questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Among the following, what is the function of the marked muscles?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Depression

The muscle marked in the above image is the lateral pterygoid muscle and its primary function is depression of the mandible (opening of the mouth). 

Bilateral contraction of the lateral pterygoid alone causes depression of the mandible (making it the primary function) whereas, protrusion is the result of bilateral contraction of both the medial and lateral pterygoid muscles. 

The lateral pterygoid has the following actions:

  1. Opening of the jaw (depression): Lateral pterygoid has a specialized role in mandibular opening mediated by its horizontal fibres. When left and right lateral pterygoid muscles contract together, the mandibular condyle is pulled forwards and slightly downwards. This protrusive movement alone has little or no function except in assisting the opening of the jaw (Gray's Anatomy 41st edition).
  2. Side-to-side movement: When the lateral pterygoid contracts unilaterally along with the adjacent medial pterygoid the jaw is pulled medially. This is used for grinding food between teeth of the same side. This action is mediated by the inferior head of the lateral pterygoid.

questions.question: All of the following are true about grey rami communicantes except:
options: Present medial to white ra‌mi communicantes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Preganglionic

The grey rami communicantes are not preganglionic fibers. They are postganglionic fibers.

The sympathetic trunks on either side of the vertebral columns consist of a series of ganglia. They are connected to the spinal nerves by white and grey rami communicantes. The cell bodies of the preganglionic sympathetic neurons are located in the lateral horn in the spinal grey matter. They leave the cord in the ventral nerve roots to form spinal nerves. These fibers enter the sympathetic trunk in white rami communicantes. They synapse with the postganglionic sympathetic neurons in the sympathetic ganglia. The axons of the postganglionic neurons return to the spinal nerve through the grey rami communicantes.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: What represents the marked area in the given histology of lymph node?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Mantle zone

The area marked in the image is the mantle zone of a lymph node.

Lymph node has primary follicle composed of small, quiescent lymphocytes, and a secondary follicle with germinal centre composed mainly of antigen-stimulated B cells.

The mantle zone is produced as surrounding cells are marginalised by the rapidly growing germinal centre. It is populated by mainly quiescent B cells with condensed heterochromatic nuclei and little cytoplasm (hence the deeply basophilic staining of this region in routine preparations), a few helper T cells, Follicular Dendritic cells and macrophages.

In peripheral lymph nodes, the marginal zone are often inapparent because they are mixed with the mantle zone cells. And often not well developed in lymph nodes.

The paracortex lies between the cortical follicles and the medulla and is populated mainly by T cells, which are not organised into follicles

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A young patient presented with hypoparathyroidism, absent thymus and tetany. Which of the following marked areas in the picture is defective in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 3

The given clinical scenario of hypoparathyroidism, absent thymus, and tetany is suggestive of DiGeorge syndrome. It is caused by defective development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouch. In the image of pharyngeal pouches, "3" points to the thymus (derivative of 3rd pharyngeal pouch). Since in the above question, the thymus is absent, option 3 will be the most appropriate answer.

DiGeorge syndrome is a complex embryopathy that is caused by the hemizygous interstitial deletion of chromosome 22. It is characterized by multiple developmental defects, including conotruncal defects, hypoparathyroidism, and dysmorphic syndrome. It is also known as velocardiofacial syndrome (palate, facial, and cardiac defects).

It has variable presentations including Cleft palate, Abnormal facies, Thymic aplasia leading to T-cell deficiency, Cardiac defects, and Hypocalcemia secondary to parathyroid aplasia (CATCH-22).

questions.question: Inferior thyroid artery is the branch of which of the following?

questions.question: Neurovascular bundle is absent in which compartment of the leg?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Posterior superficial compartment

Posterior superficial compartment of the leg does not contain any neurovascular bundle. 

The posterior compartment of the leg is divided into the deep and superficial parts by the transverse intermuscular septum. 

The contents of the posterior superficial compartment are gastrocnemius, plantaris, and soleus muscle.

Neurovascular components in various compartments of leg are as follows:

  • Anterior compartment: Anterior tibial artery and Deep fibular/peroneal nerve 
  • Posterior deep compartment: Tibial nerve and posterior tibial vessels in the deep plane. 
  • Lateral Compartment: Superficial peroneal/fibular nerve and peroneal/fibular vessel. Peroneal artery is a branch of posterior tibial artery.  

Note: MRI is the best imaging modality for evaluating the soft tissues of the leg.

questions.question: A patient presents to you with inability to form words but can make noises. He also knows what he wants to say. What area of the brain has been damaged in this patient?

Correct answer: B. Broca’s area

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Broca's aphasia in which the Broca's area will be affected.

In Broca's aphasia/ Motor aphasia / Non-fluent aphasia, areas 44 and 45 in the prefrontal and premotor facial regions of the cerebral cortex are affected. The affected individuals will have difficulty forming verbal or written words. The comprehension aspect of speech is preserved but the person cannot repeat or name the words and lacks fluency.

Patients in whom the area is severely affected may have very few words to express all of their emotions.

Posterior column–medial lemniscal pathway:

First-order axons carrying discriminative touch and vibration sensations enter the dorsal horn and continue traveling upward in the posterior white column as the fasciculus gracilis and fasciculus cuneatus.

Fibers of these fasciculi synapse on the second-order neurons of the ipsilateral nuclei gracilis and cuneatus in the medulla oblongata, respectively.

Axons of these second-order neurons then cross over as the internal arcuate fibers to form the medial lemniscus in the contralateral medulla.

These second-order axons ascend through the brainstem to reach the third-order neuronal cell bodies in the ventral posterior lateral nucleus of the thalamus. Axons from the third-order neurons then project through the posterior limb of the internal capsule to reach the primary somatosensory cortex.

  • All lymphoid organs like spleen, lymph node, and bone marrow (except thymus).
  • Glands, liver and kidneys.
  • The basement membrane of all epithelia.
  • Smooth muscle and nerve cells.

The radius and ulna are united with each other by three joints:

Finkelstein's test: On grasping the patient’s thumb and quickly abducting the hand ulnar ward, the pain over the radial styloid tip is excruciating. It’s the most pathognomonic objective sign but is also seen in other conditions like radial nerve entrapment and arthritis.

Treatment:

  • Majority of the patients are treated medically
  • Only few require the release of the 1st dorsal compartment which houses the APL and EPB tendons.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Identify the cell marked in the histological image of the cerebellum shown below :
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Purkinje cells

The cells marked in the above histological image are Purkinje cells.

Characteristics of Purkinje cells:

  • Purkinje cells are the flask-shaped cells present in the Purkinje cell layer of the cerebellum.
  • The cells are evenly spaced and are arranged in a single layer.
  • A dendrite arises from the neck of each flask-shaped cell, which passes upward to enter the molecular layer, which then branches extensively to form a dendritic tree.
  • The axon of each cell passes downwards, crosses the granular cell layer to enter the white matter.
  • Axons of Purkinje cells are the only efferents of the cerebellar cortex.
  • The initial segment of the axon receives synaptic contacts from basket cell axons.
  • The main axon terminates in one of the cerebellar or vestibular nuclei.
  • Purkinje cells are inhibitory and use GABA as their neurotransmitter.

Pathological significance:

  • Negri bodies in rabies, are usually found as eosinophilic, cytoplasmic inclusions in the neurons of the hippocampus and Purkinje cells.
  • Loss of Purkinje cells and granule cells is seen in ataxia-telangiectasia.
  • In patients with subacute cerebellar degeneration, there is the destruction of Purkinje cells. Some patients show circulating PCA­1 antibody (anti­Yo) against Purkinje cells.
  • Purkinje cells and neurons in pyramidal cell layers of hippocampus and cerebral cortex are the most sensitive neurons to hypoxia, and are likely to be damaged in cases of global cerebral ischemia.

questions.question: The long left recurrent laryngeal nerve is due to the persistence of which arch artery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 6th arch

The long left recurrent laryngeal nerve is due to the persistence of the left 6th arch artery.

During the development, the laryngeal nerves initially arise below the 6th arch artery and cross here to innervate the intrinsic muscles of the larynx. As the larynx moves cranially relative to the aortic arch arteries, the recurrent laryngeal nerves on the right and left sides are caught under the 6th arch arteries.

On the right side, the distal 6th arch artery disappears. Since there is no 5th arch artery, the right recurrent laryngeal nerve is caught under the 4th arch artery which becomes the future right subclavian artery.

On the left side, the 6th arch artery persists, which develops into ductus arteriosus, which later forms ligamentum arteriosum. Due to the persistence of the 6th arch artery, the left recurrent laryngeal nerve is caught under it and therefore, has a relatively long course.

A fontanelle tap or percutaneous ventricular puncture is performed in infants without access to a VP shunt, who require urgent ventricular decompression and have an open anterior fontanelle. The given clinical situation with a positive card test and an inability to flex the distal interphalangeal joint of the 4th and 5th digits, suggests an ulnar nerve injury. The most likely site of injury would thus be medial epicondyle: site C

Injury at the medial epicondyle damages the ulnar nerve, leading to paralysis of flexor carpi ulnaris (loss of ulnar deviation) and medial half of flexor digitorum profundus (loss of distal interphalangeal joint flexion). It leads to hypothenar paralysis (lead to atrophy) and sensory loss. Also, flexor digitorum superficialis (supplied by median nerve) and extensor digitorum (supplied by the radial nerve) are still functional. Hence complete paralysis of the 3rd and 4th digits is not seen.  The positive card test is due to the weakness of palmar interossei leading to loss of adduction.

Ulnar nerve branches and supply: 

Superficial branch supplies palmaris brevis, skin on the palmar surface of medial 1½ fingers. The deep branch runs within the concavity of deep palmar arch and supplies all intrinsic muscles of the hand (except first 2 lumbricals and thenar muscles).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A boy with a history of a fall from a tree presents with a lurching gait and dragging of his feet. Which of the following structures are involved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2

The structure involved in causing lurching gait in the child is gluteus medius (marked as 2).

The gluteus medius originates from the outer surface of the ilium between the anterior and posterior gluteal lines. Insertion of the muscle is at the lateral surface of the greater trochanter. It is supplied by the superior gluteal nerve.

Gluteus medius and minimus are powerful abductors of the hip joint. Mechanism of actions of gluteus medius and minimus:

  • When the leg on one side is lifted off the ground, the gluteus medius and minimus muscles, on the opposite supported side, exert traction on the hip bone by acting from the femur. This action results in a slight raising of the pelvis on the unsupported side, which helps maintain the trunk in the upright position.
  • The actions of these muscles are affected when there is an injury to the superior gluteal nerve, neck of the femur, or loss of normal angulation of the shaft of the femur. This occurs in conditions like paralysis of the glutei, developmental dysplasia of the hip, etc.
  • When the gluteus medius and minimus are paralyzed, the pelvis sinks down on the unsupported (normal) side, when the patient tries to stand on the affected limb. This leads to a positive Trendelenburg's sign with a characteristic lurching gait - the patient lurches towards the affected side with contralateral pelvis drop. 

Other options

1 - Gluteus maximus - involved in the extension of flexed thigh, abduction (only upper fibres), and lateral rotation at the hip joint. Insertion is at the iliotibial tract. 

3 - Piriformis - involved in lateral rotation and assists abduction at the hip joint. It is inserted into the medial side of greater trochanter of the femur. Entrapment of the sciatic nerve in the piriformis can lead to piriformis syndrome.

4 - Sciatic nerve - The nerve passes over the obturator internus, gemellus superior, gemellus inferior and quadratus femoris. It supplies knee flexors and muscles below the knee. Paralysis of this nerve results in flail foot and severe difficulty in walking.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The cell marked in the below slide is inhibitory to
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Deep nuclei of cerebellum

The structure marked in the image is a flask-shaped neuron in the cerebellar cortex, which is a Purkinje cell. It is inhibitory to deep cerebellar nuclei.  

Purkinje cells are the flask-shaped cells present in the Purkinje cell layer of the cerebellum. They are evenly spaced and arranged in a single layer between molecular and granular cell layers. The dendrite from each cell passes upward to enter the molecular layer and the axon of each cell passes downwards, crosses the granular cell layer, and terminates on the deep cerebellar nuclei. They are inhibitory and use GABA as their neurotransmitter.

Axons of Purkinje cells are the only efferents of the cerebellar cortex. They receive excitatory input from the climbing fibers from the inferior olivary nucleus and mossy fibers. 

Pathological significance of Purkinje cells:

  • Negri bodies in rabies are usually found as eosinophilic, cytoplasmic inclusions in the neurons of the hippocampus and Purkinje cells of the cerebellum.
  • In paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration, there is the destruction of Purkinje cells due to antibodies directed against them. 
  • Purkinje cells and neurons in pyramidal cell layers of the hippocampus and cerebral cortex are the most sensitive neurons to hypoxia and are likely to be damaged in cases of global cerebral ischemia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The marked structure develops from which of the following structures?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Supracardinal vein

The structure marked in the given image is the azygos vein, which develops from the supracardinal vein.

The azygos system of veins forms a connecting channel between the superior and inferior venae cavae. It occupies the upper part of the posterior abdominal wall and the posterior mediastinum. It also connects the portal, caval system, and vertebral venous systems.It drains the thoracic wall and the upper lumbar region.

Development: The azygos venous system arises from the supra cardinal veins embryologically. The right supra cardinal vein becomes the azygos vein, while the left supra cardinal vein becomes the hemiazygos vein.

  • The 4th to 11th right intercostal veins empty into the right supracardinal vein, which together with a portion of the posterior cardinal vein forms the azygos vein.
  • On the left, the 4th to 7th intercostal veins enter into the left supracardinal vein, and the left supracardinal vein, then known as the hemiazygos vein, which also empties into the azygos vein.

Other options: Cardinal veins form the main venous drainage system of the embryo. It consists of,

  • Anterior cardinal veins, which drain the cephalic part of the embryo, and
  • Posterior cardinal veins, which drain the rest of the embryo.

During the fifth to the seventh weeks, a number of additional veins are formed. It includes,

  • Subcardinal veins, which mainly drain the kidneys;
  • Sacrocardinal veins, which drain the lower extremities;
  • Supracardinal veins, which drain the body wall by way of the intercostal veins.

Pelvic diaphragm 

The muscular part of the pelvic floor is the pelvic diaphragm. It is attached to the pelvic wall on either side between the greater and lesser sciatic foramen. Levator ani and coccygeus muscles form the pelvic diaphragm and delineate the lower limit of the true pelvis. 

Levator ani is formed by pubococcygeus, iliococcygeus, and puborectalis. The muscles blend together posterior to the vagina in women and around the anus in both sexes. Posterior to the anal aperture, the form the anococcygeal body attaches to the coccyx. Urogenital hiatus is present anteriorly separating the muscles. This allows the urethra and vagina to pass through. Levator ani reinforces the external anal sphincter. In women, it functions as the vaginal sphincter. 

The coccygeus muscles, one on each side are triangular in shape and form the posterior part of the pelvic diaphragm. The apices are attached to the tips of ischial spines. The bases are attached to the coccyx and sacrum.

questions.question: Third part of vertebral artery is related to which of the following ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2

The third part of the vertebral artery (V3) is related to the area marked 2, which is the posterior arch of the first cervical vertebra or the atlas.

The given image shows the first cervical vertebra - atlas.

  • The area marked 1 is the posterior tubercle.
  • The area marked 2 is the posterior arch. The superior surface bears a groove for the of vertebral artery and venous plexus immediately behind.
  • The area marked 3 is the superior articular facet.
  • The area marked 4 is the posterior surface of the anterior arch. It gives attachment to the apex of dens from the second cervical vertebra. 

The vertebral artery arises from the first part of the subclavian artery. It passes through the foramina of transverse processes of C6 to C1 cervical vertebrae and enters the cranium through the foramen magnum. The vertebral arteries of both sides join to form the basilar artery. In its course, it is divided into four parts:

The first part, V1, begins at its origin from the subclavian artery and ends at its entry into the transverse process of the C6 cervical vertebra. This part is crossed by the inferior thyroid artery on both sides, and thoracic duct on the left side, and the right lymphatic duct on the right side. 

The second part, V2 is that part of the artery ascending through the foramina in the transverse process of the cervical vertebrae. 

The third part, V3 is curved backward behind the atlas. In this position, it lies in a groove on the posterior arch of the atlas. This part of the artery lies in the suboccipital triangle. 

The fourth part, V4 pierces the dura and arachnoid mater and unites with the contralateral vertebral artery to form the midline basilar artery at the lower border of pons.

Correct answer: A. Arterial puncture

The bone marked in the above image is the left clavicle. The most common complication of a central line insertion below this bone is an arterial puncture.

Complications of central vein catheterization are

  • Arterial puncture- this is the most common complication. 
  • Cardiac tamponade is the most important life-threatening complication. It occurs as a result of puncture of intrapericardial superior vena cava, right atrium, or right ventricle.
  • Pneumothorax- injury to the underlying pleura may lead to pneumothorax. This is more common in subclavian vein catheterization.
  • Chylothorax can occur particularly in left subclavian vein catheterisation. But it is not the most common.
  • Injury to the associated nerves like brachial plexus, stellate ganglion, phrenic nerve, or vocal cords.
  • Thromboembolism leading to venous thrombosis, pulmonary embolism is more common with femoral veins.
  • Infections

Central venous catheterization is the insertion of the catheter into a large central vein. The veins preferred largely depend on the underlying disease in the patient, the clinical setting, and the expertise of the doctor. 

The internal jugular vein is preferred when the patient has:

  • Bleeding diathesis- Bleeding from this vein can be easily detected and can be controlled with pressure. 
  • Pneumothorax- The lesser risk of injury to the lung
  • Needs cardiac pacing- right internal jugular vein is used.

Femoral or subclavian veins can be used in patients when the neck is immobilized using a cervical collar.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A patient presented with vision loss. On radiological investigation, an aneurysm causing damage to the optic chiasma was noted. Which of the following arteries is most likely to be the artery that is causing the damage?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anterior communicating artery

An aneurysm of the anterior communicating artery is most likely to be causing damage to the optic chiasma, leading to vision loss in this patient.

Circle of Willis is a large arterial anastomosis that unites the internal carotid and vertebrobasilar systems. It lies in the subarachnoid space within the basal cisterns that surround the optic chiasma and infundibulum.

Anterior communicating artery aneurysm: 

Anterior communicating artery (Acom) links the right and left anterior cerebral arteries and is directed anterior and superior to the optic chiasma. The aneurysm will protrude in the posterior direction and will impinge upon the optic chiasma from above, leading to loss of vision.

Compression of the optic chiasma (central lesion) by an ACom aneurysm, will lead to bitemporal hemianopia i.e, loss of vision in the left/temporal halves of both visual fields. Nasal fibers of each retina cross through the chiasma at this level and hence, these fibers will be compromised.

In the case of a bilateral peripheral lesion of the optic chiasma, binasal hemianopia will be seen.

Other causes of chiasmal lesions are

  • Pituitary adenoma (most common)
  • Craniopharyngioma
  • Meningioma
  • Glioma

Blood supply of optic chiasma: The left and right anterior cerebral arteries, along with the superior hypophyseal artery (branch of the internal carotid artery) form the blood supply of optic chiasma.

 

The given cadaveric image below is of the vascular structures (Circle of Willis) at the base of the brain.

 

Investigation: Digital subtraction angiogram is the definitive imaging modality for aneurysms arising from the circle of Willis. Other investigations are CT and MRI.

Other options:

Aneurysms of the anterior choroidal artery (option B) and middle cerebral artery (option C) aneurysms will not compress the optic chiasma as they are anatomically not in close proximity to be able to exert pressure on the chiasma and cause loss of vision.

Despite the anatomical proximity of the anterior cerebral artery (option D) to the optic chiasma, anterior communicating artery (Acom) aneurysm is the commonest intracranial aneurysm.

questions.question: A 34-year-old man presented with fever and massive splenomegaly. On palpation, the spleen was 15 cm and directed obliquely when measured from the right iliac fossa. Which of the following structures prevent the vertical and downward descent of the spleen?

Correct answer: C. Phrenicocolic ligament

The vertical and downward descent of the spleen is prevented by the phrenicocolic ligament.

The phrenicocolic ligament is not attached to the spleen. It attaches the splenic flexure of the colon to the diaphragm. 

When the spleen gets enlarged, the phrenicocolic ligament along with the splenic flexure of the colon restricts its downward displacement. The enlargement of the spleen occurs towards the right iliac fossa and hence the spleen is directed obliquely.

Phrenicocolic ligament Diaphragm to the splenic flexure of the colon -
Phrenicosplenic ligament The undersurface of the diaphragm to the spleen -
Splenorenal (lienorenal) ligament Hilum of the spleen to the anterior surface of the left kidney Tail of pancreas
Splenic artery and vein
Gastrosplenic ligament The greater curvature of the stomach to the upper pole of the spleen Short gastric vessels
Left gastroepiploic artery

 

Cross-sectional view of the spleen and its ligaments

 

The spleen becomes palpable when it is enlarged 2-3 times more than its normal size. A characteristic splenic notch can be felt in the medial border in an enlarged spleen. Also, fingers cannot be insinuated between the left costal margin and the enlarged spleen.

In the classical method of palpation, the right hand (with fingers pointed towards the left costal margin) is placed on the right iliac fossa. Palpation begins from the right iliac fossa towards the left hypochondrium in an upwards and lateral direction. Between each breath of the patient, the edge of the spleen can be felt.

In the hooking method, the hooked fingers of the right hand are placed under the left costal margin, and with the left hand, pressure is exerted over the posterolateral aspect of the lower thorax. Spleen is felt at the deep inspiratory phase.

The given histological image is a section of the tongue showing circumvallate papillae, the largest papillae of the tongue.

Circumvallate papillae are large cylindrical structures that are around 8-12 in number, covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.

They are arranged in a V-shaped row immediately in front of the sulcus terminalis (not on the sides of the tongue) on the dorsal surface of the tongue. It is narrower at its base than its apex. 

Numerous taste buds (around 250 taste buds for each of the 8-12 papillae) are present within the papillary walls and they contain chemosensory cells that synapse with the gustatory nerves. Serous glands of von Ebner empty via the ducts into the base of the sulcus.

Identification: They can be identified by their characteristic dome-shaped structure lined by stratified squamous epithelium.

Other options: 

Option A - Fungiform papillae are large, rounded, and red in color and are mainly present on the lingual margins and also on the dorsal surface of the tongue. They are covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium. It is supplied by the lingual nerve.

Option C- Filiform papillae are minute cylindrical or conical projections that are mainly present on the dorsal part of the anterior 2/3rd of the tongue. All except filiform papillae contain taste buds. They are covered by keratinized stratified squamous epithelium. It is supplied by the lingual nerve.

Option D - Foliate papillae are red, leaf-like mucosal ridges that are present bilaterally in two zones at the sides of the tongue near the sulcus terminalis. They are covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 7-year-old boy was brought to the hospital with multiple fractures of the humerus secondary to a fall from height. On examination, there is difficulty in flexion of the elbow and supination of the forearm, and associated loss of sensation over the lateral aspect of the forearm. Which is the nerve most likely to be injured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Musculocutaneous nerve

The given clinical vignette in a patient with difficulty in flexion of the elbow and supination of the forearm, with associated loss of sensation over the lateral aspect of the forearm, is suggestive of injury to the musculocutaneous nerve.

Fall from a height on an outstretched hand is one of the main causes of humerus fractures.

Course:

The musculocutaneous nerve (C5, C6, C7) is a branch of the lateral cord of the brachial plexus. It emerges at the lower border of the pectoralis minor and pierces coracobrachialis. It then descends between biceps brachii and brachialis where it supplies a branch to the shaft of the humerus. Then it enters the elbow and continues as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.

It innervates all the muscles of the anterior compartment of the arm i.e., 

  • Biceps brachii - involved in flexion of elbow and supination of the forearm
  • Brachialis -  involved in the flexion of the elbow
  • Coracobrachialis - flexes the arm at the glenohumeral joint

Cutaneous innervation of the lateral aspect of the forearm is by a branch of the musculocutaneous nerve, namely, the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm (C5, C6).

Hence, injury to the musculocutaneous nerve results in weakness of supination of forearm (biceps brachii), weakness in flexion of the elbow (biceps brachii, brachialis), and loss of sensation over the lateral aspect of the forearm (lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm).

Muscles of the anterior compartment of the arm:

Muscles Origin Insertion Innervation
Coracobrachialis Coracoid Process of scapula The medial side of the midshaft of the humerus Musculocutaneous nerve
Brachialis Distal half of anterior aspect of the humerus Ulnar tuberosity Musculocutaneous and radial nerve
Biceps Brachii Short head: Coracoid process 
Long head: Supraglenoid tubercle		 Radial tuberosity Musculocutaneous nerve

The below image shows the anterior compartment of the arm

Other options: 

Option A:

Median nerve injury is characterized by sensory loss over the radial 3 1/2 fingers and loss of thumb abduction. In high lesions, the long flexors of the thumb, index, and middle fingers, the radial wrist flexors, and the forearm pronator muscles are also paralyzed. Wasting of the thenar eminence is seen in long-standing cases.

Option B:

Radial nerve injury can present with wrist drop, thumb drop, and finger drop. Extension of the elbow will be spared in lesions below the elbow. The extension of the IP joints is intact due to the action of the intrinsic muscles of the hand. Loss of sensation over the first dorsal web space is observed.

Option D:

Ulnar nerve injury is characterized by ulnar claw hand, wasting of the hypothenar muscles and intrinsic muscles of the hand, and sensory loss over palmar & dorsal aspect of the medial third of the hand and medial 1 1/2 fingers.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A patient presented with jaw swelling and weight loss. Suspecting a malignancy, the submandibular gland was resected. Which is the most likely nerve to be damaged during submandibular gland resection?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lingual nerve

The most likely nerve to be damaged during submandibular gland resection is the lingual nerve.

It loops around the submandibular duct and hence is susceptible to injury during submandibular gland resection.

Course:

The lingual nerve arises from the posterior trunk of the mandibular nerve (V3 branch of the trigeminal nerve). The lingual nerve descends between the tensor veli palatini muscle and the lateral pterygoid muscle, where it is joined by the chorda tympani nerve. It then descends across the medial pterygoid muscle to enter the oral cavity. As the lingual nerve enters the floor of the oral cavity, it lies on the deep portion of the submandibular gland. It then passes into the tongue on the hyoglossus muscle where it is attached to the submandibular ganglion.

The submandibular duct lies between the lingual and hypoglossal nerves, superficial to the hyoglossus muscle. As the duct reaches the anterior border of the hyoglossus, it is crossed by the lingual nerve and lies in close proximity to the nerve. Hence lingual nerve injury is the most common.

Injury: 

The lingual nerve is at risk to be injured during submandibular gland resection because dissection of the submandibular duct from the nerve is required. Also, it is connected to the submandibular ganglion which will lead to the nerve being exposed within the operating field.

The manifestations of lingual nerve injury depend on whether the lesion is proximal or distal to where it is joined by the chorda tympani nerve.

  • Proximal injury: There is loss of sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, gingivae, oral mucosa, lower lip, and chin.
  • Distal injury: In addition to features of proximal injury, secretion from the salivary glands below the oral fissure and taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is also lost. 

Note:

The cranial nerves that are at risk during submandibular gland resection include:

  • The marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve
  • Lingual nerve
  • Hypoglossal nerve

Other options: 

Option A: Nerve to mylohyoid is a branch of the inferior alveolar nerve and lies in the mylohyoid groove inferior to the mandibular foramen, hence the risk of injury is less.

Option B: Inferior alveolar nerve enters the mandibular canal via the mandibular foramen, hence is unlikely to be injured during submandibular gland excision.

Option D: Hypoglossal nerve injury is less common than lingual nerve injury as it only lies below and parallels to the submandibular duct.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A patient underwent a coronary bypass graft with the great saphenous vein. The patient now complains of paresthesia and sensory loss over the medial aspect of the leg and foot. Which of the following nerves is most likely to be involved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Saphenous nerve

The given clinical vignette in a patient with paresthesia and sensory loss over the medial aspect of the leg and foot is suggestive of injury to the saphenous nerve.

Injury to the saphenous nerve is common following venous cut down for access to the great saphenous vein, in this case for coronary bypass graft.

Saphenous nerve:

It is the longest and largest cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve and is the longest nerve in the body. It arises from the posterior division of the femoral nerve. It then enters the adductor canal and exits it by piercing the fascia lata between the gracilis and sartorius and supplies the skin over the patella. The saphenous nerve then descends along the medial border of the tibia along with the great saphenous vein (anterior to the vein) and supplies the skin on the medial side of the knee, leg, and foot as far as up to the first metatarsophalangeal joint.

Saphenous nerve injury:

When the great saphenous vein is being harvested for coronary bypass graft, injury to the saphenous nerve is common as it closely travels with the great saphenous vein. Sensory loss over the medial side of the knee, leg, and foot is observed in saphenous nerve injury. 

Other options: 

Option A: Superficial peroneal nerve injury causes sensory loss over the lateral aspect of the leg and the dorsum of the foot.

Option C: Femoral nerve gives rise to anterior cutaneous branches, the saphenous nerve, and motor supply to the quadriceps and sartorius. Anterior cutaneous branches supply the skin on the anterior thigh and knee. If the saphenous nerve was not an option in the question, the femoral nerve would have been the next best answer. 

Option D: Sural nerve injury causes sensory loss over the posterior and lateral aspects of the distal third of the leg and lateral side of the foot and fifth toe. It is often used as an autologous peripheral nerve graft as it is readily identified and easy to harvest.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: During the clinical examination of the nervous system, which of the following nerves can be tested by touching the highlighted structure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. IX

The structure marked in the given sagittal section of the head and neck is the uvula. The sensory supply to the uvula is by the glossopharyngeal nerve and it is tested in this case.

Nerve supply by glossopharyngeal nerve:

  • Sensory fibers to the uvula, tympanic cavity, pharyngotympanic tube, tonsils, fauces, nasopharynx, and posterior third of the tongue.
  • Motor fibers to the stylopharyngeus muscle
  • Parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the parotid gland
  • Gustatory fibers for the postsulcal part of the tongue.

Pharyngeal plexus:

The nerve supply of the pharynx is mainly from the pharyngeal plexus of nerves. It is formed by the pharyngeal branches of the glossopharyngeal nerve and vagus nerve. It also has contributions from the superior cervical ganglion. The vagus nerve provides the motor supply and the glossopharyngeal nerve provides the sensory supply.

Nerve supply by the pharyngeal branch of the vagus nerve:

  • All the muscles of the soft palate(except tensor veli palatini - supplied by mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve)
  • All the muscles of the pharynx(except stylopharyngeus - supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve)

Note:

Previously cranial root of the spinal accessory nerve was thought to contribute to the motor functions of the pharyngeal plexus, but recent evidence suggests that it is not a major part of the motor drive to the pharyngeal plexus.

Innervation of the soft palate:

General sensation - It is mostly carried by the lesser palatine nerve which is a branch of maxillary nerve. The sensation from posterior part is carried by the pharyngeal branches of the glossopharyngeal nerve and from the plexus around the tonsil which is formed by the tonsillar branches of the glossopharyngeal and lesser palatine nerves. 

Taste sensation - There are taste buds in the oral surface of soft palate and sensation from them is carried by the lesser palatine nerve.

Secretomotor supply - It is by the lesser palatine nerve via postganglionic fibres from the pterygopalatine ganglion.

Motor supply - It is by the pharyngeal branch of the vagus nerve except for tensor veli palatini which is supplied by mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question:
Arrange in sequence the structures involved in the direct pathway:

1. Striatum
2. Globus pallidus
3. Substantia nigra
4. Thalamus
5. Cortex
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 5,1,2,3,4

The sequence of structures involved in the direct pathway is cortex > striatum > globus pallidus > substantia nigra > thalamus.

There are five parallel circuits that connect the frontal cortex to the striatum, pallidum, substantia nigra, and thalamus. These circuits have both direct and indirect pathways. The direct pathway stimulates the cortex to produce movement, whereas the indirect pathway inhibit it. 

The cerebral cortex projects into the striatum. The striatum is seen projected into the pallidum and substantia nigra pars reticularis. Fibres originate from different striatal cells according to their endings in the external and internal pallidum. In the direct pathway, striatal neurones project directly to the internal pallidum.  Whereas some other fibres that arise from the neurons project to the external pallidum. This is called the indirect pathway.  

The sequence of structures involved in the indirect pathway is cortex > striatum > globus pallidus externa > subthalamic nucleus > globus pallidus interna and substantia nigra >Thalamus

The striatal activity in the direct pathway is mediated by D1 dopamine receptors and in the indirect pathway by D2 dopamine receptors. 

Putamen lies lateral and the internal capsule lies medial to the pallidum. It receives fibres from the striatum and subthalamic nuclei. It acts as the main output of the basal ganglia to the thalamus and superior colliculus. The substantia nigra is seen in each cerebral peduncle of the midbrain located deep to the crus cerebri. The levels of dopamine in the substantia nigra and striata are seen reduced in parkinsonism disease.

In parkinsonism disease, due to the death of neurons in substantia nigra activity of the direct pathway is reduced and the indirect pathway is increased. This results in bradykinesia in parkinsonism disease. Whereas in Huntington's disease, the activity of the indirect pathway is affected resulting in choreic involuntary movements.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: What is the volume of the prostate in normal adult males?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 20cc

The volume of the prostate in normal adult males is 20cc.

Prostate is an accessory glandular tissue embedded in the fibromuscular stroma. It usually weighs 8 grams in the young adults and its weight ranges from 40-150 grams in men aged >50 years. 

The prostate gland is situated in the lesser pelvis and surrounds the prostatic urethra which extends from bladder base to the membranous urethra. Pubic symphysis and pubic arch lie anteriorly to the prostate whereas rectourethralis and rectal ampulla lie posteriorly to it. 

The prostate has three distinct zones as follows:

Zone Structures enclosed Clinical significance
Transitional zone Urethra  Most common site for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)
Central zone Ejaculatory ducts Atrophies secondary to BPH
Peripheral zone

Central and transitional zones Pre-prostatic urethra

 Most common site for prostatic carcinoma

 

The prostate is composed of 5 lobes. They are anterior, posterior, two lateral and one medial or middle lobe. 

The median lobe of the prostate forms the uvula vesicae. It is an elevation found in the lower part of the bladder trigone. It is the most common site of adenoma. 

 

Microstructure of the prostate gland: 

The glandular tissue of the prostate gland is composed of many follicles with frequent internal papillae. The follicular epithelium is either a single-layered or pseudostratified columnar epithelum. These follicles open into canals, which join to form the main ducts. Small eosinophilic colloid amyloid bodies called corpora amylacea are frequently seen within a follicle. 

The prostatic ducts open into the prostatic sinus in the prostatic urethra. The ducts of the prostate follicles are lined by bilayered epithelium (basal cuboidal and apical columnar). 

The secretions of the prostate are acidic and contain acid phosphatase, amylase, prostate-specific antigen (PSA), fibrin, and zinc.

The blood supply to the prostate is by the inferior vesical, internal pudendal and middle rectal arteries. It recieves nerve supply from the inferior hypogastric plexus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which ligament connects medial cuneiform to the base of the 2nd metatarsal?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lisfranc

The Lisfranc ligament connects the medial cuneiform to the base of the 2nd metatarsal.

Lisfranc ligament is a cuneometatarsal interosseous ligament. It is the strongest ligament among the three cuneometatarsal interosseous ligaments. It passes from the lateral surface of the medial cuneiform to the adjacent angle of the second metatarsal bone. 

Deformity of this ligament can lead to instability and deformity of the tarsometatarsal joint.

Other options:
Option A: Chopart's ligament is related to both calcaneocuboid and calcaneonavicular joints. It is a strong Y-shaped band, having a proximal stem and 2 distal limbs.

  • The proximal limb is attached by a stem to the anterior part of the upper calcaneal surface.
  • The distal limb divides into calcaneocuboid and calcaneonavicular parts.

Option B: Spring ligament also known as the plantar calcaneonavicular ligament connects the sustentaculum tali to the navicular. It ties the calcaneus to the navicular and maintains the medial longitudinal arch of the foot. It is made up of the superomedial calcaneonavicular portion and the inferior calcaneonavicular portion.

Option D: Deltoid ligament also called the medial collateral ligament is attached to the apex, anterior and posterior borders of the medial malleolus. It has 2 layers, superficial and deep:

  • The superficial layer consists of tibionavicular fibres anteriorly, tibiocalcaneal fibres in the middle, and superficial posterior tibiotalar fibres posteriorly.
  • Deep layer consists of anterior tibiotalar fibres, tibiocalcaneal in the middle and deep posterior tibiotalar posteriorly.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Fibres of the given structure originate from ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hippocampus

The given structure is the fornix and its fibres arise from the hippocampus. 

The fornix is a part of the connecting pathways of the limbic system. It arises from the hippocampus which wraps around the thalamus and ends in the mammillary body. It connects the hippocampus with distal brain sites. 

The fornix has two types of fibres:

  • Association fibres: They connect the various cortical regions within the same hemisphere 
  • Commissural fibres: They connect the corresponding regions of two hemispheres. It is seen in the hippocampal commissure of the fornix. 

The blood supply of fornix is by the anterior communicating artery which arises from the anterior cerebral artery. 

The limbic system is a group of structures seen between the cerebral cortex and the hypothalamus. It is involved in emotional and motivation activity, learning, and memory. 

Other options:

Option A: Amygdala is a part of the limbic system that consists of lateral, central and basal nuclei. It can Influence the body's response to enviromnental changes. In a fearful situation it can change the heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate etc. 

Option C: Caudate nucleus is a C-shaped mass of grey matter. It is divided into a head, body, and tail. Degeneration of the caudate nucleus is seen in Huntington's disease.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which structure is supplied by the nerve causing this elevation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Risorius

Risorius is supplied by the facial nerve which causes the elevation marked. The image shows the floor of the fourth ventricle and the facial colliculus is marked. 

The fourth ventricle is located between the brainstem and the cerebellum. The rhomboid fossa is a diamond-shaped depression seen on the floor of the fourth ventricle. The superior and the inferior part of the floor is triangular in shape. It is divided by a longitudinal median sulcus into two halves. Each half is again divided into the medial and lateral regions.

The facial colliculus is present in the superior part, which presents as a small elevation produced by the root of the facial nerve winding around the nucleus of the abducens nerve.  Columns are formed by groups of facial neurones, which innervate individual muscles and give branches of the facial nerve. Dorsal neurones innervate muscles in the scalp and upper face and ventral neurons supply the lower facial musculature. 

Risorius falls under the buccolabial muscle group and act as the elevator, retractor and evertor of the upper lip. Some of its peripheral attachments are the zygomatic arch, parotid fascia and fascia over the mastoid process. It is involved in actions like grinning and laughing and is innervated by the buccal branches of the facial nerve.

Other options:

Option A: Lateral rectus is an extraocular muscle that arises from the lateral part of the common tendinous ring. It is innervated by the abducens nerve. 

Option B: Superior oblique is an extraocular muscle that arises from the body of the sphenoid. It is innervated by the trochlear nerve. 

Option D: Levator palpebrae superiors is an extraocular muscle that arises from the lesser wing of sphenoid. It is innervated by the oculomotor nerve.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question:
Arrange lung hilar structures from anterior to posterior:

1. Primary bronchus
2. Bronchial artery
3. Pulmonary vein
4. Pulmonary artery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 3,4,1,2

Lung hilar structures are arranged from the anterior to posterior in the order:

  • Pulmonary vein
  • Pulmonary artery
  • Primary bronchus
  • Bronchial artery

 The medial surface of the lung is connected to the heart and trachea by a group of structures that enter or leave the hilum. It is called the pulmonary root. It is anteriorly related to the phrenic nerve, pericardiacophrenic vessels , and anterior pulmonary plexus. The vagus nerve and posterior pulmonary plexus form the posterior relation and the pulmonary ligament the inferior relation. 

The superior vena cava and right atrium are seen in front of the right root and terminal part of the azygos vein superiorly. The hilar structures are arranged from the superior to inferior as:

  • Superior lobar bronchus
  • Pulmonary artery
  • Principal bronchus
  • Inferior pulmonary vein 

The aortic arch is seen superiorly and descending thoracic aorta posteriorly of the left root. The hilar structures are vertically arranged as:

  • Pulmonary artery
  • Principal bronchus
  • Inferior pulmonary vein

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which is not a branch of facial artery in the face?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mental

Mental is not a branch of the facial artery but the branch of the maxillary artery in the face.

The first part of the maxillary artery gives rise to the mental artery as a terminal branch of the inferior alveolar artery.

The facial artery is a branch of the external carotid artery which arises in the carotid triangle, above the origin of the lingual artery. It runs upwards in the neck and curves around the anteroinferior border of the masseter to enter the face. 

Branches of facial artery in the neck Branches of facial artery in the face
Ascending palatine artery Premasseteric artery
Tonsillar branch Superior and inferior labial arteries
Submental artery Lateral nasal artery
Branches to submandibular gland Angular artery

The premasseteric artery passes along the anterior border of the masseter and the surrounding tissues are supplied by it. The inferior labial artery mainly supplies the inferior labial glands. It then anastomoses with its controlateral fellow and with the mental branch of the inferior alveolar artery. The superior labial artery supplies the upper lip whereas the lateral nasal artery supplies the dorsum and alae of the nose. Both these arteries anastomose with its controlateral fellow.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following structures passing via jugular foramen has a separate canal?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glossopharyngeal nerve

The glossopharyngeal nerve passing through the jugular foramen has a separate canal.

 The jugular foramen is formed by the occipital bone and the petrous part of the temporal bone. The spinal accessory nerve and vagus nerve also pass through this foramen.

The glossopharyngeal nerve leaves the skull through the anteromedial part of the jugular foramen in a separate dural sheath.

The branches of the nerve are tympanic, carotid, pharyngeal, muscular, tonsillar and lingual branches.

Infection, malignancy and postoperative inflammation of the tonsil and tonsillar fossa will cause referred pain in the ear. This is conducted through the tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve.

Pharyngeal branches of the glossopharyngeal nerve and vagus nerve form the pharyngeal plexus of nerves. These plexes mainly supply the pharynx. It also has contributions from the superior cervical ganglion.

Nerve supply by the pharyngeal branch of the vagus nerve are:

  • All the muscles of the soft palate(except tensor veli palatini - supplied by mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve)
  • All the muscles of the pharynx(except stylopharyngeus - supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve)

 Motor fibres to the stylopharyngeus and parasympathetic secretomotor fibres to the parotid gland are also supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve.

Sensory supply includes uvula, posterior one-third of the tongue, tympanic cavity etc.

The glossopharyngeal nerve is rarely damaged alone. Lesions will result in loss of sensation of the posterior third of the tongue, reduced gag reflex, loss of sensation over the ipsilateral soft palate etc. 

The main functions of IX and X can be tested together by assessing swallowing, phonation/articulation and sensation from the pharynx/larynx. 

Glossopharyngeal and vagus nerve examinations include:

  • Observing the position and symmetry of the palate and uvula at rest and with phonation (“aah”).
  • By assessing the strength of the cough

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: What is the nerve supply of the structure marked in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Median nerve

The median nerve supplies the 1st lumbrical which is marked. 

There are four lumbrical muscles. They originate from the tendons of the flexor digitorum profundus. It passes to the radial side of the corresponding fingers and is inserted into the dorsal digital expansion of the extensor digitorum.

The action of lumbricals is flexion at the metacarpophalangeal joint and extension of interphalangeal joints. 

Lumbricals can be tested only along with interosseous muscle. The examiner will hold the metacarpophalangeal joint of the index finger in hyperextension. Then the patient is asked to extend the proximal interphalangeal joint against resistance. The test is repeated on other fingers as well.

The median nerve innervates the first and second lumbricals. The deep terminal branch of the ulnar nerve innervates the third and the fourth. 

The median nerve is formed by the union of the lateral root (C6, 7) from the lateral cord, and the medial root (C8, T1) from the medial cord.

On the hand, it is seen proximal to the flexor retinaculum and lateral to the tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis. It also lies between the tendons of flexor carpi radialis and palmaris longus.

Its cutaneous supply in hand is as follows: 

  • Lateral 2/3rd of the palm by superficial cutaneous branch
  • Lateral 3½ fingers (palmar aspect and dorsal aspect of nailbeds) by palmar digital nerves

The muscles supplied by the median nerve in the hand are flexor pollicis brevis, abductor pollicis brevis, and opponens pollicis

The median nerve sometimes gets compressed under the fibro-osseous tunnel beneath the flexor retinaculum leading to carpal tunnel syndrome. 

Pen test is used to test the median nerve in the hand. It tests the abductor pollicis brevis muscle.  The hand must remain flat with the palm facing upwards. A pen is held above the palm and the patient is asked to touch the pen with his thumb.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A child lacks thymus and inferior parathyroid glands. Defective development of which of the following structures is likely to be the cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 3

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of DiGeorge syndrome. Defective development of the third pharyngeal pouch marked as 3 causes this condition.

A child with DiGeorge syndrome lacks thymus and inferior parathyroid glands due to defective development of the 3rd pharyngeal pouch. The child can also lack superior parathyroid glands, due to defective development of the 4th pharyngeal pouch. It is caused by chromosome 22q deletion and is characterized by the following (Mnemonic: CATCH-22)

  • Cleft palate
  • Abnormal facies
  • Thymic aplasia leading to T-cell deficiency and recurrent infections
  • Cardiac defects
  • Hypocalcemia, secondary to parathyroid aplasia. 

Derivatives of the Pharyngeal Pouches

1st Pouch

  • Tympanic cavity (middle ear cavity)
  • Auditory tube (eustachian tube) 

2nd Pouch

  • Palatine tonsils
  • Tonsillar fossa

3rd Pouch

  • Inferior parathyroid glands 
  • Thymus

4th Pouch

  • Superior parathyroid glands 
  • Ultimobranchial body - gives rise to parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid gland

 

The medulla of the thymus has Hassall’s corpuscles. They are small rounded structures formed from whorls of medullary epithelial cells with a central partially keratinized core appearing as an eosinophilic-staining mass.

questions.question: Identify which of the following structure is a merocrine gland:

Sweat gland marked 2 is a merocrine gland.

Eccrine and apocrine are the two types of sweat glands. Secretions of the sweat glands are by exocytosis hence they are also known as merocrine sweat glands.

Glands are divided into holocrine, apocrine, and merocrine on the basis of the manner in which their secretions are poured out of the cells.

In holocrine secretions, the secretory cells themselves are disintegrated as part of their terminal differentiation. Afterwhich, the terminally differentiated cells filled with lipid products are released. The sebaceous gland and hair follicles are examples.

Merocrine uses exocytosis for secretions. Most of the exocrine glands are merocrine.

In apocrine, product-filled areas of cells are released, the mammary gland is an example.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The rupture of penile urethra does not cause extravasation of blood into which of the following spaces?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ischiorectal fossa

Rupture of the penile urethra causes extravasation of blood into the superficial perineal pouch, scrotum, penis, and then up to the lower anterior abdominal wall.

The superficial perineal pouch is a compartment of the perineum enclosed by the membranous layer of the perineal fascia that surrounds the scrotum or labia and penis or clitoris.

Anteriorly, the membranous layer of perineal fascia is continuous over the pubic symphysis and pubic bones. It is later continuous with the membranous layer of the anterior abdominal wall.  Thus, the fluid that accumulates in the perineal pouch extends to the lower anterior abdomen.

In the lower lateral abdominal wall, the abdominal fascia is attached to the deep fascia of the thigh, inferior to the inguinal ligament. Thus, on trauma at the penile urethra, urine does not extravasate into the anterior thigh.

The superficial perineal pouch is closed posteriorly by attaching the membranous layer of superficial fascia to the posterior margin of the urogenital diaphragm. Thus, commonly there is no extravasation into the deep perineal pouch and the ischiorectal fossa.

Also, the membranous layer of superficial fascia attaches to the ischiopubic rami and forms the lateral borders of the urogenital triangle. Thus, the urine does not extravasate to the thigh.

But, the ischiorectal fossa would be a better answer because of the following reasons:

  1. Bulbourethral glands that lie in the deep perineal space open their ducts into the spongy urethra, which is related to the superficial perineal space. Also, the muscles surrounding these glands were recently found to be a continuation of the deep transverse perinei and tail of the external urethral sphincter, both of which are components of the deep perineal space. Injury to the penile urethra can damage bulbourethral glands' ducts, which can lead to damage to the above-mentioned structures and may cause extravasation of urine into the deep perineal space. 
  2. Previously, the perineal membrane was thought to be a triangular membrane. However, recent studies show that it is contiguous anteriorly with the structures that support the urethra. Posteriorly, it is related to the support of the perineal body and lateral vaginal wall. So damage to the urethra might damage the anterior part of the perineal membrane which can make way for extravasation of blood into the deep perineal space. 
  3. Deep perineal pouch: It was believed initially that the urogenital diaphragm was formed by 3 layers: An inferior fascia (also called the perineal membrane), deep perineal space, and a superior fascia. The superior fascia formed the inferior border of the ischioanal fossa. The Colles fascia also separates the perineal membrane from the ischioanal fossa. So, extravasation of blood into the deep perineal space is possible but extravasation into the ischioanal fossa due to penile urethral injury is highly unlikely. Recent studies have shown that this might be a slightly more complex structure.

Later, it is divided into anterior and posterior branches by the lateral circumflex femoral artery.

Option C: Lateral cutaneous nerve (a.k.a lateral femoral cutaneous nerve) of the thigh is most commonly injured at the site where it leaves the pelvis. An injury to the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh leads to pain and paresthesia over the anterolateral region of the thigh, a condition called meralgia paresthetica.

Which of the following statements are true about the internal capsule?

  1. Charcot's artery supplies the posterior limb.
  2. Retrolenticular part of the internal capsule contains optic radiation.

questions.question: Injury of the lower brachial plexus leads to Klumpke's paralysis. What is the characteristic clinical finding seen in this lesion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Claw hand

The characteristic clinical finding in Klumpke's paralysis is a complete claw hand.

Klumpke's paralysis is caused by injury of the lower trunk of the brachial plexus-mainly T1 and partially C8, due to traction injury of the lower trunk that may be seen in undue abduction of the arm (outstretched arm grabbing an object during a fall from height) or birth injury (traction of the extended arm during delivery) 

This leads to paralysis of the intrinsic muscles of the hand (T1) that are responsible for flexion at metacarpophalangeal joints (MCP) and extension at proximal and distal interphalangeal joints(PIP and DIP). The unopposed action of extensor digitorum at MCP causes hyperextension. The unopposed action of flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus at PIP and DIP causes flexion. Thus giving rise to the characteristic claw hand.

Other changes include anesthesia and analgesia along the ulnar border of the forearm, vasomotor changes, absence of sweating, and trophic changes in long-standing cases. If the C8 is also damaged, the extent of anesthesia will be greater and will involve the medial side of the forearm, hand, and medial two fingers.

Horner's syndrome (option D) may occur in one-third of the cases due to injury of sympathetic fibers to the head and neck that leave the spinal cord through nerve T1.

Correct answer: A. V

The liver segment highlighted in green in this CT section is segment V. The section of the CT given is taken below the portal vein as the cross-section of the portal vein before its bifurcation can be viewed.

A horizontal plane known as the portal plane divides the liver where the portal vein bifurcates and becomes horizontal. This divides each section of the liver into superior and inferior segments: 

  • Left lateral section: segment II above and segment III below the portal plane
  • Left medial section: segment IVa above and segment IVb below the portal plane
  • Right anterior (or medial) section: segment VIII above and segment V below the portal plane
  • Right posterior (or lateral) section: segment VII above and segment VI below the portal plane

 Shown below is a section from below the portal plane.

questions.question: Identify the given structure:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pancreatic islet cells

The above image shows pancreatic islet cells. Islet of Langerhans makes up the endocrine part of the pancreas.

Islets are characterized by secretory cells supported by reticulin fibers, and containing numerous fenestrated capillaries. There is a delicate capsule around each islet. They are paler than the surrounding exocrine cells, as they have less rough endoplasmic reticulum.

The image given below shows the histology of the pancreas.

The islets of Langerhans contain four major and two minor cell types:

  • Four main types are β, α, δ, and PP (pancreatic polypeptide) cells:
    • α or A cells- located peripherally and secrete glucagon 
    • β or B cells- located centrally and produce insulin 
    • δ or D cells- scattered between beta cells and secrete somatostatin
    • PP cells- are present in islets and also in the exocrine pancreas. They secrete a pancreatic polypeptide, which exerts several gastrointestinal effects, such as stimulation of secretion of gastric and intestinal enzymes and inhibition of intestinal motility. 
  • Minor cell types:
    • D1 cells secrete vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), a hormone that induces glycogenolysis and hyperglycemia. It also stimulates gastrointestinal fluid secretion and causes secretory diarrhea.
    • Enterochromaffin cells synthesize serotonin and are the source of pancreatic tumors that cause carcinoid syndrome.

Other options:

Option A: Lymph nodes are secondary lymphoid organs. The structure of lymph nodes consists of an outer cortex and inner medulla. The cortex contains an aggregation of B-lymphocytes (primary follicles) and quiescent secondary follicles with a pale central germinal center.

The inner medulla consists of medullary cords (lymphocytes and plasma cells) and medullary sinuses. Between the cortex and medulla, there is an ill-defined zone called the paracortex, which contains T lymphocytes.

The image given below shows the histology of the lymph node. 

Option B: Glomerulus is a rounded tuft of anastomosing capillaries. The glomerular capillary wall is the filtering membrane and consists of fenestrated endothelial cells, basement membrane, and visceral epithelial cells called podocytes, which contain foot processes.

The glomerular tuft is supported by the mesangium containing mesangial cells and a non-cellular mesangial matrix.

The image given below shows the histology of the glomerulus.

Option C: Spleen is a secondary lymphoid organ. It contains round white pulp surrounded by red pulp. The white pulp is made up of aggregations of lymphocytes that surround a small artery or arterioles. Lymphocytes surrounding the arteriole are called peri-arterial lymphatic sheath (PALS) and contain T cells. Follicles in white pulp contain B cells.

The red pulp is a modified lymphoid tissue infiltrated with all the cells of circulating blood. It is like a sponge permeated by spaces (splenic sinusoids) lined by reticular cells. The zone of red pulp immediately surrounding white pulp is the marginal zone. This zone has a rich network of sinusoids.

questions.question: A patient presents with swelling under the left ear lobule and complains of pain. Which of the following structures is the likely cause of the pain?
options: Investing layer of deep ce​rvical fascia

Correct answer: B. Greater auricular nerve

The cause of the pain in this patient complaining of pain in the parotid region is likely to be the greater auricular nerve.

The greater auricular nerve provides sensory innervation to the skin overlying the parotid gland and the ear lobule. Pain associated with swelling and inflammation in the parotid region could be transmitted through the greater auricular nerve. The parotid gland is covered by a parotid capsule that is derived from the investing layer of deep cervical fascia. Any acute inflammation of the gland such as acute sialadenitis results in pain in the pre­auricular region. The pain is mainly due to stretching of the capsule resulting in stimulation of the greater auricular nerve.

Other options:

Option A: The facial nerve is not the primary cause of pain in the parotid region due to swelling. The Hitzelberger sign(numbness in the posterosuperior meatal wall of the external auditory canal), associated with facial nerve involvement, is seen in acoustic neuroma and is not the cause of pain in this scenario. 

Option D: Investing layer of deep cervical fascia is not the correct answer because the investing layer of deep cervical fascia itself does not transmit pain sensation. The investing layer of deep cervical fascia is a layer of connective tissue that envelops the neck and extends to cover the parotid gland, forming the parotid capsule. While inflammation or swelling in the parotid gland can stretch the capsule and cause pain, the actual transmission of pain sensation is mediated by sensory nerves, such as the greater auricular nerve, which innervates the skin over the parotid gland and the ear lobule.

The greater auricular nerve (Option B) is a more appropriate answer in this context, as it is responsible for carrying the pain sensation from the area of swelling and inflammation in the parotid region.

Option C: The auriculotemporal nerve can cause referred pain due to caries tooth, ulcerative lesions of the oral cavity, temporomandibular joint disorders, and sphenopalatine neuralgia. However, it is not the primary cause of pain in the parotid region due to swelling.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Given below is the image of a 33-hour chick embryo. Which of the following is derived from the marked structure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ribs

The structure marked in the given image is the para-axial mesoderm. The ribs are derived from the para-axial mesoderm.

During the third week of embryological development, the process of gastrulation occurs, which refers to the formation of the three germ layers: ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm. This is followed by the formation of the notochord, which is the axial structure, which induces the formation of the neural tube above it. During the formation of the neural tube, some cells at the lateral border dissociate and form the neural crest cells, which is sometimes referred to as the fourth germ layer.

After the formation of the notochord, which is the axial structure, the mesoderm on either side can be seen to be organized into three layers as follows:

1. Para-axial mesoderm - Thickened plate of the mesoderm close to the midline, on either side of the notochord. This forms the somitomeres and somites, which have the following derivatives: 

  • Dermatome: Forms the segmental dermis of the skin
  • Myotome: Forms the skeletal muscle
  • Sclerotome: Forms the vertebral column and ribs

2. Intermediate mesoderm - Longitudinal strip of mesoderm that connects the para-axial with the lateral plate mesoderm. The urinary (Option A) and genital systems are derived from the intermediate mesoderm.

3. Lateral plate mesoderm - A thinner layer of mesoderm that lies laterally. This layer develops a large cavity called the intraembryonic coelom that gives rise to pericardial, pleural (Option C), and peritoneal cavities.

The neural crest cells also contribute to the formation of structures as follows:

In the trunk region, they form melanocytes, sensory ganglia (Option B), sympathetic and enteric neurons, Schwann cells, and adrenal medulla cells.
In the cranial region, they contribute to the craniofacial skeleton, neurons for cranial ganglia, satellite glial cells, and melanocytes.

The following is a summary of the intrapulmonary passages:

Trachea → Main Bronchi → Lobar Bronchi → Segmental Bronchi → Terminal Bronchiole → Respiratory Bronchiole → Alveolar Duct → Alveolar Sac → Alveoli

Bronchi and bronchioles can be distinguished by the presence of cartilage and glands in the bronchi which are not present in the bronchioles.

Terminal bronchioles represent the most distal parts of the conducting passage. Each terminal bronchiole ends by dividing into respiratory bronchioles. Terminal bronchioles contain cilia and stratified columnar epithelium, whereas respiratory bronchioles contain few or no cilia, and simple cuboidal epithelium. Another differentiating point between the two is that terminal bronchioles would not communicate with the alveoli but respiratory bronchioles would have a communication with the alveoli.

Each respiratory bronchiole ends by dividing into a few alveolar ducts. Each alveolar duct ends in a passage, the atrium, which leads into a number of rounded alveolar sacs. Each alveolar sac is studded with a number of air sacs or alveoli.

    • Associative visual agnosia - inability to visually identify objects in the absence of visual impairment, with ability to identify the object using other sensory modalities (as suggested in the scenario). Prosopagnosia is a type of associatetive visual agnosia which refers to the inability to visually identify faces.

Stereognosis is the ability to identify an object by a perception of the form and nature of an object without looking at it. Exocrine glands can be classified into three subtypes, based on the manner in which their secretions are poured out of the cells:

  2. Merocrine
  3. Holocrine

In apocrine glands, the apical parts of the cells are shed off to discharge the secretion. Examples of apocrine glands are :

  • Secretion of milk fat by mammary glands
  • Atypical sweat glands in the axilla, perianal region, periumbilical skin, mons pubis.
  • Ceruminous glands of the external auditory meatus are modified apocrine glands

Apocrine glands are large glands found in the dermis or subcutaneous fat. They are a type of sweat gland. It consists of a basal secretory coil followed by a straight duct that opens into the pilary canal above the duct of the sebaceous gland. In hairless skin, it directly opens onto the skin surface. 

Apocrine activity is minimal before puberty, after which it is androgen-dependent and responsive to emotional stimuli. It is controlled by adrenergic nerves and is sensitive to adrenaline and noradrenaline. The secretion is initially sterile and odorless, but it undergoes bacterial decomposition to generate odorous and musky compounds. Obstruction of apocrine sweat ducts and associated upper hair follicles in the axillae, breast areolae, and pubic region, mainly in women, is thought to cause Fox–Fordyce disease. It is also implicated in the causation of a painful, occasionally debilitating condition called hidradenitis suppurativa.

The trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V) is responsible for sensory input from the face, as well as motor functions such as chewing.    First-order neurons: Cell bodies are located in the trigeminal ganglion (also called the semilunar or Gasserian ganglion).

   First-order neurons: Cell bodies are located in the trigeminal ganglion.

3. Mandibular Division (V3):
   First-order neurons: Cell bodies are located in the trigeminal ganglion.

These first-order neurons carry sensory information from the face to the brainstem. Upon entering the brainstem, the fibers synapse with second-order neurons in specific nuclei:

   a.Receives input mainly from the maxillary and mandibular divisions.
   b.Located in the medulla.
   c.Second-order neurons here carry pain and temperature sensations.

After synapsing in these nuclei, the sensory information is further relayed to higher brain centers for processing and perception.

  • Roof and lateral wall - Tapetum of corpus callosum

questions.question: Which of the following marked areas in the histopathological specimen shows calcification?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 3

The given specimen is that of an epiphyseal cartilage, where zone 3 corresponds to the zone of calcification.

Epiphyseal cartilage is divided into five zones :

  • The resting zone consists of hyaline cartilage without morphological changes in the cells (option 1)
  • In the proliferative zone, chondrocytes divide rapidly and form columns of stacked cells parallel to the long axis of the bone (option 2)
  • The hypertrophic cartilage zone contains large chondrocytes whose cytoplasm has accumulated glycogen. The resorbed matrix is reduced to thin septa between the chondrocytes.
  • Simultaneous with the death of chondrocytes in the calcified cartilage zone, the thin septa of cartilage matrix become calcified by the deposit of hydroxyapatite.
  • In the ossification zone, endochondral bone tissue appears (option 4). Blood capillaries and osteoprogenitor cells formed by mitosis of cells originating from the periosteum invade the cavities left by the chondrocytes. The osteoprogenitor cells form osteoblasts, which are distributed in a discontinuous layer over the septa of the calcified cartilage matrix. Ultimately, the osteoblasts deposit bone matrix over the three-dimensional calcified cartilage matrix.

The epiphyseal cartilage is responsible for the growth in the length of bone and it disappears in adults, which is why bone growth ceases in adulthood.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following statements is true concerning the anatomy of the breast?
options: Inner quadrants contain mo‍st breast tissue
Ligaments of cooper are fo‍und only in lower quadran​ts
Tail of Spence extends acr‍oss anterior axillary fol​d
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tail of Spence extends across anterior axillary fold

The tail of Spence extends across the anterior axillary fold and is a small extension of the upper lateral quadrant of the breast.

The breast lies in the superficial fascia of the pectoral region. It is divided into four quadrants, i.e. upper medial, upper lateral, lower medial and lower lateral. 

Vertically, it extends from the second to the sixth ribs. Horizontally, it extends from the lateral border of the sternum to the midaxillary line. A small extension of the upper lateral quadrant, called the axillary tail of Spence, passes through an opening in the deep fascia and lies in the axilla. The opening is called the foramen of Langer. 

The breast lies on the deep pectoral fascia covering the pectoralis major and serratus anterior superiorly, the external abdominal oblique and its aponeurosis inferiorly, and the clavipectoral fascia laterally. Fibrous strands or sheets consisting of condensations of connective tissue extend between the posterior lamina of the superficial fascia and the dermis. These suspensory ligaments (retinacula or Cooper’s ligaments) are often well-developed in the superior parts of the breast and support the breast tissue, helping to minimize drooping.

The breasts normally comprise up to 20 discrete lobes that contain ductal-glandular tissue consisting of branching ducts and terminal secretory lobules in a connective tissue stroma. Each lobe is derived by branching from one central lactiferous duct in the nipple. The terminal duct lobular unit (TDLU or lobule) is the functional milk secretory component of the breast. 

The upper outer quadrant of the breast contains a greater volume of tissue than the other quadrants. This is the reason for the majority of the carcinomas arising in the upper outer quadrant.

Retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is derived from the neuroectoderm. The RPE develops from the outer layer of the optic cup, a structure that arises from the neural tube (neuroectodermal origin), not from neural crest cells.

Neural crest cells are a group of cells that migrate during embryonic development and give rise to various structures, including parts of the nervous system, face, and heart.

questions.question: The cranial component of the neural crest cells leads to the formation of?
