questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: In a patient with maple syrup urine disease, all of the following amino acids should be restricted in diet except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Methionine

In maple syrup urine disease (MSUD), only branched-chain amino acids are restricted, hence, methionine does not need any restriction in diet.

Branched-chain amino acids are:

  • Leucine (L)
  • Isoleucine (I)
  • Valine (V)

MSUD is an autosomal recessive disorder in which there is a partial or complete deficiency of branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase complex (BCKD). This impairs the metabolism of branched-chain amino acids. These amino acids, particularly leucine and their metabolite accumulate in the blood, causing toxic effects on the brain. Features include feeding problems, vomiting, ketosis, and a characteristic burnt sugar odor /maple syrup-like odor found in urine, sweat, and cerumen.

Laboratory investigations will show increased levels of branched-chain amino acids in the plasma and urine. Leucine levels are usually higher than isoleucine, and valine.

Treatment involves restricted intake of branched-chain amino acids using commercially available formulas and judicious supplementation of isoleucine and valine. Very high levels of leucine are removed by hemodialysis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the human genome project is false?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Next generation sequencing was used

The human genome project did not use next-generation sequencing.

The Human Genome Project (HGP) was an international, collaborative research program, which involved agencies such as UNESCO, HUGO, the National Institute of Health/Department of Energy (USA), the Medical Research Council (UK), Genethon (France), and the European Union. The primary goal of the Human Genome Project was to determine the sequence of all nucleotide base pairs, that make up human DNA and to create a single linear map of all genes from the human genome. The project was active from 1990 to 2003, taking around 13 years to complete. A total of 20500 genes were identified and mapped. Scientists used various methods of first-generation sequencing technologies including sanger's technique, SGS technique, etc. The HGP has produced a curated and accurate reference sequence for the majority of human chromosomes. The reference sequence has provided the foundation for the use of second-generation sequencing technologies such as array techniques.

Next-generation sequencing (NGS) is a new technology used for sequencing DNA and RNA and mutation detection. NGS can sequence the genome faster and in a shorter period of time than first-generation sequencing technologies. NGS allows for the detection of a spectrum of mutations, including single nucleotide substitutions, small insertions and deletions, large genomic duplications and deletions, and rare variations. Next-generation DNA sequencing technologies include

  • Illumina sequencing
  • Roche 454 sequencing
  • Ion torrent: Proton/PGM sequencing
  • SOLID sequencing.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Banding technique used for dicentric chromosomes is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. C banding

The banding technique used for dicentric chromosomes is C banding.

Heterochromatin includes non-coding regions of DNA, such as centromeric regions. The staining of these constitutive heterochromatins, is done by C-banding using silver salt staining. A dicentric chromosome having two centromeres can hence be identified by C banding.

Various techniques are used in karyotyping to study chromosomes. Staining with various compounds produces various results and helps us to understand the chromosomes better.

Common techniques used are:

  • Q banding - Fluorescence staining with quinacrine mustard.
  • G banding - Giemsa staining after partial denaturation of chromatin. It is the most common technique used in cytogenetics to produce a visible karyotype by staining condensed chromosomes.
  • R banding - Reverse Giemsa staining. In this, the light and dark areas are reversed.
  • C banding - staining of heterochromatin with silver salts.
  • T banding - staining the telomeres of chromosomes.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Affinity maturation of antibodies is because of?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Somatic hypermutation

Affinity maturation of antibodies is because of somatic hypermutation.

Affinity maturation is the process by which antibodies gain increased affinity, avidity, and anti-pathogen activity. It is a result of somatic hypermutation of immunoglobulin genes in B cells, coupled with selection for antigen binding.

Somatic hypermutation is a cellular response by which the immune system adapts to the new foreign elements that confront it. They do so by adding nucleotides in V gene regions of heavy and light chains, resulting in a better fit of antigen with the antibodies. This hence increases the affinity of antibodies to antigens. Due to this, the subset of plasma cells with these improved hypervariable regions are more strongly
selected by the antigen and therefore constitute a larger part of the population of antibody-producing cells. This process is called affinity maturation.

This process occurs in the germinal centers and proceeds for weeks after acute infection or vaccination, or for many cycles during chronic infection. The resulting antibodies can be highly mutated from their germline-encoded counterparts, with an increase in several orders of magnitude in affinity for antigen compared to the corresponding naïve B cell receptors (BCRs).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Best method for detection of mutations with low allele frequency is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Droplet digital PCR

Best method for detection of mutation with low allele frequency is Droplet digital PCR (ddPCR)

It is an advanced and more precise type of quantitative PCR which gives more consistent and reproducible results. It can accurately quantify the target nucleic acid sequence within a sample. It is useful for determining somatic mutation with low allele frequency. Mutant alleles of frequency as low as 0.25% can also be detected using this technique. 

Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is a rapid automated method for the amplification of specific DNA sequences (or genes). Reverse transcriptase PCR- The enzyme reverse transcriptase (RT) is used to synthesize a complimentary copy of DNA (cDNA) from RNA and this cDNA is then used as a template for PCR.

Other special PCR types:

Nested PCR- It involves the sequential use of two primer sets. The first primer set is used for amplification and the target sequence for the second primer is present only on the amplicon with the target sequence. Nested PCR is intended to reduce non-specific binding due to the amplification of unexpected primer binding sites.

Multiplex PCR- Multiple primers are used to amplify several DNA sequences simultaneously. As this process targets multiple genes at once, a single test run gives additional information that would otherwise require several times the reagents and technician time to perform. 

The Sanger sequencing technique is used for DNA sequencing. It is based on controlled termination of synthesis of DNA by using chain terminating agents like dideoxynucleotides.

Fluorescent In Situ Hybridisation (FISH) is a simple technique for the detection of specific genetic information on morphologically intact tissue using fluorescent probes. FISH can be performed on prenatal samples, peripheral blood cells, touch preparations from cancer biopsies, and even fixed archival tissue sections.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: In Sanger sequencing, ddNTP is used because:
options: It is used to increase DNA‍ polymerase activity
They exhibit higher affini‍ty for DNA polymerases
It doesn't allow further e‍longation of DNA
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. It doesn't allow further elongation of DNA

In Sanger sequencing, dideoxynucleotides triphosphates (ddNTP) are used because it doesn't allow further elongation of DNA.

The Sanger method is used for DNA sequencing. This method uses the mechanism of synthesis of DNA by DNA polymerases. In the process of synthesis of DNA, the 3'-hydroxyl group of primer reacts with an incoming dNTP to form a new phosphodiester bond. This reaction is catalyzed by DNA polymerase.

In the Sanger sequencing method, ddNTP is used because it halts the DNA synthesis. ddNTPs can bind to the template strand but lack the 3'-hydroxyl group which is required to add the next nucleotide. The products of this reaction are a mixture of DNA strands of varying lengths. This mixture is then separated using polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis and autoradiography. This produces a pattern of bands from which the DNA sequence can be read.

The image given below shows the steps involved in Sanger's method. 

 

Sanger’s technique was the first technique used to determine the sequence of proteins. The first protein to be sequenced by this method was insulin. Sanger’s reagent is 1- fluoro 2,4 dinitro benzene.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Misincorporation of uracil into DNA is seen in deficiency of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Folate

Misincorporation of uracil into DNA is seen in the deficiency of folate. 

Folate deficiency leads to decreased thymidylate synthesis from deoxyuridylate due to deficient methylation of deoxyuridine monophosphate (dUMP) to thymidine monophosphate (TMP). The methylation of dUMP to TMP is catalyzed by thymidylate synthase and requires tetrahydrofolate (THFA) as a methyl group donor. This decreased TMP synthesis can result in an imbalance of deoxyribonucleotides and hence leading to excessive uracil misincorporation into DNA during replication and repair.

Folic acid (vitamin B9) is a water-soluble vitamin, and its active form is tetrahydrofolate (THFA). It acts as a carrier of one-carbon groups. Tetrahydrofolate receives one-carbon fragments from donors such as serine, glycine, and histidine and transfers them to intermediates in the synthesis of amino acids, purines, and pyrimidines.

 

Folate deficiency results in:

  • Megaloblastic anemia 
  • Homocystenemia
  • Neural tube defects (spina bifida, Anencephaly) in the fetus.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Deamination of methylated cytosine forms which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Thymine

Deamination of methylated cytosine forms thymine.

Deamination is the removal of an amino group(NH2) from a chemical compound. Enzymes that catalyze this reaction are called deaminases. Deamination of 5-methylcytosine forms thymine. 

Other significant deaminations are given below:

  • Deamination of adenosine forms inosine. This is a metabolic step involved in uric acid formation by purine catabolism. It is mediated by the enzyme adenosine deaminase (ADA). ADA deficiency leads to sparse or defective T cells and B cells and patients suffer from Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID).
  • Deamination of cytosine leads to uracil formation - The production of apolipoprotein B-48 (apoB-48) in the intestine is the result of RNA editing in the intestine. This involves post-transcriptional deamination of cytosine to uracil by enzyme cytidine deaminase. This converts sense codon (CAA) in the mRNA to nonsense codon (UAA)at a single specific site. This edited mRNA translates to apoB-48.
  • Deamination of guanine forms xanthine. This is a metabolic step involved in uric acid formation by purine catabolism.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which of the following types of inhibition is depicted in the given Lineweaver-Burk plot?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Competitive inhibition

The given graph shows competitive inhibition, in which the value of Vmax remains constant and the Km value increases.

  • Km is the substrate concentration at which velocity is half maximum.
  • Vmax is the maximum velocity of a reaction.
Inhibition Km Vmax
Competitive Increases Same
Non Competitive Same Decreases
Uncompetitive Decreases Decreases

 

Competitive inhibition is when the inhibitor binds reversibly to the substrate-binding site and competes with the substrate for the active enzyme-binding site. This effect of competitive inhibition can be overcome by increasing the substrate concentration by which maximum velocity can still be achieved. Therefore, Vmax is unaltered in this type of inhibition. However, the concentration of the substrate required to achieve half of the maximum velocity is increased. Therefore, Km is increased in this condition.

The graph shows the changes in Vmax and Km in competitive inhibition.

Other options:

Option B: Non-competitive inhibition is by binding inhibitors to enzymes in locations remote from the active site. Increasing the concentration of the substrate does not overcome non-competitive inhibition. Thus, noncompetitive inhibitors decrease the Vmax of the reaction. They do not interfere with the binding of the substrate to the enzyme. Thus, the enzyme shows the same Km in the presence or absence of noncompetitive inhibitors.

The graph shows the changes in Vmax and Km in non-competitive inhibition.

Option C: In uncompetitive inhibition, inhibitors bind with the enzyme-substrate intermediate complex, and inhibit it. This leads to decrease in both Vmax and Km. An example is the inhibition of placental alkaline phosphate (ALP) by phenylalanine. 

Option D: Suicidal inhibition is a special type of irreversible inhibition. The inhibitor here makes use of the enzyme's own reaction mechanism to inactivate it and is hence known as mechanism-based inactivation. An example is allopurinol, which is oxidized by xanthine oxidase to alloxanthine. Alloxanthine in turn is a more potent inhibitor of xanthine oxidase.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Glycogen phosphorylase is activated by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Calcium

Glycogen phosphorylase is activated by calcium in the muscle.

Glycogen phosphorylase is the rate-limiting enzyme of glycogenolysis and is decreased in the fed state.

In the muscle, the increased cytosolic calcium ion concentration initiates both contraction and glycogenolysis. Muscle phosphorylase kinase has four different subunits, α, β, γ, and δ. The α and β subunits are phosphorylated by cAMP-dependent protein kinase. The δ subunit is identical to the calcium-binding protein calmodulin and binds four calcium ions. Calcium coordinates the activation of Glycogen Phosphorylase with the contraction of the muscle.

Glycogen phosphorylase catalyzes the cleavage of α1 → 4 linkages of glycogen to single units of glucose 1-phosphate. It uses pyridoxal phosphate as the coenzyme. Different isoenzymes of glycogen phosphorylase are seen in the liver, muscles, and brain.

Other options:

Option B: During glycogenolysis, glucose 6-phosphate allosterically inhibits glycogen phosphorylase. 

Option C: Insulin entirely suppresses glycogenolysis in the skeletal muscle and liver.

Option D: In glycogenolysis protein phosphatase is inactivated by inhibitor proteins in response to cAMP, to maintain the glycogen phosphorylase in an active state.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Mutation of the gene of cystic fibrosis occurs with:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Phenylalanine at 508 position, chloride channel

The mutant gene of cystic fibrosis (CF gene) produces a mutant CFTR protein with the deletion of a phenylalanine residue at 508 (F508del), characterised by impaired chloride secretion.

Cystic fibrosis is a condition with an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance. It results due to a defective mutation in the gene encoding for cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CF gene). It plays an important role in mucociliary transport along the respiratory mucosa. It also helps to regulate the amount of exocrine gland secretion.

The defect in the ion channel results in the production of hyper-viscous, adherent secretions which can obstruct the airways. Organisms such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus can grow in the sputum. The exocrine pancreas can undergo fibrotic scarring, cyst formation, and acinar tissue loss. The viscid secretions can lead to pancreatic duct obstruction. The flow of digestive enzymes to the duodenum is hence impaired.

Symptoms include sinusitis, steatorrhea, and abdominal pain. Distal intestinal obstruction is a complication due to difficulty in excreting intestinal contents. In neonates, it can present as meconium ileus. 

Detection of high levels of trypsinogen is used in newborn screening. Chloride level >60mEq/L in the sweat of affected patients is diagnostic. Hyponatremic hypochloremic alkalosis is seen.

Postural drainage, short-term antibiotics, and inhaled bronchodilators can be used for medical management. The definitive treatment is lung transplantation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: A baby is brought to the OPD with complaints of lethargy and poor feeding. On examination, it is noted that the urine had a smell of burnt sugar. A defect in which of the following enzymes causes this disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase

The diagnosis, in this case, is that of maple syrup urine disease (MSUD). This disease occurs due to a defect of the enzyme branched-chain keto acid dehydrogenase.

 MSUD is an autosomal recessive disorder that occurs due to a deficiency of branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase complex. This impairs the metabolism of branched-chain amino acids valine, leucine, isoleucine, and alloisoleucine. These amino acids, particularly leucine and its metabolite accumulate in the blood, causing toxic effects on the brain.

The affected child develops poor feeding and vomiting a few days after birth. There is a period of hypertonicity with a period of flaccidity in between. These appear as repetitive boxing and bicycling movements. The babies may also have hypoglycemia, but this is not corrected by the administration of glucose. The urine, sweat, and cerumen of the baby have a sweetish maple syrup-like odor.

Laboratory investigations will show increased levels of branched-chain amino acids in the plasma and urine. Leucine levels are usually higher than isoleucine, valine, and alloisoleucine. Since the patient excretes ketone bodies in the urine, the urine will be positive for the dinitrophenylhydrazine test.

Treatment involves controlled intake of branched-chain amino acids using commercially available formulas and judicious supplementation of isoleucine and valine. Very high levels of leucine are removed by hemodialysis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: All are true about the hexose monophosphate shunt, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Utilises ribose

The hexose monophosphate (HMP) shunt produces ribose and does not utilize it. 

The pentose phosphate pathway, also known as the HMP shunt pathway, is an alternative route for the metabolism of glucose. It contributes in two major ways:

  • Formation of NADPH for the synthesis of fatty acids and steroids and maintenance of reduced glutathione for antioxidant activity.
  • Formation of ribose for the synthesis of nucleic acid and nucleotides

The enzymes for this pathway are found in the cytosol. There are two phases:

  1. Irreversible oxidative phase: Glucose-6-phosphate is dehydrogenated and decarboxylated to form ribulose-5-phosphate which in turn gets converted to ribose-5-phosphate.
  2. Reversible non-oxidative phase: Ribulose-5-phosphate is converted back to glucose-6-phosphate.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question:
Which of the following enzymes use selenocysteine?

1. Glutathione peroxidase
2. Glutathione synthase
3. Deiodinase
4. Thioredoxin reductase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 3, 4

The enzymes that use selenocysteine are glutathione peroxidase, deiodinase, and thioredoxin reductase. 

Selenocysteine is the 21st amino acid coded by the UGA codon, which is normally a stop codon. It is formed by co-translational modification. The protein synthetic apparatus can identify a selenocysteine-encoding UGA by the presence of the selenocysteine insertion sequence (SECIS) in the untranslated region of mRNA.

Enzymes such as thioredoxin reductase, glutathione peroxidase, and deiodinase use selenocysteine to catalyze redox reactions. Defects in human selenoproteins are associated with tumorigenesis and atherosclerosis. It can cause cardiomyopathy due to selenium deficiency, which is known as Keshan disease.

Glutathione synthase is the second enzyme in the synthesis of glutathione. Glutathione plays an important role in oxidative stress, redox signalling, and regulates cell proliferation and apoptosis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: A patient presented with reduced levels of high-density lipoprotein, and ABCA1 mutation. On examination, tonsils appeared as shown in the image. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tangier's disease

The diagnosis in this case with reduced levels of high-density lipoprotein (HDL), ABCA1 mutation, and orange tonsils on examination is Tangier's disease. It is caused by a defect in ABCA1 receptors.

ABCA1 plays a role in the efflux of cholesterol from peripheral cells of HDL. LCAT (lecithin cholesterol acyltransferase) converts cholesterol to cholesterol esters, which accumulate in the core of HDL. Thus, defective ABCA1 will lead to low levels of HDL in the blood. 

Other options:

Option B: Abetalipoproteinemia is a hypolipoproteinemia caused by a defect in the MTP gene. Here, loading apolipoprotein B with lipids is defective. Hence, few very low density-lipoproteins (VLDLs) or chylomicrons are formed, leading to the accumulation of triacylglycerols in the liver and intestine.

Option C: Hyperlipoproteinemia is a disorder that causes the body to metabolize lipids incorrectly. This results in hyperlipidemia and can lead to the development of multiple small xanthomas in the skin.

Option D: Acid lipase deficiency can lead to Wolman's disease which is a lysosomal storage disease. The pathognomic feature of this condition is adrenal calcification. So patients generally present with adrenal insufficiency and are neonates.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: A baby is being evaluated for delayed developmental milestones. On examination, the child has hepatosplenomegaly. A microscopic image of the bone marrow evaluation is shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Gaucher disease

The microscopic image of the bone marrow biopsy shows Gaucher cells and the diagnosis is Gaucher disease.

Gaucher disease is a lysosomal storage disease with autosomal recessive inheritance. The condition results due to the deficiency of acid β-glucosidase. This results in the accumulation of glucosylceramide (a glycolipid substrate) in the reticuloendothelial cells. There is progressive infiltration of the liver, spleen, and bone marrow. 

There are three clinical types:

  • Type 1: Adult (non-neuronopathic form)
  • Type 2: Infantile (acute neuronopathic form)
  • Type 3: Juvenile (subacute neuronopathic form)

Type 1 is the most common. It presents with a myriad of symptoms, such as bruising secondary to thrombocytopenia, fatigue due to anemia, hepatosplenomegaly, and bone pain. Lytic lesions and osteosclerosis of the femur, ribs, and pelvis may also be seen. A few patients may have pulmonary involvement. Growth retardation may be observed in cases presenting in the first decade. 

Type 2 is rare, and presents with hypertonia, strabismus, and organomegaly. Neurodegeneration is the characteristic feature. Stridor and failure to thrive can also be the presenting features. Ultimately, death can occur due to respiratory arrest. 

Type 3 presents with intermediate symptoms, as seen in the other two types. By the age of 10-15 years, the child succumbs to death.

Gaucher cells  are reticuloendothelial cells with glucosylceramide, and have a wrinkled-paper appearance due to intracytoplasmic substrate inclusions. These cells stain strongly with periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stain. This is characteristic of Gaucher's disease.

Other options:

Option B - Acid sphingomyelinase deficiency results in Niemann-Pick disease types A and B. Both are autosomal recessive conditions. Type A has a neurodegenerative course, while type B is non-neuronopathic. The former presents with hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and psychomotor retardation. Type B is associated with hepatosplenomegaly and mild pulmonary involvement. 

Option-C - Hunter disease is an X-linked inherited disorder due to a deficiency of the enzyme iduronate sulfatase. It leads to the accumulation of dermatan and heparan sulfate. Clinical features involve coarse facies, cardiovascular involvement, and distinctive skin lesions.

Option-D - Hurler/Scheie disease is a mucopolysaccharidosis that has childhood and adult onset. It presents with cognitive degeneration.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Refsum disease is due to:
options: Absence of alpha oxidation‍ in peroxisomes
Absence of alpha oxidation‍ in lysosomes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Absence of alpha oxidation in peroxisomes

Refsum disease is due to the absence of alpha oxidation in peroxisomes.

Refsum's disease is a rare autosomal recessive disorder. The defective enzyme is phytanoyl CoA hydroxylase, which causes alpha oxidation of fatty acids and leads to elevated levels of phytanic acid in the blood.

Clinical features are dysmorphic facies and severe neurological symptoms such as polyneuropathy, retinitis pigmentosa, nerve deafness, ichthyosis, and cerebellar ataxia.

Restricted dietary intake of phytanic acid reduces the symptoms. Management includes avoiding sources of phytanic acid such as dairy products, meat, nuts, and green leafy vegetables.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which of the following describes the relationship between the melting temperature (Tm) of DNA and the concentration of G-C and A-T?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tm increases with more G-C

The correct statement about the melting temperature of DNA (Tm) is that it increases with more G-C concentration.

On heating the DNA, the temperature at which one-half of the helical structure loses its structure defines the melting temperature Tm. The two strands of the double helix structure of the DNA get separated when the hydrogen bonds between the base pairs are disrupted. Thus, the Tm is influenced by the concentrationbase composition of the DNA.

Since G-C pairing has 3 hydrogen bonds and A-T pairing has 2 hydrogen bonds, DNA rich in G-C base pairs requires higher temperatures to denature in comparison to DNA rich in A-T base pairs.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question:
An elderly patient on a vegetarian diet presenting with easy fatigability and pallor was investigated. Peripheral smear showed findings of macrocytic anemia. What is the probable cause of anemia in this patient? Other lab findings are as follows:

Hemoglobin - 9 g/dL

Mean corpuscular volume (MCV) - 112 fL

Serum homocysteine - Elevated

Serum methylmalonic acid - Normal
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Folate deficiency

The probable cause of anemia in this patient of folate deficiency.

The given clinical scenario of macrocytic anemia in a vegetarian with elevated homocysteine levels is due to megaloblastic anemia, which can be caused by the deficiency of vitamin B12 or folic acid. Vitamin B12 deficiency is associated with raised serum methylmalonic acid (MMA) levels, which are normal in this patient; hence, folic acid deficiency is the cause of megaloblastic anemia in this patient.

Folic acid deficiency is associated with the following clinical and laboratory findings:

  • Raised MCV (normal range: 80–100 fL) - macrocytosis
  • Normal MCHC (normal range: 33–36 g/dL) 
  • Increased MCH
  • Elevated RDW
  • Decreased reticulocyte count - due to destruction of abnormal erythroid precursors
  • Elevated homocysteine level
  • Normal MMA level

where MCV, mean corpuscular volume; MCHC, mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration; mean corpuscular hemoglobin, MCH; RDW, red cell distribution width

In vitamin B12 deficiency, neurological abnormalities, elevated homocysteine, and elevated MMA levels are seen.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Zellweger syndrome is due to a defect in the biogenesis of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Peroxisomes

Zellweger syndrome is due to a defect in the biogenesis of peroxisomes.

Zellweger syndrome is also known as cerebrohepatorenal syndrome. It is caused by mutations in the PEX family of genes. This results in defective beta-oxidation of very long-chain fatty acids.

The child presents with

  • Dysmorphic facial features. 
  • Weakness, hypotonia.
  • Neonatal seizures
  • Eye abnormalities.

Biochemical findings will show :

  • Accumulation of very-long-chain fatty acids, phytanic acid
  • Abnormalities in the synthesis of bile acids
  • Marked reduction of plasmalogens

There is no appropriate treatment for Zellweger syndrome. It is very severe and infants rarely survive beyond a few months.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: True statement about the action of enhancers of gene expression?
options: Work only when in close co‍njugation with promoter r​egion
Work only when in upstream‍ of promoter region
They are very specific to ‍the gene
Recruit chromatin and modi‍fy regulatory mechanisms
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Recruit chromatin and modify regulatory mechanisms

The correct statement about the action of enhancers is that they recruit chromatin and modify regulatory mechanisms.

A promoter is a sequence on DNA where RNA polymerase binds and acts as the start signal for transcription. They are present upstream or downstream but close to the gene that is undergoing transcription. 

Enhancers or repressors are proteins that regulate the expression of a gene by recruiting chromatin(DNA bound with histones) and modifying regulatory mechanisms and making it more or less accessible to transcription by RNA polymerase. They may be located upstream or downstream and can be present at any distance from the promoter region. These are not specific to any single gene and interact with many other proteins.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Increased H+ ions in the intermembrane space of mitochondria are due to?
options: Water retention in inner m‍itochondrial space
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Decreased oxidative phosphorylation

Increased H+ ions in the intermembrane space of mitochondria are due to decreased oxidative phosphorylation.

ATP is synthesized in mitochondria by a process called oxidative phosphorylation. The oxidation of substrates like carbohydrates, amino acids, or fats produces reducing equivalents (NADH, FADH2). These equivalents enter the electron transport chain and transfer a proton (H+) to the inter-membrane space. The inner mitochondrial membrane is not permeable to protons leading to the accumulation of H+ in the intermembrane space. The flow of these protons through the Fo releases the energy that phosphorylates ADP to form ATP.

Drugs that inhibit oxidative phosphorylation like oligomycin inhibit the flow of protons through Fo causing an increase in H+ ions in the intermembrane space.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Fructosamine is obtained by glycation of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Albumin

Fructosamine is obtained by the glycation of albumin.

Fructosamine is a measure of non-enzymatic glycation of circulating proteins including albumin, globulins, and lipoproteins. It is now used as a  reasonable alternative to HbA1c measurement when it is not reliable. Since albumin is the most abundant of the serum proteins, fructosamine is predominantly a measure of glycated albumin.

Fructosamine is used as a short-term marker of glucose control. It reflects the average glycemia over the preceding 2 to 3 weeks. HbA1c reflects glucose control over a period of the preceding 8 to 12 weeks.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: A patient from a Mediterranean country visits Africa, where he develops malaria. He is treated with primaquine and later develops hemolytic anemia. Deficiency of an enzyme involved in which of the following pathways could be the cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hexose monophosphate (HMP) pathway

The deficiency of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) enzyme, which is involved in the hexose monophosphate (HMP) pathway, could be the cause behind this presentation. 

G6PD is an enzyme that plays a critical role in redox reactions that occur in all aerobic cells. It is the only source of NADPH in erythrocytes, which helps in the formation of reduced glutathione. This reduced form protects erythrocytes against oxidative stress.

G6PD deficiency is an X-linked inheritance disorder. Most patients with this condition are asymptomatic. But when exposed to oxidative agents, they are prone to develop acute hemolytic anemia. The various oxidative triggers include:

  • Fava beans
  • Infections
  • Drugs such as primaquine, dapsone, and nitrofurantoin

A hemolytic attack can present with weakness and abdominal/ lumbar pain. Later, the patient can develop jaundice, hemoglobinemia, and hemoglobinuria. Investigations will show elevated levels of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and low levels of plasma haptoglobin. Anisocytosis and spherocytes can be seen on peripheral smear. Acute renal failure is a complication seen in adults. 

Other options:

Option A - Glycolysis, the main pathway of glucose, can occur either aerobically or anaerobically. A deficiency of the enzyme pyruvate kinase can present as hemolytic anemia. Fatigue can be the presentation when there is phosphofructokinase. Both these are enzymes of glycolysis. 

Option B - Gluconeogenesis is the process by which non-carbohydrate precursors are used to synthesize glucose. Pyruvate carboxylase, phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase, and glucose-6-phosphatase are the enzymes in the pathway. Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency leads to von Gierke disease, which is a glycogen storage disorder. Defective gluconeogenesis results in hypoglycemia.

Option D - Luebering–Rapoport pathway is a shunt mechanism that generates and dephosphorylates 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG). 2,3-BPG mutase is the enzyme involved. A deficiency of this enzyme can cause erythrocytosis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which of the following disorders follows autosomal recessive inheritance pattern?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cystic fibrosis

Cystic fibrosis is a condition with an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance. 

It results due to a defective mutation in the gene encoding for cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR gene). It functions as an epithelial anion channel. It plays an important role in mucociliary transport along the respiratory mucosa. It also helps regulate the amount of exocrine gland secretion.

The defect in the ion channel results in the production of hyper viscous, adherent secretions which can obstruct the airways. Organisms such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus can grow in the sputum. The exocrine pancreas can undergo fibrotic scarring, cyst formation, and acinar tissue loss. The viscid secretions can lead to pancreatic duct obstruction. The flow of digestive enzymes to the duodenum is hence impaired.

Symptoms include sinusitis, steatorrhea, and abdominal pain. Distal intestinal obstruction is a complication due to difficulty in excreting intestinal contents. In neonates, it can present as meconium ileus. 

Detection of high levels of trypsinogen is used in newborn screening. Chloride level >60mEq/L in the sweat of affected patients is diagnostic. Hyponatremic hypochloremic alkalosis and hypokalemia may also be seen.

Postural drainage, short-term antibiotics, and inhaled bronchodilators can be used for medical management. The definitive treatment is lung transplantation.

In autosomal recessive inheritance, multiple affected members are seen in the same generation. Other generations are not affected. The following pedigree chart depicts an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance.

Other options:

Option A - Huntington's disease is a trinucleotide (CAG) repeat disorder with an autosomal dominant mode of inheritance. It is characterized by involuntary movements known as chorea.

Option B - Treacher Collins syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder that presents as mandibular and malar hypoplasia.

Option D - Achondroplasia has an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern and presents with short limbs, saddle nose, and spinal deformity.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which of the following helps in the transport of fatty acids across the inner mitochondrial membrane?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Carnitine

Carnitine is responsible for the transport of fatty acids or long-chain acyl-CoA across the inner mitochondrial membrane.

Fatty acids are oxidized in the mitochondria to produce acetyl-CoA to produce energy. They must first be converted to acyl-CoA (active fatty acid) before they can be catabolized. 

Carnitine palmitoyltransferase - I (CPT- I) transports acyl-CoA across the inner mitochondrial membrane only in the presence of carnitine. The acyl group of acyl-CoA is transferred to carnitine. The acylcarnitine so formed can penetrate the inner mitochondrial membrane via the carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase. This transporter transfers the acyl group back to CoA, restoring acyl-CoA and liberating carnitine, which is moved back to the intermembrane space. Carnitine palmitoyltransferase -II catalyzes this reaction. The deficiency of this enzyme is a common cause of recurrent myoglobinuria.

Carnitine deficiency can lead to hypoglycemia and restrictive or dilated cardiomyopathy. It can also cause hepatic steatosis.

Other options:

Option A - Acyl carrier protein is a component of the fatty acid synthase complex involved in the biosynthesis of fatty acids. It has vitamin pantothenic acid (vitamin B5).

Option C - Lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT) is present in the plasma and plays an important role in the esterification of cholesterol. Deficiency leads to low levels of lysolecithin and cholesteryl esters.

Option D - The long-chain fatty acids are bound to albumin in the plasma. But albumin does not transport fatty acids across the inner mitochondrial membrane. Albumin is a negative acute-phase reactant synthesized by the liver. It is a carrier for acidic drugs.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: A single mutation in a nucleotide base pair resulting in a termination codon is known as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Nonsense mutation

A single mutation in a nucleotide base pair resulting in a termination codon is known as a nonsense mutation. 

A codon is a sequence of three bases present on the mRNA (messenger RNA), and it codes for amino acids. Out of the 64 codons possible, only 61 code for the 20 amino acids. Three codons, UAA, UAG, and UGA  do not code for any of the 20 amino acids. These are known as nonsense/punctator/termination/stop codons and function as translation termination signals. The UGA codon is traditionally considered a stop codon, but it codes for selenocysteine (21st amino acid).

The tRNA (transfer RNA) contains the anticodon which recognizes specific codons present on the mRNA. The sequence of the anticodon is complementary to the codon. The pairing between the codon and anticodon can wobble at the third base. For example, GGU, GGC, and GGA all pair with the anticodon CCI. The wobble phenomenon along with degeneracy reduces the effect of mutations.

A mutation involving a single nucleotide base is known as a point mutation. A nonsense mutation is a type of point mutation where a codon previously coding for an amino acid is changed to a stop codon. This results in premature termination of translation and the formation of a truncated protein. mRNA containing premature stops are removed by the nonsense-mediated degradation pathway.

Other options:

Option A: A missense mutation is a type of point mutation where the new codon, formed by the changed base, codes for a different amino acid.

Option C: Stop mutation is a term that can be used interchangeably with nonsense mutation. Here, nonsense mutation is the best answer.

Option D: Silent mutations are point mutations where the new codon formed still codes for the same amino acid as the codon before the mutation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: DNA packing is done by which of the following ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Histone

The proteins involved in DNA packing are histones. 

Chromatin contains double-stranded DNA molecules and small basic proteins known as histones. In addition, nonhistone proteins are present that are involved in DNA replication and repair, and RNA synthesis. Histones play a role in condensing the DNA.

Nucleosomes are the organizational unit of chromatin and contain an octamer of histones around which 150 base pairs of DNA are packed. There are various types of histone proteins. H2A, H2B, H3, and H4 groups are components of nucleosomes and are known as core histones. They undergo post-translational modifications such as acetylation and methylation. This plays a critical part in chromatin structure and function. 

The DNA in the nucleosome is arranged in a left-handed helical configuration over the histone octamer.

Other options:

Option B - Glycoproteins are proteins with oligosaccharide chains (glycans) bound to amino acids. Certain plasma proteins, peptide hormones, and cell membrane proteins are examples. Structural changes in the glycoproteins present in cancer cells may play a role in metastasis.

Option C - Nucleic acids can be either DNA or RNA. DNA is thought to be arranged in a double-stranded helix model. RNA on the other hand exists as a single strand. There are different types of RNA such as mRNA (messenger RNA), tRNA (transfer RNA), and rRNA (ribosomal RNA).

Option D - Adenine is a purine base that when linked to ribose forms adenosine, a nucleoside. When a nucleoside is esterified with a phosphate group a nucleotide is formed. Guanine is the other purine base. Cytosine is the pyrimidine base common to DNA and RNA. Thymine is present only in DNA and Uracil in RNA.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: An adolescent male patient presents to you with exercise intolerance. He gives a history of developing cramps on exertion. Which of the following enzyme deficiencies could be the cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Myophosphorylase

The clinical scenario points to a diagnosis of McArdle disease, which results due to a deficiency of the enzyme myophosphorylase (muscle glycogen phosphorylase).

McArdle disease, also known as type V glycogen storage disorder, is an autosomal recessive condition. It typically presents during late childhood or in the second decade of life. The muscle glycogen phosphorylase enzyme deficiency interferes with ATP generation by glycogenolysis in the muscles. This causes muscle glycogen accumulation.

Symptoms are exercise intolerance associated with muscle cramps. A second wind phenomenon, where the symptoms subside after a short period of rest, can also be seen. Myoglobinuria secondary to rhabdomyolysis leads to the passage of burgundy-colored urine in some patients. 

Rarely, it can present during infancy as hypotonia, muscle weakness, and respiratory complications. It is generally fatal. 

Muscle biopsy to measure glycogen content is the standard diagnosis. Avoiding strenuous exercise prevents symptoms. Glucose administration before exercise can improve tolerance. Vitamin B6 is also recommended.

Other options:

Option B - Hexokinase is a glycolytic enzyme. Its deficiency leads to hemolytic anemia. Splenomegaly may be another presenting feature. 

Option C - Glucose-6-phosphatase is an enzyme involved in gluconeogenesis. Its deficiency leads to von Gierke disease also known as type I glycogen storage disease.

Option D - Hepatic glycogen phosphorylase deficiency results in type VI glycogen storage disease, also known as Hers disease.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which of the following enzyme activities can be estimated in red blood cells to diagnose vitamin B2 deficiency?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glutathione reductase

Glutathione reductase activity in red blood cells can be estimated to diagnose vitamin B2 deficiency.

Vitamin B2, also known as riboflavin, is a water-soluble vitamin. Its active forms are FMN (flavin mononucleotide) and FAD (flavin adenine dinucleotide). Glutathione reductase is a FAD-containing enzyme (flavoenzyme). Hence, riboflavin deficiency can be detected by measuring erythrocyte glutathione reductase activity. Red blood cell and urinary concentrations of riboflavin can also be estimated to detect a deficiency.

Deficiency of riboflavin can present as anemia, corneal vascularization, mucocutaneous lesions, and personality changes. Milk and other dairy products are important dietary sources.

Other options:

Option A - Transketolase contains thiamine diphosphate as a coenzyme. Estimation of erythrocyte apotransketolase (enzyme protein) after in vitro addition of thiamine diphosphate, can be used to assess thiamine nutritional status. Thiamine deficiency can result in peripheral neuritis, beriberi, and Wernicke encephalopathy with Korsakoff psychosis.

Option C - Kynureninase is an enzyme that requires pyridoxal phosphate as a coenzyme. It converts 3-hydroxykynurenine, a tryptophan metabolite, to 3-hydroxyanthranilate. In vitamin B6 deficiency, this is impaired and results in the formation and subsequent urinary excretion of xanthurenate. This can be used for diagnosis. 

Option D - Pyruvate is decarboxylated by pyruvate dehydrogenase for which thiamine diphosphate acts as the cofactor. Therefore thiamine deficiency results in the accumulation of pyruvate. This leads to pyruvic and lactic acidosis, commonly seen in alcoholics.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: The following is due to the deficiency of?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitamin A

The given image depicts Bitot's spots characteristically seen in deficiency of vitamin A. Bitot's spots are seen as white patches of keratinized epithelium on the sclera. It is more commonly bilateral and on the temporal side.

Vitamin A deficiency arises mostly due to the inadequate amounts of vitamin A in diet. It can present as night blindness, conjunctival xerosis, Bitot's spots, and keratomalacia. In later stages, it can lead to xerophthalmia. It also increases the risk of developing measles, diarrhea, and dysentery. Skin manifestations include xerosis, scaling, and dermomalacia. Phrynoderma may also be seen as keratotic follicular papules affecting the thighs and upper arms. It is shown in the image below.

In patients above the age of 1 year, vitamin A deficiency is treated with 200,000 IU of vitamin A orally or 100,000 IU by intramuscular route. It should be repeated the next day and two weeks later.

Vitamin A is a fat-soluble vitamin that plays an essential role in vision, reproduction, and maintenance of epithelial integrity. The various forms of vitamin A include retinol (storage form), retinal, retinoic acid, and beta-carotene. It is stored in the liver perisinusoidal stellate (Ito) cells as retinyl ester (retinyl palmitate).

Other options:

Option A - Vitamin C is a water-soluble vitamin that aids in iron absorption and collagen maturation. It cannot be synthesized in humans because of the absence of L-gulonolactone oxidase. Vitamin C deficiency results in scurvy.

 Option C - Vitamin B deficiency has clinical manifestations pertaining to each type. 

Option D - Vitamin E deficiency can present as posterior column and spinocerebellar symptoms. Peripheral neuropathy, ophthalmoplegia, and pigmented retinopathy are other features seen.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: A child presents to you with anemia, thrombocytopenia, and bony pain. On examination, hepatosplenomegaly was noticed. If light microscopy of bone marrow aspirate reveals "crumpled tissue paper" appearance, what is the enzyme defect?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Glucocerebrosidase

The clinical scenario points to a diagnosis of Gaucher's disease, where there is a defect in the enzyme glucocerebrosidase.

Gaucher's disease is a lysosomal storage disease with autosomal recessive inheritance. The condition results due to the deficiency of beta-glucocerebrosidase. This results in the accumulation of glucosylceramide (glycolipid substrate) in the reticuloendothelial cells. There is progressive infiltration of the liver, spleen, and bone marrow. 

There are three clinical types:

  • Type 1: Adult (non-neuronopathic) form
  • Type 2: Infantile (acute neuronopathic) form
  • Type 3: Juvenile (subacute neuronopathic) form

Type 1 is the most common. It presents with a myriad of symptoms, such as bruising secondary to thrombocytopenia, fatigue due to anemia, hepatosplenomegaly, and bone pain. Pathologic fractures and lytic lesions of the femur, ribs, and pelvis may also be seen. A few patients may have pulmonary involvement. Growth retardation may be observed in cases presenting in the first decade. 

Type 2 is rare, and presents with hypertonia, strabismus, and organomegaly. Neurodegeneration is the characteristic feature. Stridor and failure to thrive can also be the presenting features. Ultimately, death can occur due to respiratory arrest. 

Type 3 presents with intermediate symptoms, as seen in the other two types. By the age of 10–15 years, the child succumbs to death.

The Gaucher cells, which are the reticuloendothelial cells with glucosylceramide, have a wrinkled-paper appearance due to intracytoplasmic substrate inclusions. These cells stain strongly with periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stain. This is characteristic of Gaucher's disease.

Other options:

Option B - Acid sphingomyelinase deficiency results in Niemann-Pick disease types A and B. Both are autosomal recessive conditions. Type A has a neurodegenerative course, while type B is non-neuronopathic. The former presents with hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and psychomotor retardation. Death occurs by the age of 3 years. Type B is associated with hepatosplenomegaly and mild pulmonary involvement. 

Option C - Hexosaminidase deficiency causes Sandhoff disease. It has an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance. Clinical features include ataxia, dysarthria, and mental retardation.

Option D - Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency leads to von Gierke disease, which is a glycogen storage disorder.  It is an autosomal recessive condition. The affected children have characteristic doll-like facies. Hyperuricemia, lactic acidosis, and triglyceridemia can be seen. Hepatomegaly and renal enlargement is also associated.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: The electron transport chain is a series of redox reactions that result in ATP synthesis. Which of the following is a cytochrome complex IV inhibitor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cyanide

Cyanide is an inhibitor of cytochrome complex IV or cytochrome a+a3 (cytochrome c oxidase). It is a component of the electron transport chain. 

The electron transport chain (ETC) is a specialized set of electron carriers that can accept electrons. Energy-rich molecules like glucose are oxidized to produce water and carbon dioxide. The intermediate substrates in these reactions can pass on electrons to certain coenzymes such as nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) and flavin adenine dinucleotide (FADH2). The reduced forms can then donate electrons to the ETC by which they lose most of their free energy which is used to move H+ through the inner mitochondrial membrane. The H+ gradient thus produced results in the production of ATP. ATP synthesis together with electron transport is known as oxidative phosphorylation. 

The reactions in oxidative phosphorylation and the arrangement of complexes that form the ETC are shown below.

These complexes can accept or donate electrons to coenzyme Q (CoQ) and cytochrome c, which are mobile electron carriers. Certain site-specific inhibitors can inhibit ATP synthesis. 

Complexes of ETC Inhibitors
Complex I Piericidin A, amobarbital, rotenone
Complex II TTFA (thenoyltrifluoroacetone), carboxin, malonate
Complex III BAL(British anti-lewisite), antimycin A
Complex IV Hydrogen sulfide, carbon monoxide, cyanide

Other options:

Option B - Carbon dioxide along with water is produced by the oxidation of energy-rich molecules in oxidative phosphorylation.

Option C - Oligomycin, an antibiotic, blocks the flow of protons through ATP synthase. This inhibits oxidative phosphorylation.

Option D - Ouabain is a cardiac drug that inhibits the Na+ - K+ ATPase of cell membranes by acting on the extracellular surface.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which of the following zymogens requires gamma-glutamyl carboxylase?
options: Factors II, VII, IX, and X‌
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Factors II, VII, IX, and X

Clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X are zymogens of serine proteases that contain glutamic acid residues. These residues undergo vitamin-K-dependent carboxylation via gamma-glutamyl carboxylase to form gamma-carboxyglutamic acid residues. These residues chelate calcium ions, allowing the binding of clotting factors to the platelet surface.

Zymogens are the proprotein form of enzymes (proenzymes) that require proteolytic activation to carry out their function.

The reduced form of vitamin K acts as a cofactor in the post-synthetic modification of these zymogens and their activation. This reduced form of vitamin K is recycled back from its oxidized form by the enzyme vitamin K epoxide reductase, which is inhibited by warfarin.

The absence of vitamin K or the presence of warfarin inhibits carboxylation of the glutamate residues, leading to the release of abnormal precursors of clotting factors in the blood.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: A patient presented with diarrhea, dermatitis, and dementia. Which of the following vitamin deficiencies would you suspect in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vitamin B3 deficiency

The given clinical scenario of a patient with diarrhea, dermatitis, and dementia is suggestive of niacin/vitamin B3 deficiency.

Niacin deficiency causes pellagra, found mostly among people eating corn/maize-based diets, which are low in niacin and tryptophan. Excess leucine in jowar and maize disrupts the conversion of tryptophan to niacin.

Niacin can be synthesized in the body from tryptophan. Two compounds, nicotinic acid and nicotinamide, have the biological activity of niacin. The nicotinamide ring of the coenzymes nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP) participate in oxidation/reduction reactions.

The initial symptoms of pellagra include loss of appetite, generalized weakness, irritability, abdominal pain, and vomiting. This is followed by bright red glossitis and a characteristic pigmented, scaly skin rash in sun-exposed areas. This rash is known as Casal’s necklace when it forms a ring around the neck. 

The 4Ds of pellagra:

  • Diarrhea
  • Dermatitis
  • Dementia, leading to
  • Death

It is diagnosed by measuring urinary levels of 2-methyl nicotinamide and 2-pyridone.

It is treated by oral supplementation of 100–200 mg of nicotinamide or nicotinic acid three times daily for 5 days.

Option B: Vitamin B1/Thiamine deficiency can manifest as wet beriberi (CVS features like heart failure and edema) or Shoshin beriberi, an acute and fulminant form of wet beriberi, dry beriberi (peripheral neuritis), or as Wernicke encephalopathy with Korsakoff psychosis (in alcoholics). Dietary deficiency of thiamine inhibits pyruvate dehydrogenase. Chronic alcoholics may develop potentially fatal pyruvic and lactic acidosis. 

Option C: Vitamin B6/Pyridoxine deficiency is rare but has been observed in alcoholics, newborns, formulas low in vitamin B6, and women taking oral contraceptives. Isoniazid, an anti-TB drug, leads to pyridoxine deficiency resulting in peripheral neuropathy. Hence pyridoxine supplementation is included in ATT regimens.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: A young boy presents to the OPD with hypoglycemia and muscle cramps, on exertion or while playing.  Then he becomes normal after resting for a while. These episodes are recurrent after a period of activity. He has decreased serum lactate and glucose levels. Which of the following diseases is he most likely to be suffering from?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. McArdle disease

A clinical scenario of a patient with muscle cramps, pain, weakness with exertion, myoglobinuria, and the muscle biopsy specimen showing vacuolar myopathy are suggestive of McArdle's disease, which is due to the deficiency of muscle glycogen phosphorylase. 

McArdle disease, also known as type V glycogen storage disorder, is an autosomal recessive condition. It typically presents during late childhood or in the second decade of life. The muscle glycogen phosphorylase enzyme deficiency interferes with ATP generation by glycogenolysis in the muscles. This causes muscle glycogen accumulation.

Symptoms are exercise intolerance associated with muscle cramps. Due to high-intensity exercise, sudden persistent muscle contraction occurs. This leads to severe muscle damage resulting in a massive release of muscle proteins and myoglobin in the blood. Myoglobinuria secondary to rhabdomyolysis leads to the passage of burgundy-colored urine in some patients. 

A unique feature associated with McArdle is the improvement in symptoms after rest for a few minutes. This is termed as the second wind phenomenon. This occurs due to the increased blood flow to the muscles and increased utilization of free fatty acids (FFAs) for energy production after resting for a few minutes. This compensates for the impaired ATP generation from glycogenolysis. Patients with McArdle disease can benefit from engaging in regular aerobic exercises, such as walking or cycling, which can help increase their exercise tolerance and cardiovascular fitness. However, they should avoid high-intensity exercises or activities that can trigger muscle cramps and rhabdomyolysis. Glucose administration before exercise can improve tolerance. Vitamin B6 is also recommended.

Standard diagnosis includes muscle biopsy, which shows periodic acid Schiff (PAS)-positive vacuoles (Shown in the image below) of high glycogen content due to lack of myophosphorylase and genetic testing (PYGM gene sequencing).

 

Other options:

Option B: Hers disease (type VI glycogen storage disorder) - It is caused by the deficiency of liver glycogen phosphorylase. Patients with Hers disease exhibit growth retardation, hepatomegaly, and mild hypoglycemia. They do not typically present with muscle cramps and myoglobinuria.

Option C: Cori's disease (type III glycogen storage disorder) - It is caused by a deficiency of glycogen debranching enzyme. Patients with Cori's disease present with hepatomegaly, growth retardation, and hypoglycemia. Muscle weakness may be present but not muscle cramps or myoglobinuria.

Option D: Andersen disease (type IV glycogen storage disorder) - It is caused by the deficiency of glycogen branching enzyme. This disease presents with hepatomegaly, cirrhosis, and liver failure. It does not cause muscle cramps or myoglobinuria.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: A family consumes only polished rice. Which of the following combination of vitamin deficiency and enzymatic defect will be present in this family?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Thiamine-transketolase

The consumption of polished rice leads to thiamine deficiency which leads to defective transketolase activity.

Polished rice is rice that has had its husk, bran, and germ removed, leaving only the endosperm. This processing method results in a loss of nutrients, including thiamine. 

Thiamine pyrophosphate (Vit B1) is the cofactor of transketolase. This reaction requires two cofactors:

  • Mg2+
  • Thiamine diphosphate (vitamin B1)

Transketolase and transaldolase are involved in the non-oxidative phase of the HMP pathway.

Thiamine deficiency can lead to beriberi, a condition characterized by peripheral neuropathy, weakness, and cardiovascular symptoms. In severe cases, it can also lead to Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, which is characterized by confusion, ataxia, and vision disturbances. Thiamine deficiency can be prevented by consuming a balanced diet that includes unprocessed grains, legumes, and other sources of thiamine. Diagnosis of thiamine deficiency can be established by erythrocyte transketolase activity assessment.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: A chronic alcoholic patient presented to the casualty with confusion, ataxia, and painful eye movements. What could be the vitamin deficiency seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vitamin B deficiency

The above clinical history is suggestive of Wernicke encephalopathy, which is caused by vitamin B1 (Thiamine) deficiency.

Vitamin B1/thiamine deficiency leads to following conditions:

  1. Wernicke encephalopathy:
    • An acute, neuropsychiatric syndrome characterized by nystagmus and ophthalmoplegia, mental status changes (confusion), and unsteadiness of stance and gait.
    • Wernicke’s encephalopathy is a medical emergency, and thiamine should be initiated immediately, either intravenously or intramuscularly.  
    • The current standard of treatment for patients with symptoms of Wernicke's encephalopathy is to give thiamine 100 mg intravenously before administering glucose-containing IV fluids.
       
  2. Korsakoff psychosis: 
    • Korsakoff syndrome is characterized by a pronounced anterograde and retrograde amnesia along with potential impairment in visuospatial, abstract, and other types of learning.
    • Symptoms are similar to that of Wernicke encephalopathy, but also include memory loss and confabulation.
    • Permanent in at least a partial form in about 50% of the people affected.
         
  3. Beriberi: It can present with:
    • Dry beriberi: sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy, muscle weakness
    • Wet beriberi: tachycardia, cardiomegaly, high-output cardiac failure

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: A 4-year-old child presents with easy fatiguability. The mother also complains that the child has increased hunger between meals, which is relieved after food. Liver examination revealed no glycogen. The enzyme most likely deficient is _________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glycogen synthase

The most likely enzyme deficiency in a child with fatigue, excessive hunger between meals, and absent liver glycogen is glycogen synthase deficiency.

Glycogen is a storage carbohydrate synthesized from glucose (glycogenesis) and is stored in the liver, muscles, and brain. Glycogen synthase is a regulating enzyme for glycogenesis.

Glycogen synthase exists in both phosphorylated (inactive) and dephosphorylated (active) forms. Phosphorylation is stimulated by epinephrine, norepinephrine, and glucagon via cAMP. Dephosphorylation is stimulated by insulin via phosphodiesterase.

A deficiency of glycogen synthase leads to glycogen storage disorder and presents in infancy with early morning drowsiness and fatigue, fasting hypoglycemia, pallor, emesis, and hypoglycemic convulsions. It leads to a marked decrease in liver glycogen stores. Hepatomegaly is absent.

Laboratory investigations reveal prolonged hyperglycemia, glycosuria, ketosis, lactic acidosis, low alanine levels, and normal insulin levels after glucose administration. A liver biopsy is diagnostic.

Treatment involves protein-rich frequent meals, and nighttime supplementation with cornstarch to prevent hypoglycemia and hyperketonemia.

 Other options:

Option A: Glycogen phosphorylase deficiency, also known as McArdle's disease or glycogen storage disease type V, primarily affects skeletal muscle glycogen metabolism. Affected individuals experience muscle weakness, cramps, and exercise intolerance, but it doesn't typically cause the symptoms mentioned in the question.

Option C: Debranching enzyme deficiency, also known as Cori's disease or glycogen storage disease type III, presents with hepatomegaly, hypoglycemia, and growth retardation. The liver would still contain glycogen, albeit with an abnormal structure.

Option D: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency, known as von Gierke's disease or glycogen storage disease type I, is characterized by severe fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, and hepatomegaly. In this case, glycogen is present in the liver but cannot be broken down efficiently into glucose.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: A child was brought with pedal edema and cheilosis. Cardiomegaly was present. What is the vitamin deficiency associated with this clinical presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Thiamine

The given clinical presentation with pedal edema and cardiomegaly is suggestive of wet beriberi due to thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency.

Early symptoms of thiamine deficiency include peripheral neuropathy, irritability, loss of deep tendon reflexes and proprioception. As the disease progresses, increased intracranial pressure, meningismus and coma develop.

Wet beriberi results due to cardiac and renal dysfunction which leads to fluid accumulation. It is associated with tachycardia, cardiomegaly, cardiac failure, and edema. It is commonly seen in the refugee camps where people consume polished rice-based monotonous diets.

Dry beriberi is associated with neurological deficits such as peripheral neuropathy, optic atrophy, ataxia, and irritability. Complications include lactic acidosis and Wernicke encephalopathy in adults.

Diagnosis of thiamine deficiency can be established by erythrocyte transketolase activity assessment.

Other options:

Option A: Riboflavin deficiency can present with cheilosis, but it does not typically cause pedal edema and cardiomegaly.

Option C: Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) deficiency can cause neurological symptoms, anemia, and dermatitis but is not associated with pedal edema, cardiomegaly, and cheilosis.

Option D: Niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency leads to pellagra, characterized by the triad of dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia. It is not associated with pedal edema, cardiomegaly, and cheilosis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: A chronic alcoholic patient is diagnosed with gouty arthritis. What biochemical changes will be seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Increased urate and lactate levels

This patient with chronic alcoholism and gouty arthritis will most likely have elevated levels of lactate and urate.

The oxidation of ethanol to acetate by alcohol dehydrogenase is accompanied by the reduction of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) to NADH. This results in a high concentration of NADH, leading to an increased NADH/NAD+ ratio (Option A). 

Due to this, the following metabolic reactions that require NAD+ are inhibited:

  1. Glycolysis
  2. Citric acid cycle (ketogenesis favored)
  3. Pyruvate dehydrogenase
  4. Fatty acid oxidation

Decreased fatty acid oxidation leads to increased esterification and production of triacylglycerol, which causes fatty liver.

Also, there is an increase in two reactions:

  • Pyruvate to lactate 
  • Oxaloacetate to malate

Increased lactate leads to hyper-lactic-acidemia, which leads to increased renal reabsorption of urate and decreased excretion of uric acid. This results in aggravation of gout. Alcoholics are deficient in thiamine which inhibits pyruvate dehydrogenase and leads to lactic acidosis.

A decrease in pyruvate and oxaloacetate levels, which are substrates for gluconeogenesis, leads to a decrease in blood glucose levels, causing symptoms of agitation, impaired judgment, and combativeness.

Other options:

Increased urea and urate levels are not specifically associated with alcoholism and gouty arthritis. While urate levels may be increased due to gout, urea levels are not directly related to the condition (Option B).

Increased levels of alkaline phosphatase can be seen in alcohol-induced hepatitis due to intrahepatic cholestasis but is not directly related to gouty arthritis in a chronic alcoholic patient. Therefore, this option is less relevant compared to increased urate and lactate levels (Option D).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: A child presents with erythematous scaly patches in the perioral region, mucosal ulcers, and impaired epithelial wound healing. The most likely mineral deficiency associated with this condition is ________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Zinc deficiency

The clinical features of periorificial dermatitis and stomatitis in a young child are suggestive of acrodermatitis enteropathica, seen in zinc deficiency. 

Acrodermatitis enteropathica is a genetic disorder that results in the inability to absorb dietary zinc.

The clinical features develop after weaning and the infant presents with:

  • Failure to thrive
  • Skin manifestations such as symmetrical vesiculobullous dermatitis in the perioral, perianal, and acral regions
  • Anorexia, diarrhea
  • Recurrent infections due to T-cell immunodeficiency
  • Alopecia with a reddish tint
  • Impaired wound healing
  • Male hypogonadism, growth retardation
  • Neurological manifestations like tremors, nystagmus, photophobia, hypogeusia, irritability, and night blindness

Oral zinc supplementation is the treatment of choice.

Other options:

Option A- Iron deficiency is the most common micronutrient deficiency globally. It presents with iron-deficiency anemia and neurocognitive impairment. It presents clinically with pallor, fatigue, atrophic glossitis, and pica.

Option C- Calcium deficiency leads to rickets as a result of early weaning. It presents with typical symptoms of rickets, including failure to thrive; protruding abdomen; muscle weakness; fractures; craniotabes; delayed dentition; caries; enlargement of wrists and ankles; and hypocalcemic symptoms of tetany, stridor, and seizures.

Option D- Copper deficiency leads to anemia, growth retardation, defective keratinization and pigmentation of hair, hypothermia, degenerative changes in aortic elastin, osteopenia, and mental retardation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: A patient presenting with bleeding gums and easy bruisability was diagnosed with scurvy. This is due to ______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Defective collagen formation

Bleeding gums and easy bruisability seen in scurvy are due to defective collagen formation.

Scurvy results from the deficiency of vitamin C, which is required for the hydroxylation of prolyl and lysyl residues of collagen reactions. Hence, deficiency of vitamin C results in a defective prolyl hydroxylase activity, leading to defective collagen formation and resulting in generalized bleeding tendencies.

Hemorrhagic manifestations of scurvy include petechiae, purpura, ecchymoses at pressure points, epistaxis, gum bleeding, and characteristic perifollicular hemorrhages. Other manifestations are poor wound and fracture healing, hyperkeratosis of hair follicles, arthralgia, and muscle weakness. It also results in defective osteoid formation. Costo-chondral separation leads to the formation of tender nodules that are sharply angulated and are also known as the scorbutic rosary. 

The cutaneous manifestations of scurvy include 

  • Phrynoderma over posterolateral arms which can then generalize over the back and thighs and legs.
  • Corkscrew hairs -  fractured and coiled hairs due to impaired keratin cross‐links by disulfide bonds
  • Perifollicular hemorrhage and purpura
  • Lower limb edema 
  • Splinter hemorrhages

It is treated with vitamin C supplementation. 

Other options:

Option A: Low calcium levels do not cause scurvy; they may contribute to other clinical conditions like osteoporosis or muscle cramps.

Option C: Inhibition of clotting factors is not responsible for scurvy. Vitamin K deficiency, however, can lead to the inhibition of clotting factors and cause bleeding tendencies.

Option D: Increased keratinization of epithelium is not the cause of scurvy. Vitamin A deficiency, on the other hand, can result in hyperkeratoses and epithelial changes, such as xerosis and Bitot's spots.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which of the following is seen in low insulin:glucagon ratio?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Activation of hormone-sensitive lipase

Low insulin:glucagon ratio occurs in the fasting state. Since insulin has an inhibitory effect on hormone-sensitive lipase (lipolytic hormone), low insulin:glucagon ratio results in the activation of hormone-sensitive lipase.

In adipose tissues, decreased insulin results in the inhibition of lipogenesis and activation of intracellular hormone-sensitive lipase. The stored triglycerides are broken down (lipolysis) by hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) into free fatty acids (FFAs) and glycerol. In the fasting state, glucose is spared for the brain and glycerol is used as a substrate for gluconeogenesis.

In diabetic patients, low insulin level corresponds to an increase in HSL activity, promoting the breakdown of lipids and the release of FFAs from adipose tissue. HSL activity is accelerated by hormones like epinephrine, norepinephrine, glucagon, ACTH, TSH, GH, ADH, and melanocyte-stimulating hormones (MSH).

 

Well-fed state (Insulin) During fasting (Glucagon)
Lipogenesis increased Lipogenesis inhibited
Lipolysis inhibited Lipolysis increased
Insulin inhibits HS-lipase Glucagon activates HS-lipase
Lipoprotein lipase active Lipoprotein lipase inactive

Other options:

Option A: Activation of lipoprotein lipase (LPL) is promoted by insulin, not low insulin: glucagon ratio. LPL is involved in the breakdown of triglycerides and is active in the well-fed state. In low insulin: glucagon ratio, lipoprotein lipase activity is reduced, leading to decreased hydrolysis of triglycerides.

Option B: Activation of glycogen synthase is promoted by insulin. In low insulin: glucagon ratio, glycogen synthase activity is reduced, leading to decreased glycogenesis. Instead, glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis are promoted to maintain blood glucose levels.

Option C: Activation of phosphofructokinase 1 (PFK1) is promoted by insulin. PFK1 is a rate-regulating enzyme in glycolysis. In low insulin: glucagon ratio, glycolysis is downregulated, and gluconeogenesis is upregulated to maintain blood glucose levels.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: An infant is brought by his parents with complaints that his urine turns black on standing. Which of the following metabolic disorders is likely?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Alkaptonuria

Blackening of urine on standing is characteristic of alkaptonuria.

Alkaptonuria is an autosomal recessive disorder of tyrosine metabolism, that develops due to the defect in homogentisate oxidase/homogentisic acid 1, 2 - dioxygenase, which oxidizes homogentisate to maleylacetoacetate. The defect in this enzyme leads to the accumulation of homogentisate, which is then excreted in the urine. 

Alkaptonuria is characterized by homogentisic aciduria, ochronosis, and arthropathy (joint pain).

Homogentisic aciduria is the black discoloration of urine on prolonged exposure to air caused due to oxidation of the excreted homogentisate. 

Ochronosis, which is bluish-black pigmentation in connective tissue, generally occurs after the third decade of life, and it occurs due to the accumulation of homogentisic acid and its oxidation products like benzoquinone acetic acid in connective tissue.

Arthritis generally begins in the third decade. Arthritis often begins in the spine and resembles ankylosing spondylitis in its large-joint distribution. Radiographs of the spine showing flattened and calcified intervertebral discs are pathognomonic. Other findings include degeneration of the intervertebral discs, followed by disc calcification and eventually fusion of the vertebral bodies. Osteophyte formation and calcification of the intervertebral ligaments also occur.

Diagnosis: Blackish discoloration of urine on standing is diagnostic of alkaptonuria (shown below). The ferric chloride test will be positive. The blackening of urine occurs due to the excretion of homogentisic acid in the urine.

Image A - Normal urine
Image B - Alkaptonuria

Other options:

Option A: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is a metabolic disorder resulting from a deficiency of the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase. It does not lead to black urine. Patients with PKU have a musty or mousy odor due to phenylacetic acid accumulation.

Option C: Homocystinuria is an inborn error of methionine metabolism caused by a deficiency of the enzyme cystathionine β-synthase. It is characterized by tall stature, long limbs, dislocation of the lens of the eye, and predisposition to thromboembolism, but it does not lead to black urine.

Option D: Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD) is an inherited metabolic disorder caused by a deficiency of branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase. It does not cause black urine. Patients with MSUD have urine with a characteristic sweet odor, resembling maple syrup.
