questions.question: A child presents with bone pain and hepatosplenomegaly. A trephine biopsy and aspirate show the following finding. Which of the following is the most likely enzyme deficient in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glucocerebrosidase

The given clinical scenario of a child with bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly, and biopsy showing Gaucher's cell with a characteristic crumpled tissue paper appearance is suggestive of Gaucher's disease. The deficient enzyme is glucocerebrosidase (also known as beta-glucosidase).

Gaucher's disease is an inborn error of metabolism caused due to a deficiency of beta-glucocerebrosidase. It is the most common lysosomal storage disorder and the mode of inheritance is autosomal recessive. There is an accumulation of lipid-laden macrophages in the spleen, liver, and other tissues.

There are three clinical subtypes - type I (chronic non-neuronopathic), type II (acute neuronopathic), and type III (intermediate). Clinical features include anemia, thrombocytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, and neurological features depending on the subtype. 

Gaucher's cells - These are formed as a result of the accumulation of massive amounts of glucocerebrosides within the phagocytes. The cells have a fibrillary cytoplasm and give a crumpled tissue paper appearance.

Option A: Deficiency of hexosaminidase A is seen in Tay-Sachs disease. The deficiency of beta-hexosaminidase A and B causes Sandhoff's disease. Clinical features are seizures, macrocephaly, and hyperacusis. 

Option C: Deficiency of sphingomyelinase leads to Niemann-Pick disease. It is characterized by the presence of foam cells in the bone marrow. There may be pulmonary infiltrates leading to lung failure. 

Option D: Pompe's disease (type 2 glycogen storage disease) occurs due to alpha 1,4-glucosidase (acid maltase) deficiency. It is the only glycogen storage disease that is a lysosomal storage disease and causes lysosomal glycogen accumulation in cardiac, skeletal, and smooth muscle cells. The clinical symptoms of Pompe disease are hypotonia (floppy infant), skeletal muscle weakness, hepatomegaly, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and macroglossia.

questions.question: A child presents with mental retardation, bone pain, and inability to walk. On funduscopy examination, a cherry red spot is seen. There is no organomegaly. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Correct answer: A. Tay-Sachs disease

The given clinical scenario, along with the fundoscopy image showing a macular cherry-red spot, indicates that the most likely diagnosis is Tay-Sachs disease. 

Tay-Sachs disease is a lysosomal storage disease caused by the deficiency of β-hexosaminidase. It can present during infancy with macrocephaly, increased startle reaction, gradual loss of motor skills, and a macular cherry-red spot. Affected children usually die by the age of 10–15 years. 

It is of two types—juvenile-onset and adult-onset. The symptoms of the juvenile-onset form include ataxia and dementia. Dysarthria, lower motor neuron signs, and psychiatric disorders are common in the adult-onset type.

Options B - Niemann-Pick disease is an autosomal recessive inborn error of lipid metabolism. It results due to the deficiency of the sphingomyelinase enzyme. The clinical features include a combination of hepatosplenomegaly, developmental delay, failure to thrive, severe psychomotor regression, interstitial lung disease, and a cherry-red spot in the macula.

Presentation is usually at 6–24 months with corneal clouding, coarse facial features, joint stiffness, and skeletal dysplasia. Glaucoma, retinal degeneration, and nasal discharge are the other features. The condition is generally fatal.

Option D - Gaucher disease is a glycolipid storage disorder that can present with hepatosplenomegaly, mental retardation, and erosion of long bones. It is caused by the deficiency of β-glucosidase. The Gaucher cell has a wrinkled-paper appearance due to intracytoplasmic inclusions, which is a characteristic feature.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: A 12-year-old boy with type 1 diabetes mellitus presents with unconsciousness. His urine is subjected to a test and the results are shown below. What is the test done?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Rothera's test- Ketone bodies

The given clinical scenario points towards a diagnosis of diabetic ketoacidosis. Rothera’s test as shown in the image is a specific test used for the determination of ketone bodies in the urine.

Type I diabetes mellitus is a low insulin state. There is an increased conversion of fatty acids to acetyl-CoA which in turn leads to increased ketone body production. The presence of ketosis can be established by the detection of ketone bodies in urine by Rothera's test.

The test involves the saturation of 5 mL of urine with solid ammonium sulfate. This is followed by the addition of a few drops of freshly prepared sodium nitroprusside followed by 2 mL of liquor ammonia along the sides of the test tube. The development of a purple ring indicates the presence of ketone bodies in urine. Strip tests based on the same principle are also available.

Other options-

Option A: Seliwanoff's test will distinguish glucose and fructose. The reagent is resorcinol in HCl. 3 ml of the reagent and 0.5 ml of urine are heated for 30 seconds up to a boiling point. A red color indicates the presence of fructose.

Option B: Benedict's test is a test commonly used in the follow-up of diabetics for the detection of glucose in urine (glucosuria). It uses Benedict's reagent containing sodium carbonate, copper sulfate, and sodium citrate. Reducing sugars (containing a free aldehyde/ keto group) will reduce Benedict's reagent. Examples include glucose, fructose, and lactose. The test is a semi-quantitative test. The blue color indicates no reducing sugar. 

Option C: Fouchet's test is used for detecting the presence of bile pigments in urine. Here, urine is heated with barium sulfate, which adsorbs bilirubin. Ferric chloride is added, which oxidizes the adsorbed bilirubin to biliverdin which produces a green color. Principle for all tests to detect bile pigments: Oxidizing agents readily oxidize bilirubin to biliverdin to form a green color.

questions.question: The template DNA strand is 5'CATTCAATATCGATC3'. The resulting mRNA sequence after transcription is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 5'GAUCGAUAUUGAAUG3'

5'GAUCGAUAUUGAAUG3' will be the sequence of mRNA produced from this fragment of template DNA.

The non-template strand or coding strand or sense/plus strand in the DNA will have the same sequence of the RNA that is produced, except that the non-template or coding strand has T is in place of U. 

As all sequences are written in the 5′ to 3′ direction, unless otherwise specified, an RNA sequence of GAUCGAUAUUGAAUG would correspond to a DNA sequence, on the non-template strand, of CATTCAATATCGATC. Both the non-template strand and RNA produced will be a complementary sequence to the template strand.

Note:

Template strand - known as minus or antisense or non-coding strand.

Coding strand- known as plus or sense or non-template strand.

The thermic effect is highest in proteins.

Specific dynamic allowance (previously called the thermic effect of food): This refers to the increased heat production or increased metabolic rate following the intake of food (diet-induced thermogenesis).

The values of SDA are

  • 30% for proteins: This means that out of every 100 grams of proteins consumed, the energy available for doing useful work is 30% less than the calculated value - i.e 30% of the energy content in protein is used in its own metabolism.

  • 5% for carbohydrates.

  • Resting metabolic rate
  • Thermic effect of food (formerly termed specific dynamic action)
  • Physical activity

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Ketone bodies are not utilized by the liver because it lacks:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Thiophorase

Ketone bodies are not utilized in the liver because it lacks the enzyme thiophorase.

Ketone bodies are synthesized in the liver mitochondria (by ketogenesis) and transported in the blood to the peripheral tissues. Here they are utilized by the following steps:

  1. β-hydroxybutyrate (the most predominant ketone body) is oxidized to acetoacetate by β-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase producing NADH.
  2. Acetoacetate is then activated to acetoacetyl CoA by transferring a CoA molecule from succinyl CoA by succinyl CoA-acetoacetyl CoA transferase (thiophorase).
  3. Acetoacetyl CoA is cleaved into two acetyl CoA molecules by thiolase and oxidized into CO2 by the TCA cycle.

Thiokinase or Acyl CoA synthetase catalyzes the only energy-requiring step in fatty acid oxidation. In the presence of ATP and coenzyme A, thiokinase catalyzes the conversion of a fatty acid to acyl-CoA. Acyl-CoA is the active form of fatty acid. This step uses one high-energy phosphate and forms AMP and PPi.

When higher than normal ketone bodies are present in the blood or urine, it is called ketonemia or ketonuria, respectively. The overall condition is called ketosis. The metabolism of free fatty acids to produce ketone bodies is exaggerated in pathologic states such as starvation and diabetes mellitus, thus causing ketosis. The continued buffering and excretion of ketone bodies deplete the alkali reserve, causing ketoacidosis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question:
Which of the following methods can detect the alterations in DNA sequence?

  1. Restriction fragment length analysis
  2. Flow cytometry
  3. Pyrosequencing
  4. FISH
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1 and 3

The alterations in DNA sequence can be detected by restriction fragment length analysis and pyrosequencing.

Restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP) is also called cleaved amplified polymorphic sequence (CAPS) assay. RFLP is a technique in which organisms may be differentiated by variations in their DNA sequence by restriction endonucleases. This technique involves cutting a particular region of DNA with known variability, with restriction enzymes, then separating the DNA fragments by agarose gel electrophoresis and determining the number of fragments and relative sizes. 

Pyrosequencing is a synthesis type of approach of DNA sequencing. This technique employs four enzymatic reactions in a single tube to monitor DNA synthesis. Nucleotides are incorporated into the reaction and pyrophosphate (PPi) is released. PPi triggers a series of reactions resulting in the production of light, which is proportional to the amount of DNA and number of incorporated nucleotides. The generated light is detected and recorded by a detector system in the form of a peak signal, which reflects the activity of all four enzymes in the reaction. 

The practical applications of recombinant DNA technology include:

  • Gene mapping using techniques such as fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH).
  • Producing proteins such as:
    • Interferons, tPA (tissue plasminogen activator)
    • Insulin, growth hormone
    • Hepatitis B vaccine
  • Molecular analysis of disease, to detect gene variations and mutations.
  • Restriction Fragment Length polymorphism (RFLP) and single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)
  • Microsatellite DNA polymorphisms
  • Gene therapy and bone marrow transplantation

Flow cytometry is a laser-based method that analyzes the cells and cell components based on the presence of certain cell surface molecules which are named as per cluster of differentiation (CD) nomenclature. It is very effective for the study of the immune system and its response to infectious diseases and cancer. It cannot detect the alterations in DNA sequence.

Fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) is a technique where cells are stained with fluorescent stains. It uses DNA probes that recognize sequences specific to particular chromosomal regions. It cannot detect the alterations in DNA sequence. FISH can be performed on prenatal samples, peripheral blood cells, touch preparations from cancer biopsies, and even fixed archival tissue sections. Uses include :

  • Numerical abnormalities of chromosomes e.g., aneuploidy.
  • Subtle microdeletions and rearrangements.
  • Complex translocations that are not demonstrable by routine karyotyping.
  • Gene amplification of HER2 in breast cancer or NMYC amplification in neuroblastomas.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which of the following is not involved in the repair of DNA following double-stranded breaks?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. MSH2

MSH2 is involved in mismatch repair and is not involved in the repair of double-stranded DNA breaks as the repair involves the correction of a single mismatch base pair e.g. C to A, instead of T to A. 

DNA mismatch repair proteins function as spell checkers during DNA replication by correcting the incorrect pairing. In HNPCC, the proofreading function of the mismatch repair systems (majorly MLH1 and MSH2) is lost, leading to the accumulation of errors throughout the genome. The genomes of these patients show microsatellite instability, which is characterized by changes in the length of short repeats.

Double-strand breaks (DSBs) in DNA pose a significant concern.  Genetic recombination events can give rise to chromosomal translocation, chromosomal breakage, and ultimately cellular demise. Double-strand breaks (DSBs) have the potential to undergo repair through two distinct mechanisms: homologous recombination and non-homologous end joining. Homologous recombination is observed in yeasts, whereas in mammals, non-homologous end joining predominates.

Non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) is a mechanism by which a group of proteins mediates the recognition, processing, and direct ligation of the ends of two DNA fragments where a double-strand break in DNA has occurred. This is in contrast to homologous repair (HR), another mechanism, where an undamaged homologous DNA template is required to replace an adjacent damaged one.

The type of repair depends on the phase of cell cycles:

Phase of the cell cycle  Repair mechanism
G0 /G1 Phase Nonhomologous End Joining Repair
S, G2, M Phase Homologous Repair

Other options:

Option A: The protein known as ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM) serves as a crucial kinase that triggers a wide range of cellular stress responses through its signalling activity. The activation of ATM is induced by DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) and oxidative stress, resulting in the phosphorylation of a wide range of target proteins. Recent advancements in molecular biology have brought to light the participation of the ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM) protein in a range of cellular mechanisms triggered by DNA damage. These mechanisms encompass the repair of double-strand breaks (DSBs), the halting of cell cycle progression through checkpoint activation, the initiation of programmed cell death (apoptosis), and the cessation of transcriptional activity. The compromised precision of repair resulting from the combinational failure of stress responses leads to heightened sensitivity to ionizing radiation (IR) in ataxia-telangiectasia (A-T) cells.

Option B: CtIP which is a DNA repair protein involved in Homologous Repair whose function is dependent on phosphorylation at serine 327 as well as the recruitment of BRCA 1.

Option D: The Ku heterodimer, consisting of Ku70 and Ku80 subunits, plays a pivotal role in the nonhomologous end-joining (NHEJ) pathway, which is responsible for the repair of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs). Ku protein mediates the binding of the damaged DNA fragment and orchestrates the recruitment of additional proteins to enable the subsequent processing and ligation of the broken DNA end.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: 2-3 BPG binds to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Globin part of Hemoglobin

2,3 bisphosphoglycerate binds to the globin chains of the hemoglobin while oxygen binds to the heme part of the hemoglobin.

A single unit of 2,3-BPG forms a complex with one tetrameric unit of deoxyhemoglobin within the central cavity of its four subunits. The centre pocket of this structure contains two -globin chains that are positively charged, such as histidine and lysine. Ionic bonds, also known as salt bridges, are established through the interaction between amino acids that carry a positive charge, specifically those found in globins, and phosphate groups that possess a negative charge, specifically those present in 2,3-BPG.  The stabilization of deoxygenated haemoglobin (in its T-form) is achieved through the cross-linking of the α-chains by the binding of 2,3-BPG. Upon oxygenation of haemoglobin, the molecule 2,3-BPG is released from its binding site, resulting in the transformation of oxyhemoglobin into the R-form conformation.

A relaxed (R) configuration, exposes more O2 binding sites. The quaternary structure of haemoglobin determines its affinity for O2. In deoxyhemoglobin, the globin units are tightly bound in a tense (T) configuration, which reduces the affinity of the molecule for O2. When O2 is first bound, the bonds holding the globin units are released, producing a relaxed (R) configuration, which exposes more O2 binding sites. The net result is a 500-fold increase in O2. In tissues, these reactions are reversed, resulting in O2  dissociation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which of the following is complementary to the active site of the enzyme?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Substrate

The substrate is complementary to the active site of the enzyme.

The Lock and Key concept was put forth by Emil Fischer. This model is the initial proposition aimed at elucidating the mechanism of an enzymatic catalytic process. Based on this concept, it can be inferred that the enzyme's structure or conformation exhibits a state of rigidity. The substrate effectively conforms to the binding site, which is now referred to as the active site, in a manner analogous to a key fitting precisely into its corresponding lock or a hand fitting snugly into a well-fitting glove. The active site of an enzyme can be described as a stiff and pre-configured template that selectively accommodates a certain substrate for binding. 

The induced fit or Koshland theory states that the active site does not possess a firm and pre-determined conformation. The emerging active site exhibits the fundamental characteristics of the substrate binding site. The substrate's contact with the enzyme elicits a conformational change in the enzyme, leading to the establishment of a robust binding site for the substrate. Moreover, as a result of induced fit, the enzyme undergoes conformational changes that lead to the repositioning of the specific amino acids involved in the formation of the active site, hence facilitating the catalytic process. The induced fit model has garnered substantial empirical support through X-ray diffraction studies. Koshland's model additionally elucidates the mechanisms by which allosteric modulators and competitive inhibition exert their effects on enzymes.

The substrate strain theory states that the substrate experiences strain as a result of the conformational alteration generated by the enzyme. It is plausible that upon the binding of a substrate to the preexisting active site, the enzyme elicits a strain on the substrate. The presence of a stressed or strained substrate facilitates the generation of the desired product. The enzymatic action is believed to involve a combination of the induced fit model and substrate strain.

Other options:

Option A: The complementary active site of the enzyme binds to the substrate to form the product.

Option C: The active site of the enzyme is not complementary to the allosteric activator. Allosteric sites are separate and specific sites on the enzyme that are modulated with allosteric effect modifiers and hence are complementary to them.

Option D: The active site of the enzyme binds to the substrate which form a transitional state which is unstable and later dissociates to form a product.

questions.question: Cytochrome P450 monooxygenase utilises which of the following cofactors during the phase 1 reaction of detoxification of xenobiotics?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. NADPH

The microsomal cytochrome P450 system, located in the liver, facilitates the process of drug and foreign substance detoxification through hydroxylation processes that rely on the availability of NADPH.

Phase 1 reactions include oxidation, reduction, or hydrolytic reaction. CYPs- Cytochrome P family of enzymes play a major role in phase 1 reactions. Reactions carried out by phase 1 enzymes usually lead to the inactivation of a drug. The addition of functional groups does little to increase the water solubility of the drug but alters its biological properties. 

The importance of NADPH is enumerated as follows:

  • NADPH is needed for the reductive biosynthesis of fatty acids and steroids, hence HMP shunt is more active in lipogenesis tissues like adipose tissue and the liver.
  • Along with Glutamate dehydrogenase helps in the synthesis of various amino acids.
  • Maintaining reduced glutathione is critical for RBC membrane integrity. NADPH keeps haemoglobin's ferrous iron (Fe2+) lowered to prevent methemoglobin (Fe3+) buildup.
  • High concentrations of NADPH are also required to maintain the transparency of the lens.

The cytochromes are a class of proteins that possess a conjugated heme group. The latter is comprised of a porphyrin ring containing an iron atom. The heme group present in cytochromes exhibits distinct characteristics when compared to the heme group observed in the structures of haemoglobin and myoglobin. The heme iron within cytochromes undergoes a cyclic process of oxidation (Fe3+) and reduction (Fe2+), playing a crucial role in facilitating electron movement throughout the electron transport chain (ETC). This stands in opposition to the heme iron found in haemoglobin and myoglobin, which remains in the ferrous (Fe2+) form. The cytochromes were initially assigned the designations of a, b, and c based on the specific heme type they contained and their corresponding absorption spectra. Subsequent discoveries led to the identification of additional cytochromes, including c1, b1, b2, a3, among others.

Other options

Option A: Flavin adenine mononucleotide (FMN) is a phosphorylated form of riboflavin which functions as a cofactor for various enzymes. Some of these include as a cofactor for blue-light photoreceptors and oxidoreductases.

Option C:  Flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) is nothing but phosphorylated riboflavin and is used in the electron transport chain and also is a cofactor for various enzymes. Some of these include oxidative phosphorylation, DNA repair, beta-oxidation of fatty acids as well as amino acid catabolism.

Option D: Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) consists of the vitamin B3 (niacin) and also serves as a coenzyme for various enzymatic reactions in the body. Some of these include oxidative phosphorylation (ATP production), DNA repair and intracellular calcium signalling.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which biochemical cycle/process is used by monoclonal antibodies in hybridoma technology?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Purine salvage pathway

It is the purine salvage pathway that is utilized by monoclonal antibodies in hybridoma technology.

Monoclonal antibodies refer to the antibodies produced by a group of lymphocytes that produce antibodies against a single antigen. These antibodies are produced by hybridoma technology. 

In this technology, the B-lymphocytes of mice spleen are immunized with an antigen to produce a specific antibody. These specific antibody-producing B lymphocytes are then fused with myeloma cells that can multiply indefinitely.

The myeloma cells are deficient in the hypoxanthine-guanine-phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT) gene and do not produce immunoglobulins. Therefore, the resulting hybrid cell is producing antibodies against a single antigen indefinitely. These hybrid cells are cultured in a HAT medium (containing hypoxanthine, aminopterin, and thymidine) and the monoclonal antibodies are obtained. It is well-established that nucleotides present in DNA and RNA consist of purine and pyrimidine bases. The synthesis of these nucleotides can occur through either the De novo pathway or the salvage pathway. Consequently, the inclusion of aminopterin in the HAT medium effectively inhibits the De novo pathway, thereby rendering the synthesis of purine dependent on the salvage pathway. However, it should be noted that the salvage pathway exclusively takes place in the presence of the enzymes HGPRT and thymidine kinase. The hybridoma cell is uniquely capable of proliferating on the HAT medium due to its distinct composition. Specifically, the myeloma component of the hybridoma possesses the capacity for repetitive cellular division, while the plasma cell component contains the enzyme HGPRT. Consequently, the hybridoma cells can sustain growth and viability over an extended period when cultivated on the HAT medium.

Hybridoma technology is a method for producing large numbers of identical antibodies (monoclonal antibodies).

Hybridomas are somatic cell hybrids produced by fusing the antibody-forming spleen cells with myeloma cells. The resultant hybrid thus has both the antibody-producing ability of the B-cell and the ability to multiply indefinitely of the myeloma. 

The following are the steps involved in hybridoma technology:

  • Mice are immunized with an antigen.
  • After several weeks of immunization, blood samples are obtained from mice for measurement of serum antibodies.
  • When the antibody titer is high enough, mice are commonly boosted by injecting antigen without adjuvant, intraperitoneally or intravenously.
  • Then the mice are euthanized and their spleens removed for in vitro hybridoma cell production.
  • Fusing antibody-producing spleen cells, which have a limited life span, with myeloma cells (derived from an immortal tumour of lymphocytes) results in a hybridoma that is capable of unlimited growth.
  • The cells are cultured in a medium containing hypoxanthine, aminopterin, and thymidine (HAT medium) which allows only the fused cells to survive in culture.
  • Monoclonal antibodies are then harvested.

Applications of hybridoma technology

  • Listing lymphocyte subpopulations
  • Specific cell quantitative preparation
  • As an immunosuppressant in therapeutic settings
  • Blood component nephelometric assays
  • ELISA testing
  • Quantitative purification of antigens.
  • Common therapeutic applications for monoclonal antibodies

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: The following Lineweaver-Burk plots depict enzymatic action in the presence of enzyme inhibitors. The enzyme action without inhibitor is represented by a blue line. What type of inhibitors are depicted in images 1 and 2?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1- Noncompetitive inhibition 2- Competitive inhibition

The Lineweaver-Burk plot in image 1 depicts non-competitive inhibition, and that in image 2 depicts competitive inhibition.

Important parameters in a reaction include:

  • The affinity of the enzyme for its substrate, given by the Michaelis constant or Km. A low Km reflects a high affinity of the enzyme for substrate and vice versa. The value of Km is given by the substrate concentration at which the reaction velocity is equal to one-half Vmax. It does not change with changes in enzyme concentration.
  • Vmax is the maximum velocity of a reaction.

Competitive inhibition is when the inhibitor binds reversibly to the substrate-binding site and competes with the substrate for the active enzyme-binding site. This effect can be overcome by increasing the substrate concentration by which maximum velocity can still be achieved. Therefore, Vmax is unaltered in this type of inhibition. However, the concentration of the substrate required to achieve half of the maximum velocity is increased. Therefore, Km is increased in this condition.

In a Lineweaver-Burk plot, the addition of a competitive inhibitor causes plots with the same y-intercept (Vmax is unaffected) but different x-intercepts (due to increased Km).

Noncompetitive inhibition is by binding of inhibitors to enzymes in locations remote from the active site. Increasing the concentration of the substrate does not overcome non-competitive inhibition. Thus, noncompetitive inhibitors decrease the Vmax of the reaction. They do not interfere with the binding of the substrate to the enzyme. Thus, the enzyme shows the same Km in the presence or absence of noncompetitive inhibitors.

In a Lineweaver-Burk plot, the addition of a non-competitive inhibitor causes plots with the same x-intercept (Km is unaffected) but different slopes and y-intercepts (due to decreased Vmax).

In uncompetitive inhibition, inhibitors bind with the enzyme-substrate intermediate complex and inhibit it. This leads to a decrease in both Vmax and Km.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: FISH technique helps to identify all except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Point mutation

Fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) is not useful in identifying point mutation. Point mutations are identified by other means like sequencing studies and restriction fragment length polymorphism.

FISH is a method of molecular analysis of genetic lesions involving large deletions, duplications, or more complex rearrangements that are not readily amenable to detection using polymerase chain reaction or DNA sequencing approaches. 

FISH uses DNA probes that recognize sequences specific to particular chromosomal regions. To perform FISH, large fragments of cloned genomic DNA spanning up to 200 kb are labeled with fluorescent dyes and applied to metaphase chromosome preparations or interphase nuclei. The probe hybridizes to its homologous genomic sequence and thus labels a specific chromosomal region that can be visualized under a fluorescent microscope.

FISH can be performed on prenatal samples, peripheral blood cells, touch preparations from cancer biopsies, and even fixed archival tissue sections. It is used to detect numeric abnormalities of chromosomes (aneuploidy), subtle microdeletions and complex translocations that are not demonstrable by routine karyotyping, and gene amplification (e.g., HER2 in breast cancer or NMYC amplification in neuroblastomas).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which of the following micronutrients are associated with decreased sexual maturation and hypogonadism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Zinc

Zinc deficiency is associated with decreased sexual maturation and hypogonadism.

Zinc is the second most common trace element in the body after iron. As a component of zinc finger proteins, zinc regulates gene transcription and participates in nucleic acid metabolism, protein synthesis and thereby cell growth. Zinc is a major antioxidant being part of the enzyme superoxide dismutase. 

Zinc is derived mainly from animal protein. Diets based on cereals, plants and legumes are associated with zinc deficiency due to dietary phytic acid decreasing the bioavailability of zinc.

Zinc is absorbed throughout the small intestine by a process of facilitated diffusion. Almost 90% of the total body zinc is localized in bone and skeletal muscle.

Deficiency - 

  • Poor physical growth is an important feature of zinc depletion in preschool and school-age children. Delayed sexual maturation and hypogonadism are prominent features of zinc deficiency in adolescents. Other features include anemia, anorexia, diarrhea, alopecia, impaired immune function and poor wound healing.
  • Acrodermatitis enteropathica is an autosomal recessive disorder of severe zinc deficiency, caused by impaired intestinal absorption due to a defect in intestinal zinc transporter protein. It presents in early infancy with vesiculobullous, dry, scaly, or eczematous skin lesions chiefly in the periorificial and acral areas.

Normal requirements for children range between 3.5 and 5.0 mg/day. Acquired zinc deficiency stats can be treated with 0.5 to 1.0 mg/kg/day for several weeks. Malnourished children have much higher requirements of 2-4mg/kg/day.

Other options :

Option B - Copper deficiency results in microcytic, hypochromic anemia unresponsive to iron therapy, depigmentation of hair, neutropenia, neurological problems and osteoporosis. Disruption in copper transport is linked to Wilson's disease and Menke's disease.

Option C - Selenium deficiency is a cause of Keshan disease, a form of cardiomyopathy in young children seen in some regions of China. In combination with iodine deficiency, lack of selenium can result in myxedematous endemic cretinism.

Option D - Iron deficiency causes anemia, irritability, anorexia, pica, angular stomatitis, leg cramps and congestive heart failure.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which of the following is not a heme breakdown product?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. ALA

Aminolevulinic acid (ALA) is not a product of heme breakdown; rather it is an intermediate in the synthesis of heme molecules.

The process of heme breakdown occurs over a series of reactions. In the reticuloendothelial system of the liver, spleen and bone marrow, heme is degraded by microsomal heme oxygenase. It requires NADPH and cytochrome c. In this process, the alpha methenyl bridge of the heme molecule is liberated as carbon monoxide. The Fe+ liberated is oxidized to Fe3+++ and taken up by transferrin.

The linear tetrapyrrole formed is biliverdin (green pigment), which is further reduced to bilirubin (red-yellow pigment) by an NADPH-dependent biliverdin reductase. The bilirubin is transported in the plasma bound to albumin and is taken up by the liver, where it is conjugated with glucuronic acid to make it water-soluble, which is finally excreted in the bile.

The intestinal bacteria deconjugate the bilirubin, which is reduced to urobilinogen. It is further reduced to stercobilinogen, which is excreted through feces.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which type of mutation results in the reversal to wild type of phenotype when the mutant gene is suppressed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Mutations in tRNA

Mutations in tRNA are known to suppress the mutant gene and cause reversal to wild phenotype. Such mutations are called suppressor mutations.

Suppressor mutations are secondary mutations that alter the phenotypes caused by an existing mutation. This is not to be confused with reversion mutations in which the original mutation has been lost. Instead, suppressor mutations return the phenotype caused by the original mutation to a more wild-type phenotype despite the presence of the original mutation. The suppressor mutation’s effect on the phenotype can vary from partial restoration to full restoration of the wild-type phenotype.

In prokaryotic and lower eukaryotic organisms, abnormally functioning tRNA molecules have been discovered that are themselves the results of mutations. Some of these abnormal tRNA molecules are capable of binding to and decoding altered codons, thereby suppressing the effects of mutations in the structural genes.

These suppressor tRNA molecules, usually formed as a result of alterations in their anticodon regions, are capable of suppressing certain missense mutations, nonsense mutations, and frameshift mutations. An example of suppressor mutation is illustrated below.

A primary mutation occurs changing the original codon sequence from UGG (Trp) to UAG (Stop). A secondary mutation occurs in the gene for a glutamine tRNA leading to the anticodon switch from a GUC to AUC. This mutant tRNA can recognize the UAG stop codon and insert glutamine in place of the stop, allowing translation to continue past the stop and suppressing the original mutation. 

In the laboratory context, such suppressor tRNAs, coupled with mutated variants of aminoacyl- tRNA synthetases, can be utilized to incorporate unnatural amino acids into defined locations within altered genes that carry engineered nonsense mutations. The resulting labeled proteins can be used for in vivo and in vitro cross-linking and biophysical studies.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which of the following is not a post-transcriptional modification?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Glycosylation

Glycosylation is not a post-transcriptional modification; it is a post-translational modification.

A primary transcript is the initial, linear, RNA copy of a transcription unit. The collection of all the primary transcripts synthesized in the nucleus by RNA polymerase II is known as heterogeneous nuclear RNA (hnRNA). The pre-mRNA components of hnRNA undergo extensive co- and posttranscriptional modification in the nucleus and become mature mRNA. These modifications usually include the following :

  • Addition of a 5′ cap - This is the first of the processing reactions for pre-mRNA. The cap is a 7-methylguanosine attached to the 5′ terminal end of the mRNA and is resistant to most nucleases. Creation of the cap requires the removal of the γ-phosphoryl group from the 5′ triphosphate of the pre-mRNA, followed by the addition of guanosine monophosphate. Methylation of this terminal G occurs in the cytosol and is catalyzed by guanine- 7-methyltransferase. Additional methylation steps may occur (options A and B).
  • Addition of a 3′-poly-A tail - Most eukaryotic mRNA have a chain of 40 to 250 adenylates (adenosine monophosphates) attached to the 3′ end. This poly-A tail is added by the nuclear enzyme, polyadenylate polymerase. The poly-A tail terminates eukaryotic transcription. In addition, it helps stabilize the mRNA, facilitates its exit from the nucleus, and aids in translation. 
  • Splicing - Maturation of eukaryotic mRNA usually involves removal from the primary transcript of RNA sequences (introns) that do not code for protein (endonuclease cleavage). The remaining coding (expressed) sequences, the exons, are joined together to form the mature mRNA. The process of removing introns and joining exons is called splicing. The molecular complex that accomplishes these tasks is known as the spliceosome (option D).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question:
Match the following conditions :

1) Glycogen accumulation in liver and renal cells and lactic acidemia, associated with hypoglycemia a)Cori disease
2) Glycogen accumulation in lysosomes b)McArdle disease
3) Exercise intolerance c)Von Gierk disease
4) Accumulation of branched structures d)Pompe disease
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 -c, 2 -d, 3 -b, 4 -a

The correct answer is option B: 1 -c, 2 -d, 3 -b, 4 -a

1) Glycogen accumulation in liver and renal cells and lactic acidemia, associated with hypoglycemia c) Von Gierk disease
2) Glycogen accumulation in lysosomes d)Pompe disease
3) Exercise intolerance b)McArdle disease
4) Accumulation of branched structures a)Cori disease


Von Gierke disease (type I glycogen storage disorder) occurs due to the deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase enzyme in the liver, kidney, and intestinal mucosa. Patients present commonly by 3-4 months of age with hypoglycemia (leading to seizures), lactic acidosis, and hepatomegaly. Affected children often have a doll-like face with fat cheeks, relatively thin extremities, short stature, and a protuberant abdomen due to massive hepatomegaly. The kidneys are also enlarged, whereas spleen and heart are not involved. Laboratory findings include hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, and hyperlipidemia.

Pompe's disease (type II glycogen storage disorder) occurs due to a mutation in alpha-1,4-glucosidase (also known as acid maltase), a lysosomal enzyme. A defect in this enzyme leads to the accumulation of glycogen in the lysosomes of peripheral, voluntary muscles and progresses to involve the cardiac muscle and diaphragm. Clinical features include hypotonia (floppy baby syndrome), cardiomyopathy, hepatomegaly, and failure to thrive. Myozyme can prevent worsening or can reverse cardiac and skeletal abnormalities.

Cori disease (type III glycogen storage disorder) occurs due to a deficiency of the glycogen debranching enzyme. The features of Cori disease include hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, and hyperlipidemia but with normal blood lactate and uric acid levels. Muscle weakness and atrophy can also occur in these patients. Liver biopsy shows the accumulation of glycogen in the form of limit-dextrins (branched structures).

McArdle disease (type V glycogen storage disorder) typically presents during late childhood or in the second decade of life. The muscle glycogen phosphorylase enzyme deficiency interferes with ATP generation by glycogenolysis in the muscles. This causes muscle glycogen accumulation. Symptoms are exercise intolerance associated with muscle cramps. This leads to severe muscle damage resulting in a massive release of myoglobin in the blood.

questions.question: All are true statements regarding folate deficiency except
options: Increased levels of homocy​steine and normal methylm​alonic acid
Folate supplementation on ​diagnosis of pregnancy pr​events neural tube defect‍
It is important to treat c​o-existing vitamin B12 de​ficiency before initiatin‍g folate therapy

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Folate deficiency is commonly seen in children with hemolytic anemia

Folate deficiency is seen in children with macrocytic anemia and not with hemolytic anemia. 

Folic acid (vitamin B9) is the synthetic form of folate used in supplements and fortification of foods. Folic acid plays a key role in one-carbon metabolism, essential for the biosynthesis of several compounds. Tetrahydrofolate (THF), the reduced, coenzyme form of folate, receives one-carbon fragments from donors such as serine, glycine, and histidine and transfers them to intermediates in the synthesis of amino acids, purine nucleotides, and thymidine monophosphate (TMP), a pyrimidine nucleotide incorporated into DNA.

Leafy vegetables such as spinach, turnip, lettuce and fortified cereal products are rich sources.

Folate deficiency is caused by increased demand (e.g., pregnancy and lactation), poor absorption caused by pathology of the small intestine, alcoholism, or treatment with drugs (e.g., methotrexate) that are dihydrofolate reductase inhibitors. Children with hemolytic anemia have high folate requirements due to increased erythropoiesis predisposing them to deficiency (option B). Its manifestations are :

  • Anemia -  A primary result of folic acid deficiency is megaloblastic anemia, caused by diminished synthesis of purine nucleotides and TMP, which leads to an inability of cells to make DNA and, therefore, an inability to divide. 
  • Neural tube defects - Maternal deficiency of folate, during pregnancy, is implicated in neural tube defects. Periconceptional folate supplements, begun 1 month before conception and continued for 3 months after, are recommended to reduce the risk.
  • Hyperhomocysteinemia - Folate, along with vitamin B12, is involved in converting homocysteine to methionine, as depicted below. Hence, folate deficiency results in increased levels of homocysteine. 

However, levels of methylmalonic acid are normal. Methylmalonic acid levels are elevated in deficiency of vitamin B12, which is required as a coenzyme in the conversion of methylmalonyl CoA to succinyl CoA (option A).

Treatment: In patients with megaloblastic anemia, it is imperative to exclude and treat vitamin B12 deficiency before treating with folate. Otherwise the neurological signs of vitamin B12 deficiency may develop and progress irreversibly (option C). Deficiency is corrected using folic acid at a dose of 0.5-1mg/day orally for 3-4 weeks.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Congenital lactic acidosis is seen due to a defect in which of the following enzymes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pyruvate dehydrogenase

Congenital lactic acidosis is seen due to a defect in pyruvate dehydrogenase.

The major source of acetyl CoA for the tricarboxylic acid (TCA)cycle is the oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate by the multienzyme pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDHC). The PDHC is a protein aggregate of multiple copies of three enzymes, pyruvate decarboxylase (E1), dihydrolipoyl transacetylase (E2), and dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase (E3). Each catalyzes a part of the overall reaction.

A deficiency of the E1 component of the PDHC is the most common biochemical cause of congenital lactic acidosis. The deficiency results in a decreased ability to convert pyruvate to acetyl CoA, causing pyruvate to be shunted to lactate via lactate dehydrogenase. This creates particular problems for the brain, which relies on the TCA cycle for most of its energy and is particularly sensitive to acidosis. Symptoms include neurodegeneration, muscle spasticity, and, in the neonatal-onset form, early death. The inheritance pattern is X- linked dominant, with both males and females affected. Although there is no proven treatment for PDHC deficiency, dietary restriction of carbohydrates and supplementation with thiamine may reduce symptoms in select patients. 

Other options :

Option B - Branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency results in maple syrup urine disease. There is defective oxidative decarboxylation of leucine, isoleucine and valine. The disease is characterized by feeding problems, ketoacidosis, changes in muscle tone, and coma.

Option C -  Defective transketolase is a rare disorder of pentose phosphate metabolism with symptoms apparent in infancy including developmental delay and intellectual disability, delayed or absent speech, short stature, and congenital heart defects. 

Option D -  Isocitrate dehydrogenase is an enzyme of the TCA cycle which converts isocitrate to alpha-ketoglutarate. Defects in this enzyme are linked to carcinogenesis.

questions.question:
Which of the following is not associated with G6PD deficiency?

Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD)
options: Equal incidence in males a​nd females
Predisposes the patient to​ oxidative stress

Correct answer: A. Equal incidence in males and females

G6PD Deficiency does not have an equal incidence in males and females. It is an X-linked recessive (XLR) disorder, hence males are more affected than females.

Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency causes congenital hemolytic anemia due to enzyme deficiency. G6PD is required to generate NADPH while oxidizing glucose-6-phosphate in the hexose monophosphate pathway (HMP). G6PD deficiency leads to reduced NADPH levels (option B) which then reduces the level of reduced glutathione. Reduced glutathione is required to protect the cells against oxidative stress to RBCs and hemolysis. 

Clinically, most patients are asymptomatic. When exposed to triggers like fava beans, infections, drugs such as primaquine, chloroquine, sulfonamides/sulfones, dapsone, and nitrofurantoin patient develops:

  • Episodic hemolysis, both intravascular and extravascular
  • Hemolytic anaemia
  • Hemoglobinemia
  • Hemoglobinuria

Increased oxidative damage to RBCs leads to the formation of denatured precipitates known as Heinz bodies. These bodies can damage the RBC membrane leading to intravascular hemolysis. Additionally, when such RBCs pass through the splenic cords, macrophages pluck out these precipitates, giving them the characteristic appearance of bite cells.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which of the following is not a neurotransmitter derived from aminoacids ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Creatine

Creatine is not a neurotransmitter derived from amino acids.

Creatine is an intermediate product in the process of formation of creatinine. The steps involved in the formation are as follows:

  • The amidino group of arginine is transferred to glycine to form guanidoacetic acid. This step occurs in the kidneys and pancreas.
  • Guanido acetic acid is methylated by S-adenosyl methionine to form creatine. This step occurs in the liver.

Creatine is phosphorylated to creatine phosphate by the enzyme creatine kinase, which is present in the muscle, brain and liver. The reaction needs hydrolysis of ATP. The stored creatine phosphate in the muscle serves as an immediate store of energy in the muscle. During muscle contraction, the energy is first derived from ATP hydrolysis. Thereafter, the ATP is regenerated by the hydrolysis of creatine phosphate. This is called the Lohmann's reaction.

The creatine phosphate may be converted to its anhydride, creatinine, which is excreted in the urine. Creatinine level in the blood is an indicator of renal function.

Other options :

Option A - Gamma amino butyric acid (GABA) functions in brain tissue as an inhibitory neurotransmitter. It is formed by decarboxylation of glutamate by L-glutamate decarboxylase.

Option B - Dopa is a precursor in the formation of the neurotransmitters dopamine, norepinephrine and epinephrine. It is formed by the hydroxylation of tyrosine by tyrosine hydroxylase. 

Option C - 5 Hydroxytryptamine is an important neurotransmitter in the brain, where it functions as an antidepressant. It is derived from the amino acid tryptophan, in a process of hydroxylation followed by decarboxylation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which of the following methods is used to test the blood taken from a neonate for metabolic disease screening?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tandem Mass Spectrometry

Tandem mass spectrometry is used to screen a blood sample for metabolic diseases.

Mass spectrometry is a very sensitive quantitative analytical technique used to measure a wide range of clinically relevant analytes. It identifies molecules based on their mass or molecular size. A sample is vaporized such that a positive charge is produced on the molecule. An electric field is applied so that particles move. At the same time, a magnetic field is applied, so the cations are deflected and hit on the detector. For molecules of identical charge, the time required for the molecule to reach the detector is inversely proportional to the mass of the molecule.

In tandem mass spectrometry, two mass spectrometers (MS) are arranged sequentially. The first MS separates big peptides, based on their mass. From this observation, the parent ion can be directed into the second MS. Here the ions collide with argon gas molecules and are broken into smaller ions. These daughter ions are detected and quantified by their mass spectrum in the second instrument. 

Tandem MS is used to screen blood samples from newborns for the presence and concentrations of amino acids, fatty acids and other metabolites. Abnormalities in metabolite levels can serve as diagnostic indicators for a variety of genetic disorders like phenylketonuria.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Familial hypercholesterolemia is a result of a defect in which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. LDL receptor

Familial hypercholesterolemia occurs due to a defect in the LDL (low-density lipoprotein) receptor.

The primary function of LDL particles is to provide cholesterol to the peripheral tissues (or return it to the liver). They do so by binding to plasma membrane LDL receptors that recognize apo B-100. 

After binding, the LDL–receptor complex is endocytosed. The pH of the endosome falls, which allows the separation of the LDL from its receptor. The receptors can be recycled, whereas the lipoprotein remnants in the vesicle are transferred to lysosomes and degraded by lysosomal acid hydrolases, releasing free cholesterol, amino acids, fatty acids, and phospholipids. These compounds can be reutilized by the cell. 

Defects in the synthesis of functional LDL receptors cause a significant elevation in plasma LDL-C. Patients with such deficiencies have type IIa hyperlipidemia /familial hypercholesterolemia (FH). This autosomal dominant condition predisposes individuals to premature atherosclerosis and coronary artery disease.

Patients with homozygous FH must be treated aggressively to delay the onset and progression of CVD. Two drugs that reduce the hepatic production of VLDL and thus LDL, a small-molecule inhibitor of the microsomal TG transfer protein (MTP) and an antisense oligonucleotide to apoB, and an antibody that inhibits ANGPLT3 are approved and should be considered in patients who have insufficient response to statins and PCSK9 inhibitors. LDL apheresis should be considered in patients who have persistently elevated LDL-C levels despite drug therapy. 

Other options :

Option B - Defects in apo-E lead to type III hyperlipoproteinemia / familial dysbetalipoproteinemia.  It is characterized by defective clearance of chylomicron remnants and intermediate-density lipoproteins by the liver. This leads to hypercholesterolemia, xanthomas, and atherosclerosis. 

Option C - Defective apo-C II results in type I hyperlipoproteinemia/ familial lipoprotein lipase deficiency. The resulting inactive lipoprotein lipase leads to slow clearance of chylomicrons and VLDL, and low levels of LDL and HDL. Patients present with eruptive xanthomas and acute pancreatitis.

Option D - Apo-B 48 is involved in the assembly of chylomicrons. Defects in this protein are not associated with familial hypercholesterolemia.

questions.question: In a patient with Diabetes Mellitus, the liver produces more TG and VLDL. What is the cause of the same?

In diabetes, low insulin leads to decreased LPL activity which corresponds to an increase in VLDL and TG.

This results in increased production of triglycerides and VLDL in the liver.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question:
Match the following with appropriate precursors

i. Melatonin      a. Tyrosine
ii. Histamine  b. Tryptophan
iii. Norepinephrine  c. Cystine
iv. Glutathione    d. Histidine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. i-b, ii-d, iii-a, iv-c

The correct matched sequence is : i-b, ii-d, iii-a, iv-c.

i. Melatonin b. Tryptophan
ii. Histamine d. Histidine
iii. Norepinephrine a. Tyrosine
iv. Glutathione c. Cystine

i. Melatonin – b. Tryptophan

Tryptophan is an essential amino acid and the precursor for the synthesis of melatonin, produced by the pineal gland. The process begins with tryptophan being converted into serotonin, and then serotonin is further converted into melatonin.

ii. Histamine – d. Histidine

Histamine is derived from the amino acid histidine. The conversion of histidine into histamine is catalyzed by the enzyme histidine decarboxylase. Histamine is involved in local immune responses, acts as a neurotransmitter, and plays a role in regulating gastric acid secretion.

iii. Norepinephrine – a. Tyrosine

Norepinephrine (noradrenaline) is synthesized from tyrosine. Tyrosine is first converted to L-DOPA by the enzyme tyrosine hydroxylase, and then L-DOPA is converted into dopamine. Finally, dopamine is hydroxylated to form norepinephrine. Norepinephrine is a neurotransmitter involved in the sympathetic nervous system's fight-or-flight response.

iv. Glutathione – c. Cystine

Glutathione is a tripeptide composed of glutamate, cystine, and glycine. The cystine component is crucial because it contains a thiol (-SH) group, which is responsible for the antioxidant properties of glutathione.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: In the current scenario treatment for urea cycle disorder is available. Administration of amino acid phenylbutyrate can decrease ammonia formation. Which amino acid provides phenylbutyrate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Glutamate

The amino acid that provides phenylbutyrate in the treatment of urea cycle disorders is glutamate.

Ammonia to Urea cycle: Ammonia gets converted to glutamate (non toxic form) through transamination.  Glutamate is transported to the liver as glutamine (by glutamine synthase). In the liver, ammonia is released from glutamine, converting it to alpha keto glutatamte. The released ammonia enters the urea cycle.

In acetylation therapy, Phenylbutyrate (a prodrug) which is metabolized to phenylacetate. Phenylacetate combines with glutamine (a nitrogen-rich amino acid) to form phenylacetylglutamine. Phenylacetylglutamine is water-soluble and is excreted in the urine. This process helps trap excess nitrogen, bypassing the urea cycle.

Other drugs that can be used to achieve the same outcome (ammonia scavengers) include:

  • Phenylacetate
  • Benzoate

Option D: Glycine: The combination of benzoate and glycine forms hippuric acid, a non-toxic compound. When Benzoate is administered to the body, it acts as a nitrogen-scavenging agent. Hippuric acid is water-soluble and is excreted in the urine, effectively removing one nitrogen molecule from the body per molecule of hippuric acid formed. This mechanism is similar to how phenylacetate acts as a scavenger for glutamate.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question:
Which among the following are appropriate techniques for chromosomal aneuploidy?

i.  In situ hybridization

ii. Conventional cytogenetics

iii. Sanger sequencing

iv. Polymerase chain reaction
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. i,ii,iii,iv

In situ hybridization, Conventional cytogenetics, Sanger sequencing and Polymerase chain reaction are appropriate techniques for chromosomal aneuploidy.

Techniques to detect aneuploidy:

  1. In situ hybridization: Fluorescent In Situ Hybridisation (FISH) helps in the detection of specific genetic information using fluorescent probes. FISH is used to detect chromosomal aneuploidy, subtle microdeletions and rearrangements, complex translocations, and gene amplification.
  2. Conventional cytogenetics: This technique involves the study of chromosomes under a microscope, typically using methods like karyotyping, which arranges chromosomes by size, shape, and number. The analysis allows the identification of large chromosomal abnormalities, such as aneuploidy or structural changes.
  3. Sanger sequencing: DNA sequencing that uses chain-termination to identify the exact sequence of nucleotides in a DNA molecule. Simple Senger sequencing can detect aneuploidy only with massive parallel sequencing.
  4. Polymerase chain reaction: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is a rapid automated method for the amplification of specific DNA sequences (or genes). It can accurately quantify the target nucleic acid sequence within a sample. It is useful for determining somatic mutation with low allele frequency. Quantitative Fluorescence (QF) PCR is a method of rapid aneuploidy detection. It is less expensive and allows simultaneous processing of large number of samples of FISH.
  5. Array Comparitive Genomic Hybridization: microarray based technique which can reveal imbalances across the genome.
  6. Multiplex Ligation Probe Amplification: to detect gene dosage.

questions.question:
Enzyme used in recombinant DNA technology are?

  1. Isomerase
  2. Phosphatase
  3. Terminal transferase
  4. Crispr Cas9
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2,3,4

Phosphatase, Terminal transferase and Crispr Cas9 are used in recombinant DNA technology.

Recombinant DNA technology is a technique where DNA from different sources is combined to create new genetic material. Applications of recombinant DNA technology include producing insulin, growth hormones, vaccines, gene therapy, and studying gene functions and disease mechanisms.

Phosphatase dephosphorylates 5′ ends of RNA and DNA. It is primarily used for the removal of phosphate groups pror to kinase labelling and it is also used to prevent self ligation.

Terminal transferase catalyzes the addition of nucleotides to the 3' terminus of a DNA molecule. It is used in homopolymer tailing. 

CRISPR-Cas9 acts as an RNA-directed nuclease. It is a DNA editing/gene regulatory system.  It involves two essential components: Cas9, an endonuclease that causes a double-stranded DNA break, allowing modifications to the genomic DNA to be made; and a synthetic single-guide RNA, or sgRNA, responsible for guiding Cas9 to its target.

Isomerase is a class of enzymes that catalyze the structural rearrangement of molecules, converting one isomer into another. Isomerase is not commonly used directly in recombinant DNA technology, it has broader applications. They are used in metabolic pathways and as biocatalysts in industrial processes.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: A patient underwent gastrectomy for gastric adenocarcinoma. Which of the following vitamins needs to be supplemented in this patient?

Correct answer: A. Vitamin B12

A patient who has undergone gastrectomy for gastric adenocarcinoma needs to be supplemented with vitamin B12.

Vitamin B12 absorption is a complex process that relies on several factors. Intrinsic factor, a glycoprotein secreted by the parietal cells in the stomach, is essential for this process. Gastric acid and pepsin release vitamin B12 from dietary proteins, allowing it to bind with cobalophilin in the saliva. In the jejunum, cobalophilin is broken down, freeing vitamin B12 to bind with intrinsic factor. This complex is then absorbed in the distal ileum through specific receptors.  Following gastrectomy, the production of intrinsic factor is impaired due to the removal of gastric tissue, making vitamin B12 absorption difficult. Therefore, vitamin B12 supplementation is necessary after gastrectomy to prevent deficiency.

Other complications of gastrectomy include:

  • Nutritional deficiencies- Iron deficiency anemia (most common), Vitamin B12 deficiency, and osteoporosis
  • Dumping syndrome: early and late
  • Diarrhea
  • Duodenal stump leak/blow out
  • Bile reflux gastritis and esophagitis
  • Gall stones
  • Roux syndrome

questions.question: A 10-year-old child from a southern Indian state, hailing from a poor family, presents with rough and scaly skin. The child’s diet lacks vegetables and fruits. After treatment with linseed oil, Vitamin A, and Vitamin B, the symptoms subsided. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Phrynoderma are keratotic follicular papules commonly present over the elbows and knees. They can also extend to the shoulders, neck, back, thighs, buttocks, and abdomen. It is also known as toad skin, due to the rough cone-shaped elevated papules. It can caused by deficiency of vitamins A, B complex, C, and E and essential fatty acids. 

When it occurs due to vitamin A deficiency, it is associated with ophthalmic symptoms like xerophthalmia, night blindness, and Bitot's spots and cutaneous symptoms like xerosis, scaling, and acne.

Management includes nutritional improvement through diet, multivitamin supplementation, and treatment of the underlying cause.

A patient presents to the emergency department with severe abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. The laboratory results show serum triglyceride levels > 2000 mg/dl. Which deficiency could be contributing to the patient's condition?

LDL- low density lipoprotein
HDL- high density lipoprotein

Correct answer: A. Apolipoprotein C II

The elevated triglyceride levels and symptoms of acute pancreatitis are likely related to a deficiency in apolipoprotein C II.

Apolipoprotein C2 is a lipoprotein lipase cofactor that catalyzes cleavage of chylomicrons. Defective apo C II results in type I hyperlipoproteinemia/ familial lipoprotein lipase deficiency. The resulting inactive lipoprotein lipase leads to slow clearance of chylomicrons and VLDL, and low levels of LDL and HDL. Patients present with eruptive xanthomas and acute pancreatitis.

Lipoprotein lipase is an extracellular enzyme that is present in the capillary walls of most tissues. It is chiefly synthesized by the adipose tissue, and cardiac and skeletal muscles. A deficiency of lipoprotein lipase or apo C-II leads to type 1 hyperlipoproteinemia or familial chylomicronemia which leads to an increased risk of acute pancreatitis.

questions.question: After the age of 12, the boy had an intellectual disability. On examination, fingernail abrasions, excessive biting of lips, and increased levels of serum uric acid were observed. What is the likely diagnosis?

Correct answer: B. Lesch-Nyhan disease

The above clinical scenario with findings showing self-mutilation and laboratory values of hyperuricemia is most likely suggestive of Lesch-Nyhan disease.

Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is an X-linked recessive disorder due to a complete deficiency of the hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT). This deficiency results in an inability to salvage hypoxanthine or guanine leading to increased levels of phospho-ribosyl pyrophosphate (PRPP). Increased PRPP leads to increased purine synthesis, which is later degraded to uric acid. Increased hypoxanthine is also converted to uric acid.

The patients have intellectual disability, behaviors of self-injury like lip and finger biting, developmental delay, muscle dystonia, and extrapyramidal symptoms.

Diagnosis is made by the elevated levels of uric acid and by HGPRT enzyme assay.

Orange diaper syndrome can be an early indicator of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. At birth, individuals with Lesch-Nyhan syndrome typically appear asymptomatic, with normal prenatal growth and development. The condition is often first detected through the presence of orange-coloured crystals in the diaper, resulting from hyperuricemia. Since hyperuricemia is a common feature across all variants of HGPRT deficiency, which causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, predicting associated neurodevelopmental abnormalities requires enzyme activity testing.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: A neonate was brought with features of lethargy, and poor oral intake. On examination, a cataract was seen. Urine Benedict's test was positive but negative for Glucose. What will be the enzyme deficiency in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase

The given clinical scenario of a neonate presenting with lethargy, and poor oral intake, with examination revealing a cataract and urine benedict's test was positive but negative for glucose, is suggestive of classical galactosemia and enzyme deficient is galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase.

Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase deficiency leads to classical galactosemia. It is an autosomal recessive disorder. Normally, newborns receive up to 40% of their intake as lactose (glucose + galactose). The deficiency of this enzyme leads to an inability to convert galactose-1-phosphate to uridine diphosphate galactose. This leads to the accumulation of galactose 1-phosphate and causes injury to the kidney, liver, and brain. 

Clinical features:

  • Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate in the liver causes liver damage & leads to hepatomegaly, vomiting, and convulsions.
  • Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate depletes the liver of inorganic phosphate leading to diminished ATP synthesis which affects gluconeogenesis resulting in hypoglycemia.
  • Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate in the nerves causes intellectual disability.
  • Accumulation of galactitol in the lens causes oil-drop cataracts.
  • Patients with galactosemia are at an increased risk of developing Escherichia coli neonatal sepsis.

In uridyl transferase deficiency, the epimerase is present in adequate amounts, so that the galactosemic individual can still form UDPGal from glucose. This explains how normal growth and development of affected children can occur despite the galactose-free diets.

Urinary reducing sugar (Benedict's test) and mucic acid test are positive. Direct enzyme assay using erythrocytes establishes the diagnosis.

Treatment is a galactose-free diet.

Other options:

Option A: Hexokinase is a glycolytic enzyme, involved in maintaining intracellular glucose concentration by catalysing the first step in glucose metabolism, i.e., phosphorylation of intracellular glucose.  Its deficiency leads to hemolytic anaemia. Splenomegaly may be another presenting feature. 

Option B: Galactokinase is the enzyme responsible for the conversion of galactose to galactose 1-phosphate. Only cataract is seen in the deficiency of this enzyme because galactose-1-phosphate is not formed. Hence no toxic effects of this compound are manifested. 

Option D: Phosphofructokinase is a key regulatory enzyme of glycolysis and is necessary for the ATP-dependent conversion of fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-diphosphate. Tauri's disease is type VII glycogen storage disorder that results due to the deficiency of phosphofructokinase.

questions.question: A patient diagnosed with a rare homozygous recessive condition presented with ectopia lentis. In the peripheral smear, there was no megaloblastic anemia. Correct answer: B. Pyridoxine

The vitamin that can be used as supplementation in this patient with homocystinuria is pyridoxine (vitamin B6). 

Classical homocystinuria is an autosomal recessive disease most commonly caused by a deficiency of the cystathionine β-synthase. The deficiency of this enzyme leads to an accumulation of homocysteine in the blood and a clinical syndrome of intellectual disability, subluxated ocular lenses, long and slender extremities, arachnodactyly, and arterial and venous thrombi. The skeletal features of homocystinuria often mimic Marfan syndrome. Folic acid and vitamin B12 deficiency can also lead to homocystinuria with megaloblastic anemia.

Demonstration of elevated total homocysteine in the blood confirms the diagnosis. 50% of the cases of homocystinuria are termed pyridoxine-responsive because large doses of pyridoxine can enhance the activity of deficient enzymes in these patients. Administration of large doses of pyridoxine (vitamin B6) restores the activity of the deficient enzyme in half of all cases of homocystinuria.

Folate supplementation is also added to overcome any folate deficiency that might occur due to increased conversion of homocysteine to methionine. For the other 50% of the patients, the treatment consists of methionine restriction and cysteine supplementation. In addition, betaine (methyl group donor), folate and vitamin B12 may be added.

questions.question: You received a text message from your friend JOHN DOE about occupational exposure after he visited his doctor as shown below. What is the test used to diagnose?

Correct answer: B. Lead poisoning

The test for coproporphyrinogen levels is used as a screening test to diagnose lead poisoning.

Lead inhibits the enzymes delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) dehydratase and ferrochelatase, which are involved in heme synthesis. ALA is converted to porphobilinogen by ALA dehydratase, inhibited by lead. So, serum porphobilinogen levels are decreased in lead poisoning.

  • An elevated level of protoporphyrin in blood and elevated ALA and coproporphyrinogen in urine
  • Microcytic anemia with basophilic stippling in peripheral smear due to ineffective heme synthesis

In the later phase, the findings are colic abdominal pain, constipation, nerve palsy, encephalopathy, and disturbance of the genito-urinary and cardiovascular systems.

Diagnosis of lead poisoning:

Coproporphyrin in urine >150 mcg/L Screening test- indicates exposure
Aminolevulinic acid (ALA) in urine >5 mg/L Indicates lead absorption
Lead in blood >70 mcg/dL Clinical symptoms appear

Basophilic stippling of RBCs   Sensitive indicator

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: A 3-year-old child is brought to the OPD with complaints of persistent delayed developmental milestones, and hyperpigmented macular lesions on the body which are more pronounced on exposure to sunlight. What is the error in DNA multiplication?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Nucleotide excision repair

The history points to a diagnosis of xeroderma pigmentosum. It is characterized by defective nucleotide excision repair.

UV radiation leads to pyrimidine dimerization in DNA strands, preventing further replication by DNA polymerase. The nucleotide excision repair mechanism corrects the dimer formation in DNA. Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder characterized by an inability to repair DNA pyrimidine dimers caused by UV exposure. This leads to clinical and cellular hypersensitivity to ultraviolet (UV) radiation.

In XP the skin is normal at birth and has a three-stage progression:

  • Diffuse erythema, scaling, and freckle-like areas over the sun-exposed regions of the body at around 6 months of age.
  • The second stage is characterized by poikiloderma. This results in skin atrophy, telangiectasias with mottled hyperpigmentation, and hyperpigmentation.
  • In the third stage appearance of cutaneous malignancies like squamous cell carcinomas, malignant melanoma, basal cell carcinoma, and fibrosarcoma. 

Most of the cases with XP have ocular manifestations. Initially, it appears as photophobia, conjunctivitis, ectropion, and symblepharon with ulceration. Accumulation of pyrimidine dimer causes corneal opacification and neovascularization. Ocular malignancies are common in the lids, conjunctiva, and cornea as they are exposed to as much as facial skin. XP is ultimately fatal, and early detection of the skin lesions and their management with prevention of UV ray exposures prolong life.

A patient with a family history of coronary heart disease presented with tendon xanthomas. His lipid profile showed serum LDL to be 280 mg/dL and triglyceride levels was 398 mg/dl. What is the likely defect in this patient?

LDL - Low-density lipoprotein

Correct answer: A. LDL receptor defect

The clinical presentation with tendon xanthomas, elevated serum LDL  and elevated serum triglycerides points to a diagnosis of familial hypercholesterolemia and is due to a defect in LDL receptors.

Familial hypercholesterolemia  (type IIa hyperlipoproteinemia) is an inherited disorder due to defects in LDL receptors. This defect causes a decrease in the uptake of LDL and cholesterol. As a result, the blood levels of both LDL and cholesterol are elevated. Such patients are at increased risk of developing atherosclerosis and coronary artery disease.

Features of FH: 

  • Painful polyarthritis and tendinitis are common.
  • Physical findings seen are corneal arcus and tendon xanthomas over the Achilles tendon and the dorsum of the hands. Xanthomas are tumorous masses produced by foamy cell clusters (lipid-laden macrophages) found in the connective tissue of the skin and in tendons.

Diagnosis is done clinically based on hypercholesterolemia with 

  • LDL > 190 mg/dl, 
  • Family history of hypercholesterolemia and/or
  • Premature coronary artery disease.

Treatment includes lifestyle changes, restriction of a fatty diet, and pharmacotherapy with statins in heterozygous FH patients.

Recent drugs for specific treatment of homozygous FH are:

  • Lomitapide, a microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTP) inhibitor, and
  • Mipomersen, an antisense oligonucleotide against apoB.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which food item among these is the primary source of thiamine in Indians?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 4

Among the various food items given on the plate, the primary source of thiamine (vitamin B1) in the Indian diet is option 4 i.e. chapati and rice.

The thiamine content in various foods in decreasing order are as follows:

  • Gingelly seeds
  • Groundnut
  • Bengal gram
  • Whole wheat
  • Rice

Gingelly (sesame) seeds have the highest content of thiamine.

Thiamine is lost from rice during the process of milling. As it is a water-soluble vitamin, washing, and cooking rice cause further losses. Hence, it is advisable to avoid highly polished rice and eat parboiled or under-milled rice.

Thiamine is essential for energy metabolism, particularly in carbohydrate processing. Its active form, thiamine diphosphate, acts as a coenzyme for three critical enzyme complexes: pyruvate dehydrogenase, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and branched-chain keto acid dehydrogenase. This coenzyme facilitates oxidative decarboxylation by forming a reactive carbanion that attaches to carbonyl groups like those in pyruvate, leading to the release of CO2. Thiamine diphosphate is also vital for transketolase in the pentose phosphate pathway.

Thiamine triphosphate, another form of thiamin, helps regulate nerve function by activating chloride channels in nerve membranes.

A thiamine deficiency can cause several conditions such as beriberi, characterized by peripheral neuritis, which can also involve heart failure and edema. Additionally, thiamine deficiency can lead to Wernicke's encephalopathy and Korsakoff's psychosis, commonly associated with alcohol or drug abuse. The lack of thiamine impairs the conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, leading to increased levels of lactate and pyruvate in the blood, which can result in dangerous lactic acidosis, especially in those consuming high-carbohydrate diets.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: A young female comes to the emergency department after ingesting 10 tablets of Phenobarbital. Which of the following components of the ETC is inhibited by this drug?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Complex I to Q

Phenobarbital is a barbiturate that inhibits complex I to Q of the electron transport chain. 

Complex I of the electron transport chain is NADH-Q oxidoreductase. It oxidizes NADH and reduces coenzyme Q. Phenobarbital inhibits complex I to Q so that the electrons will not be able to be transferred from NADH to coenzyme Q, which is the first step in the electron transport chain. As a result, the rate of oxygen consumption will decrease.

The electron transport chain (ETC) represents the final pathway through which electrons, originating from the oxidation of carbohydrates, fatty acids, and amino acids, are channeled toward a final reaction with oxygen to produce water and ATP. The ETC complexes are embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane.

The oxidation of compounds by ETC complexes leads to the release of free energy. This is used to pump H+ to the intermembrane space. This results in the formation of a proton motive force that is used for the phosphorylation of ADP to ATP. Thus, oxidation is coupled with phosphorylation to generate ATP. NADH generates 2.5 ATP and FADH2 generates 1.5 ATP.

questions.question: A child presents to you with bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly, and pancytopenia. A trephine biopsy aspirate shows the following finding. Which of the following is the most likely enzyme deficient in this patient?

Gaucher's disease is an inborn error of metabolism caused due to a deficiency of beta-glucocerebrosidase. It is the most common lysosomal storage disorder and the mode of inheritance is autosomal recessive. There is an accumulation of lipid-laden macrophages in the spleen, liver, and other tissues.

There are three clinical subtypes - type I (chronic non-neuronopathic), type II (acute neuronopathic), and type III (intermediate). Clinical features include anemia, thrombocytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, and neurological features depending on the subtype. 

Gaucher's cells are formed as a result of the accumulation of massive amounts of glucocerebrosides within the phagocytes. The cells have a fibrillary cytoplasm and give a crumpled tissue paper appearance.
