questions.question: A 32-year-old lady comes with complaints of erythematous scaly rash, loose stools, and cognitive dysfunction. The rash involved her forearm, neck, and face. She seems to have difficulty remembering things from the recent past. Her electrolytes are within normal range. She admits to having shifted to a corn-based diet due to economic reasons. Which of the following would improve her symptoms?

Correct answer: A. Oral Nicotinamide supplementation

The given clinical features suggests the diagnosis of pellagra, due to her corn-based diet. Oral nicotinamide supplements can improve her symtpoms. 

Niacin can be synthesized in the body from tryptophan. Two compounds, nicotinic acid and nicotinamide, have the biological activity of niacin. The nicotinamide ring of the coenzymes nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP) participate in oxidation/reduction reactions.

The initial symptoms of pellagra include loss of appetite, generalized weakness, irritability, abdominal pain, and vomiting. This is followed by bright red glossitis and a characteristic pigmented, scaly skin rash in sun-exposed areas. This rash is known as Casal’s necklace when it forms a ring around the neck. 

The 4Ds of pellagra:

  • Diarrhea
  • Dermatitis
  • Dementia, leading to
  • Death

It is diagnosed by measuring urinary levels of 2-methyl nicotinamide and 2-pyridone.

While cognitive dysfunction can result from thiamine deficiency, rash and loose stools do not fit with thiamine deficiency. Therefore, thiamine would not address the full spectrum of this patient’s symptoms.

Option C: Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy, which is associated with symptoms like bleeding gums, bruising, joint pain, and fatigue. Scurvy is not associated with a rash like the one described, nor does it typically cause cognitive dysfunction or diarrhea. Hence, high-dose vitamin C would not improve this patient’s symptoms.

Option D: Corn-based diets are low in niacin and tryptophan, leading to pellagra over time, especially if the diet is not balanced with other niacin-rich foods. While stopping the corn-based diet could prevent further niacin deficiency, it will not immediately address the existing deficiency and symptoms like rash, diarrhea, and cognitive dysfunction. The patient would still need niacin supplementation to resolve the current symptoms.

questions.question: A patient presented with multiple yellowish raised plaques on eyelids, xanthomas on the achilles tendon. What is the likely cause for the patient's presentation?

The clinical presentation with yellowish, raised plaques on eyelids, and tendon xanthomas points to a diagnosis of familial hypercholesterolemia (FH).

Familial hypercholesterolemia (type IIa hyperlipoproteinemia) is an inherited disorder due to defects in LDL receptors and Apo B100. This decreases the uptake of Low-density lipoprotein and cholesterol leading to their increased levels in the blood. The increased LDL accumulates in the blood vessels causing atherosclerosis (premature coronary artery disease)and in the Achilles tendon causing tendon xanthomas. Xanthomas are tumorous masses produced by foamy cell clusters (lipid-laden macrophages) found in the connective tissue of the skin and tendons. Patients can also have yellowish plaques around the eyes (Xanthelasma) and corneal arcus.

Treatment includes lifestyle changes, restriction of a fatty diet, and pharmacotherapy with statins in heterozygous FH patients.

questions.question:
A child presented to the OPD with complaints of fatigue and muscle weakness while exercising. Laboratory investigations found that LCFA oxidation was affected. A muscle biopsy was done which revealed the presence of fat vacuoles. What is the probable diagnosis?

LCFA- Long-chain fatty acid

LPL- Lipoprotein lipase

LDL- Low-density lipoprotein
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Carnitine deficiency

The clinical scenario of a child with fatigue and muscle weakness on exercise with laboratory findings of LCFA oxidation deficiency and fat vacuoles on muscle biopsy suggests a diagnosis of carnitine deficiency.

Carnitine deficiency is a defect in fatty acid oxidation that leads to hypoketotic hypoglycemia and hyperammonemia. Carnitine transports activated LCFA (long chain fatty acyl CoA) from the cytoplasm to the mitochondria for beta-oxidation (as they cannot cross the mitochondrial membrane), carnitine deficiency impairs this transport causing accumulation of lipids (skeletal muscle weakness). This excess fatty acid inhibits the urea cycle causing hyperammonemia. Since beta-oxidation cannot occur, energy production is reduced, and there is hypoglycemia without a corresponding increase in ketone bodies (hypoketotic) during times of glucose depletion such as exercise.

The role of carnitine in the metabolism of fatty acids is demonstrated in the image below:

Clinical features of carnitine deficiency begin in childhood and include poor feeding, lethargy, liver dysfunction and hepatomegaly, hypotonia, and dilated cardiomyopathy. Treatment involves oral supplementation of carnitine.

Other options:

Option A: An increase in LDL can cause hyperlipoproteinemia, and reduced LDL can cause defective absorption of fat-soluble vitamins.

Option B: LPL is involved in hydrolysis of lipoproteins in the blood to free fatty acid and glycerol which are then taken up by the tissues. A defective LPL can cause type 1 familial chylomicronemia syndrome presenting as pancreatitis.

Option C: Fatty acid synthase is a multienzyme complex involved in fatty acid synthesis in the cytosol which when defective may impair energy production, essential fatty acids, and affect metabolic pathways. There is no accumulation of fat vacuoles since fatty acids are not synthesised.

questions.question: A mother came back home to see her child suffering from difficulty breathing. The child had contact with rotenone while trying to bathe their pet. In the given clinical vignette, inhibition of NADH-Q oxidoreductase by rotenone was the likely cause of breathlessness, followed by death in this child.

questions.question: A child suffering from phenylketonuria was started on necessary dietary modifications but the neurological symptoms persisted. Phenylalanine hydroxylase levels in the serum are normal. Which of the following enzymes is likely to be deficient in this case?

Correct answer: C. Tetrahydrobiopterin synthase

This child with phenylketonuria with neurological symptoms not improving despite dietary modifications and normal serum phenylalanine hydroxylase level is suggestive of tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) synthase deficiency.

A diet low in phenylalanine (eg: tapioca) is the mainstay of treatment for classic phenylketonuria but may not be sufficient in BH4 deficiency where supplementation with BH4 and deficient neurotransmitter precursors (L-dopa) is required to overcome the block.

Phenylketonuria (PKU) is an inborn error of metabolism seen due to a defect in the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase (classic phenylketonuria) and less commonly, due to a defect in BH4 synthase (non-classical). These defects result in the impaired conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine. The patient develops clinical features due to elevated levels of phenylalanine metabolites and decreased levels of tyrosine. The excess phenylalanine in the blood is metabolized to phenylpyruvate (positive ferric chloride) and phenylacetate (mousy odour) which are excreted in the urine. Infants appear normal at birth and gradually develop symptoms of hyperreflexia, seizures, hypopigmentation, low IQ, hyperactivity, and tremors.

Tandem mass spectroscopy is the investigation of choice. Guthrie test is a screening test that shows with absence of growth of Bacillus subtilis. The ferric chloride test is positive with the development of a transient blue-green colour.

questions.question: Which micronutrient is most likely deficient in a patient with the radiographic findings given below along with anemia, neutropenia, depigmented hair and skin?

The given clinical features of anaemia and neutropenia, along with depigmented hair and skin and the radiological findings suggestive of pelkan spurs, trummerfeld zone, Frenkel's line, and Wimberger's ring sign point to the diagnosis of Menke's disease. Patients with this condition have low serum levels of copper.

Menke's disease or Menke-Kinky hair syndrome is an X-linked recessive condition caused due to a mutation in the ATP7A gene on chromosome X. This causes impaired transport of dietary copper from the small intestine to the liver leading to low levels of copper-containing enzymes.

The final step of collagen synthesis involves the formation of covalent cross-links. This is done by the enzyme lysyl oxidase, a copper-containing protein. This is essential for the strength and rigidity of collagen. As a result of deficiency of copper in Menkes disease, this step of collagen synthesis is affected. 

The patient presents with depigmented kinky hair, failure to thrive, neurodegenerative symptoms (loss of developmental milestones, truncal hypotonia, epilepsy), multiple fractures, anaemia due to ceruloplasmin and hephaestin deficiency (converts ferrous to ferric to be bound to transferrin), neutropenia, and recurrent infections.

Lab investigations show low serum copper (<65 μg/dL) and low ceruloplasmin(<20 mg/dl). The disease is fatal and has no curative treatment.

A variety of distinct anomalies that are representative of scurvy and acquired copper insufficiency can be seen on radiographs of people with menke's disease.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: In the given Lineweaver-Burk plot, the blue line represents the action of an enzyme, and the red line represents the action of the same enzyme in the presence of an inhibitor.  What is the type of inhibition shown here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Competitive inhibition

The given graph shows competitive inhibition, in which the value of Vmax remains constant and the Km value increases. The intercept on the y-axis remains unchanged while the intercept on the x-axis shifts close to zero forming a steeper slope.

Competitive inhibition is when the inhibitor binds reversibly to the substrate-binding site and competes with the substrate for the active enzyme-binding site. This effect of competitive inhibition can be overcome by increasing the substrate concentration by which maximum velocity can still be achieved. Therefore, Vmax (maximum velocity of the reaction) is unaltered in this type of inhibition. However, the concentration of the substrate required to achieve half of the maximum velocity is increased. Therefore, Km is increased in this condition.

The graph below shows the changes in Vmax and Km in competitive inhibition.

Other options:

Option B: Non-competitive inhibition is by binding inhibitors to enzymes in locations remote from the active site. Increasing the concentration of the substrate does not overcome non-competitive inhibition. Thus, noncompetitive inhibitors decrease the Vmax of the reaction. They do not interfere with the binding of the substrate to the enzyme. Thus, the enzyme shows the same Km in the presence or absence of noncompetitive inhibitors.

The graph shows the changes in Vmax and Km in non-competitive inhibition.

Option C: In uncompetitive inhibition, inhibitors bind with the enzyme-substrate intermediate complex, and inhibit it. This leads to a decrease in both Vmax and Km. An example is the inhibition of placental alkaline phosphate (ALP) by phenylalanine. 

Option D: In Allosteric inhibition, inhibitors bind to a site other than the active site i.e. allosteric site, and induce a conformational change (change in the shape of the active site unlike in non-competitive inhibition) thus, inhibiting the enzyme. ATP is an allosteric inhibitor of Phosphofructokinase in glycolysis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: How much drug will remain at the end of 6 hours when a patient is given 200 mg drug, 75 mg excreted in 90 min and if the drug follows first-order kinetics?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 30.5 mg

In first order kinetics, a constant fraction of the drug is excreted in a given time. 

Since 75 mg of 200 mg is excreted in 90 minutes, the fraction of drug excreted in each 90 mins is 75/200, which is 3/8. Thus, the fraction of the drug that remains in the body is 5/8. 

There will be 4 cycles of excretion of the drug (6 hours = 360 mins, and 360/90 = 4). Thus, with a starting dose of 200mg, the drug remaining in the body after 4 hours will be:

200 x 5/8 x 5/8 x 5/8 x 5/8 = 30.5mg

Alternate way to calculate: 

75 mg of 200 mg is excreted in 90 minutes, thus 75/200 = 0.375 is eliminated 

After 90 minutes; 200 mg-75 mg = 125 mg remains.
The second 90 minutes (after 180 minutes) = 125 x 0.375 = 46.875 mg is eliminated, and 125-46.875 = 78.125 mg remains
The third 90 minutes (after 270 minutes) = 78.125 x 0.375 = 29.297 mg is eliminated, and 78.125-29.297 = 48.828 remains
The fourth 90 minutes (after 360 minutes) = 48.828 x 0.375 = 18.310 mg is eliminated, 48.828-18.310 = 30.518 mg remains after 6 hours.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: A patient with Prinzmetal angina is administered isosorbide mononitrate and is noticed to have symptomatic relief. What is the mechanism of action of nitrate in this case?
options: Increased left ventricular‌ end diastolic volume
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Endothelium independent coronary vasodilation

The mechanism of action of nitrates in prinzmetal angina is endothelium-independent coronary vasodilatation.

Prinzmetal angina occurs due to vasospasm of the coronary arteries. Nitrates relax the smooth muscles of epicardial coronary arteries and relieve coronary artery spasm.

In the case of stable angina, the primary mechanism of action of nitrates is preferential dilatation of veins (by increasing cGMP). Venous dilatation leads to a decrease in the venous return to the heart (preload). This decreases the ventricular end-diastolic volume and thereby a decrease in myocardial oxygen consumption. The diastolic perfusion pressure (aortic blood pressure in diastole - left ventricular pressure in diastole) is increased.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: What is the mechanism of action of vancomycin?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cell wall synthesis inhibition

The mechanism of action of vancomycin is cell wall synthesis inhibition.

The bacterial cell wall has long chains of peptidoglycan and is cross-linked to each other by the action of the enzyme transglycosylase. Vancomycin is a glycopeptide group of antibiotics that binds to the D-alanyl-D-alanine terminus of the synthesized peptidoglycan. The drug and cosmetics act initially passed in 1940 and amended in 2016 provides a definition of misbranded, spurious, and adulterated drugs.

A drug is considered misbranded if it fulfills any of the following three conditions:

  • If the appearance of the drug has been altered to conceal physical damage or make it appear of greater therapeutic value than it actually is (or)
  • If it is not labeled in the prescribed manner (or)
  • If the label or container of the drug makes a false or misleading claim about the drug. In this case, the packet states that there is 500 mg of paracetamol present as opposed to the 200 mg that is actually present.

A drug is considered spurious if it fulfills the following conditions:

  • If the drug is imported under a name that belongs to another drug (or)
  • If the drug is an imitation of another drug with the intent to deceive (or)
  • If the label depicts a manufacturer that is either fictitious or a real company with no ties to the product (or)
  • If it has been substituted wholly or in part by another drug or substance.

A drug is considered adulterated if it fulfills the following conditions:

  • If it consists wholly or in part of any filthy, putrid, poisonous, or decomposed substance (or)
  • If it has been manufactured under unsanitary conditions (or)
  • If it bears a coloring other than the one prescribed (or)
  • If it has been mixed with any substance that may reduce its quality or strength.

*Note: The term counterfeit drugs is a broad term and is used by the WHO. This may also be conceived to include misbranded, spurious, or adulterated drugs. However, the term misbranded drugs would be a more appropriate answer here since it is likely that the reference used is from CDSCO.

Low apparent volume of distribution of a drug indicates that it is not extensively distributed in the tissues.

Apparent Volume of distribution (Vd) = dose administered I.V/ plasma concentration E.g: If a 500 mg of drug A is given i.v (100% bioavailability) and the plasma concentration reached is 10 mg/ liter then the apparent volume of distribution (Vd) is 500/10= 50 liters.

But the normal blood volume is about 5 liters. A high Vd is due to accumulation of drug A in extravascular tissues resulting in low plasma concentration. Therefore, the apparent volume of distribution is an imaginary volume throughout which the drug is distributed if the plasma concentration remains the same throughout.

Option A: t1/2 relationship with volume of distribution (Vd) and clearance (Cl) is given by the formula t 1/2 = 0.693 x Vd /Cl. t1/2 is directly proportional to Vd but it is also inversely proportional to clearance. If a drug has a low volume of distribution but clearance is very low, t1/2 can still be high. So low Vd doesn't always imply low t1/2. So the best answer among the given options is D. 

Option B and C: Low Vd does not indicate low bioavailability or low efficacy.

Correct answer: C. Drug deposition in the oropharynx

The given image shows a metered-dose inhaler (MDI). The most common side effect of this device is drug deposition in the oropharynx. 

Most material inhaled using this device will be swallowed and absorbed, entering systemic circulation after undergoing the first-pass effect in the liver. Some drug will also be absorbed into the systemic circulation from the lungs.

The use of a large-volume spacer will reduce the amount of drug deposited in the oropharynx, thereby reducing the amount swallowed and absorbed from the GI tract, thus limiting the systemic effects of the drug.

The given image shows the use of spacer with MDI:

 

Spacers reduce the velocity and size of particles entering the upper airways. This reduces the amount of drug that impinges on the oropharynx and increases the proportion of the drug inhaled into the lower airways.

Spacer devices are useful in delivering inhaled drugs to small children, as young as 3 years of age, who are not able to use a pMDI (pressurized MDI), as seen in the image below:

 

Pressurized metered-dose inhalers: Drugs are propelled from a canister in the pMDI with the aid of a propellant. These devices are convenient, portable, and typically deliver 50–200 doses of the drug.

Dry powder inhalers: Drugs may also be delivered as a dry powder using devices that scatter a fine powder dispersed by air turbulence on inhalation. Children less than 7 years of age find it difficult to use a DPI. DPIs have been developed to deliver peptides and proteins, such as insulin, systemically but have proved to be problematic because of the consistency of dosing.

The given image shows various types of dry powder inhalers:

 

Nebulizers: Two types of nebulizers are available. Jet nebulizers are driven by a stream of gas (air or oxygen), whereas ultrasonic nebulizers use a rapidly vibrating piezoelectric crystal and thus do not require a source of compressed gas.

The nebulized drug may be inspired during tidal breathing, and it is possible to deliver much higher doses of the drug as compared to pMDI. Nebulizers are therefore useful in treating acute exacerbations of asthma and COPD, for delivering drugs when airway obstruction is extreme (e.g., in severe COPD), for delivering inhaled drugs to infants and small children who cannot use the other inhalation devices, and for giving drugs such as antibiotics when relatively high doses must be delivered.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true regarding the dose-response curve shown in the image below?
options: C is more p​otent than A
B is more p​otent than A
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. B is competitive antagonist

In the above image, drug B is a competitive antagonist.

In competitive antagonism, the DRC is shifted to the right whereas in non-competitive antagonism the DRC is flattened.

Thus in the above image Drug B is the Competitive antagonist while drug C is the non-competitive antagonist.

Potency:

  • It is defined as the amount of drug needed to produce a given response.
  • A highly potent drug evokes a given response at low concentrations and vice-versa.
  • The more the curve is on the left in a dose-response curve (DRC), the greater is its potency.
  • Thus, in the above image, the potency is drug A > drug C > drug B.

Efficacy:

  • It is defined as the maximum effect produced by the drug.
  • It expresses the effect produced by the receptors when bound by a certain drug.
  • In the log dose-response curve, the perpendicular height represents the drug efficacy.
  • Thus, in the above image, the efficacy is drug A = drug B > drug C.

questions.question: Apparent volume of distribution of a drug is very high (6L/kg). Which of the following is true regarding the distribution of that drug?

Correct answer: C. Sequestered in body tissues

In the present case, the volume of distribution of the drug is 6L/kg (420 L in a normal adult with reference weight 70kg) which is very high when compared to the total body water of 42L. Therefore, it can be implied that the drug is having high sequestration in tissues.

The apparent volume of distribution (Vd) is an imaginary volume throughout which the drug is distributed if the plasma concentration remains constant throughout. 

Vd = Dose administered IV/ plasma concentration

The difference in the volume of distribution based on drug type:

  • Low Vd 
    • Restricted to the intravascular compartment 
    • Seen in drugs with high molecular weight (e.g., heparin) or high protein binding (e.g., warfarin - 9.8L)
  • Medium Vd 
    • Lipid insoluble drugs (e.g., gentamicin - 20L) do not enter the cells and are distributed in the extracellular fluid volume
    • Small water-soluble molecules (e.g., ethanol - 42L) are distributed in the total body water
  • High Vd
    • Sequestered and accumulated in the tissues
    • Small lipophilic molecules (e.g., chloroquine - 13000L)

questions.question: What is the mechanism of resistance by lactamases​ to β-lactam antibiotics?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Degradation of antibiotics

Resistance by lactamases is through the degradation of antibiotics.

The bacterial cell wall is made of heteropolymeric peptidoglycan that confers mechanical stability. The β-lactam antibiotics inhibit the last step in peptidoglycan synthesis by acylating the transpeptidase via cleavage of the –CO–N– bond of the β-lactam ring. These transpeptidase targets are collectively called Penicillin Binding Proteins (PBPs)

Beta-lactamases are enzymes produced by certain bacteria that inactivates β-lactam antibiotics by hydrolysis of the β-lactam ring in their structure.

The resistance to penicillins and other beta-lactam antibiotics can be conferred through one of the four mechanisms:

  1. Inactivation of antibiotic by lactamases
  2. Modification of target PBPs
  3. Impaired penetration of drug to target PBPs
  4. Antibiotic efflux

questions.question: A female patient is on first-line pharmacological therapy for bipolar disorder for 6 months. She is fasting for a few days due to religious reasons and presented with seizures, coarse tremors, confusion, and weakness of limbs. Which of the following investigations should be done to help diagnose her condition?

Correct answer: B. Serum lithium level

The clinical features given in the question are most likely suggestive of lithium toxicity, and hence serum lithium levels should be measured to confirm it.

Lithium is a mood stabilizer with a very narrow therapeutic index and is the first line of management in bipolar disorder.

The kidney handles both lithium and Na+ in the same way via ENac channel. Thus during fasting/dehydration, along with Na+ reabsorption in renal tubules, there will be an increase in the reabsorption of lithium leading to lithium toxicity.

Lithium has a very narrow therapeutic index of 0.8-1.2 mEq/L. The severity of lithium toxicity is often divided into the following three grades: 

Grade

Sr. lithium concentration (in mEq/L)

 Symptoms
Mild symptoms 1.5-2.5  nausea, vomiting, tremor, and fatigue
Moderate intoxication 2.5-3.5  confusion, agitation, delirium, tachycardia, and hypertonia
Severe intoxication >3.5  coma, seizures, hyperthermia, and hypotension

A fine tremor is common in patients taking lithium at therapeutic doses. Therapeutic lithium tremor is generally symmetric, limited to the arms, and nonprogressive. The tremor from lithium toxicity is coarser and more disabling, may also affect the legs, and occurs with other symptoms of toxicity. Other adverse effects include mental confusion, hypothyroidism, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, and edema.

As lithium is readily dialyzed, lithium overdose or toxicity is treated with hemodialysis.

*Note - Serum Na+ levels are significant with respect to lithium toxicity, where as serum potassium levels becomes significant in digoxin toxicity. Hypokalemia increases the risk of digoxin toxicity.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: Which of the following is false about the selection of essential drugs?
options: Adequate safety profile ne​eds to be established
Cost to benefit has to be ​considered
Fixed drug combination is ​preferred over single dru‌gs
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fixed drug combination is preferred over single drugs

Fixed drug combinations are not preferred over single drugs while selecting essential drugs.

Criteria for selection of essential medicines as per WHO:

  • There should be adequate data on the safety and efficacy of the drug.
  • The drug should be available in a form where its quality including bioavailability and stability on storage is assured.
  • The choice of the drug depends on the pattern of prevalent diseases, financial resources, availability of trained personnel and facilities, genetic, demographic, and environmental factors.
  • The cost-benefit ratio is an important factor.
  • Pharmacokinetic properties of the drug and the local manufacture and storage facilities are also considered.
  • Essential drugs should preferably be single compounds.
  • Fixed combinations are used only when the dosage of each component meets the requirement of the population in which it is used. It should also have the advantage in safety, therapeutic effect, adherence, and prevention of drug resistance when compared to single compounds.
  • The selection of essential drugs is a continuous process and changes are to be made with developments in public health and the availability of better drugs.
  • The selection should be based on rationally developed treatment guidelines.

Note:

In 1977 WHO brought the first "Model List of Essential Drugs". India made its "National Essential Drug List" in 1996 and revised the list in 2011 and renamed it as "National List of Essential Medicines". The latest edition of WHO Model List of Essential Drugs is the 21st edition published in 2019.

questions.question: A 34-year-old man with hypertension is diagnosed with stage 4 chronic kidney disease, with eGFR of <30. His doctor wants to prescribe a thiazide diuretic. Which of the following can be given?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Metolazone

The thiazide diuretic that can be used as an antihypertensive in this patient with chronic kidney disease is metolazone.

In patients with chronic renal failure, thiazide diuretics are ineffective. But metolazone, despite being a thiazide diuretic, is effective as antihypertensives in patients with chronic renal failure.

Metolazone is useful even in severe renal failure (GFR of ∼15 mL/min). It has an additive action when combined with loop diuretics like furosemide. It also has an additional proximal tubular action (thiazides mainly act on DCT). It is commonly used for edema and is occasionally used as an antihypertensive.

Diuretics in hypertension:

Thiazides are the diuretics of choice for uncomplicated hypertension.

Mechanisms of antihypertensive action:

  • Decreases plasma and ECF volume by diuresis thereby decreasing cardiac output
  • Even when the compensatory mechanisms restore the Na+ levels and plasma volume, a low BP is maintained by a reduction in total peripheral resistance.
  • This reduction in total peripheral resistance is due to the persistence of a small sodium and volume deficit even after compensation. The decreased intracellular sodium is responsible for increased compliance of the vessel wall and a  reduced response to constrictor stimulus.

Advantages of thiazide as an antihypertensive:

  • It can be given as once a day dose and has a flat dose-response curve.
  • Decreased incidence of postural hypotension and relative freedom from CNS side effects
  • No tolerance
  • No fluid retention
  • Decreased risk of osteoporotic fractures due to its hypocalciuric action
  • Low cost
  • Effectiveness in isolated systolic hypertension

Thiazides are ineffective both as antihypertensive and diuretic in patients with chronic renal failure.

High ceiling diuretics: Furosemide is the prototype drug in this class and it is a weaker antihypertensive agent than thiazides. They are given in hypertension only in the presence of the following complications:

  • Chronic renal failure - As thiazides are ineffective
  • Coexisting refractory congestive heart failure
  • Resistance to combination regimen with thiazides
  • Marked fluid retention with the use of potent vasodilators.

Potassium-sparing diuretics - They are only used in combination with thiazides to prevent the loss of potassium.

Side effects of diuretics include hypokalemia, carbohydrate intolerance, dyslipidemia, and hyperuricemia.

If there is downregulation of this enzyme it will cause a decrease in the efficacy of clopidogrel and can lead to thrombotic events like stroke. Drugs that inhibit CYP2C19 can also decrease the antiplatelet effect of clopidogrel. Therapeutic uses: Clopidogrel is used to reduce the rate of stroke and myocardial infarction. It also decreases the rate of deaths in patients with recent myocardial infarction or stroke. Other uses are acute coronary syndrome and peripheral arterial disease.

Adverse effects: Increased risk of bleeding especially when given with an anticoagulant or aspirin. Rarely thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura can occur.

CYP2C19: Common drugs that are metabolized include omeprazole, phenytoin, diazepam, and propanolol. Inducers of the CYP2C subfamily are rifampicin and carbamazepine. Omeprazole is an inhibitor.

Other options:

CYP1A1/2: It metabolizes few drugs like theophylline, paracetamol, caffeine and carbamazepine. It plays an important role in the activation of procarcinogens. Inducers are rifampicin, carbamazepine, polycyclic hydrocarbons, charbroiled meat, and cigarette smoke.

CYP2E1: It is involved in the oxidation of alcohol, halothane, and minor metabolism of other drugs. It is important to note that it is involved in the formation of hepatotoxic N-acetyl benzoquinone imine from paracetamol. Chronic alcoholism is responsible for the induction of this enzyme.

questions.question: Which of the following steps does Vancomycin act on?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 4

Vancomycin acts on step 4 in the given image.

Mechanism of action of vancomycin: It is a cell wall synthesis inhibitor. It binds to the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of the newly formed peptidoglycan pentapeptide and inhibits the transglycosylase enzyme. This would prevent further elongation of the peptidoglycan and its cross-linking.

Vancomycin is a bactericidal agent for gram-positive organisms. It is also active against many gram-positive anaerobes like Clostridium difficile. Resistance against vancomycin in enterococci is due to the alternation in its binding site where D-Ala is replaced by D-Lactate.

Clinical uses:

  • Parenteral vancomycin is given for bloodstream infections and endocarditis caused by MRSA.
  • Vancomycin plus gentamicin is given as an alternative regimen for enterococcal endocarditis with penicillin allergy.
  • In combination with other agents for suspected meningitis or meningitis due to penicillin-resistant pneumococcus.
  • Oral vancomycin is given for Clostridium difficile colitis.

Adverse effects:

  • Injection site phlebitis
  • Nephrotoxicity
  • "Redman" syndrome due to histamine release following infusion

Other options:

Fosfomycin inhibits step 1 in the image. It acts at a very early stage in cell wall synthesis and inhibits the cytoplasmic enzyme enol pyruvate transferase. This would block the addition of phosphoenolpyruvate to UDP-N-acetylglucosamine. This prevents the formation of UDP-N-acetylmuramic acid which is the precursor N-acetylmuramic acid. N-acetylmuramic acid is a component of the bacterial cell wall and hence cell wall synthesis is inhibited.

Cycloserine inhibits step 2 in the image. It is a structural analog of D-alanine and inhibits the enzymes alanine racemase that converts L-alanine to D-alanine and d-alanyl-d-alanine ligase. This would thereby inhibit the incorporation of D-alanine into the peptidoglycan pentapeptide. It is mainly used in the management of tuberculosis where there is resistance to the first-line agents.

Bacitracin inhibits step 3 in the image. It is a cell wall synthesis inhibitor that interferes with dephosphorylation in the cycling of the lipid carrier which transfers peptidoglycan subunits to the growing cell wall. It is only given for topical application because of its severe nephrotoxicity when given systemically.

Note:

Beta-lactam antibiotics prevent cross-linking by inhibiting the transpeptidases. (Last step in the images)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: The elimination rate constant of a drug is 0.05/hr. What is its half-life?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 13.8 hours

The half-life of the given drug is 13.8 hours.

The half-life of a drug or t1/2 is the time taken for the plasma concentration to be reduced by 50%. The elimination rate constant or k value of a drug reflects the fraction of drug removed from the body compartment per unit of time.

The half-life of a drug and its elimination rate constant are inversely proportional to each other. They are represented by the equation: 

k t1/2 =  0.693

Therefore, t1/2 = 0.693/ k

The given value for elimination rate constant 𝑘 is 0.05, therefore the half-life of the given drug would be:

 0.693/ 0.05 = 13.8

Therefore, the half-life of the drug would be 13.8 hours.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: Category A, B, C, D, X in drug classification are indicative of which of the following?
options: Cost ratio from cheap to e​xpensive
As per safety or therapeut​ic index
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Safety in pregnancy

Category A, B, C, D, X in drug classification are indicative of their safety in pregnancy.

The united states food and drug administration (FDA) system for teratogenic potential attempts to quantify teratogenic risk from category A (safe) to category X (definite human teratogenic risk).

Category A: The possibility of fetal harm is remote and studies in women have failed to demonstrate any evidence of risk to the fetus. Examples: doxylamine, folic acid, levothyroxine.

Category B: Either animal-reproduction studies have not demonstrated a fetal risk, but there are no controlled studies in pregnant women, or animal-reproduction studies have shown an adverse effect that was not confirmed in controlled studies in pregnant women. Example: Amoxicillin, loratadine, ondansetron.

Category C: Either studies in animals have revealed adverse effects on the fetus, that is, teratogenic or embryocidal but there are no controlled studies in women, or studies in women and animals are not available. These drugs should be given only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus. Example: fluconazole, metoprolol, sertraline.

Category D: Though there is evidence of human fetal risk, the benefits from use in pregnant women may be acceptable despite the risk, for example, if the drug is needed in a life-threatening situation or for a disease for which safer drugs cannot be used or are ineffective. Example: lisinopril, lithium, phenytoin.

Category X: There is evidence of fetal risk based on human or animal experience and the risk of the use of the drug in pregnant women clearly outweighs any possible benefit. The drug is contraindicated in women who are or may become pregnant. Example: methotrexate, simvastatin, warfarin.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: Identify the false statement regarding suicidal inhibition.
options: The inhibitor can bind wit​h any site resulting in s‌uicidal inhibition
The binding of the enzyme ​to the substrate analogue‌ is irreversible
They are enzyme specific a​nd used in rational drug ‌design
The inhibitor forms a prod​uct with the enzyme and t‌he product inhibits it
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. The inhibitor can bind with any site resulting in suicidal inhibition

The false statement regarding suicidal inhibition is the inhibitor can bind with any site resulting in suicidal inhibition.

In suicidal inhibition, the inhibitor can only bind with the active site of an enzyme and is unreactive outside the confines of the enzyme's active site. 

The enzyme inhibition helps to modify the rate of reactions it catalyzes and this inhibition can either be reversible or irreversible. Reversible inhibitors bind to enzymes through non-covalent bonds. Irreversible inhibitors usually bind to an enzyme through covalent bonds and do so strongly so that it can no longer dissociate.

Suicide inhibitors are a category of irreversible inhibitors also called mechanism-based inhibitors. They are specialized substrate analogs that contain a chemical group that reacts with the catalytic machinery of the target enzyme. In these types of inhibitors, the substrate analog irreversibly ties up with the binding site of an enzyme, deceiving the enzyme by concealing its functional group resulting in the formation of a highly reactive molecule, which brings about self-inactivation of the enzyme.

Suicide inhibitors bind to the enzyme by means of covalent bonds; they are enzyme-specific and unreactive outside the confines of the enzyme’s active site.

An example of this would be the binding of clavulanic acid to the active site of beta-lactamases in bacteria. Clavulanic acid mimics the structure of a beta-lactam antibiotic and forms a covalent adduct with the β-lactamase active site. This leads to a rearrangement that creates a much more reactive derivative, which is subsequently attacked in its active site to irreversibly acylate the enzyme and inactivate it. Thus, amoxicillin and clavulanic acid are combined to overcome bacterial resistance to amoxicillin alone.

The development of clavulanic acid to target beta-lactamase-producing bacteria is also an example of the rational design of drugs. Rational design of drugs refers to the ability to predict the appropriate molecular structure of a drug on the basis of information about its biological receptor.

questions.question: What is the mechanism of action of remdesivir?

The mechanism of action of remdesivir is inhibition of the enzyme RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.

Remdesivir is an adenosine nucleotide prodrug. It distributes into cells where it is metabolized to form remdesivir triphosphate (RDV-TP). It binds to the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase and inhibits viral replication by prematurely terminating RNA transcription. 

Remdesivir (under Emergency Use Authorization) is used in the treatment of COVID-19. It may be considered in patients with moderate to severe disease, requiring supplemental oxygen, within 10 days of onset of the illness.

  • Patients <12 years of age
  • Patients who are not on oxygen support or in-home settings

Option A- RNA-dependent DNA Polymerase / reverse transcriptase inhibitors prevent the conversion of viral RNA into proviral DNA. They help to prevent infection of susceptible cells but do not eradicate the virus from cells that are integrated with proviral DNA. Options C and D- Entry/fusion inhibitors include enfuvirtide and maraviroc. Enfuvirtide inhibits the fusion of viral and cell membranes mediated by gp41 and CD4 interactions. Maraviroc is a chemokine receptor antagonist and binds to host cell CCR5 receptor to block binding of viral gp120. They are also used to manage HIV infection.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: Administration of which of the following drugs would increase the bioavailability of saquinavir?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ritonavir

Administration of ritonavir would increase the bioavailability of saquinavir.

Saquinavir is an HIV protease inhibitor that inhibits replication of both HIV-1 and HIV-2. It is metabolized predominantly by the hepatic enzyme CYP3A4. Inhibition of CYP3A4 results in an increase or a boost in the concentration of saquinavir.  Ritonavir is one such drug that inhibits CYP3A4. Therefore combining it with a protease inhibitor like saquinavir results in:

  • Enhanced bioavailability
  • Inhibition of systemic clearance
  • Inhibition of first-pass metabolism, and
  • Longer half-life of the co-administered HIV protease inhibitor.

This allows for a reduction of drug dose and dosing frequency of saquinavir.

All protease inhibitors except for nelfinavir are predominantly metabolized by CYP3A4. Therefore, the administration of CYP3A4 inhibitors like ritonavir or cobicistat can increase the bioavailability of these protease inhibitors. This phenomenon is known as boosting protease inhibitors by CYP inhibitors. The dosage of ritonavir, when given as a booster drug, is 100 to 200mg once or twice daily.

Option C: Cimetidine is a histamine 2 receptor antagonist which is used to promote gastric and duodenal ulcer healing. It is used in the management of gastroesophageal reflux disease. It also inhibits CYPs, but only ritonavir and cobicistat are used for boosting protease inhibitors.

Option D: Ganciclovir is a guanine nucleoside analogue which has inhibitory activity against all herpes viruses, especially cytomegalovirus (CMV).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question:
The table below gives the AUC of drug B alone and that of drug B when combined with another drug A. If the 𝑝 value is <0.01, then which of the following statements is true?
Drug  Area Under Curve (AUC)
Drug B  570 seconds ± 127 seconds
Drug B + Drug A  820 seconds ± 124 seconds
options: Drug A decreases intestina​l absorption of Drug B
Drug A reduces first pass ​metabolism of Drug B
Drug A increases the metab​olism of Drug B
Drug A increases renal eli​mination of Drug B
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Drug A reduces first pass metabolism of Drug B

Drug A reduces the first-pass metabolism of Drug B.

The area under the plot of plasma concentration of a drug versus time after dosage is called the area under the curve or AUC. It can be used as a measure of the bioavailability of a drug and to calculate its clearance rate from the body.

Bioavailability refers to the extent to which an administered dose of the drug reaches its site of action; if the metabolic and excretory capacity of the intestine or liver for the drug is large, bioavailability is reduced substantially and this is called the first-pass metabolism whereas bioavailability is increased if intestinal absorption of the drug is increased.

The greater the AUC, the greater is the bioavailability of the drug.

In the question, is observed that when drug A was given along with drug B, the total AUC has increased (820 seconds ± 124 seconds) when compared to the AUC when drug B is administered alone (570 seconds ± 127 seconds).

The null hypothesis for the above question would be that drug A doesn't increase the AUC for drug B and for this to be true, 𝑝 value should be >0.05.

As given 𝑝 value is <0.01, it is significant and the null hypothesis is rejected, which means that drug A has indeed increased the AUC for drug B.

This indicates increased bioavailability of drug B when administered with drug A, which shows that drug A has either increased the intestinal absorption of drug B or has reduced its first-pass metabolism.

Other options:

Option A: If drug A decreased the intestinal absorption of drug B, this would mean that the AUC for drug B, when administered with drug A, would be reduced. This is due to decreased bioavailability of drug B when given with drug A.

Option C: If drug A increases the metabolism of drug B, this would lead to a shorter t1/2 and duration of action of drug B, thereby decreasing the AUC for when drug B and drug A are given together.

Option D: If drug A increased the elimination of drug B, the AUC for drug B when given with drug A would be reduced due to reduced duration of action of drug B.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question:
What is the mechanism of action of cyclosporine?

AMP - Adenosine monophosphate
IMP - Inosine monophosphate
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Inhibition of calcineurin

The mechanism of action of cyclosporine is inhibition of calcineurin activity.

Calcineurin is a calcium/calmodulin-dependent phosphatase required for the induction of T cell lymphokine production and proliferation. Cyclosporine is an immunomodulatory drug that inhibits calcineurin activity by forming a complex with cyclophilin, a cytoplasmic-receptor protein present in target cells, to form a cyclosporine-cyclophilin complex. This drug-receptor complex specifically and competitively binds to and inhibits calcineurin, a calcium and calmodulin-dependent phosphatase. This in turn, inhibits the translocation of a family of transcription factors (NF-AT), leading to reduced transcriptional activation of cytokine genes for interleukin (IL)-2, tumour necrosis factor (TNF)-alpha, IL-3, IL-4, CD40L, granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor, and interferon-gamma. Ultimately, the proliferation of T lymphocytes is reduced, resulting in immunomodulation.

Its uses are :

  • In solid organ transplantation, to treat organ rejection in kidney, liver, and heart allogeneic transplants.
  • In patients with rheumatoid arthritis, when the disease has not adequately responded to methotrexate.
  • It is approved to treat amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS or Lou Gehrig disease) and its variants.
  • In nephrotic syndrome, to treat focal segmental glomerulosclerosis not responding to corticosteroids.

Adverse effects of cyclosporine include a decrease in glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and metabolic disturbances like hypomagnesemia, hyperkalemia, dyslipidemia, gynecomastia, hypertrichosis; neurotoxicity in the form of convulsions. There is an increased risk of developing skin and lymphoproliferative malignancies in cyclosporine-treated psoriasis patients.

Other options:

Option B: AMP kinase is stimulated by metformin, a first-line orally administered drug in the management of type-2 diabetes mellitus.

Option C: IMP dehydrogenase is inhibited reversibly by the drug mycophenolate mofetil, which is indicated in the prophylaxis of transplant rejection.

Option D: Dihydro-orotate dehydrogenase is inhibited by leflunomide, a pyrimidine synthesis inhibitor indicated for the management of rheumatoid arthritis in adults.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: Anionic and weakly acidic drugs bind to which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Albumin

Anionic and weakly acidic drugs bind to albumin.

After being distributed in the circulating blood, drugs bind to serum proteins to varying degrees. Among serum proteins, albumin and alpha-1 acid glycoprotein play important roles in protein binding for many drugs, which affects their distribution in the body.

Albumin is a major carrier of and binds to acidic drugs like phenytoin, NSAIDs. Whereas, α-1 acid glycoprotein binds basic drugs like lignocaine,disopyramide, quinidine and propranolol.

Importance of plasma protein binding:

Conditions resulting in acute phase reaction response leading to elevated levels of alpha-1 acid glycoprotein like Crohn’s disease, myocardial infarction, arthritis, cancer, etc. enhance binding of basic drugs. Conditions causing hypoalbuminemia result in decreased binding sites for acidic drugs. 

When a drug is bound to the plasma proteins, it is kept in the blood, while the unbound (free) drug can produce a therapeutic effect, be metabolized, or excreted. In the majority of the drugs, this does not have a significant effect, but in drugs with a narrow therapeutic index like warfarin, it is clinically relevant as excessive free warfarin can produce toxicity.

Many drugs displace other drugs from their protein binding sites. This may cause an increase in the pharmacological effect of the displaced drug. 

A drug bound to a plasma protein cannot cross membranes and this bound fraction of a drug is also not available for metabolism or glomerular filtration which can make the drug long-acting.

Other options:

Option B- Globulins are of three types - α,β, and γ-globulins. Globulins bind glucocorticoids and progesterone in the blood.

Option C- Lipoproteins like VLDL, LDL can bind anti-cancer drugs like 5-fluorouracil and doxorubicin.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: A 14-month-old boy was diagnosed with Hemophilus influenza meningitis. The initial treatment plan was to start on ampicillin but later was shifted to ceftriaxone. What could be the probable reason?
options: Hemophilus alters penicill​in binding protein sites,‌ hence resistant to ampic‍illin
Easier to administer IV ce​ftriaxone than IV ampicil‌lin
Cotrimoxazole is the drug ​of choice, but patient is‌ allergic to sulfa drugs
Hemophilus produces beta l​actamase, hence resistant‌ to ampicillin
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hemophilus produces beta lactamase, hence resistant to ampicillin

The probable reason why the drug to be administered was changed from ampicillin to ceftriaxone is because Hemophilus produces beta-lactamase and hence, is resistant to ampicillin.

A considerable percentage of isolates of Hemophilus influenzae produce beta-lactamase, rendering them resistant to ampicillin, a beta-lactam antibiotic. However, these strains are still sensitive to second and third-generation cephalosporins.

In H. influenzae, the resistance to ampicillin and other β-lactam antibiotics is generally due to the production of a β-lactamase. In the case of β-lactamase-negative ampicillin-resistant strains, resistance is due to the presence of altered penicillin-binding proteins. 

Ceftriaxone is a third-generation cephalosporin that is effective against Hemophilus Influenzae and considerably resistant to beta-lactamase. It has a very long half-life which permits once-daily dosing of the drug. Because of the efficacy of third-generation cephalosporins in the therapy of meningitis caused by Hemophilus Influenzae type b, ceftriaxone administered at the rate of 50 mg/kg/dose given 12th hourly should be a part of the initial empirical therapy.

Vancomycin combined with a third-generation cephalosporin like ceftriaxone is the recommended empirical antibiotic regimen in a suspected case of meningitis, beyond the neonatal period.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: A patient who is a known case of cirrhosis of the liver presents with abdominal distension and swelling of the lower limbs. The preferred diuretic for this patient would be
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Eplerenone

The preferred diuretic for this patient with cirrhosis presenting with abdominal distension and lower limb swelling is eplerenone.

Eplerenone is a mineralocorticoid receptor/aldosterone antagonist. High doses of mineralocorticoid receptor/aldosterone antagonists decrease total body sodium in cirrhotic patients with ascites by natriuresis. 

Patients with liver cirrhosis have a decreased effective arterial blood volume because of splanchnic vasodilatation. This stimulates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and results in hyperaldosteronism. This causes increased sodium and water retention and leads to the development of ascites. This also contributes to resistance to loop diuretics. 

Normally, aldosterone (AL) enters the cells of the late distal tubule and collecting ducts by diffusion and binds to a specific mineralocorticoid receptor (MR) in the cytoplasm. This AL-MR complex mediates Na+ reabsorption, which drives the secretion of K+ and H+into the tubules.

Eplerenone competitively blocks this MR, preventing it from binding with aldosterone. The net effect is sodium diuresis and potassium retention. It is a potassium-sparing diuretic. Other mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists include spironolactone, canrenone, potassium canrenoate.

Some clinical uses of MR antagonists are - 

  • Hypertension due to primary hyperaldosteronism 
  • Edema associated with liver cirrhosis, congestive cardiac failure, chronic kidney disease
  • They may reduce mortality in patients with myocardial infarction

Hyperkalemia is the major side effect of MR antagonists, the risk being greater in patients with renal disease or those already taking ACE inhibitors. Other important side effects are gynecomastia and decreased libido due to the anti-androgenic effect of spironolactone but eplerenone does not cause gynecomastia and decreased libido.

Other options : 

Option A- Triamterene directly inhibits renal epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) in the late distal tubule and collecting duct. It is a potassium-sparing diuretic and is generally used along with other diuretics in the treatment of hypertension and edema. Triamterene is metabolized in the liver, hence triamterene toxicity may be enhanced in patients with hepatic disease. It is used in the management of Liddle syndrome.

Option C- Chlorthalidone is a thiazide-like diuretic. It inhibits Na+-Cl- symporter in the early distal tubule and increases the excretion of sodium and chloride. Thiazide diuretics may be used for the treatment of hypertension, heart failure, nephrolithiasis due to idiopathic hypercalciuria, and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

Option D- Furosemide is a loop diuretic. It acts by inhibiting the Na+-K+-2Cl- symporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle resulting in increased excretion of sodium and chloride. It also has mild carbonic anhydrase inhibitory activity and also increases urinary excretion of bicarbonate and phosphate. Cirrhotic patients are often resistant to loop diuretics due to decreased secretion of the drug into tubular fluid and high aldosterone levels. Furosemide may be given along with eplerenone, but the best answer here is eplerenone since aldosterone antagonists are the main therapy for cirrhotic edema.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question:
Which of the following is the most effective drug in smoking cessation?

SR: Sustained release
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Varenicline

Varenicline is the most effective drug in smoking cessation.

Nicotine is the principal constituent of tobacco responsible for its addictive behaviour. One of the newest agents introduced to aid in smoking cessation is varenicline.

Varenicline works by blocking the effects of nicotine on the brain. It blocks α-4, β-2 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor subtypes and varenicline inhibits dopaminergic activation produced by smoking through their partial agonism, and decreases the craving and withdrawal syndrome that occurs with cessation attempts. It prevents nicotine stimulation of the mesolimbic dopamine system associated with nicotine addiction, thus helping to occlude the "rewarding" effect of smoking.

Varenicline is prescribed only to patients 18 years or older. Varenicline is taken orally and the dose taken is 0.5 mg once daily on days 1 to 3, increased to 0.5 mg twice daily on days 4 through 7 and 1 mg twice daily after day 8 for 11 weeks. Therapy should start one week before the target quit date. It can be continued for another 12 weeks (1 mg BD) to maintain abstinence.

The adverse effects include nausea, which can be mitigated by starting at lower doses and gradually increasing the dose. Other symptoms include disturbed sleep, sleepwalking, agitation, drowsiness, and constipation and may also increase the risk of pancreatitis. Varenicline has also been implicated in specific skin syndromes such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome, erythema multiforme, and photosensitivity. Varenicline can cause renal failure and kidney stones, thus renal function must be monitored.

The FDA has issued a warning about mood and behavioral changes associated with its use, and there is some evidence of increased cardiovascular risk.

Other options:

Option B: Buspirone sustained release is a partial agonist at 5HT receptors but affinity for D2 receptors may also be present. Its effects are slow onset, over a couple of weeks and is used in the management of generalised anxiety states.

Option C: Nicotine gum has nicotine which is an agonist at Nn type nicotinic cholinergic receptors and is also advised for smoking cessation along with psychotherapy. However, varenicline was more effective when compared with single‐product nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) and was similarly effective compared with combination NRT.

Option D: Rimonabant is an inverse agonist at cannabinoid receptor CB1 which decreases neurotransmitter release at GABAergic and glutamatergic synapses; its usage for smoking cessation and treat obesity was stopped after serious side effects notably severe depression and increased risk of suicide. However, it continues to be used off-label for smoking cessation.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: A patient who was on warfarin therapy for atrial fibrillation is prescribed a cephalosporin antibiotic for the treatment of a lower respiratory tract infection. He reports back to the hospital after having developed hemarthrosis. Which of the following cephalosporins is likely to have caused this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cefoperazone

The cephalosporin antibiotic most likely to have caused hemarthrosis in this patient on warfarin therapy is cefoperazone.

Cephalosporins containing a methylthiotetrazole (NMTT) group can prolong the prothrombin time. This results in clinically significant bleeding in patients already on anticoagulant therapy or having vitamin K deficiency. 

This is because NMTT cephalosporins inhibit the enzyme vitamin K epoxide reductase in the liver, which is the key enzyme for vitamin K-dependent carboxylation, a posttranslational modification that is essential for the biological functions of coagulation factors. 
NMTT group containing cephalosporins include latamoxef, cefmenoxime, cefoperazone, cefotetan, cefamandole.

Vitamin K epoxide reductase is also the target of anticoagulants like warfarin. Oral administration of vitamin K can prevent this problem.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: Which of the following is a novel anti-depressant?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vilazodone

Vilazodone is the novel antidepressant.

The antidepressant effect of vilazodone is due to its enhancement of serotonergic activity in the CNS through selective inhibition of serotonin reuptake. It binds with high affinity to the serotonin reuptake site but not to the norepinephrine or dopamine reuptake site. As a result, vilazodone potently and selectively inhibits the reuptake of serotonin.

Vilazodone is also a partial agonist at serotonergic 5-HT1A receptors; the result of this activity on serotonergic transmission also plays a role in its antidepressant effect.

Thus it offers a novel combination of selective serotonin reuptake inhibition (SSRI) and serotonergic (5-HT1A) receptor partial agonist activity. Because of these characteristics, vilazodone has been termed a serotonin partial agonist–reuptake inhibitor (SPARI).

Vilazodone is never combined with a monoamine oxidase (MAO) inhibitor or given within 14 days of discontinuing or initiating MAO inhibitor therapy due to the serious risk of serotonin toxicity.

Other options:

Option A: Lurasidone is a second-generation antipsychotic that is a 5-HT2A and D2 receptor antagonist. it is used in the treatment of schizophrenia and bipolar depression (as monotherapy or as an adjunct).

Option C: Asenapine is a second-generation antipsychotic which is also a 5-HT2A and D2 receptor antagonist, used in the management of schizophrenia and acute mania.

Option D: Blonanserin is a second-generation antipsychotic, which acts as an antagonist at D2, D3, and 5-HT2A receptors. Blonanserin has a low affinity for 5-HT2C, adrenergic α1, histamine H1, and muscarinic M1 receptors, but displays a relatively high affinity for 5-HT6 receptors. It is used in the management of schizophrenia.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: A 57-year-old man was brought to the hospital with complaints of dizziness and breathlessness. During his physical examination, you notice the following discolouration over his face. He is presently being treated with amiodarone, metoprolol, verapamil, lisinopril, and amlodipine. Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Amiodarone

The image shows grey-blue discoloration over this patient's face and the drug responsible for this is amiodarone.

Long-term treatment with amiodarone is responsible for skin pigmentation. Elderly men are at an increased risk of developing this. 

Ultraviolet light reacts with amiodarone and its metabolites to cause local vasodilatation. This increases the diffusion of amiodarone and its metabolites, resulting in their deposition in the tissues, causing pigmentation. Therefore, it is usually seen in sun-exposed areas.

Cessation of amiodarone, avoiding exposure to sunlight using sunscreen cream is recommended.

Amiodarone is an iodine-containing compound that is structurally related to thyroid hormone. It is a class III antiarrhythmic drug, which increases the duration of an action potential by blocking potassium channels. It thereby increases the time taken for repolarization. It also prolongs the refractory period and suppresses abnormal automaticity. It also has weak calcium channel blocking, sodium channel blocking, and adrenergic blocking actions.

It is used to maintain normal sinus rhythm during atrial fibrillation and prevent recurrent ventricular tachycardia. 

Adverse effects of amiodarone:

  • Prolonged usage of amiodarone causes interstitial lung disease.
  • Heart blocks, bradycardia and QT prolongation
  • Hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism
  • Corneal micro-deposits and vortex keratopathy, optic neuropathy

Drug interactions of amiodarone

  • Causes digoxin toxicity by decreasing its renal clearance.
  • Increases concentration of quinidine and procainamide
  • Potentiates the anticoagulant effect of warfarin when given simultaneously

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question:
The anti-epileptic drugs which can also be used for the treatment of neuropathic pain are

  1. Pregabalin
  2. Carbamazepine
  3. Lamotrigine
  4. Gabapentin
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2 and 4

The anti-epileptic drugs which can also be used for neuropathic pain are 1, 2, and 4 which are pregabalin, carbamazepine and gabapentin respectively.

Pregabalin is an anti-epileptic drug that acts by binding to α2δ, a protein that is a subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels and causes a decrease in glutamate release at excitatory synapses. It is used in the management of neuropathic pain associated with diabetic peripheral neuropathy, spinal cord injury or postherpetic neuralgia.

Gabapentin is an anti-epileptic drug that, like pregabalin, acts by binding to α2δ protein. It is used in the management of neuropathic pain due to postherpetic neuralgia in adults.

The binding of gabapentin and pregabalin, also called "gabapentinoids" due to their structural similarity to GABA, to calcium channel subunit a2δ protein, is considered to mediate the anti-convulsant effects of gabapentin and pregabalin. They are used in focal onset seizures with or without progression to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures when used in addition to other anti-epileptic drugs.

Carbamazepine is an iminostilbine derivative. It blocks voltage-activated sodium channels, slowing their rate of recovery and limiting the repetitive firing of action potentials. It is used in the treatment of:

  • Generalized, focal-to-bilateral and idiopathic tonic-clonic seizures
  • Focal seizures
  • Neuropathic pain associated with trigeminal and glossopharyngeal neuralgias.

Lamotrigine is an anti-folate agent whose mechanism of action is similar to that of carbamazepine i.e. it delays the recovery from inactivation of recombinant sodium channels. It also inhibits the release of glutamate by acting directly on the sodium channels. Therefore, when used concurrently with carbamazepine, is associated with toxicity in some patients due to increase in 10,11- epoxide of carbamazepine. It is useful in the management of:

  • Focal and secondarily generalized tonic-clonic seizures in adults
  • Lennox-Gastaut syndrome - a childhood disorder characterized by multiple type seizures, mental retardation, and refractoriness to anti-seizure medication.

Pharmacologic management of osteoporosis:

Bisphosphonates: These are pyrophosphate analogs that act by directly inhibiting bone resorption. The antiresorptive action is mainly due to its direct inhibitory effect on osteoclasts. It causes osteoclast apoptosis as well as the prevention of hydroxyapatite dissolution. Long-term bisphosphonates therapy is given for durations of 3-5 years, depending on the fracture risk of the patient. Since they are associated with osteonecrosis of the jaw and atypical femur fractures, a drug holiday may be advised after long-term management.

Teriparatide is a recombinant PTH analog that has an anabolic effect on bone homeostasis by increasing osteoblastic activity. It increases bone mineral density and decreases the risk of fractures in postmenopausal women. Indications of teriparatide therapy include the history of osteoporotic fracture, multiple risk factors for fracture, intolerance, or failure of previous osteoporosis therapy. It is only approved for 2 years of use. Clinical trials that used teriparatide prior to bisphosphonate have been proven effective.

Denosumab is a human monoclonal antibody with a mechanism of action similar to that of osteoprotegerin (OPG). It binds to RANK Ligand (RANKL), thereby inhibiting its binding to the RANK receptor of the surface of osteoclasts. This prevents RANK receptor activation and subsequent bone resorption.

Selective estrogen receptor modulators (SERMs) - Estrogen has a protective effect that prevents accelerated bone loss. This is carried out by reducing the bone resorption effects of parathyroid hormone (PTH). Keeping in line with these effects, osteoporosis prevention in postmenopausal women has been attributed to the use of SERMs such as raloxifene. It acts as an estrogen agonist on the bone and liver.

Calcium and Vitamin D supplementation: Calcium supplementation in the elderly suppresses bone turnover and improves bone mineral density. 1200mg of calcium is daily required in adults of more than 50 years of age. Vitamin D supplementation with 400-800IU/day improves intestinal calcium absorption, suppresses bone remodeling, and improves bone mineral density.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: What formula is the dosing rate of a drug based on?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Clearance x plasma concentration

The formula for drug dosing rate is clearance x plasma concentration.

The equation for dose rate given here is based on steady-state concentration. When a drug is given repeatedly at short intervals it will accumulate in the body until the elimination of the drug matches its input. So steady-state concentration is the plasma concentration at which the drug elimination and drug input balance each other.

Steady-state concentration(Cpss) = Dose rate / Clearance

From this equation dose rate for a target steady-state plasma concentration is calculated as 

Dose rate = Clearance(CL) x target plasma concentration(Cpss)

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: A patient on digoxin, potassium chloride, clarithromycin, atenolol, and triamterene developed atrial fibrillation with controlled ventricular rate. Serum digoxin levels were raised. Which of his medications is responsible for the same?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Clarithromycin

Elevated serum digoxin levels and the development of atrial fibrillation with controlled ventricular rate are suggestive of digoxin toxicity. Clarithromycin when given along with digoxin can cause digoxin toxicity.

P-glycoprotein pumps play a major role in the elimination of digoxin. Drugs that inhibit P-glycoprotein can thereby decrease the elimination of digoxin and lead to digoxin toxicity. Macrolide antibiotics like clarithromycin and erythromycin are inhibitors of the P-glycoprotein. So clarithromycin when given along with digoxin can cause digoxin toxicity.

Other drugs that inhibit P-glycoprotein are - Amiodarone, quinidine, verapamil, diltiazem, cyclosporine, itraconazole, propafenone, and flecainide.

Digoxin is one of the cardiac glycosides which is derived from the digitalis plant and used clinically.

It inhibits Na+/K+ ATPase, a membrane-bound transporter to increase intracellular sodium. As a result, there is less expulsion of calcium from the cell by sodium-calcium exchanger (NCX). Increased calcium inside the myocyte leads to an increase in cardiac contractility.

The most common cardiac manifestations of digitalis toxicity include atrioventricular junctional rhythm, premature ventricular depolarizations, ventricular bigeminy, ventricular tachycardia, and second-degree AV blockade.

Factors that increase the risk of digoxin toxicity are:

  • Hypercalcemia
  • Hypomagnesemia
  • Hypokalemia- It increases the binding of the digoxin to the Na+/K+ ATPase pump. 
  • Drugs causing hypokalemia- loop and thiazide diuretics, amphotericin B, corticosteroids
  • Drugs that decrease digoxin elimination (inhibitors of P-glycoprotein)
  • Renal failure
  • Hypothyroidism

 Triamterene, atenolol, and potassium chloride cause hyperkalemia, and therefore do not cause digoxin toxicity.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: The extent of drug absorption is represented by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Area under the curve

The extent of drug absorption is represented by the area under the curve.

The rate and extent of absorption of a drug from dosage form administered by any route refer to the bioavailability of a drug. Bioavailability is determined by the concentration-time curve in blood or by its excretion in urine. The area under the blood concentration-time curve (AUC) is proportional to the dose and the extent of bioavailability of a drug.

Bioavailability is defined as the fraction of unchanged drug that reaches systemic circulation. It can be represented by the formula:

Bioavailability(F) = Quantity of drug reaching systemic circulation/ Quantity of drug administered.

Bioavailability depends on two factors:

  • Absorption
  • 1st pass metabolism

The area under the plot of plasma concentration of a drug versus time after dosage is called the area under the curve or AUC. It can be used as a measure of the bioavailability of a drug and to calculate its clearance rate from the body.

N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI) is a metabolite of paracetamol drug toxicity. 

Paracetamol is an analgesic and antipyretic with weak anti-inflammatory action. It is mainly metabolized in the liver by conjugation with glucuronic acid and sulfate and is excreted in the urine.

Paracetamol poisoning is the most common cause of liver failure necessitating transplantation.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: Identify the false statement about eicosanoids.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Synthesized from arginine

A false statement about eicosanoids is they are synthesized from arginine. Eicosanoids are synthesized from arachidonic acid (Option B)

Eicosanoids are the most universally distributed autocoids in the body. Prostaglandins, thromboxanes, and leukotrienes comprise eicosanoids. Every cell is capable of synthesizing one or more eicosanoids. Platelets primarily synthesize thromboxanes (Option D).

Eicosanoids are synthesized from arachidonic acid. Arachidonic acid is derived from membrane phospholipids. The release of arachidonic acid (AA) from the membrane phospholipids is mainly mediated by phospholipase A.

AA is metabolized by cyclooxygenases to produce prostaglandins and lipoxygenases to produce leukotrienes and lipoxins.

Inhibitors of metabolism of arachidonic acid:

  • Corticosteroids cause inhibition of prostaglandin synthesis by inhibiting phospholipase A2.
  • Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory (NSAIDs) drugs inhibit the synthesis of prostaglandins by inhibiting the enzyme cyclooxygenase.
  • Zileuton inhibits the enzyme lipoxygenase thereby decreasing the synthesis of leukotrienes.

Chemically, all prostaglandins are considered to be derivatives of prostanoic acid, having a five-carbon ring (Option C).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.question: The given diagram shows the steps in bacterial cell wall formation. Identify the site of action of beta-lactam antibiotics.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 4

Beta lactams act on step 4 in the given image.

Mechanism of action of beta-lactams: They are the cell wall synthesis inhibitor. The β-lactam antibiotics inhibit this last step in peptidoglycan synthesis. They inhibit the enzyme transpeptidase which is required for cross-linking of the peptidoglycan chain. Transpeptidases cleave the terminal D-alanine of the peptide chains and form cross-linkages between them. This cross-linking provides rigidity and stability to the cell wall.   

Transpeptidases and other related proteins constitute penicillin-binding proteins(PBP) and, are located in the bacterial cell membrane. β-lactam antibiotics are bactericidal. This is because bacterias swell and burst due to deficient cell walls when they divide in the presence of β-lactam antibiotics. Penicillins, cephalosporins, monobactams, and carbapenems are examples of β-lactam antibiotics.

Gram-positive bacteria are more susceptible to β-lactam antibiotics than gram-negative because their cell wall is almost entirely made of peptidoglycan.

Resistance to β-lactam antibiotics develops due to the production of the beta-lactamase enzyme and the development of altered penicillin-binding proteins like in methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). β-lactamases inactivate β-lactam antibiotics by opening the β-lactam ring. This could be overcome by using drugs that inhibit this enzyme. Examples of β-lactamase inhibitors are clavulanic acid, sulbactam, and tazobactam.

Other options:

Option A: Fosfomycin inhibits step 1 in the image. It inhibits the cytoplasmic enzyme enol pyruvate transferase that catalyses the initial step in the bacterial cell wall and hence cell wall synthesis. It is used for the treatment of urinary tract infections.

Option B: Bacitracin inhibits step 2 in the image. It is a cell wall synthesis inhibitor that interferes with dephosphorylation in the cycling of the lipid carrier which transfers peptidoglycan subunits to the growing cell wall. It is only given for topical application because of its severe nephrotoxicity when given systemically.

Option C: Vancomycin inhibits step 3 in the image. It binds to the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of the newly formed peptidoglycan pentapeptide. This prevents further elongation of the peptidoglycan and its cross-linking. It is used against MRSA and Clostridium difficile infection. Redman syndrome due to histamine release following infusion is an important side effect.

Note: The FDA has approved the use of cefepime-enmetazobactam, a combination of a fourth-generation cephalosporin and beta-lactamase inhibitor for use in complicated UTIs (including pyelonephritis).

questions.question: Phospholipase C acts via which of the following G protein-coupled receptors?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Gq

Phospholipase C acts via the Gq type of G protein-coupled receptors.

G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are cell membrane receptors that span across the membrane 7 times. They also serve as receptors for various peptide hormones, neurotransmitters, amino acids, etc.

Subtypes of GPCRs are distinguished by their alpha subunits. The important subtypes of GPCRs are Gs, Gp, Gq, and Go.

GPCRs act via various second messengers. The important ones with their action on the effector are:

  • Gs causes activation of adenylyl cyclase and results in Ca2+ channel opening.
  • Gi causes inhibition of adenylyl cyclase and results in K+ channel opening.
  • Go causes Ca2+ channel inhibition.
  • Gq causes activation of phospholipase C which generates the second messengers inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3) and diacylglycerol (DAG). The water-soluble IP3 diffuses to the cytosol and mobilizes Ca2+ from endoplasmic reticular depots.
