questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.question: A 35-year-old man presented with high fever, bleeding gums, myalgia, and hepatosplenomegaly. His TLC is 3100, Hb- 11 g/dl, hematocrit- 55%, and platelets - 25,000 cells. What is the most important prognostic factor in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hematocrit

The given clinical history of a patient with a fever, myalgia, gum bleeding, hepatosplenomegaly, and laboratory investigations showing anaemia, leukopenia, raised hematocrit and low platelets is suggestive of dengue with warning signs and hematocrit is the most important prognostic factor in this patient.

Hematocrit is the percentage of red blood cells in a given blood volume, and a rising hematocrit is a sign of hemoconcentration due to plasma leakage. As plasma leakage signifies the severity of the disease, hematocrit is monitored to assess prognosis.

Dengue is an arbovirus disease transmitted by Aedes aegypti and causes a clinical spectrum:

  • Probable dengue: fever with myalgia, nausea, vomiting, leukopenia or a positive tourniquet test.
  • Dengue with warning signs: abdominal pain, tenderness, persistent vomiting, fluid accumulation (pleural effusion, ascites), mucosal bleed, hepatomegaly(>2cm), rapid rise in hematocrit and fall in platelet count
  • Severe dengue: severe plasma leakage causing dengue shock syndrome, respiratory distress, severe hemorrhagic manifestations, severe organ involvement (AST or ALT >1000U/L, CNS manifestations, AKI, pancreatitis, DIC)

Other options:

Options B and C- Although dengue causes anaemia and leukopenia, they do not determine the prognosis of the disease.

Option D- Reduced platelet count is a warning sign but does not correlate with plasma leakage. Therefore hematocrit monitoring would be a better option.

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman presented with painful blisters on the skin and oral mucosa. Direct immunofluorescence is given below. Which of the following is false regarding the same?

questions.question: ALK positivity is seen in which of the following neoplasms:

Correct answer: D. Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour

ALK (anaplastic lymphoma kinase) positivity (translocation) is seen in Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor of lung.

ALK positivity means the rearrangements in the ALK gene on chromosome 2p23.

These rearrangements break the ALK locus leads to the formation of chimeric genes encoding signalling pathways.

ALK rearrangements carry a very good prognosis as they show good response to treatment with ALK kinase inhibitors. The tumours lacking ALK rearrangements have a substantially worse prognosis.

  • Neuroblastoma

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: Which of the following is true regarding the internal iron homeostasis in iron-deficiency anaemia?
options: Ferritin mRNA concentratio​n iron-responsive element​ increases and ferritin s‌ynthesis decreases
Transferrin receptor 1 iro​n-responsive elements inc​reases transferrin recept‌or mRNA concentration and​ synthesis
Transferrin receptor 1 iro​n responsive elements dec​reases transferrin recept‌or mRNA concentration and​ synthesis
Ferritin mRNA concentratio​n iron responsive element​ decreases and ferritin s‌ynthesis increases
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Transferrin receptor 1 iron-responsive elements increases transferrin receptor mRNA concentration and synthesis

In iron deficiency anaemia, there is an increase in transferrin receptor mRNA concentration and synthesis.

Iron absorbed through diet or which is released from circulation is bound to transferrin (iron transfer protein). When erythropoiesis is stimulated, iron-transferrin complexes act as transferrin receptors on the surface of bone marrow erythroid cells. Through receptor-mediated endocytosis, this complex is internalised. 

This iron is then made available for heme synthesis while the transferrin-receptor complex is recycled to the surface of the cell, from where the transferrin is released back into circulation and the transferrin receptor re-anchors into the cell membrane. The excess iron after hemoglobin synthesis binds to apoferritin (storage protein), forming ferritin. 

Senescent RBCs undergo phagocytosis in the cells of the reticuloendothelial system. The hemoglobin is broken down, the globin and other proteins are returned to the amino acid pool, and the iron is shuttled back to the surface of the reticuloendothelial cell, where it is taken up by transferrin via ferroportin (iron export channel).

There is no regulated excretory pathway for iron, and the only mechanisms by which iron is lost are blood loss (via gastrointestinal bleeding, menstruation, or other forms of bleeding) and the loss of epithelial cells from the skin, gut, and genitourinary tract. The normal daily iron loss from the body is 1-2 mg.

Variables Iron-deficient state  Iron-excess state
Iron uptake ↑ ↓
Transferrin receptor synthesis ↑ ↓
Transferrin receptor mRNA concentration ↑ ↓
Iron storage ↓ ↑
Ferritin synthesis ↓ ↑
Ferritin mRNA concentration No change No change

Histopathological image shows acellular periodic acid Schiff (PAS)-positive nodules suggestive of nodular glomerulosclerosis/intercapillary glomerulosclerosis/Kimmelstiel–Wilson disease, which occurs in patients with diabetic nephropathy.

These lesions appear as ovoid or spherical, often laminated, PAS-positive nodules within the mesangial core of the glomerular lobules.

These nodular lesions are frequently accompanied by prominent accumulations of hyaline material in capillary loops (“fibrin caps”) or adherent to Bowman capsules (“capsular drops”).

Renal failure is the second common cause of death in diabetes mellitus, the first being myocardial infarction.

Three renal lesions are encountered in diabetic nephropathy:

1. Glomerular lesions:

  1. Capillary basement membrane thickening
  2. Diffuse mesangial sclerosis
  3. Nodular glomerulosclerosis/Kimmelstiel–Wilson disease

2. Renal vascular lesions, principally hyaline arteriolosclerosis

3. Pyelonephritis, including necrotizing papillitis

Renal histopathology in

  • Amyloidosis: Glomerular deposits appearing as thickenings of the mesangial matrix, forming interlacing broad ribbons of amyloid
  • Lupus nephritis: Immune complex deposits in the mesangium or along the entire basement membrane (wire loop lesions), with mesangial cell proliferation
  • Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis: Focal and segmental hyalinosis and sclerosis of the capillary wall; lipid droplets in the sclerosed area.

T lymphocytes develop in the thymus from precursors that arise from hematopoietic stem cells. Mature T cells are found in the blood, where they constitute 60% to 70% of lymphocytes, and in T-cell zones of peripheral lymphoid organs.

  • Each T cell recognizes a specific cell-bound antigen by means of an antigen-specific T-cell receptor (TCR).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: Which of the following is not an intermediate filament?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tubulin

Tubulin is a part of microtubules and is not an intermediate filament.

There are three major classes of cytoskeletal proteins: microfilaments, intermediate filaments, and microtubules.

1. Actin microfilaments:

These fibrils formed from the globular protein actin (G-actin) noncovalently polymerize into long filaments (F-actin) that intertwine to form double-stranded helices.

2. Intermediate filaments:

These rope-like intermediate filament fibers are found predominantly in a polymerized form within cells and do not possess the quality of active reorganization like actin and microtubules. They are responsible for cellular tensile strength, which allows the cells to bear mechanical stress.

Type of intermediate filament Description
Lamin A, B, and C These proteins are localized in the nuclear lamina of all cells. Mutations in lamin proteins are associated with certain disorders such as familial partial lipodystrophy type 2, Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome, and familial dilated cardiomyopathy.
Vimentin These are mainly found in mesenchymal cells (fibroblasts, endothelium).
Desmin Present in sarcomeres in muscle cells.
Neurofilament These are found in neuronal axons, imparting strength and rigidity.
Glial fibrillary acidic protein Present in glial cells around neurons.
Cytokeratins

These proteins are the most diverse among IFs and constitute type I (acidic) and type II (basic) IF proteins.

There are at least 30 isoforms of this protein divided into two groups: Epithelial keratins (found in epithelial cells) and trichocytic keratins (found in hair-keratin).

3. Microtubules:

These are formed by non-covalent polymerization of a dimer of two globular proteins, alpha-tubulin, and beta-tubulin. The microtubules in most cells extend outward from a microtubule-organizing center (MTOC), in which the minus ends of microtubules are anchored.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: Which test evaluates the extrinsic pathway?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. PT

Prothrombin time (PT) evaluates the extrinsic pathway of coagulation.

PT measures the clotting time of plasma in the presence of an optimal concentration of tissue extract (thromboplastin). This indicates the overall efficiency of the extrinsic clotting system.

Causes of prolonged PT:

  • Administration of oral anticoagulant drugs - vitamin K antagonists
  • Liver disease - obstructive jaundice
  • Vitamin K deficiency
  • Disseminated intravascular coagulation
  • Previously undiagnosed factor VII, X, V or prothrombin deficiency or defect (rare)

Activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) measures the clotting time of plasma after the activation of contact factors and the addition of phospholipid and CaCl2, but without added tissue thromboplastin. It indicates the overall efficiency of the intrinsic pathway.

Causes of prolonged APTT:

  • Disseminated intravascular coagulation
  • Liver disease
  • Massive transfusion with plasma-depleted red blood cells
  • Administration of or contamination with heparin or other anticoagulants
  • A circulating anticoagulant (inhibitor)
  • Deficiency of a coagulation factor other than factor VII
  • Intake of oral anticoagulant drugs
  • Vitamin K deficiency

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: Which of the following is not a hemostatic agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Boric acid

Boric acid is not a hemostatic agent. 
 
Topical hemostatic agents used in practice include:
  • Hemostatic field dressings
  • Surgical hemostatic agents

1. The hemostatic field dressings are the granular and gauze-based agents which are used to facilitate coagulation and hemostasis. The active ingredients used in various hemostatic field dressings are kaolin, mineral zeolite, and chitosan.

 
Mechanism of action
Advantage
Disadvantage
Kaolin
Cation based activation of the intrinsic pathway of the coagulation cascade
It is non-granular compound. Hence, it does not leave any residue upon removal of the dressing
Clots may be disrupted upon removal. It is less effective in functional or dilutional coagulopathies.
Mineral zeolite
Adsorbs the water, thereby increasing the concentration of the clotting factors, platelets, RBCs.
It is available in two forms:
 
Granular zeolite is effective for pouring into low-flow wounds.
 
The mesh-embedded product is useful in high flow wounds.
The chemical reaction which causes adsorption of water is an exothermic reaction. This causes local tissue damage. The granules may be difficult to be removed.
Chetosan
Poly-N-acetylglucosamine is commonly known as chitin. The deacetylated form of chitin is called chitosan. It has mucoadhesive properties which causes the dressing to adhere to the tissues. It induces vasospasm and attracts RBCs and platelets to the site of bleeding.
It has antimicrobial properties. It can be easily applied and has a long shelf-life.
As the dressing material adheres to the tissues, it may cause disruption of the clots upon removal.

 

2. The surgical hemostatic agents are further divided into the following groups based on the nature of the agent:

 
  • Caustic agents: They act by causing local tissue destruction, which leads to protein coagulation and precipitation. This further leads to thrombus formation and sealing of the small blood vessels. The agents include Monsel solution (a20% ferric nitrate solution), silver nitrate, and aluminum chloride.
 
  • Biological physical agents: They act by promoting platelet activation and formation of three-dimensional matrix for the formation of clots. These agents are used in several operations including neurosurgical, orthopedic, thoracic, abdominal, and vascular procedures. The agents include gelatin, oxidized cellulose, and microfibrillar collagen.
 
  • Physiologic agents: These agents activate a specific step of the coagulation cascade and promotes the clot formation. These agents include thrombin and fibrin glue/sealant.
 
  • Combination or polymer agents: These agents include several different combinations of the above agents and various synthetic hemostatic agents. Examples include gelatin-thrombin agent, polyethylene glycol hydrogel, and glutaraldehyde cross-linked albumin.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: An affected male does not have affected children but an affected female always has affected children. Type of inheritance?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Mitochondrial

In mitochondrial inheritance, if the mother is affected and the father is normal, then all their children (both male and female) will be affected. However, children born to an affected father and a normal mother will not be affected.
 
The mitochondrial inheritance pattern is as shown in the image below:

The unique feature of mitochondrial inheritance is maternal inheritance, as the disease is transmitted through the affected mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), which is derived from the maternal mitochondria.
 
The ovum contains several mitochondria, while the spermatozoa has very few mitochondria if present. Hence, the mitochondrial DNA of the zygote is entirely derived from the ovum.
 
Therefore, affected mother transmits the disease to all the offsprings (both male and female), and only the daughters of the affected mother, will further transmit the disease.
 
Characteristic features of mitochondrial inheritance:
  • The mitochondrial DNA encodes enzymes required for oxidative phosphorylation. Therefore, organs that are most dependent on the oxidative phosphorylation are the ones most affected in diseases due to mutations in mtDNA. These organs include central nervous system, skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle, liver, and kidneys.
  • There are several thousands of copies of mtDNA in each mitochondria, of which only a few copies are affected in case of mutation. Therefore, a diseased individual possesses copies of both wild type mtDNA and mutant mtDNA in each mitochondria  This phenomenon is called heteroplasmy. 
  • The disease manifests if a minimum number of copies of mutant mtDNA are present in the mitochondria that can lead to oxidative dysfunction, called the threshold effect. In most cases, this threshold effect is reached in the organs as mentioned above.
  • Also, during a cell division, the wild and mutant copies of the mtDNA are unequally distributed among the daughter cells. As a result, the expression of the disease varies even among different cells of an organ.

Anaphylactoid reactions are those reactions that are similar to the anaphylactic reactions but are not IgE mediated. These reactions are caused by direct degranulation of the mast cells or basophils, which causes the release of mediators.

Unlike the classic anaphylaxis which occurs on re-exposure to the allergen, the anaphylactoid reaction can occur even on the first exposure. The most common agents that can cause an anaphylactoid reaction include NSAIDs and radiocontrast media.

In 2014, World Allergy Organisation has introduced two new terms:

  • Immunologic anaphylaxis - It includes anaphylactic reactions mediated by IgE, IgG (in animals), and immune complex/ complement-mediated reactions.
  • Non-immunologic anaphylaxis (previously called anaphylactoid reaction) - It includes reactions caused by agents which cause massive degranulation of mast cells or basophils in the absence of immunoglobulin.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: Hepcidin inhibits iron transfer from the enterocyte to the plasma by binding to _____
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ferroportin

Hepcidin inhibits iron transfer from the enterocytes into the plasma by binding to ferroportin, which is an iron efflux channel in the enterocyte.

Iron metabolism is regulated by hepcidin, a protein and acute phase reactant produced by the liver. It binds to ferroportin and degrades it. This inhibits the transfer of iron from the enterocyte to the plasma via ferroportin. As a result, iron becomes trapped within the duodenal cells (enterocytes) in the form of mucosal ferritin and is lost in feces when these cells are shed off.

Transcription of hepcidin is increased by the following factors:

  • Increased levels of iron
  • Inflammatory cytokines

Transcription of hepcidin is decreased by the following factors:

  • Iron deficiency
  • Hypoxia
  • Ineffective erythropoiesis

Hepcidin is encoded by the HAMP gene and its mutations are associated with hereditary hemochromatosis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: Which of the following is true regarding glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency?
options: Cells don't lyse in hypoto‌nic solution
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cells are spherical

G6PD deficiency has spherical red cells (Spherocytes).

Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) is an enzyme that helps in the synthesis of NADPH. NADPH helps in keeping glutathione in a reduced state (GSH). This reduced glutathione acts as a defense against oxidative damage. In G6PD deficiency, RBCs are exposed to oxidants. These cross-linking of the reactive sulphydryl groups in the globin chain of hemoglobin. These are then deposited as inclusions in RBC membranes as Heinz bodies. When these RBCs pass-through spleen, macrophages pluck out these membrane inclusions. The remaining cells are seen as bite cells. Less severely damaged cells lose a part of their membrane, forming spherocytes.

Spectrin is a part of the RBC membrane skeleton. It is commonly defective in hereditary spherocytosis. 

Normal biconcave RBCs have a bit of an 'extra space'. They can accommodate a little fluid when exposed to a hypotonic solution. But spherocytes have already lost a part of its membrane, so are relatively full. Hence if they are placed in a hypotonic solution, they absorb more fluid and result in lysis of RBCs. This forms the basis of testing spherocytes in Hereditary spherocytosis or G6PD and is known as osmotic fragility testing.

On the other hand, placing RBCs in a hypertonic solution may cause them to lose water and shrink in size. But hardly any hemolysis takes place.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: A 24-year-old man met with an RTA and was brought to the casualty after 6 hours. His B.P. was 90/60 mm Hg, heart rate was 110/min, and SpO2 was 92%. A blood transfusion was done. After a few hours, the patient is febrile, tachypneic, and starts bleeding from the IV and NG tube sites. His SpO2 levels started falling. What could be the cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Transfusion reaction

The symptoms of this patient (bleeding from the IV catheter and nasogastric tube sites) are suggestive of DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation) within a few hours of blood transfusion. Hence, the most likely cause of this presentation is an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction.

These reactions are mediated by pre-existing IgM antibodies that act against the polysaccharide blood group antigens A or B. They bind to the red cells and cause complement-mediated lysis which further leads to intravascular hemolysis and hemoglobinuria. Severe cases may present with DIC, which is a consumptive coagulopathy with bleeding manifestations. Other complications include shock, acute kidney injury, and sometimes, death.

 

The various blood transfusion reactions according to their time of occurrence are as follows:

  • Anaphylactic reaction - Within a few seconds to minutes of the transfusion
  • Allergic/Urticarial reactions - Within 2-3 hours of transfusion
  • Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction (AHTR) - Within 24 hours of transfusion
  • Febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction (FNHTR) - Within 6 hours of transfusion
  • Delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction (DHTR) - After 24 hours of transfusion

 

Other options:

Option b- Acute adrenal crisis usually presents as an unexplained shock that is refractory to fluids and vasopressors.

Option c- Fat embolism is associated with fractures of the long bones. It develops within 2-3 days of fracture/trauma. Moreover, a history of petechial rash is characteristic of fat embolism.

Option d- Hemorrhagic shock presents as tachypnea, tachycardia, narrow pulse pressure, and oliguria. Cold extremities and delayed capillary refill time are other features. In this case, hemorrhagic shock might occur as a consequence of bleeding due to DIC, but the cause of this presentation is transfusion reaction.

Methanol is not a crosslinking fixative. It is a dehydrant coagulant fixative.

Fixation of tissues can be done by physical or chemical methods.

Chemical methods: These methods are commonly used in the processing of tissue for various histopathological diagnoses. It includes the use of:

  • Cross-linking fixatives: These fixatives add covalent reactive groups which may induce cross-links between proteins, individual protein moieties within nucleic acids, and between nucleic acids and proteins. Eg: Formaldehyde and Glutaraldehyde.
  • Dehydrant coagulant fixatives: These fixatives remove free water from tissues and precipitate or coagulate the proteins. Eg: ethanol, methanol, and acetone.
  • Compound fixatives: Fixatives, which are the mixtures of reagents are referred to as compound fixatives. Eg: alcoholic formalin fixes tissues in two ways i.e firstly, by adding covalent hydroxymethyl groups and crosslinking proteins and secondly, by coagulation and dehydration.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: JAK2 mutation is most commonly associated with _____
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Polycythemia vera

Polycythemia vera is strongly associated with activating point mutations in the tyrosine kinase JAK2.

A mutation in JAK2, a key member of the cytokine intracellular signaling pathway, can be found in 90–95% of patients with polycythemia vera.

It is characterized by :

  • Increased marrow production of red cells, granulocytes, and platelets (panmyelosis)
  • Low erythropoietin levels and elevated hematocrit
  • Blood viscosity and sludging lead to both thrombosis and bleeding.
  • Headache, dizziness, hypertension, dizziness, venous thrombosis (Budd Chiari syndrome due to hepatic vein thrombosis), bowel infarction, and stroke.
  • Intense pruritus especially aquagenic pruritus 
  • Peptic ulceration, hyperuricemia
  • 15% to 20% of patients after an average period of 10 years ->Myelofibrosis and extensive extramedullary hematopoiesis,
  • PCV transforms into AML in 2% of patients.

Primary myelofibrosis

  • Marrow fibrosis associated with extramedullary hemopoiesis in the spleen.
  • Activating mutation in JAK2 (more commonly) or MPL.
  • Presence of neoplastic megakaryocytes, which are responsible for the release of fibrogenic factors like PDGF (platelet-derived growth factor) and TGF-β.
  • Bone marrow aspiration yields dry tap due to fibrosis of the bone marrow.
  • So, bone marrow biopsy is the investigation of choice, which shows the presence of hypocellularity with increased deposition of reticulin inside the marrow, abnormal megakaryocytes and the characteristic finding of dilated marrow sinusoids.
  • Blood shows mild leukocytosis, decreased Hb and hematocrit levels, and elevated LAP scores.
  • Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) occurs in 5% to 20% of cases.

Essential thrombocytosis (ET) may also be associated with JAK2, MPL, or CALR mutations.

  • Essential thrombocytosis (ET) is often associated with activating point mutations in JAK2 (50% of cases) or MPL (5% to 10% of cases), a receptor tyrosine kinase that is normally activated by thrombopoietin.
  • In addition, recent DNA sequencing studies have revealed that most of the remaining cases have mutations in calreticulin (CALR), a protein with several functions in the endoplasmic reticulum and the cytoplasm. Since JAK2 and calreticulin mutations are mutually exclusive, it is hypothesized that the calreticulin mutations also increase JAK-STAT signaling through mechanisms that are currently unknown.

CML is the consequence of the balanced translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22 (t[9;22]).

PV, PMF, and ET are characterized by driver mutations that directly or indirectly constitutively activate JAK2, a tyrosine kinase essential for the function of the erythropoietin andthrombopoietin receptors and also utilized by granulocyte colony stimulating factor receptor.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: Rees and Ecker diluting fluid is used in ______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. RBC Pipette

Rees and Ecker's solution is used as a diluting fluid in the RBC pipette for performing platelet counts. Its composition is:

Components Value
Sodium citrate 3.8 g
Formaldehyde (40 %) 0.2 ml
Brilliant cresyl blue 0.1 g
Distilled water 100 ml

The steps involved in platelet count are:

I - Filling the pipette

  • Diluting fluid is drawn to mark 1 of the RBC pipette and expelled
  • Blood is aspirated to 0.5 mark of the RBCs diluting pipette
  • Diluting fluid is aspirated to 101 mark
  • Blood and diluting fluid are mixed mechanically for 5 min

II - Filling the counting chamber

  • Allow the counting chamber to stand for 20-30 minutes to allow the platelets to settle.
  • To prevent drying out of the preparation, it should be kept in a moist atmosphere, this is most easily arranged by placing the filled counting chamber in the bottom of a clean Petri dish, alongside which arrange a small piece of cotton wool which has been soaked in water and squeezed out. Petri dish lid is additionally put over the dish.
  • After 20-30minutes, the counting chamber can be removed and carefully transferred to the microscope stage.

III - Counting the number of platelets

  • Focus on the surface of the hemocytometer chamber with a high power dry objective. Dim the light to make the thrombocytes visible, and count all of the thrombocytes in the entire center 1 mm² (erythrocyte counting area) of both sides of the hemocytometer. This gives the number of thrombocytes in 0.2 l of 1: 200 dilution of blood.
  • The number of thrombocytes counted X 1000 = number of thrombocytes/l of undiluted blood.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: Which fixation technique is used for fat in the histopathological examination?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Frozen section

A frozen section is done for the fixation of fats. This ensures that the tissue need not go through routine processing, which can remove lipids.

When the tissue sample goes through rapid freezing, it becomes firmer. The ice acts as an embedding media allowing the tissue to be sectioned. 

The temperature range in the cryostat machine usually ranges from 0⁰C to -35⁰C. The majority of the tissue can be appropriately sectioned between -15⁰C to -25⁰C. Tissue samples that contain water can be sectioned at a higher temperature. The tissues that contain more fat will need to be cut at a lower temperature.

The stain used for fat is the oil red O stain. It can identify neutral lipids and fatty acids in smears and tissues. It is used in the following conditions:

  • Fat emboli in lung tissue
  • Renal cell carcinoma
  • Sebaceous gland tumors of the skin
  • Lipid-rich carcinomas

Fixatives containing alcohols, or routine processing with clearing, will remove lipids. Fixation can be achieved by the following methods:

  • Physical methods - heating, microwaving, cryopreservation
  • Chemical methods - immersion of specimen in fixative, perfusing vascular system with a fixative

 Given below are a few fixatives with their uses:

Technique/Tissue Fixative
Electron microscopy Glutaraldehyde
Trephine biopsy-bone marrow Zenker's fluid (AZF fixative)
GI biopsies Bouin's fixative
Brain Formalin ammonium chloride
Adrenal biopsy Orth's fluid
Pap smear Ethanol

 The most commonly used fixative is 10% neutral buffered formalin.

questions.question: Which of the following clotting factor deficiency will not affect clotting in vivo?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Factor XII

Factor XII deficiency will not affect the clotting in vivo.

Unlike the clotting cascade in the lab (in vitro), the cascade in the body (in vivo) differs slightly - as tissue factor (TF) is the major initiator of the cascade. The TF/VIIa complex is the most important activator of factor IX and factor IXa/factor VIIIa complex is the most important activator of factor X. Factor V is involved in both the pathways as shown in the image below.

The coagulation cascade in the laboratory:

  • Extrinsic pathway sequence (in a test tube):  Tissue factor → Factor VII → Factor X.
  • Intrinsic pathway sequence (in a test tube): Factor XII →  Factor XI → Factor IX → Factor X 

Laboratory methods to initiate clotting include:

  • Intrinsic pathway - adding phospholipids, calcium, and either a negatively charged substance such as glass beads
  • Extrinsic pathway - a source of tissue factor

Thromboelastography (TEG) tests the entire coagulation pathway. It measures coagulation cascade, platelet function, and fibrinolysis.

It is a test that quantitatively measures the ability of whole blood to form a clot. The advantages are:

  • Global assessment of blood coagulability, including coagulation cascade, platelet function, and fibrinolysis
  • Rapid real-time bedside test with a simple methodology (point-of-care testing)
  • Diagnosis of coagulopathic bleeding
  • Guide transfusion therapy and decrease the use of blood products
  • Detect dynamic changes in blood coagulation during resuscitation
  • Predict the clinical efficacy of therapeutic agents affecting blood coagulability

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Zollinger ellison syndrome

The eosinophilic appearing cells marked as A are the parietal cells, the absence of which is not associated with Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome. The cells marked as B are Chief cells. 

Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome is caused by gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumors, which leads to parital cell hyperplasia. Gastrinomas are almost always found in the small intestine or pancreas. The most remarkable feature found in the stomach is an increase in oxyntic mucosal thickness due to massive parietal cell hyperplasia.

 

Other options:

Option A and C: Pernicious anemia is an autoimmune disease characterized by the presence of autoantibodies that impairs the production or activity of the intrinsic factor (IF) that is released from the parietal cells, which is required for the uptake of vitamin B12. There are three types of autoantibodies namely, type I, II, and III. The action of each of these include:

  • Autoantibody type I prevents the binding of vitamin B12 to the intrinsic factor (IF).
  • Autoantibody type II prevents the binding of vitamin B12-IF complex to the ileal receptors.
  • Autoantibody type III acts against the α and β subunits of the gastric proton pump, which impairs the production of intrinsic factor.

These patients also develop chronic atrophic gastritis, characterized by loss of parietal cells, infiltration of lymphocytes and plasma cells, and megaloblastic changes in mucosal cells.

Option B: Gastric carcinoid tumors originate from gastric enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells. They are referred to as well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumors. The peak incidence of carcinoid tumors is in the 6th decade. These tumors occur throughout the GI tract, most commonly in the appendix, ileum, and rectum, in decreasing order of frequency.

Gastric carcinoid tumors may be associated with endocrine cell hyperplasia, autoimmune chronic atrophic gastritis, MEN-I, and Zollinger–Ellison syndrome. Ileal carcinoid may cause carcinoid syndrome which is characterized by cutaneous flushing, sweating, bronchospasm, colicky abdominal pain, diarrhea, and right-sided cardiac valvular fibrosis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: Identify the correct statement regarding immune surveillance.
options: Anti CTLA 4 Ab is a new mo‌dality in the treatment o​f advanced cancers
Mutation of tumor supresso‌r genes decreases antigen​ toxicity
PD1/ PDL1 activation leadi‌ng to tumor supression
Binding of CD28 leads to i‌mmune tolerance
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anti CTLA 4 Ab is a new modality in the treatment of advanced cancers

Anti-CTLA-4 antibody ipilimumab was the first drug to achieve a significant improvement in survival of advanced-stage melanoma. Cytotoxic T lymphocyte antigen 4 (CTLA-4) plays an important inhibitory role in the control of T-cell activation.

Ipilimumab is a fully-humanized IgG1 monoclonal antibody that inhibits cytotoxic T lymphocyte antigen-4 (CTLA-4).

It has been postulated that anti-CTLA-4 antibodies act by blocking inhibitory signals from effector T-cells, allowing costimulatory signaling and generation of antitumor T-cell responses. In vitro studies demonstrated also that the antitumor activity of CTLA-4 blockade is mediated by Fc gamma receptor-expressing macrophage and hypothesized a possible role of regulatory T-cell depletion in the tumor microenvironment.

Option B - Mutation of tumor supressor genes is associated with increased risk of cancer. Antigen toxicity is when the immune response to an antigen is excessive or misdirected, causing damage to tissues or organs.

Option C - PD1/PDL1 is an immune checkpoint whose activation inhibits T-cell function and helps with immune tolerance. Blocking PD-1/PD-L1 interaction using immune checkpoint inhibitors reactivates T cells and enhances immune responses against tumors.

Option D - CD28 is primarily involved in providing the second signal required for T cell activation. The first signal comes from the interaction between the T cell receptor (TCR) and the antigen presented by the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) on antigen-presenting cells (APCs). Without CD28-mediated costimulation, T cells that only receive the TCR signal (without the second signal) can become anergic.

Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) is seen in HIV, SLE, CLL, and Hepatitis B.

MPGN is caused due to immune-mediated injury. It often presents with a nephritic-nephrotic picture.

The causes of MPGN are as follows:

  • Primary MPGN (Idiopathic)
  • Secondary MPGN

    • Malignancies - chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL)

  • Type I - It is characterized by the deposition of immune complexes and mesangiocapillary proliferation.
  • Type II - It is now known as dense-deposit disease. It belongs to a group of disorders called C3 glomerulopathies.

  • Lobular glomeruli with proliferating mesangial cells, capillary endothelium, and infiltrating leukocytes (endocapillary proliferation)
  • Duplication of the basement membrane gives a double contour or tram-track appearance. It is especially evident in silver or PAS stains.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements is correct regarding Peutz Jeghers syndrome?

  1. Arborizing pattern of smooth muscle
  2. Loss of heterozygosity in the STK11 gene
  3. Multiple GI polyps
  4. Autosomal recessive
  5. Congenital hypertrophy of retinal pigment epithelium is seen
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2, and 3

Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is an autosomal dominant, hereditary disorder characterized by multiple intestinal hamartomatous polyps having an arborizing pattern of smooth muscle. Germline heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the STK11 gene are present in approximately half of individuals with familial Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.

It is also characterized by mucocutaneous dark blue to brown melanin pigmentation, which is particularly evident on the face, buccal mucosa, hands, feet, perianal and genital regions. This rare syndrome presents at a median age of 11 years.

The hamartomatous polyps seen in Peutz-Jeghers syndrome are characterized by a branching network of smooth muscle fibers continuous with the muscularis mucosa that supports the glandular epithelium of the polyp.

Complications:

  • Peutz-Jeghers polyps can cause intussusception, which is occasionally fatal.
  • It is associated with a markedly increased risk of many malignant conditions. Lifetime risk is approximately 40% and regular surveillance is recommended from a very young age for sex cord tumors of the testes.
  • During later life, there is a risk for gastric and small intestinal cancers, and subsequently for colon, pancreatic, breast, lung, ovarian, and uterine cancers.

Allograft rejection: It is the primary concern that requires close surveillance. Both classic cellular rejection and antibody-mediated rejection is recognized. Cellular rejection is characterized by interstitial lymphocytic inflammation, with associated myocyte damage.

Allograft arteriopathy: It is the single most important long-term limitation for cardiac transplantation. It is a late, progressive, diffusely stenosing intimal proliferation in the coronary arteries, leading to ischemic injury. It can lead to silent myocardial infarction since transplant patients have denervated hearts and do not experience angina. Progressive congestive heart failure and sudden cardiac death can also occur.

Other postoperative problems include infection and malignancies, especially Epstein–Barr virus-associated B-cell lymphomas.

Fever is characterized by an elevation of body temperature, usually by 1° to 4°C. It is one of the most prominent manifestations of the acute-phase response, especially if associated with infection.

Anaplasia refers to a lack of differentiation.

The term anaplasia means to form backward implying a reversal of differentiation to a more primitive level. The extent to which neoplastic cells resemble normal cells, both morphologically and functionally, is called differentiation.

Anaplasia is an important morphological feature of malignant transformation.

The morphological features of malignancy include:

  • Increased N: C ratio (nucleus: cytoplasmic ratio) - around 1:4 in normal cells, increases to 1:1 in malignant cells
  • Hyperchromasia - coarsely clumped and darkly stained chromatin within irregular nuclei
  • Increased mitosis - atypical, bizarre mitotic figures
  • Loss of polarity - sheets or large masses of tumor cells grow in an anarchic, disorganized fashion

Metastatic tumors of bone:

Metastatic tumors are the most common form of skeletal malignancy, greatly outnumbering primary bone cancers.

Skeletal metastases are typically multifocal. However, carcinomas of the kidney and thyroid may present with solitary lesions. Most metastases involve the axial skeleton (vertebral column, pelvis, ribs, skull, and sternum). The red marrow in these areas, with its rich capillary network and slow blood flow, facilitates implantation and growth of the tumor cells.

The radiographic appearance of metastases may be purely lytic (bone destroying), purely blastic (bone forming), or mixed lytic and blastic. Furthermore, some cancers are associated with predominantly one pattern or the other.

For example, prostatic adenocarcinoma is predominantly blastic whereas carcinomas of the kidney, lung, and gastrointestinal tract and malignant melanoma produce lytic lesions.

Correct answer: C. Elastase

α1-antitrypsin is the major inhibitor of the enzyme neutrophil elastase.

  • Lysosomal enzymes, if unchecked, can potentiate further inflammation by damaging tissues.
  • These harmful proteases, however, are normally controlled by a system of antiproteases in the serum and tissue fluids.
  • α1-antitrypsin is the prototype member of the serine protease inhibitor (serpin) superfamily of proteins.

Clinical correlate:

  • Alpha 1 anti-trypsin deficiency (α1-ATD) is caused by mutations in the SERPINA1 gene located in the long arm of chromosome 14.

  • The resulting protease excess in alveoli destroys alveolar walls and causes emphysema.

questions.question: A 50-year-old man presented with a retroperitoneal mass. Biopsy from the lesion is shown in the image below. Molecular analysis revealed t(12;16).  What is the most likely condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Myxoid Liposarcoma

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of myxoid liposarcoma. 

The image shows abundant ground substance, with branching capillaries and a few immature adipocytes. 

Liposarcoma is the most common sarcoma in adults and is usually seen in the 5th to 6th decade of life. They commonly occur in the deep soft tissues of the proximal extremities and in the retroperitoneum.

Histologically the liposarcomas are divided into three subtypes:

  • Well-differentiated liposarcoma: It consists of mature adipocytes and scattered spindle cells with hyperchromatic nuclei. It is associated with amplification of 12q13-q15.
  • Myxoid liposarcoma: It contains abundant basophilic extracellular matrix with branching capillaries. Few immature adipocytes are found scattered within the matrix. It is associated with t(12;16).
  • Pleomorphic liposarcoma: It consists of sheets of anaplastic cells with bizarre nuclei and few immature adipocytes.

Among the three subtypes, the pleomorphic liposarcoma is the most malignant and often metastasizes, while the well-differentiated is least malignant. Myxoid liposarcoma has intermediate malignancy behaviour.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: Which of the following is true about the pathogenesis of Hirschsprung disease?
options: Failure of migration of ne‌ural crest cells
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Failure of migration of neural crest cells

Hirschsprung disease occurs due to the failure of migration of the neural crest cells to the bowel wall.

During normal embryogenesis, the neural crest cells migrate from the caecum to the rectum. The enteric neuronal plexuses develop from these migrated neural crest cells.

In Hirschsprung disease, there is an arrest in the migration of these cells, which leads to the development of a distal intestinal segment that is devoid of Meissner (submucosal) and the Auerbach (myenteric) plexus. Hence this segment is referred to as the aganglionic segment.

As a result, there is a lack of coordination in the peristaltic contractions and functional obstruction, which further leads to the dilation of the intestine proximal to the affected segment, leading to congenital megacolon. Diagnosis is confirmed by demonstrating the absence of ganglion cells in biopsy sections.

Some conditions may cause acquired megacolon. These include:

  • Chagas disease, due to the loss of ganglion cells
  • Visceral myopathy
  • Obstruction by neoplasm or inflammatory stricture
  • Toxic megacolon complicating ulcerative colitis
  • Functional psychosomatic disorders

Reperfused myocardium shows eosinophilic contraction bands on light microscopy. They occur in irreversibly injured myocytes with damaged membranes, when blood supply is restored 12-24 hours after MI.

On microscopic examination, the irreversibly injured myocytes exhibit contraction bands that are intensely eosinophilic intracellular stripes. These contraction bands are composed of closely packed sarcomeres.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: All-trans retinoic acid is used in the treatment of tumor that is associated with which of the following genetic aberrations?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. PML-RARA

All-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) is used in the treatment of acute promyelocytic leukemia (APML), which is associated with PML-RARA fusion gene.

Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APML) is associated with a reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 15 and 17 producing a PML-RARA fusion gene. This fusion gene encodes for a chimeric protein, which consists of a part of the PML protein and a part of the retinoic acid receptor-α (RARα).

The normal RARα binds to the DNA and activates the transcription in the presence of retinoids. However, the chimeric protein produced by PML-RARA has reduced affinity for retinoids. This causes inhibition of transcription, thereby preventing gene expression for cellular differentiation. This leads to the accumulation of myeloid progenitor cells.

The condition is treated with all-trans retinoic acid. It binds to the PML-RARA chimeric protein. This causes conformational change such that the protein regains its normal function and activates DNA transcription.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: What is the cell of origin of Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia/Small Lymphocytic Lymphoma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Naive B cells

The cell of origin of Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia (CLL)/ Small Lymphocytic Lymphoma (SLL) is either naive B cells or post-germinal centre memory B cell. 

The CLL and SLL differ only in the degree of peripheral blood lymphocytes. CLL is the most common leukemia of adults in the western world. The median age of diagnosis is 60 years. The most common genetic anomalies seen are deletions of 13q14.3, 11q, and 17p and trisomy 12q. Loss of tumor suppressor genes in chromosome 13 results in overexpression of the anti-apoptotic protein BCL2.

The growth of CLL/SLL cells is confined to the proliferation centers (pathognomonic for CLL/SLL), where the tumor cells receive critical factors from the surrounding environments, such as NF-κB for cell survival, MYC for cell growth, Bruton Tyrosine Kinase (BTK) signaling pathway, etc.,

The tumor cells express CD19, CD20, CD23, and CD5. Smudge cells are also characteristic of CLL. Clinical features include easy fatiguability, weight loss, anorexia, generalized lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, hemolytic anemia, etc. CLL/SLL has a tendency to transform to a more aggressive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL)  - this is called Richter syndrome.

Factors with a bad prognosis include:

  1. Presence of deletions of 11q and  17p.
  2. Lack of somatic hypermutation.
  3. Expression of ZAP-70, a protein that augments signals produced by the Ig receptor.
  4. Presence of NOTCH1 mutations

BTK inhibitors and BCL2 inhibitors produce sustained therapeutic responses in a higher fractions of people with CLL/SLL.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: Human Papilloma Virus inactivates RB gene by which of the following proteins?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. E7

E7 protein of Human Papilloma Virus (HPV) binds to the hypophosphorylated RB protein and displaces the E2F transcription factors, thereby promoting G1/S transition.

RB gene is a key negative regulator of the cell cycle at the G1/S transition. RB gene exists in an active hypophosphorylated state in resting cells and in an inactive hyperphosphorylated state in cells undergoing G1/S transition.

E7 protein from the high-risk types of HPV (such as HPV 16) binds to the hypophosphorylated RB through the same pocket that RB uses to bind and sequester the E2F transcription factors, thereby displacing the E2F which leads to the progression of the cell cycle and thus the proliferation of tumor cells. E7 proteins also inactivate the CDK inhibitors p21 and p27. E7 proteins from high-risk HPVs (types 16,18 and 31) also bind and presumably activates cyclins  A and E.

Oncogenic activities of protein E6:

The E6 protein binds to and helps in the degradation of p53 and stimulates the expression of telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT), which is the catalytic subunit of telomerase, thereby helping in the longevity of the cells. E6 from high-risk HPV types has a higher affinity for p53 than E6 from low-risk types.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question:
Mediators involved in the early phase of type 1 hypersensitivity are?

  1. Mast cell
  2. Histamine
  3. Neutrophils
  4. Prostaglandins
  5. Leukotrienes
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2, 4, 5

The mediators involved in the early phase of type 1 hypersensitivity are, 

  • Mast cells, 
  • Histamine,
  • Prostaglandins (D2) and 
  • Leukotrienes (C4 and D4).

Early phase of type 1 hypersensitivity:

The mediators produced by the mast cells are responsible for most of the immediate hypersensitivity reactions. Histamine and leukotrienes are released rapidly from the sensitized mast cells and trigger intense immediate reactions characterized by edema, mucus secretion and smooth muscle spasm.

Other mediators involved in the early phase are, 

  • Enzymes: neutral proteases (chymase, tryptase) and acid hydrolases
  • Proteoglycans: heparin and chondroitin sulfate
  • Lipid mediators: Platelet-activating factor (PAF)

Late-phase of type 1 hypersensitivity:

The late phase reaction is characterized by the recruitment of leukocytes, that amplify and sustain the inflammatory response without exposure to the triggering antigen.

Mediators involved in the late phase of type 1 hypersensitivity reaction are:

  • Cytokines: TNF, IL-1, IL-4, IL-5, and chemokines (eotaxin)
  • Leukocytes (eosinophils)
  • Major Basic Protein (MBP)
  • Eosinophil cationic protein

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: Given below is an image of activation of the coagulation cascade, following closed endothelial injury. Identify the factor ‘L’ which combines with tissue factor to activate factor IX.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Factor VII

The factor marked as ‘L’ is factor VII, which combines with tissue factor that is produced following a close endothelial injury to activate factor IX. 

As the image represents the in vivo coagulation cascade, the tissue factor is the major initiator of coagulation. It is believed that in vivo, factor VIIa/tissue factor complex is the most important activator of factor IX and that factor IXa/factor VIIIa complex is the most important activator of factor X. 

Tissue factor is expressed on the surfaces of the subendothelial cellular components of the vessel wall, such as smooth muscle cells and fibroblasts. This tissue factor is exposed to blood when there is a vascular damage. This activates the in vivo extrinsic pathway of coagulation cascade, which is as follows:

  • Tissue factor binds with serine protease factor VIIa
  • This complex then activates factor IX to factor IXa
  • Factor IXa then activates factor X to factor Xa
  • Factor Xa can be formed through the actions of either the tissue factor-factor VIIa complex or factor IXa (with factor VIIIa as cofactor)
  • Factor Xa then converts prothrombin to thrombin, which is the pivotal protease of the coagulation cascade.
  • The cofactor essential for this conversion is factor Va.
  • The thrombin then formed converts the soluble plasma fibrinogen to an insoluble fibrin matrix.
  • Thrombin also activates factor XIII, which is the fibrin stabilizing factor, to factor XIIIa. This factor XIIIa forms covalent cross-links and thereby stabilizes the fibrin clot.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question:
Arrange the following cellular events of inflammation in the correct sequence:

  1. Rolling
  2. Cytokine-mediated integrin activation
  3. Adhesion
  4. Migration
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, 3, 4

The correct sequence of cellular events that occurs during inflammation is as follows: Rolling, Cytokine-mediated integrin activation, Adhesion, Migration.

The recruitment of leucocytes to the site of inflammation is a multi-step process that is mediated by adhesion molecules and cytokines called chemokines. This process can be divided into sequential phases:

  1. In the lumen: margination, rolling and adhesion to the endothelium occurs.
  2. Migration of the leucocytes across the endothelium and vessel wall
  3. Migration in the tissues towards a chemotactic stimulus.

The process of leucocyte recruitment is as follows:

  • Margination: Because of the dilation of the inflamed postcapillary venues, there is stasis of blood flow, and hence, more leucocytes assume a peripheral position along the endothelial surface; this process of leucocyte redistribution is called margination.
  • Rolling: The slowed down leucocytes then sense the signals from the endothelium and start rolling on the vessel wall.
  • Cytokine-mediated integrin activation: The attachment of leucocytes to the endothelial cells requires adhesion molecules that are activated by cytokines. The major families of proteins involved in adhesion and migration are selectins and integrins and their ligands.
  • Adhesions: The weak rolling interactions slow down the leucocytes and allow them to bind more firmly to the endothelium. Chemokines that were produced at the site of injury bind to the endothelial cell proteoglycans. These chemokines then bind to the rolling leucocytes and activate them. This, in turn, converts the ligands for β1 and β2 integrins, VLA-4, and LFA-1 present on the leucocytes to a high-affinity state.
  • This combination of cytokine-induced expression of integrin ligands on the endothelium and increased integrin affinity on the leucocytes leads to firm adhesion of leucocytes to the endothelium at the site of inflammation.
  • Leucocyte migration: This is the movement of leucocytes through the intact endothelium, called transmigration or diapedesis. This occurs in postcapillary venules. This migration occurs through the inter-endothelial gap towards the chemical concentration gradient created by the chemokines at the site of injury. This occurs with the help of adhesion molecules present in the intercellular junctions such as platelet endothelial cell adhesion molecule (PECAM-1) or CD31.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: Which of the following is used in the treatment of sideroblastic anemia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitamin B6

Vitamin B6 (Pyridoxine) is used in the treatment of sideroblastic anaemia.

Pyridoxine 200mg per day for 2-3 months is administered routinely to all cases of sideroblastic anaemia. This cofactor is essential for ALA-synthase activity, and mutations in the pyridoxine binding site of the enzyme have been found in several responsive patients. Blood transfusion and other supportive therapy are also indicated. In cases of secondary sideroblastic anaemia, the primary focus is the removal of the offending agent. But no definitive treatment is available for hereditary and idiopathic types of sideroblastic anaemia.

Sideroblasts are nucleated red cells (normoblasts) containing siderotic granules which stain positively with Prussian blue stain. Based on aetiology, sideroblastic anaemia are classified into hereditary and acquired types.

Hereditary sideroblastic anaemia is an X-linked disorder caused due to a defect in the activity of aminolevulinic acid (ALA) synthetase required for heme synthesis. Affected females act as carriers while males have moderate to marked anaemia and manifest in childhood or during early adulthood

Acquired sideroblastic anaemia:

I) Primary acquired:

  • Also called idiopathic or refractory acquired sideroblastic anaemia
  • Occurs in middle-aged and older individuals of both sexes
  • Due to the reduced activity of the enzyme ALA synthetase, there is disturbed growth and maturation of the erythroid precursors at the level of hematopoietic stem cell
  • Moderate to severe anaemia, which appears insidiously
  • Neutropenia and thrombocytopenia may also be seen
  • Regarded as a myelodysplastic disorder in the FAB classification and thus considered preleukaemic

II) Secondary acquired:

May appear secondary to 

  • Drugs, chemicals and toxins: Isoniazid, Cycloserine, Chloramphenicol, Cyclophosphamide, Alcohol, Lead, etc.,
  • Haematological disorders: myelofibrosis, polycythemia vera, acute leukaemia, myeloma, lymphoma and hemolytic anaemia.
  • Miscellaneous: Carcinoma, myxoedema, rheumatoid arthritis and SLE.

Laboratory findings:

  • Peripheral smear: Hypochromic, microcytic (sometimes normocytic) anaemia
  • Absolute values: MCV, MCH and MCHC are reduced except in acquired type, where MCV is raised.
  • Bone marrow: Erythroid hyperplasia with macronormoblastic erythropoiesis. Marrow iron stores are raised. Pathognomonic ring sideroblasts are present.
  • Serum ferritin: Raised
  • Serum iron: Raised
  • TIBC: Normal
  • Haemoglobin electrophoresis: Normal

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: A 5-year-old child who presented with proptosis of one of the eyes was found to have a desmin positive tumour. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma

The clinical picture of a 5-year-old child with proptosis and a desmin positive tumor suggests a diagnosis of embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma.

Rhabdomyosarcoma is a malignant mesenchymal tumor with skeletal muscle differentiation. There are four subtypes: alveolar, embryonal, pleomorphic, and spindle cell/sclerosing. Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common soft tissue sarcoma of childhood and adolescence and is usually of the alveolar and the embryonal variety. Pleomorphic rhabdomyosarcoma is seen predominantly in adults. Spindle cell/sclerosing type affects all ages. The pediatric forms often arise in the sinuses, head and neck, and genitourinary tract.

Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma has sheets of both primitive round and spindled cells in a myxoid stroma. Rhabdomyoblasts with visible cross-striations may be present. Sarcoma botryoids is a variant of embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma in the walls of hollow, mucosal-lined structures, such as the nasopharynx, common bile duct, bladder, and vagina with cambium layer. Alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma has a network of fibrous septae that divide the cells into clusters or aggregates, creating a crude resemblance to pulmonary alveoli.

Clinically, the tumor is usually aggressive, with unilateral proptosis when the orbit is involved. Swelling and redness of the overlying skin, diplopia may be present. Immunohistochemistry is positive for desmin, myoglobin, myogenin, MyoD1, and vimentin

Treatment involves surgical resection and chemotherapy, with or without radiotherapy. The best prognosis is for the botryoid variant while the pleomorphic has variant has the worst prognosis.

Other options:

A) Ewing's sarcoma: CD99 positive

C) Leukaemia: CD45 positive

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: A 17-year-old boy presented with intussusception and was taken up for surgery. He was found to have multiple polyps. The resected section was sent for histopathology and the whole mount image of the specimen is given below. Identify the lesion.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hamartomatous polyp

The given clinical feature of intussusception and multiple polyps and the histologic picture showing an arborizing pattern of connective tissue, smooth muscle, lamina propria, and glands are suggestive of Peutz–Jeghers Syndrome, which is a type of hamartomatous polyp of the small intestine.

It is an autosomal dominant condition characterized by hamartomatous polyps of the intestinal tract and melanosis of the mouth and the lips. 

Clinical features:

  • Hamartomatous polyps of the intestinal tract
  • Hyperpigmentation of the buccal mucosa, lips, perianal skin, and digits
  • Increased (2% to 10%) risk for cancer of the intestinal tract, with cancers reported throughout the intestinal tract, from the stomach to the rectum.
  • Increased risk for extraintestinal malig­nant neoplasms, including cancer of the breast, ovary, cervix, fallopian tubes, thyroid, lung, gallbladder, bile ducts, pancreas, and testicles.

Management:

  • Surgery is indicated in cases where there are bleeding, obstruction, intussusception, or adenomatous changes of the polyp.
  • If surgery is done for these indications attempts should be made to remove as much as polyps as possible. 
  • Regular screening with endoscopic studies should be done due to the increased risk of malignancies.
  • Screening of other malignancies like breast and cervix are also important.

Other options:

A) Tubulovillous adenoma:

These are a mixture of tubular and villous adenoma and consist of small, pedunculated polyps composed of rounded or tubular glands and larger, sessile polyps which are covered by slender villi. These adenomas are characterized microscopically by the presence of epithelial dysplasia. The hallmarks of epithelial dysplasia are nuclear hyperchromasia, elongation and stratification.

 

 

 

C) Adenocarcinoma:

Presents with occult bleeding, changes in bowel habits, or cramping and left lower quadrant discomfort. Morphologically, they present as polypoid, exophytic masses or annular lesions that produce ‘napkin-ring’ construction and luminal narrowing. Microscopically, these tumours consist of tall columnar cells with elongated, hyperchromatic nuclei and necrotic debris in the gland lumen.

D) Hyperplastic polyp:

Hyperplastic polyps, most commonly found in the left colon are smooth, nodular protrusions of the mucosa, often on the crests of mucosal folds. Histologically, they are composed of mature goblet and absorptive cells with a serrated surface architecture.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question:
Which of the following is true?

  1. BRCA1 is an oncogene.
  2. HER2neu is amplified only in a fraction of breast cancer.
  3. EGFR(+) is seen in non-small cell lung cancer.
  4. N-MYC is a tumour suppressor gene.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2, 3

Of the given statements, 2 and 3 are true. BRCA1 is a tumor suppressor gene and MYC is a proto-oncogene.

BRCA1 is a tumor suppressor gene located on chromosome 17q21 and its function is to repair the double-stranded breaks in DNA. It is associated with familial breast and ovarian carcinoma. BRCA1-associated breast cancers are commonly poorly differentiated.

All breast cancers are separated into 3 major groups based on the expression of two proteins, ER and HER2 (also known as ERBB2). HER2 cancers are defined as cancers overexpressing HER2 and can be either ER-positive or ER-negative. Thus HER2neu is expressed only in a fraction of people with breast cancer.

EGF-receptor family has two proto-oncogenes: ERBB1 that codes for EGFR and ERBB2 that codes for HER. Mutation in EGFR results in adenocarcinoma of the lung, which is one of the main subtypes of non-small cell lung carcinoma.

MYC is a proto-oncogene, that is expressed in all eukaryotic cells and belongs to the immediate-early response genes, which are rapidly induced by RAS/MAPK signaling following growth factor stimulation of quiescent cells. Normally, MYC protein concentration are tightly controlled at the level of transcription, translation and protein stability. The mechanisms by which MYC promotes neoplastic cell growth may be follows:

  • MYC activates the expression of many genes like D cyclins, that are involved in cell cycle progression
  • MYC regulates the expression of telomerase
  • MYC is one of the transcriptional factors that can act together to reprogram somatic cells into pluripotent stem cells

MYC gene is deregulated in a number of cancers such as Burkitt lymphoma, breast, colon, lung and other cancers. The functionally identical NMYC and LMYC genes are also amplified in neuroblastomas and small cell cancers of the lung, respectively.

questions.question: Identify the given condition.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pemphigus vulgaris

The given histologic picture shows a suprabasal blister suggesting the diagnosis of pemphigus vulgaris. 

It is caused due to the production of antibodies mainly against desmoglein 3. Rarely antibodies against desmoglein 1 can also be found. The antibodies are commonly IgG antibodies.

Desmoglein 3 is mainly present in the basal and suprabasal layers of the skin and mucosa. The patients, therefore, present with flaccid bullae over the skin and mucosal ulcerations. Oral mucosa is commonly affected. Other areas where ulceration can be seen are conjunctiva, nasopharynx, larynx, etc. Cutaneous lesions are more common over the scalp, face, neck, upper chest, and back.

Direct immunofluorescence will show the deposition of antibodies around the keratinocytes in the epidermis. It is treated with steroids, azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, rituximab, etc.

Other options:

B) Leprosy: Tuberculoid leprosy shows granulomatous lesions, without much bacilli. Hence called paucibacillary leprosy. Lepromatous lesions contain large aggregates of lipid-laden macrophages (lepra cells), often filled with masses (globi) of acid-fast bacilli. Because of the presence of abundant bacteria, it is also called as multibacillary.

The lesions may be pruritic or even asymptomatic.  Histological hallmarks include: 1. Sézary-Lutzner cells - cells with cerebriform nuclei (infolded/ hyper-convoluted nuclear membrane), 2. Pautrier's microabscesses - tumor cells invade the epidermis as single cells and small clusters, forming a collection of atypical lymphocytes in the epidermis and 3. Epidermotropism - pronounced invasion of the tumor cells into the epidermis.

Given below is the arrow pointing at Paurtier's microabcess.

Other clinical features seen in Klinefelter’s syndrome are: 

  • Disproportionately long arms and legs,
  • Gynecomastia
  • Eunuchoid body habitus
  • Mitral valve prolapse
  • Mental retardation; IQ: 60-80,
  • Minor developmental and learning disabilities,
  • Lack of secondary sexual characteristics (due to a decrease in androgen production)

  • Testicular dysgenesis with small penis
  • Infertility/azoospermia
  • Type 2 diabetes mellitus
  • Metabolic syndrome

  • Most common sex aneuploidy in males
  • Classically karyotype is 47, XXY. Other variants can have 48 XXXY; rarely, 49 XXXXY; or mosaics with some cells containing normal 46, XY and others 47, XXY
  • Results from meiotic nondisjunction of sex chromosomes (mostly during 1st meiotic division)

A variant of Klinefelter’s syndrome—49, XXXXY—presents with short stature

  • Nipples widely spaced

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: A 20-year-old athlete suddenly collapsed while playing football and was taken to the hospital where he was declared dead. His autopsy image is given below. Which of the following is the most likely cause of death?
options: Valvular heart disease due‌ to RHD
Sudden cardiac death due t‌o arrhythmia
Sudden cardiac death due t‌o Hypertrophic cardiomyop​athy
Sudden cardiac death due t‌o atherosclerosis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sudden cardiac death due to arrhythmia

The given image shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy and along with the scenario, it is suggestive of sudden cardiac death due to arrhythmia. Patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy have an increased risk of sudden cardiac death from ventricular tachyarrhythmias. In fact, arrhythmias are the most important/most common cause of death in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is one of the most common causes of sudden, otherwise unexplained death in young athletes. HCM is characterized by reduced stroke volume due to impaired diastolic filling, which is a consequence of the massively hypertrophic left ventricle. There is a dynamic obstruction to the left ventricular outflow as the anterior mitral leaflet moves towards the ventricular septum during systole. This compromised cardiac output in combination with a secondary increase in pulmonary venous pressure is the reason for exertional dyspnea at times of increased oxygen demand.

Major clinical problems in HCM are atrial fibrillation, stroke, intractable cardiac failure, ventricular arrhythmias and also sudden death. There is a harsh systolic ejection murmur caused by the ventricular outflow obstruction. Mutations causing hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) are most commonly seen in the genes encoding β-myosin heavy chain (MHC/MYH7) or myosin-binding protein C (MYBP-C). 

HCM is mostly an autosomal dominant disorder. The most important histologic features of HCM myocardium are as follows:

  1. Massive myocyte hypertrophy particularly of transverse myocyte diameters
  2. Myofiber disarray including that of bundles of myocytes, individual myocytes, and contractile elements
  3. Interstitial and replacement fibrosis

Most of the patients can be treated with β blockers to decrease heart rate and contractility. Implantable cardioverter-defibrillators are used in patients with increased risk of ventricular arrhythmias. Some patients can also be treated by surgical excision of the septal muscle or by carefully controlled septal infarction through a catheter-based infusion of alcohol.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: Which of the following can be prevented by transfusing irradiated RBCs?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Graft versus host disease

Transfusion of irradiated RBCs prevent the incidence of graft versus host disease (GVHD) associated with the transfusion.

GVHD occurs when immunologically competent cells or their precursors are transplanted into immunologically compromised recipients and the transferred cells recognize the alloantigens in the host and attack host tissues. It is seen most commonly during hematopoietic stem cell transplantation but may occur following transplantation of solid organs too. 

GVHD maybe of two types: acute and chronic.

Acute GVHD occurs within days to weeks after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. It mainly involves the immune system and the epithelia of the skin (in the form of generalized rash), liver( in the form of jaundice), and intestines (in the form of bloody diarrhea). But the affected tissues are not heavily infiltrated by lymphocytes.

Chronic GVHD may follow acute GVHD or may occur insidiously. These patients have extensive skin damage, with destruction of skin appendages and fibrosis of the dermis, resembling systemic sclerosis. Cholestatic jaundice and esophageal strictures are also common. There will be involution of the thymus and depletion of lymphocytes in the lymph nodes. There will also be recurrent bouts of life-threatening infections. Some may even develop autoimmunity, owing to the grafted CD4+ helper T cells reacting with host B cells and stimulating them, which may result in autoantibodies production.

Depletion of donor T cells by irradiation, before transfusion can eliminate the occurrence of GVHD. But irradiation also has its side effects such as recurrence of tumor in leukemic patients, increased incidence of graft failures and EBV-related B-cell lymphoma.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question:
Which of the following statements are correct regarding the effect of Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase deficiency?

  1. Decrease in reduced glutathione
  2. Decreased NADPH
  3. Decreased lipid peroxidation
  4. Decreased RBC membrane damage
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 & 2 are correct.

Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency causes decrease in reduced glutathione and decreased NADPH.

G6PD is an important enzyme involved in the hexose monophosphate shunt. Defective enzyme function reduced the ability of red cells to protect themselves against oxidative injuries, thereby increasing lipid peroxidation and lead to hemolysis. 

  • G6PD reduces NADP to NADPH while oxidizing glucose-6-phosphate.
  • This NADPH then provides reducing equivalents needed for conversion of oxidized glutathione to reduced glutathione.
  • This reduced glutathione acts as a cofactor in reactions that neutralize compounds such as H2O2, thereby protecting against oxidant injury.
  • Exposure of G6PD deficient red cells to oxidative stress leads to crosslinking of reactive sulfhydryl groups on globin chains, which then becomes denatured and form membrane-bound precipitates called ‘Heinz bodies’, thereby producing membrane damage.
  • When these inclusion bearing RBCs pass through the splenic cords, macrophages pluck out these Heinz bodies.
  • The resultant cells are called ‘Bite cells’. 

Clinical features:

  • Episodic hemolysis, both intravascular and extravascular
  • Hemolytic anaemia
  • Hemoglobinemia
  • Hemoglobinuria

The episode of hemolysis is self-limiting, since only the older RBCs are at risk for lysis, leaving the G6PD-replete younger RBCs in circulation. The recovery phase is heralded by reticulocytosis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: Which of the following is not likely to be seen in a patient with Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH)?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Leukemia

Leukemia is least likely to be seen in patients with Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH).

Clinical manifestations of PNH include:

  • Hemolytic anemia
  • Pancytopenia
  • Intermittent hemoglobinuria- acute hemolytic episodes occur at night owing to a slight fall in pH during sleep
  • Haemosiderinuria
  • Venous thrombosis (a leading cause of death in PNH)
  • Patients diagnosed with PNH can later develop aplastic anemia and vice versa

PNH is an acquired disorder resulting from the mutation in the phosphatidylinositol glycan complementation group A gene (PIGA), an enzyme that is essential for the synthesis of membrane-associated complement regulatory proteins. PNH blood cells are abnormally susceptible to lysis or injury by complement since they are deficient in three GPI- linked proteins that regulate complement activity: 

  • Decay-accelerating factor or CD55
  • Membrane inhibitor of reactive lysis or CD59 (Inhibitor of C3 convertase) and
  • C8-binding protein 

Diagnosis:

  • Ham’s test: The abnormal sensitivity of red blood cells, leukocytes, and platelets to complement can be demonstrated in vitro using red cell lysis at acidic pH.
  • Flow cytometry detects the red cells that are deficient in GPI-linked proteins such as CD59.

Treatment:

Eculizumab, a monoclonal antibody, that prevents the conversion of C5 to C5a has been proven effective in PNH. The definitive treatment is hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.

questions.question: A child presented with bilateral proptosis. From the peripheral smear, he was suspected to have chloroma. What is the next investigation of choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Bone marrow biopsy

The next investigation of choice, in a child suspected to have a chloroma, is a bone marrow biopsy.

Chloroma, also called myeloid sarcoma, granulocytic sarcoma, or myeloblastoma is an extramedullary tumor that occurs in 2% to 14% of patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Frequent sites of involvement are the skin, lymph nodes, gastrointestinal tract, bone, soft tissue, testis, and peritoneum.

Isolated orbital involvement of myeloid sarcoma is rare. Proptosis is the most common presentation. Other symptoms include lacrimal swelling, conjunctival mass lesion, retinal hemorrhages, ptosis, dystopia. Decreased visual acuity and ocular movement restriction have also been reported.

Most cases of chloroma can be diagnosed on peripheral smear examination, which is easily available and is relatively inexpensive. Sometimes it may not be associated with any peripheral smear abnormality, and hence bone marrow aspirate and biopsy should be done to confirm AML. The diagnosis can also be made if Auer rods are detected. Myeloid sarcomas have immunophenotypic features that are identical to AML.

Although myeloid sarcomas are radiosensitive, they are managed with systemic chemotherapy in most cases, even in the absence of bone marrow involvement. Surgery and/or radiation therapy may be indicated for symptomatic lesions or tumors causing local organ dysfunction or obstruction.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: A person working in an industry for a long time developed progressive breathlessness. The histopathological image of his lung biopsy is given below. What industry was he most likely working in?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Asbestos

From the clinical history of progressive breathlessness and the histopathological image showing asbestos bodies, ferruginous bodies, and fibrosis, the patient is most likely working in the asbestos industry.

Asbestosis occurs due to the inhalation of crystalline hydrated silicates (asbestos). It is characterized by diffuse parenchymal interstitial fibrosis. It usually begins in the lower lobes of the lungs and may present with dyspnoea and cough, usually after 20-30 years of exposure. Other asbestos-related diseases include pleural plaques, recurrent pleural effusions, lung carcinoma, and mesothelioma.

Asbestos bodies are a hallmark finding. They appear as golden brown, fusiform, or beaded rods. These are formed when the asbestos fibers are phagocytosed by the macrophages and are coated by iron-containing proteinaceous material derived from phagocyte ferritin. Similar iron-protein complexes coat other inorganic particulates other than asbestos which are termed as ferruginous bodies.

The image below shows asbestos bodies.

Other options:

Option A: Silicosis is due to the inhalation of crystalline silicon dioxide (silica) as seen in individuals employed in sandblasting or rock mining. Macrophages phagocytose inhaled silica particles, thereby activating and releasing inflammatory mediators (IL-1, IL-8) that cause fibroblast recruitment. Subsequently, collagen is deposited in the interstitium.

Microscopy reveals coalescent nodules of whorled collagen fibers surrounded by a peripheral zone of silica-laden macrophages. 

Shown below is an image of a silicotic nodule with collagen whorls as seen in this condition.

 

Option C: Anthracosis/coal workers' pneumoconiosis is a pulmonary condition seen in coal miners. The inhaled carbon pigment is engulfed by alveolar or interstitial macrophages, which accumulate in the connective tissue. Initially it causes simple coal workers pneumoconiosis with little or no pulmonary dysfunction. With continued exposure, lung tissue undergoes progressive massive fibrosis which is called as complicated coal workers pneumoconiosis. The upper lobes of the lungs are commonly involved.

Microscopic features consist of coal-laden macrophages, black pigment, and dense collagenous interstitial fibrosis. 

The image below shows anthracosis- black pigment engulfed within macrophages as well as in the form of deposits.

 

Option D: Cotton dust causes byssinosis and can induce occupational asthma.
