questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: A patient presented with complaints of dyspnea on exertion for 1 month. Echocardiography showed the presence of mitral stenosis and left ventricular hypertrophy. Identify the histopathological finding given below and the probable diagnosis.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Aschoff body; Rheumatic heart disease

The lesion shown in the histopathological slide is Aschoff's body and the most probable diagnosis is rheumatic heart disease (RHD).

Aschoff's bodies are the lesions found in the heart during acute rheumatic fever. They are composed of foci of T lymphocytes, activated macrophages called Anitschkow cells, and occasional plasma cells. Anitschkow cells have abundant cytoplasm and central round-to-ovoid nuclei with chromatin that is centrally condensed into a slender, wavy ribbon. Hence, they are also called caterpillar cells.

Rheumatic fever is the leading cause of mitral stenosis. During acute rheumatic fever, Aschoff bodies may be found in any of the three layers of the heart that results in pericarditis, myocarditis, or endocarditis. 

Chronic inflammation leads to diffuse thickening and fibrosis of the valve leaflets, often with calcific deposits. Fibrinoid necrosis occurs due to inflammation of the endocardium and the left-sided valves. Over these areas of necrosis, small vegetations called verrucae develop along the lines of closure. Irregular thickenings present in the subendocardium are called MacCallum plaques.

In chronic RHD, the mitral valve leaflet is thickened, with commissural fusion and shortening. There is thickening and fusion of the tendinous cords. This can lead to narrowing the mitral orifice, leading to a fish mouth appearance (button hole).

Some major manifestations of rheumatic Fever are:

  • Migratory polyarthritis of the large joints 
  • Pancarditis (myocarditis, pericarditis, or endocarditis)
  • Subcutaneous nodules (typically on extensor surfaces of extremities)
  • Erythema marginatum, an irregular circinate skin rash 
  • Sydenham chorea, a neurologic disorder with involuntary rapid movements

Image showing button hole appearance seen in mitral stenosis in case of rheumatic heart disease.

Image show Aschoff bodies seen in RHD.

Other options:

Option B: Degenerative calcific deposits in the mitral valve typically develop in the fibrous annulus. They are seen grossly as irregular, stony hard, occasionally ulcerated nodules at the base of the leaflets. Usually, it does not affect valvular function. However, occasionally it can lead to regurgitation, stenosis, or arrhythmias.

The image below shows severe calcification of the mitral valve annulus with focally thickened shortened and fused chordae.

Option C: In sarcoidosis, the involved tissues contain well-formed non-necrotizing granulomas. They are composed of aggregates of tightly clustered epithelioid macrophages, often with giant cells, usually without central necrosis. As the lesions become chronic, fibrous rims or hyaline fibrous scars enclose the granulomas.

The image below shows non-necrotizing granulomas in the wall of a bronchiole in sarcoidosis.

Option D: In tuberculosis, sites of active involvement of tuberculosis are marked histologically by a characteristic granulomatous inflammatory reaction composed of both caseating and non-caseating tubercles. Usually, granuloma shows central granular caseation surrounded by multinucleate giant cells. Central caseation may be absent in non-caseating granulomas. Staining should be done to detect acid-fast bacilli when granulomas are present. 

The image below shows a caseating granulomatous lesion with areas of caseation (on the right half) bordered by collections of epithelioid cells, Langhans giant cells, and lymphocytes.

Image showing non-necrotizing granuloma seen in pulmonary tuberculosis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: A patient with lytic lesions on the skull is suspected of a diagnosis of Langerhan cell histiocytosis. Which of the following is a characteristic finding on electron microscopy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Birbeck granules

The presence of Birbeck granules in the cytoplasm is a characteristic finding of Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) on electron microscopy.

Birbeck granules have a dilated terminal end producing a tennis racket–like appearance. It contains the protein langerin (CD207). It is seen on electron microscopy.

The image below shows Birbeck granules on electron microscopy seen in LCH.

 

Histopathologically, Langerhans cells have a single large nucleus with a characteristic folded or grooved nucleus (coffee-bean appearance) with small inconspicuous nucleoli. Birbeck granules are seen in the cytoplasm. The tumor cells specifically express HLA-DR, S-100, and CD1a and langerin (CD207) markers.

The image below shows histopathological image of Langerhan cells with folded nuclei.

 

Langerhans cell histiocytosis occurs due to the proliferation of a special type of immature dendritic cells, called Langerhans cells. Their normal function is to present antigens. The most common mutation is BRAFV600E gain-of-function mutation.

It is characterized by single or multiple osteolytic bone lesions and can also infiltrate nearly every organ, like the skin (of the scalp), lungs, liver, spleen, bone marrow, or the central nervous system. 

LCH can present as the following clinical entities:

  • Multifocal multisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosis (Letterer-Siwe disease)
  • Unifocal and multifocal unisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosis (eosinophilic granuloma)- The combination of bone defects, diabetes insipidus, and exophthalmos is called the Hand-Schüller-Christian triad.
  • Pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis

The below image shows lytic lesion of skull seen in LCH.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: A 60-year-old patient presented with scrotal swelling and ataxia. Which among the following could likely be a cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma

The most likely cause in the following case is Non-Hodgkin lymphoma(NHL). Diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL), a type of NHL is the most common lymphoma. NHL affects the elderly age group and extranodal presentation is common. DLBCL can involve CNS, and CNS involvement is particularly common if there is involvement of the testes, paranasal sinuses, or bone marrow as well.

Primary testicular lymphoma is common in NHL when compared to Hodgkin lymphoma. Primary testicular lymphoma(PTL) is an aggressive and uncommon form of non-Hodgkin lymphoma(NHL) usually affecting the elderly age group(>60y). It typically presents as a painless, firm testicular mass. Constitutional symptoms are uncommon, and if present, warrant a systemic involvement. Metastasis involves the central nervous system (CNS), skin, contralateral testis, and pleura resulting in local complications.

Even though ataxia is seen as a paraneoplastic symptom due to cerebellar degeneration in Hodgkin lymphoma, testicular involvement is very rare and so far only 5 cases have been reported. Hodgkin lymphoma arises in a single node or chain of nodes and spreads first to anatomically contiguous lymphoid tissues. The extranodal presentation is rare. The extranodal disease can occur at any site like lung, liver, bone, and bone marrow is most common if it occurs. The central nervous system and the testis are exceptionally rare sites for Hodgkin's lymphoma. Thus Hodgkin's lymphoma can be ruled out.

Other options:

A) Glioblastoma multiforme is a highly malignant tumor, common in older adults in the fifth and sixth decades. The most common locations are the frontal and temporal lobes. The tumor may spread and invade the other hemisphere, resulting in a characteristic butterfly appearance. Extracranial metastases of malignant gliomas are extremely rare due to:

  • Absence of a lymphatic system in the brain and spinal cord for systemic dissemination
  • Dense dura around intracranial veins, preventing the penetration of the tumor
  • Lack of nurturing stroma in other organs prevents the proliferation of glioblastoma cells

Therefore the tumor metastasizing to the testis is very much unlikely and glioblastoma can be ruled out.

Image showing MRI(magnetic resonance imaging) of glioblastoma

Option D) Testicular cancer is the most common cancer in men aged from 15 to 35 years. Germ cell tumors(GCT) account for 90%–95% of cases.  Non-seminomatous form (NSGCT) metastasizes to the lungs, liver, central nervous system, and bone in order of frequency. The frequency of brain metastases is very low, not exceeding 1.2%. 

Note: This is a controversial question. A more detailed clinical history and examination than what is provided in the stem are required for us to arrive at a definitive diagnosis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: A patient with cirrhosis and ascites presented to you. The gross appearance of his liver is as shown below. Which among the following is true about it?
options: Dark areas represent necro‌sis, white areas represen​t viable liver tissue
Dark areas represent viabl‌e liver tissue, white are​as represent necrosis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dark areas represent necrosis, white areas represent viable liver tissue

The gross image of the liver shows a nutmeg appearance, seen in heart failure. The dark areas represent necrosis, white areas represent viable liver tissue.

Nutmeg liver refers to the mottled appearance of the liver which resembles the cut section of nutmeg. This occurs as a result of hepatic venous congestion following right heart failure. The dark centrilobular zones reflect sinusoidal congestion. Congestion is seen around the central veins usually from right-sided heart failure. The pale periportal zones reflect normal or fatty liver tissue.

The liver derives its blood supply from the portal venous system and the hepatic artery. The portal triad constitutes:

  • Branches of the hepatic artery
  • Portal vein 
  • Bile duct

The blood from the portal vein and the hepatic artery flow through the intervening sinusoids and drains into the central vein. The central veins from adjacent lobules form interlobular veins, which then unite as hepatic veins and finally drain into the inferior vena cava. 

The hepatic lobule is divided into three zones:

  • Zone 1 is the periportal area 
  • Zone 2 is the intermediate zone
  • Zone 3 is the area closest to the central vein

Right-sided cardiac failure leads to passive congestion of the liver. Left-sided cardiac failure leads to hypoperfusion and hypoxia of hepatocytes around central veins. The combination of hypoperfusion and retrograde congestion causes centrilobular hemorrhagic necrosis, leading to this mottled appearance of the liver, known as nutmeg liver. 

The microscopic image below of a nutmeg liver shows perisinusoidal fibrosis, hepatic venule dilation, and dilation of the sinusoids in zone III.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question:
A 6-year-old boy came with bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy. What is the probable diagnosis, cell, and virus associated with the image given below?

RS cell: Reed-Sternberg cell

HIV: Human immunodeficiency virus

CMV: Cytomegalovirus

EBV: Epstein-Barr virus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hodgkin's lymphoma, RS cell, EBV

The probable diagnosis, cell, and virus from the given clinical scenario and the histopathological image are Hodgkin's lymphoma, Reed-Sternberg cells (RS cells), and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) respectively.

Hodgkin's lymphoma arises in a single lymph node or chain of nodes and spreads first to anatomically contiguous lymphoid tissues. It usually presents as painless lymphadenopathy. The distinctive feature of Hodgkin's lymphoma is the presence of Reed-Sternberg cells.

RS cells are giant neoplastic cells derived from germinal centre or post–germinal centre B cells. They appear as large cells with multiple nuclei or a single nucleus with multiple nuclear lobes. Each cell contains large inclusion-like prominent nucleoli, and abundant, usually slightly eosinophilic, cytoplasm, depicting an owl-eye appearance, as shown in the image below.

WHO classifies Hodgkin's lymphoma into 5 subtypes:

  • Nodular sclerosis: Frequent lacunar cells
  • Mixed cellularity
  • Lymphocyte-rich
  • Lymphocyte depletion
  • Nodular lymphocyte predominance

The first 4 subtypes are considered classical Hodgkin's lymphoma. The RS cells are CD 15+ and CD30+. The lymphocyte predominant type is considered non-classical Hodgkin's lymphoma with CD15-, CD30-, CD20+ and EB -.

Type RS-cell EB Virus Prognosis
1. Nodular sclerosis (most common in the world) Frequent lacunar cells and occasional diagnostic RS cells Rare Very good
2. Mixed cellularity (most common in India) Frequent mononuclear and diagnostic RS cells 70% Good
3.Lymphocyte Rich

Frequent mononuclear and diagnostic RS cells

 40% Very good
4.Lymphocyte depleted Reticular variant: frequent diagnostic RS cells and variants and a paucity of background reactive cell 90%(Max) Poorest

5.Lymphocyte predominant		 L&H variant (Popcorn cell) variants in the background of follicular dendritic cells 0%(Min) Excellent

The image below shows a popcorn cell seen in lymphocytic predominant Hodgkin's lymphoma.

Other options: 

Option A: RS cells are diagnostic of Hodgkin's lymphoma, not non-Hodgkin's lymphoma. The histopathologic findings in non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) are varied and depend on the subtype.

Option B: Kaposi sarcoma is a vascular neoplasm caused by human herpesvirus 8 (HHV8), also known as Kaposi sarcoma herpesvirus. Cutaneous lesions of Kaposi sarcoma are composed of spindle cells, mostly in the dermis or subcutaneous tissues, with small vessels and slit-like spaces with red cells.

The image shows lesions seen in Kaposi's sarcoma.

Option D: Infectious mononucleosis is caused by EBV. The peripheral blood smear shows absolute lymphocytosis with mononucleosis cells which are atypical activated T lymphocytes. They have abundant cytoplasm with multiple vacuolations and azurophilic granules, and an oval, indented, or folded nucleus and are shown below.

About 5-7% of the cases of infectious mononucleosis can be caused by the cytomegalovirus (CMV), which can also cause pneumonia. CMV-infected pneumocytes with large, intranuclear, basophilic inclusions with haloes at their periphery as well as small, granular cytoplasmic inclusions are seen below with an owl-eye appearance.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: A person was brought to the emergency department with facial swelling, itching, and hypotension following a bee sting. The mentioned clinical features are due to the increase in which immunoglobulin?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. IgE

The given clinical features suggest type 1 hypersensitivity reaction and are mediated by immunoglobulin E (IgE).

Immediate (Type I) hypersensitivity reactions refer to allergic reactions or allergies.

It is a rapid immunologic reaction that is triggered by the binding of an antigen to IgE antibody on the surface of mast cells. It occurs in a previously sensitized individual. These reactions are induced by environmental antigens (allergens) that stimulate strong TH2 responses and IgE production in genetically susceptible individuals. 

Activation of TH2 cells is mediated by IL-4 and in turn, TH2 cells produce IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13. These cytokines act on B cells to stimulate IgE and activation of eosinophils. IgE coats mast cells by binding to the FcεRI receptor. Re-exposure to the allergen leads to cross-linking of the IgE and FcεRI which in turn causes activation of mast cells releasing powerful mediators. The principal mediators are:

  • Histamine
  • Proteases
  • Prostaglandins
  • Leukotrienes
  • Cytokines like TNF, IL-1, and chemokines. 

The clinical manifestations may be local or systemic and range from mildly annoying rhinitis to fatal anaphylaxis.

It occurs in two phases: 

  • The immediate phase is characterized by vasodilation, vascular leakage, smooth muscle spasm (in asthma), or glandular secretions. These changes occur within minutes after exposure to an allergen and subside in a few hours.
  • Late-phase reaction is characterized by infiltration of tissues with eosinophils, neutrophils, basophils, monocytes, and CD4+ T cells. Late-phase reaction sets in 2 to 24 hours later and may last for several days.

Image: Sequence of events in immediate (type 1) hypersensitivity.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: All of the following are associated with massive splenomegaly except :
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Aplastic anemia

All the above are associated with massive splenomegaly except aplastic anemia.

Aplastic anemia is a syndrome of chronic primary hematopoietic failure. This results in pancytopenia (anemia, neutropenia, and thrombocytopenia). Important causes include 

  • Alkylating agents, antimetabolites
  • Benzene
  • Whole-body irradiation
  • Viral infections: Hepatitis (unknown virus), Cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, Herpes zoster
  • Fanconi anemia

The patient will have

  • Decreased red blood cells leading to anemia
  • Decreased white blood cells leading to recurrent infections
  • Decreased platelets leading to petechiae and ecchymoses.

Many other leukemias and lymphomas may have a similar presentation. However, splenomegaly is characteristically absent in these patients. 

The bone marrow is markedly hypocellular. It is largely devoid of hematopoietic cells. Marrow aspirates yield a dry tap having only fat cells, fibrous stroma, lymphocytes, and plasma cells. Aplasia is best appreciated in marrow biopsies. The following image shows a hypocellular bone marrow with little hematopoiesis and several fat cells.

Stem cell transplantation is the treatment of choice in those with a suitable donor. Immunosuppressive therapy is responsive in old patients or in patients without suitable donors.

Other options:

Option A- Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) is a myeloproliferative neoplasm with the presence of BCR-ABL fusion gene translocation mutation. The marrow is markedly hypercellular because of increased numbers of maturing granulocytic precursor cells. This results in decreased hematopoiesis within the bone marrow. The spleen is often greatly enlarged as a result of extensive extramedullary hematopoiesis. Extramedullary hematopoiesis can also produce mild hepatomegaly and lymphadenopathy.

Option C- Hairy cell leukemia is a memory B-cell neoplasm predominantly seen in middle-aged male patients. It occurs due to activating BRAF mutations. Infiltration of the bone marrow, liver, and spleen with tumor cells result in splenomegaly. Sometimes, this can be the only finding in the patient. Pancytopenia results from marrow involvement.

Hairy cells have round, oblong, or reniform nuclei and moderate amounts of pale blue cytoplasm with thread-like or bleb-like extensions. Immunophenotyping shows hairy cell leukemias typically express the pan-B-cell markers CD19 and CD20 and certain relatively distinctive markers, such as CD11c, CD25, CD103, and annexin A1.

 Option D- Lymphomas cause splenomegaly due to the infiltration of neoplastic cells in the spleen.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: A 42-year-old female patient presents with cough, low-grade fever, and hemoptysis. Investigations reveal a cavitary lesion on her right lung apex, which on biopsy reveals caseous necrosis. The underlying pathophysiology is :
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Type 4 hypersensitivity reaction

The clinical scenario with complaints of cough, low-grade fever, hemoptysis is suggestive of pulmonary tuberculosis. The diagnosis is further supported by a cavitary lesion in the apex of the lung and a biopsy showing caseous necrosis. The pathophysiology is a type 4 hypersensitivity reaction mediated by activated macrophages.

Tuberculosis is a chronic pulmonary and systemic disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Granulomatous inflammation and tissue damage are by Th-1 mediated macrophage activation and killing of bacteria. Interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) released by Th-1 cells is the critical mediator that activates the macrophages. This activation differentiates the macrophages into epithelioid cells that aggregate to form granuloma. This is a T-cell mediated (Type 4) hypersensitivity reaction.

Pulmonary TB due to exogenous (new infection) or endogenous (reactivation of a dormant primary lesion) infection in a sensitized individual is called post-primary or reactivation or secondary or adult-type TB.

The apical and posterior segments of the upper lobe and superior segments of the lower lobe are most commonly involved in post-primary TB due to increased ventilation in these segments than the lower zones. Patients often present with fever, productive cough, blood-streaked sputum, night sweats, malaise, loss of appetite, and weight loss.

Radiological findings include ill-defined opacification in the upper lobes, consolidation, collapse, and cavitation development.

  • Typically, the disease is parenchymal without nodal enlargement.
  • Cavitation is a distinguishing feature of postprimary TB.
    • Typical cavities are thick-walled and irregular.
    • Air-fluid levels are uncommon in TB. The presence of air-fluid levels indicates superadded infections.
  • Upper-lobe involvement with cavitation and the absence of lymphadenopathy distinguishes postprimary TB from primary TB.

The image below shows chest X-ray findings of a post-primary TB with a cavity (black arrows) in the right upper lobe and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates (white triangles) in the apical regions.

Image shows a gross picture of caseous necrosis. Notice the characteristic "cheesy appearance" due to its white appearance of the area of necrosis.

Image below shows tuberculoid granuloma associated with caseous necrosis (upper right) and surrounding epithelioid cells, Langhans' multinucleated giant cells.

Other options:

Option A: Enzyme degradation is seen in liquefactive necrosis which is characterized by digestion of the dead cells, resulting in transformation of the tissue into a viscous liquid. It is seen in focal bacterial or fungal infections. Eg: Brain abscess.

Option C: Fibrinoid deposition is seen in fibrinoid necrosis. It is seen in immune reactions involving blood vessels with deposition of fibrinoid material which is combination of immune complexes and plasma proteins. Eg: Vasculitis syndromes

Option D: Sudden cut-off of blood supply causes coagulative necrosis. It is a form of necrosis in which the original architecture of dead tissue is preserved with firm texture. Eg: Ischemic injury in all organs, except the brain.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question:
A 45-year-old male patient was diagnosed with iron deficiency anemia. Which of the following is true about intracellular regulation of iron in the above condition?

IRP- Iron regulatory protein

IRE- Iron response elements
options: Ferritin translation is in‌creased by binding IRP to​ IRE
Ferritin translation is de‌creased by binding IRP to​ IRE
Transferrin receptor 1 tra‌nslation is unaffected by​ binding IRP to IRE
Transferrin receptor 1 tra‌nslation is decreased by ​binding IRP to IRE
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ferritin translation is decreased by binding IRP to IRE

In iron deficiency anemia, ferritin translation is decreased by binding iron regulatory protein to iron response elements.

Dietary iron is carried in the blood by transferrin and enters cells via endocytosis, mediated by the transferrin receptor. Excess iron is stored by binding to ferritin. The levels of transferrin, transferrin receptor (TfR), and ferritin are therefore crucial to cellular iron homeostasis.

The synthesis of these three proteins is regulated in response to iron availability and aconitase (enzyme in citric acid cycle).

When a cell is depleted of iron, the aconitase enzyme is converted to apoaconitase. Apoaconitase is identical to iron regulatory protein 1 (IRP-1) and is closely related to IRP-2. It regulates iron metabolism.

The iron regulatory proteins (IRPs) are two cytoplasmic RNA-binding proteins that control iron metabolism. They bind to regions in the mRNA containing the ferritin and transferrin receptor. These mRNA sequences are part of hairpin structures known as iron response elements (IREs). 

  • When the IRPs bind to the 5' untranslated IRE sequence in the ferritin mRNA, IRPs block ferritin translation, thus decreasing ferritin.
  • When IRPs are bound to the 3' end of the untranslated IRE sequence, they stabilize the mRNA, prevent its degradation and increase the copies of transferrin receptor per mRNA molecule.

Hence, in iron-deficient cells, iron storage (bound to ferritin) is reduced and iron uptake (via transferrin receptor) becomes more efficient.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: A 65-year-old male patient with chronic fatigue and lymphadenopathy presents to the outpatient department. His peripheral smear shows the presence of smudge cells. Which of the following additional investigations will you do to arrive at a diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Flow cytometry

An elderly patient with chronic fatigue and lymphadenopathy, and a peripheral smear showing the presence of smudge cells suggest a diagnosis of chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Immunophenotyping using flow cytometry is the investigation done to arrive at the diagnosis. The classical immunophenotypic feature of CLL is CD 19+, CD20+, CD 23+, CD5+.

Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL) is a peripheral B-cell neoplasm usually affecting adults, more commonly men. Patients are often asymptomatic at diagnosis. When symptomatic, it presents non specifically with easy fatigability, weight loss, and anorexia. Generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly are present in most symptomatic patients. 

The chromosomal defects in CLL include:

  • Deletion of 13q (commonest and has a good prognosis)
  • Deletion of 11q
  • Trisomy 12q
  • Deletion of 17p (poor prognosis)

The peripheral blood smear in cases of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) contains small round lymphocytes having condensed chromatin and scant cytoplasm. Some of these cells may get disrupted while preparing the smears, producing smudge cells. An absolute lymphocyte count of >5000/mm3 is required for diagnosis. Hypogammaglobulinemia is commonly seen, making the patient susceptible to infections. A few patients may develop hemolytic anemia or thrombocytopenia due to autoantibodies made by non-neoplastic B cells.

On lymph node biopsy: Lymph nodes are composed of small lymphocytes admixed with larger activated lymphocytes. The large lymphocytes contain mitotically active cells and gather in loose aggregates referred to as proliferation centers. These proliferation centers are pathognomic to CLL when present.

Expectant management is the treatment of choice for asymptomatic patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia. The gold standard for therapy is a combination of fludarabine, cyclophosphamide, and rituximab.

Richter’s syndrome is a complication of CLL in which there is a transformation to an aggressive lymphoma, most commonly diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL).

The image shows small round lymphocytes and smudge cells seen in CLL.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: Oil red O stain is used in which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Frozen section

Oil red O (ORO) stain is used in frozen section.

Oil red O stains lipid/ fats and gives a characteristic orange/red appearance. It is used in the unfixed frozen sections as the fixation of fats with other routine processes may lose the lipid content. 10% Neutral buffer formaldehyde (NBF) is the preferred fixative in histopathological sections staining with Oil red O. Zenker's fixative and Helly's fixative are best avoided during staining with ORO.

Oil red O stains the lipid in the vacuoles in the pulmonary vasculature. It can be useful in identifying fat emboli in lung tissue, diagnosing renal cell carcinoma, and sebaceous gland tumors of the skin.

 Other stains used for lipids or fats:

  • Nile blue sulfate. The preferred fixative is formal calcium.
  • Osmic acid is used in the frozen section. 10% NBF is the preferred fixative
  • Sudan black B is used in the frozen section. The preferred fixative is 10% NBF.

Other Options:

Option A: Formalin fixation- Formalin as 10% neutral buffered formalin (NBF) is the most common fixative used in diagnostic pathology.

Option C: Ethyl alcohol- Ideal fixative for cytological smears because they act quickly and give good nuclear detail.

Option D: Glutaraldehyde- Preferred fixative in electron microscopy. The standard solution is a 2.5% buffered glutaraldehyde.

Image below shows microscopy of a oil red O stained bronchoalveolar lavage sample from a patient with acute lung injury.

The image shows the lipid vesicles in the adipocytes stained using oil-red-O staining.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: A boy presents with fever, night sweats, and neck swelling. The biopsy of swelling showed a starry sky appearance. What is the most likely genetic abnormality seen in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. MYC

The given clinical scenario and the classical histopathological finding of starry sky appearance suggest the diagnosis of Burkitt's lymphoma and the most likely genetic abnormality is the translocation of the MYC gene on chromosome 8.

Burkitt's lymphoma arises from mature germinal center B-cells that express surface IgM, CD19, CD20, CD10, and BCL6.

It is divided into endemic and sporadic types, both of which occur mainly in children or young adults.

  • African (endemic) Burkitt lymphoma often presents as a mass involving the mandible and may involve the abdominal viscera, particularly the kidneys, ovaries, and adrenal glands. 
  • Sporadic (non-endemic) Burkitt lymphoma most often appears as a mass involving the ileocecum and peritoneum. 
  • A subset of aggressive lymphomas occurs in individuals infected with HIV.

All forms of Burkitt lymphoma are associated with translocations of the MYC gene on chromosome 8 that lead to increased MYC protein levels. Essentially all endemic Burkitt lymphomas are latently infected with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV).

The tumor shows a high mitotic index with numerous apoptotic cells. The nuclear remnants of these apoptotic cells are phagocytosed by interspersed benign macrophages. The phagocytes have abundant clear cytoplasm, creating a characteristic starry sky pattern.

Burkitt lymphoma is very aggressive but responds well to intensive chemotherapy.

The image below shows the starry sky appearance seen in Burkitt's lymphoma.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: An electron microscopic picture of a cut section of a nerve fiber is given.  Identify the area which will be affected in the most common variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2

The most common variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome is acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (AIDP). The area affected in this condition is the myelin sheath (marked as 2 in the image). 

Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is an acute autoimmune disease that causes fulminant polyradiculoneuropathy. It is a T-cell mediated immune response. 

GBS is usually associated with a history of upper respiratory infection (URI) or acute gastroenteritis (AGE) 1-3 weeks prior. The causative organisms may be Campylobacter jejuni, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae.

It presents with the following features:

  • Ascending motor paralysis (lower limbs > upper limbs)
  • Sensory deficits may or may not be seen
  • Deep tendon reflexes - absent 
  • Transient bladder dysfunction - severe cases
  • Autonomic manifestations - loss of vasomotor control, postural hypotension, cardiac dysrhythmias 

Histological examination shows inflammation of peripheral nerves, manifested as perivenular and endoneurial infiltration by lymphocytes, macrophages, and a few plasma cells. On electron microscopy, an early effect on myelin sheaths is seen. There is segmental demyelination induced by the actions of activated macrophages.

There are several types of Guillain–Barre syndrome:

  • Demyelinating
    • Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (AIDP) - most common
  • Axonal
    • Acute motor axonal neuropathy (AMAN)
    • Acute motor-sensory axonal neuropathy (AMSAN)
  • Regional GBS syndromes: Miller–Fisher syndrome (MFS)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: A 70-year-old patient presented with cough, fatiguability, and weight loss. He was diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) on bronchoscopy. The resected specimen had a hilar lymph node that was 1cm in size and showed a black pigment. What is the black pigment likely to be?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anthracotic pigment

The black-colored pigment in the hilar lymph node of the resected bronchoscopic specimen is likely to be an anthracotic pigment.

The black color is due to the deposition of carbon particles. The inhaled carbon particles are engulfed by the lung macrophages and then transported to the hilar lymph nodes. This accumulates and causes the blackening of the lung tissues or anthracosis. 

It is commonly seen in people who work in environments where there is high air pollution with carbon particles, such as coal mines. It is also the most common exogenous pigment found in the human body as a result of air pollution in urban areas. The aggregates of the carbon dust may induce fibroblastic reaction or emphysema that may lead to a condition called coal worker's pneumoconiosis.

The following image shows anthracosis with deposition of black carbon particles, within the cytoplasm of macrophages.

Option B: Melanin is brown-black in color which occurs as a result of oxidation of tyrosine in melanocytes, as shown in the following histopathology of a lymph node. 

Option C: Lipochrome or lipofuscin (brown lipid) is seen as a yellow-brown pigment in histopathological sections of the liver and heart of normal aging patients, patients with severe malnutrition, and cancer cachexia. It is derived through lipid peroxidation and indicates free radical injury and lipid peroxidation. The following image shows a cardiac myocyte with fine yellow-brown lipofuscin granules in the perinuclear region.

Option D: Hemosiderin is a hemoglobin-derived golden-yellow colored pigment seen in conditions associated with iron overload such as hemochromatosis. The following image shows extensive intra-alveolar hemosiderin deposition following pulmonary hemorrhage.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: A 34-year-old female patient presented to the outpatient department with migratory arthritis and examination revealed a pan-systolic murmur. An echocardiography was performed which was suggestive of mitral regurgitation. A biopsy specimen was obtained and the image is provided below. What is the most likely lesion shown in the histopathology slide?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Aschoff's bodies

The given clinical findings of migratory arthritis, pan-systolic murmur, and mitral regurgitation are suggestive of acute rheumatic fever. The most likely lesion shown in the histopathological slide is Aschoff's bodies.

Aschoff's bodies are the lesions found in the heart during acute rheumatic fever. They are composed of foci of T lymphocytes, occasional plasma cells, and plump-activated macrophages called Anitschkow cells. Anitschkow cells have abundant cytoplasm and central round-to-ovoid nuclei with chromatin that is centrally condensed into a slender, wavy ribbon. Hence they are also called caterpillar cells.

During acute rheumatic fever, Aschoff bodies may be found in any of the three layers of the heart that results in pericarditis, myocarditis, or endocarditis. 

Fibrinoid necrosis can occur due to inflammation of the endocardium and the left-sided valves. Over these areas of necrosis, small vegetations can be seen along the lines of closure, called verrucae. Irregular thickenings called MacCallum plaques can be present In the subendocardium.

In chronic RHD, the mitral valve shows leaflet thickening, commissural fusion and shortening, and thickening and fusion of the tendinous cords. Calcification and fibrous bridging of the valve can lead to narrowing the mitral orifice and giving it a fish mouth appearance.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question:
A 30-year-old male complained of fatigue for the past 1 year. Examination revealed massive splenomegaly. His blood workup shows the following findings. Which of the following is the most sensitive investigation in this case?

  • Anemia
  • Total leucocyte count - 1,50,000/microL
  • Peripheral blood smear - 
    • Neutrophils- 60%
    • Basophils- 6%
    • Eosinophils - 4%
    • Myeloblasts, myelocytes, and metamyelocytes
  • Myeloid to erythroid ratio- 18:1
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. FISH and PCR

The clinical presentation with fatigue, splenomegaly, and the peripheral blood smear findings are suggestive of chronic myelogenous leukemia(CML). The BCR-ABL gene which is specific for CML is detected by fluorescence in situ hybridization(FISH) or polymerase chain reaction(PCR) based tests.

Chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) is a myeloproliferative disorder with the peak incidence in the fifth to sixth decade of life. The chimeric BCR-ABL gene is created by a reciprocal (9;22)(q34;q11) translocation(Philadelphia chromosome). This BCR-ABL gene distinguishes CML from other myeloproliferative disorders and is detected by fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) or polymerase chain reaction (PCR).

Clinical features:

Mild to moderate anemia and hypermetabolism, fatigability, weakness, weight loss, and anorexia. Dragging sensation in the abdomen caused by splenomegaly, or the acute onset of left upper quadrant pain due to splenic infarction. The spleen is often greatly enlarged as a result of extensive extramedullary hematopoiesis. Extramedullary hematopoiesis can also produce mild hepatomegaly and lymphadenopathy.

Peripheral blood:

  • Leukocytosis with leukocyte count, often exceeding 100,000 cells/mm3, which consists predominantly of neutrophils, band forms, metamyelocytes, myelocytes, eosinophils, and basophils.
  • Blasts are usually less than 10% of the circulating cells.
  • Platelet count is usually increased

Bone Marrow:

  • Markedly hypercellular marrow because of massively increased numbers of maturing granulocytic precursors. There is usually an elevated proportion of eosinophils and basophils.
  • There is also an increase in megakaryocytes and usually include small, dysplastic forms and erythroid progenitors are present in normal or mildly decreased numbers. Typically there is an increased reticulin deposition, but overt marrow fibrosis is rare early in the course.
  • Sea-blue histiocytes - These are scattered macrophages with abundant wrinkled,green-blue cytoplasm.

Other options:

Immunophenotyping and flow cytometry: Flow cytometry refers to the measurement of cellular antigens as they flow in a fluid stream. Immunophenotyping is employed using labeled antibodies against specific epitopes of cellular antigens. The technique that is usually used in immunophenotyping is flow cytometry. It has a limited role in the diagnosis of CML. It is mainly used in identifying CML blast transformation.

LAP score: Leucocyte alkaline phosphatase(LAP) score is decreased in cases of CML. It is only a first-line test in the diagnosis of CML and the diagnosis needs to be confirmed by other tests including bone marrow biopsy, molecular diagnostics, and cytogenetic analysis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: A girl presents with short stature, webbed neck, thick calves, shield-shaped chest, swelling of the ankle, and increased carrying angle. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Turner syndrome

The clinical presentation of short stature, webbed neck, thick calves, shield-shaped chest, swelling of the ankle, and increased carrying angle is suggestive of Turner syndrome.

Turner syndrome occurs due to complete or partial monosomy of X-chromosomes. It produces hypogonadism in phenotypic females. It is the most common sex chromosome abnormality in females.

Important features associated with Turner's syndrome:

  • Short stature
  • Webbing of neck
  • Broad chest and widely spaced nipples
  • Cubitus valgus
  • Streak ovaries, infertility, amenorrhea
  • Peripheral lymphedema at birth
  • Low posterior hairline
  • Poor breast development
  • Pigmented nevi
  • Cardiac manifestations – Coarctation of aorta, bicuspid aortic valve
  • Horse shoe kidney

Image showing the features of Turner syndrome

Other options:

Option B: Important features associated with Down’s syndrome (Trisomy 21) include 

  • Intellectual disability
  • Congenital heart defects
  • Epicanthic folds and flat facial profile
  • Simian crease
  • Umbilical hernias
  • Predisposition to leukemia

Option C: Important features associated with Patau syndrome (Trisomy 13):

  • Microphthalmia
  • Microcephaly and intellectual disability
  • Cleft lip and palate
  • Rocker-bottom feet
  • Cardiac and renal defects

Option D: Important features associated with Edward syndrome (Trisomy 18):

  • Prominent occiput, micrognathia, low set ears
  • Intellectual disability
  • Renal and cardiac malformations
  • Limited hip abduction, rocker-bottom feet

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: A patient with occupational exposure to benzene presents with repeated infections, easy fatigability, weight loss, and evening rise of temperature. This occupational exposure will predispose him to which of the following cancers?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Leukemia

Occupational exposure to benzene predisposes to leukemia. The given clinical history of repeated infections, easy fatigability, weight loss, and evening rise of temperature with benzene exposure points towards a diagnosis of leukemia.

Benzene is oxidized to an epoxide through hepatic CYP2E1. The epoxide and other metabolites disrupt progenitor cell differentiation in the bone marrow and lead to marrow aplasia and acute myeloid leukemia.

Acute myeloid leukemia is a tumor of hematopoietic progenitors caused by acquired oncogenic mutations that impede differentiation. This leads to the accumulation of immature myeloid blasts in the marrow. The replacement of the marrow with blasts produces marrow failure and complications related to anemia, thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia.

Other options: 

Option B: Exposure to arsenic and its compounds, asbestos, beryllium and its compounds, chromium compounds, nickel compounds, radon, and its decay products can cause lung cancer.

Option C: Exposure to aryl amines, particularly 2-naphthylamine and related compounds, cyclophosphamide, cigarette smoking, irradiation can cause bladder cancer.

Option D: Exposure to UV rays, arsenic, and its compounds can cause skin cancer.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: In iron deficiency anemia, all of the following is increased except
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Transferrin saturation

Transferrin saturation is decreased in iron deficiency anemia.

Clinical presentation may include fatigue, pallor, reduced exercise capacity. Cheilosis (fissures at the corners of the mouth) and koilonychia (spooning of the fingernails) are signs of advanced tissue iron deficiency. 

Laboratory findings are:

  • Reduced hemoglobin and hematocrit values.
  • hypochromia, microcytosis, and poikilocytosis.
  • serum iron and ferritin levels are low.
  • The total plasma iron-binding capacity that reflects the elevated transferrin levels is high.
  • Low serum iron with increased iron-binding capacity results in a reduction of transferrin saturation to below 15%.
  • RBC protoporphyrin levels are increased. Protoporphyrin is an intermediate in the heme synthesis pathway. Under conditions in which heme synthesis is impaired, protoporphyrin accumulates within the red cell.
  • Bone marrow reveals a mild to moderate increase in erythroid progenitors. The absence of stainable iron in macrophages is a diagnostically significant finding.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: Which of the following is a poor prognostic marker of multiple myeloma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. β-2 microglobulin

β-2 microglobulin is a poor prognostic marker of multiple myeloma.

Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell neoplasm commonly associated with lytic bone lesions, hypercalcemia, renal failure, and acquired immune abnormalities.

Poor prognostic factors for multiple myeloma:

  • Serum β2-microglobulin. It is the single most powerful predictor
  • Deletion of 17pITP53 sequences and the translocations t(14;16) and t(14;20)
  • Polyclonal serum Immunoglobulins
  • Elevated lactate dehydrogenase
  • High C-reactive protein
  • Increased plasma cell proliferative activity
  • High degree of bone marrow replacement
  • Presence of plasmablastic morphology
  • Elevated serum soluble receptor for IL6

Multiple myeloma usually presents as destructive plasma cell tumors involving the axial skeleton. The bones most commonly affected in descending order of frequency are the vertebral column, ribs, skull, pelvis, femur, clavicle, and scapula. 

Radiographically, bone lesions appear as punched-out defects, usually 1 to 4 cm in diameter, and consist of soft, gelatinous, red tumor masses.

Radiograph of the skull showing punched out lesions:

Morphology:

  • Malignant plasma cells have a perinuclear clearing due to a prominent golgi apparatus and an eccentrically placed nucleus.
  • Relatively normal-appearing plasma cells, plasmablasts with vesicular nuclear chromatin and a prominent single nucleolus, or bizarre, multinucleated cells may predominate.
  • Other cytologic variants include flame cells, Mott cells.
  • Flame cells have fiery red cytoplasm, Mott cells contain multiple grapelike cytoplasmic droplets, a variety of other inclusions, including fibrils, crystalline rods, and globules. The globular inclusions are referred to as Russell bodies (if cytoplasmic) or Dutcher bodies (if nuclear).
  • Rouleaux formation is characteristic but not specific. High levels of M protein in the blood causes red cells to stick to one another in linear arrays in smears leading to rouleaux formation.

Image showing Mott cell:

Image showing Russell and Dutcher bodies:

Peripheral smear of multiple myeloma:

Bence Jones proteins are excreted in the kidney and causes myeloma kidney. Most myelomas are associated with more than 3 g/dL of serum Ig and/or more than 6 mg/dL of urine Bence Jones protein. The most common monoclonal Immunoglobulin (M protein) is IgG followed by IgA.

The clinicopathologic diagnosis of multiple myeloma can be done based on the identification of clonal plasma cells in the marrow and the presence of CRAB criteria (hypercalcemia, renal dysfunction, anemia, and bone lesions).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: A pap smear taken from a patient revealed hyperchromatic nuclei, irregular nuclear borders, and low maturation index involving the whole thickness but did not breach the basement membrane. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dysplasia

The hyperchromatic nuclei, irregular nuclear borders, and intact basement membrane are all suggestive of dysplasia.

Dysplasia is characterized by the loss in the uniformity of the individual cells and their architectural orientation. The features of dysplasia include:

  • Pleomorphism
  • Hyperchromatic nuclei
  • High nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio
  • Increased mitotic figures

When the dysplastic changes involve the entire thickness of the epithelium without breaching the basement membrane it is considered preinvasive and is termed carcinoma-in-situ. If the tumor invades the basement membrane it is said to be invasive. 

Dysplasia can be considered as a precursor to malignant but it does not always progress to cancer. Dysplasia usually occurs in the metaplastic epithelium but all metaplastic epithelium is not dysplastic.

Other options:

Metaplasia: It refers to the replacement of one cell type with another type. It is almost always associated with tissue damage, repair, and regeneration. The most common epithelial metaplasia is columnar to squamous. 

Carcinoma: In carcinoma, there is the invasion of the basement membrane.

Hyperplasia: It refers to the increase in the number of cells in a tissue or organ. It can be physiologic or pathological. Enlargement of the female breast during pregnancy is physiologic hyperplasia. Endometrial hyperplasia is an example of pathological hyperplasia.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: The mother of a 12-year-old girl was worried that her daughter is shorter when compared with her classmates. On examination, the child had a webbed neck, low hairline, and shield chest. A provisional diagnosis of Turner's syndrome was made. Which of the following is a likely finding to be seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Bilateral small streak ovaries

The likely finding seen in a patient with Turner syndrome is bilateral small streak ovaries.

Turner syndrome results from complete or partial monosomy of the X chromosome. It is characterized by hypogonadism in phenotypic females. It is the most common sex chromosome abnormality in females. Three types of karyotypic abnormalities are seen

  • Missing an entire X chromosome - this results in a 45X karyotype.
  • Structural abnormalities of the X chromosomes - isochromosome of the long arm and loss of the short arm, 46X,i(X)(q10), deletion of portions of both long and short arms that lead to the formation of a ring chromosome, 46X,r(X), deletion of portions of the short or long arm, 46X,del(Xq) or 46X,del(Xp).
  • Mosaics - they will have 45X along with one or more karyotypically normal or abnormal cell types. Examples are 45X/46XX, 45X/46XY, 45X/47XXX, 45X/46X,i(X)(q10).

Important features associated with Turner's syndrome:

  • Short stature
  • Webbing of neck
  • Broad chest and widely spaced nipples
  • Cubitus valgus
  • Streak ovaries
  • Infertility, amenorrhea
  • Peripheral lymphedema at birth
  • Low posterior hairline
  • Broad chest and widely spaced nipples
  • Pigmented nevi
  • Coarctation of aorta

There is failure to develop normal secondary sex characteristics at puberty. The genitalia remain infantile, breast development is inadequate, and there is little pubic hair. Short stature and amenorrhea are of particular importance in establishing the diagnosis in an adult.

Other options:

Aortic dissection, subluxation of lens, and mitral valve prolapse are seen in Marfan syndrome.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question:
An 18-year-old male presented to the outpatient department with gum bleeding and fever for the past 2 months. General examination showed pallor and the systemic examination was unremarkable. Laboratory examination revealed Hb level- 3 gm/dl, TLC- 1500/microL, platelet count- 15000/microL. Peripheral smear shows macrocytes and the reticulocyte count is 0.5. Bone marrow examination revealed fatty streaks and absent megakaryocytes but no immature cells. What is the likely diagnosis?

Hb- Hemoglobin

TLC- Total leucocyte count
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Idiopathic acquired aplastic anemia

The given clinical scenario showing a young male with gum bleeding, fever, pancytopenia, and a low reticulocyte count with bone marrow showing fatty streaks and no immature cells is suggestive of idiopathic acquired aplastic anemia.

Aplastic anemia is a syndrome characterized by chronic hematopoietic failure and pancytopenia. The common causes include:

  • Acquired 
    • Idiopathic (most common cause, about 65% of the cases)
    • Acquired stem-cell defects 
    • Immune-mediated
  • Chemical agents 
    • Dose-related (alkylating agents, antimetabolites, benzene, chloramphenicol, inorganic arsenals) 
    • Idiosyncratic (chloramphenicol, phenylbutazone, organic arsenicals, carbamazepine, penicillamine, gold salts) 
  • Physical agents 
    • Whole-body irradiation
    • Viral infections (hepatitis, Cytomegalovirus, Epstein–Barr virus, Varicella-Zoster virus)
  • Inherited 
    • Fanconi anemia 
    • Telomerase defects 

Pathogenesis involves an extrinsic immune-mediated suppression of bone marrow and an intrinsic abnormality of the stem cells. 

Clinical features and diagnosis:

There is no age or sex predisposition for aplastic anemia. It presents insidiously with features of pancytopenia such as pallor, petechiae, and ecchymosis. Recurrent infections and fever occur as a result of neutropenia. Reticulocytopenia is seen and splenomegaly is characteristically absent. Bone marrow biopsy is used for diagnosis.

Histology:

Bone marrow aspirate usually results in a dry tap. Examination shows a hypocellular marrow devoid of hematopoietic cells with remnant fat cells, fibrous stroma, and scattered lymphocytes. Red cells are usually slightly macrocytic and normochromic. The following image shows a hypocellular bone marrow with little hematopoiesis and several fat cells.

Other options: 

Option B - Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) is an acquired disorder resulting from the mutation in the phosphatidylinositol glycan complementation group A gene (PIGA), an enzyme that is essential for the synthesis of membrane-associated complement regulatory proteins. Red cells deficient in these proteins are susceptible to intravascular hemolysis. Patients with PNH usually present with pancytopenia and reticulocytosis with bone marrow biopsy showing a cellular marrow with marked to massive erythroid hyperplasia.

Option C - Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) are a group of clonal stem cell disorders. It is a consequence of maturation defects that result in ineffective hematopoiesis with a high predisposition to conversion to AML. They are characterized by a hypercellular marrow with dysplastic cells on bone marrow aspirate. Marrow changes seen in MDS are given in the pearl below.

Option D - Pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis and patients often present with fever, productive cough, blood-streaked sputum, night sweats, malaise, loss of appetite, and weight loss.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: A child is presenting with palpable blanching purpura, abdominal pain, and pain in the knee joint resulting from arthritis. Urine examination showed hematuria and proteinuria. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Henoch-Schonlein purpura

The clinical presentation and the investigations are suggestive of Henoch-Schonlein purpura.

Henoch-Schönlein purpura is a systemic immune disorder characterized by a purpuric rash, abdominal pain, polyarthralgia, and renal abnormalities. It is most commonly seen in the age group of 3-8 years. The patient may present with the following clinical features:

  • Skin lesions- characteristically involve the extensor surfaces of arms and legs, and also the buttocks
  • Abdominal manifestations- include pain, vomiting, and intestinal bleeding.
  • Renal manifestations- include gross or microscopic hematuria, nephritic syndrome, or nephrotic syndrome. Renal manifestations are more severe in adults. A rapidly progressive form of glomerulonephritis is seen in some cases.

This condition usually occurs following an upper respiratory tract infection and there is a history of atopy in one-third of the cases. IgA is deposited in the glomerular mesangium in a distribution similar to that of IgA nephropathy.

Microscopic findings:

  • IgA deposition in the mesangial region. Sometimes there is the deposition of IgG and C3 along with IgA.
  • Renal lesions show focal or diffuse mesangial proliferation, and/or endocapillary proliferation to crescentic glomerulonephritis.
  • Skin lesions show subepidermal hemorrhages and necrotizing vasculitis of small vessels.

Other options:

Option A: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura(ITP): It occurs due to antibody-mediated destruction of platelets. It can be acute or chronic. Acute ITP is usually self-limiting in nature. Cutaneous bleeding can be in the form of petechiae and ecchymoses. The patient can also have hematuria, melena, or excessive menstrual flow. 

Option B: Dengue: It is a viral illness caused by the dengue virus. The clinical manifestations include fever, headache, musculoskeletal pain, and rash. The rash which is maculopapular in nature begins on the trunk and then spreads centrifugally to the face and extremities.

Option C: Churg- Strauss syndrome (Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis): It is characterized by eosinophilic vasculitis of multiple organs. The features of this condition include asthma, peripheral eosinophilia, pulmonary infiltrates, neuropathy, paranasal sinus abnormality, and the presence of eosinophilic vasculitis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question:
A 54-year-old patient presents to the outpatient department with fatigue, tiredness and cervical lymphadenopathy. The TLC and DLC were normal. No immature cells. A lymph node biopsy was performed which shows diffuse effacement of the lymph node architecture, cells with an indented nucleus, prominent nucleolus, and are atypical. CD10 and BCL2 are positive. What is the likely diagnosis?

TLC- Total leucocyte count

DLC- Differential leucocyte count
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Follicular lymphoma

The given clinical scenario showing fatigue, tiredness and cervical lymphadenopathy with CD10 positive BCL2 positive cells is highly suggestive of follicular lymphoma.

Follicular lymphoma presents at middle age with no sex predilection. The most common presenting symptom is painless generalized lymphadenopathy. A lymph node biopsy is adequate for the diagnosis of follicular lymphoma. Immunophenotyping of the cells showing CD19, CD20, CD10, BCL2 positive, and CD5 negative is suggestive that the cells originate from the germinal centre. 

The majority of follicular lymphomas have characteristic (14;18) translocation. This juxtaposes the IGH locus on chromosome 14 and the BCL2 locus on chromosome 18. This chromosomal rearrangement results in the overexpression of BCL2 protein, which is an inhibitor of apoptosis that contributes to lymphoma cell survival.

Histopathology:

Lymph nodes exhibit a nodular or nodular and diffuse growth pattern. Two cell types are predominantly present in varying proportions: 

  • Centrocytes (small cleaved cells) - Small cells with a cleaved nucleus and scant cytoplasm
  • Centroblasts - Large cells with open nuclear chromatin, several nucleoli, and modest amounts of cytoplasm

In most cases, there is a majority of centrocytes.

The peripheral blood smear shows lymphocytosis and bone marrow tap reveals paratrabecular lymphoid aggregates.

The following image shows a lymph node biopsy in follicular lymphoma:

Other options - 

Option B - Burkitt lymphoma is an aggressive type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL). It is also known as small non-cleaved-cell lymphoma and is characterized by the translocation and deregulation of the c-MYC gene on chromosome 8 to chromosome 14 or 22 - t(8:14) or t(8:22). Histopathology of the tumor reveals a starry sky appearance created by apoptotic cells and macrophages containing clear cytoplasm.

Option C - Mycosis fungoides is the most common type of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. The histological hallmark of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides type) is the presence of Pautrier microabscess. The presence of B-cell markers in the question rules out the differential of mycosis fungoides.

Option D - Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML) is a myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by the presence of chimeric BCR-ABL gene which is a result of a reciprocal (9;22)(q34;q11) translocation (Philadelphia chromosome). The presence of lymphadenopathy in the given scenario rules out the possibility of CML as it is a myeloid disorder.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: A software engineer presents to the outpatient department with easy fatiguability. He gives a history of sitting in front of the computer for 12 - 14 hours. He consumes a lot of junk food with very less fruits and vegetables. Hb is 9gm/dl and MCV 120 fl. What is the most likely cause of this patient's anemia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Folic acid deficiency

The given laboratory values showing anemia and increased MCV are suggestive of megaloblastic anemia. This could be due to cyanocobalamin deficiency or folic acid deficiency. The history of inadequate intake of fruits and vegetables points towards folic acid deficiency.

Dietary sources of Vit-B12 are animal products such as meat, fish, milk, and eggs. Dietary sources of folic acid are green vegetables such as lettuce, spinach, asparagus, and broccoli.

Megaloblastic anemia can occur due to Vit-B12 or folic acid deficiency. Inadequate intake, intrinsic factor deficiency, pernicious anemia, gastrectomy, malabsorption, ileal resection, alcoholism, anticonvulsants, oral contraceptives, pregnancy, infancy, disseminated cancer, markedly increased hematopoiesis, folic acid antagonists are some of the causes.

Patient can present with anorexia, weight loss, diarrhea, constipation, glossitis, angular cheilosis, reversible melanin skin hyperpigmentation, paresthesias, muscle weakness, dementia, or psychotic disturbances.

In megaloblastic anemia, DNA synthesis is impaired that leading to ineffective hematopoiesis and distinctive morphologic changes.

Peripheral blood examination shows oval macrocytes, usually with anisocytosis and poikilocytosis. MCV is usually >100 fL. The normal value of MCV is between 80-100 fL. Most macrocytes lack the central pallor of normal red cells and even appear hyperchromic, but the MCHC is not elevated. The reticulocyte count is low. Neutrophils are larger than normal and show nuclear hypersegmentation with five or more nuclear lobules.

Marrow is markedly hypercellular. Megaloblastic changes are seen at all stages of erythroid development. There is nuclear-to-cytoplasmic asynchrony, where nuclear maturation is slower than cytoplasmic maturation. Granulocytic precursors are seen in the form of giant metamyelocytes and band forms. Megakaryocytes may be abnormally large with bizarre, multilobate nuclei. 

Peripheral blood smear showing hypersegmented neutrophil:

Other options:

Option A - In cyanocobalamin deficiency, MCV will be increased. But the dietary sources of cyanocobalamin are mainly of animal products. In the given clinical scenario there is inadequate intake of fruits and vegetables. Hence, this is not the answer.

Option C - In iron deficiency anemia, MCV will be decreased.

Option D - In hereditary spherocytosis, MCV will be normal.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: A chronic alcoholic patient presented with increasing abdominal girth. On examination, shifting dullness was present and the liver span was less than 7cm. Histopathological examination revealed the presence of intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions in hepatocytes. What is the content of these inclusions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Intermediate filaments

The clinical scenario given here describes alcoholic hepatitis. In this condition, there are intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions called Mallory Denk bodies and they contain intermediate filaments. 

The liver undergoes inflammation and fibrosis in alcoholic hepatitis. This leads to injured and swollen hepatocytes with cleared-out cytoplasm and cytoskeletal damage. These hepatocytes are called ballooned hepatocytes. When the cytoskeletal damage is extensive, there is the formation of Mallory Denk/ Mallory hyaline bodies. These are remnants of partially degraded intermediate filaments and are composed of keratin filaments. 

Cytoskeletal proteins include intermediate filaments, microfilaments (made up of actin - option B), and microtubules (option - C).

Intermediate filaments provide a flexible scaffold to organize cytoplasm and prevent external forces from acting on the cell. They are of five types:

  • Keratin filaments (epithelial cells)
  • Neuro filaments (neurons)
  • Desmin filaments (muscles)
  • Vimentin filaments (connective tissues)
  • Glial filaments (glial cells)

Fibronectin (option D) is an adhesive glycoprotein. Its presence in cervicovaginal secretions before rupture of membranes is a possible marker for impending preterm labor.

The given image shows intracytoplasmic eosinophilic Mallory bodies.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: A 65-year-old female patient is diagnosed with pure red cell aplasia and a mediastinal mass. Which of the following can be the likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Thymoma

The most probable diagnosis for the clinical presentation of mediastinal mass with pure red cell aplasia is thymoma. 

Thymoma refers to the tumors of the thymic epithelial cells. Most of the thymic tumors occur in the anterior mediastinum. Clinical features can be chest pain, dyspnea, cough, or superior vena cava syndrome.

It is associated with paraneoplastic syndromes like myasthenia gravis, pure red cell aplasia, or hypogammaglobulinemia. It is rarely associated with limbic encephalitis, hemolytic anemia, aplastic anemia, and other autoimmune conditions like Sjogren's syndrome.

Pure red cell aplasia: It is a marrow disorder where the erythroid progenitors are only suppressed. The complete absence of red cell progenitors is seen in severe cases.

Causes of pure red cell aplasia: It can be hereditary or acquired. Diamond-Blackfan anemia or congenital pure red cell aplasia is the hereditary cause. Causes of acquired pure red cell aplasia are given below:

  • Cancer
    • Thymoma

  • Drugs

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: All of the following are seen in anemia of chronic disease except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Low serum ferritin

Low serum ferritin levels are not seen in anemia of chronic disease.

Anemia of chronic disease is anemia resulting due to chronic diseases which produce systemic inflammation. During chronic inflammation, inflammatory mediators like interleukin - 6(IL-6) stimulate the production of hepcidin from the liver. Hepcidin is an acute phase reactant that inhibits ferroportin on macrophages and also decreases iron from stores to developing RBC precursors. This results in decreased proliferation of erythroid progenitors due to impaired iron utilization.

By decreasing available serum iron, the body defends itself from certain bacteria(Eg, Hemophilus influenza) that require iron for their pathogenicity. The lab findings seen in anemia of chronic disease are:

  • Low serum iron
  • Decreased total iron-binding capacity
  • Abundant stored iron
  • Increased hepcidin levels
  • Increased serum ferritin

The chronic illnesses associated with  anemia of chronic disease can be grouped into three categories:

  1. Chronic microbial infections, such as osteomyelitis, bacterial endocarditis, and lung abscess
  2. Chronic immune disorders, such as rheumatoid arthritis and regional enteritis
  3. Neoplasms, such as carcinomas of the lung and breast and Hodgkin lymphoma

Note: Hepcidin is the main regulator of iron absorption which is encoded by the HAMP gene and is defective in hemochromatosis.

Most of the adrenocortical neoplasms are aldosterone-producing adenomas. Conn syndrome is primary hyperaldosteronism caused by a solitary aldosterone-secreting adenoma.

The clinical features of hyperaldosteronism are secondary hypertension and various neuromuscular manifestations resulting from hypokalemia.

Microscopically, aldosterone-producing adenomas are found to have eosinophilic, laminated cytoplasmic inclusions, known as spironolactone bodies, found after treatment with the antihypertensive drug spironolactone.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question:
Identify the true statement/s regarding clear cell carcinoma of the kidney

  1. Most common sporadic renal tumour
  2. Associated with loss of long arm of chromosome 3
  3. Arises from distal convoluted tubule
  4. Cells show intracellular accumulation of glycogen and fat
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 4

True statements regarding clear cell carcinoma of the kidney are 1, 4. Clear cell carcinoma is the most common sporadic renal cell cancer and cells show intracellular accumulation of glycogen and fat.

Clear cell cancer arises from the proximal tubular epithelium and usually occurs as solitary unilateral lesions.

Most of the cases are sporadic, but can also occur either in familial forms or in association with von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease. They are associated with the loss of sequence of the short arm of chromosome 3. Those with VHL disease inherit a germline mutation of the VHL gene on chromosomal band 3p25 and lose the second allele by somatic mutation.

The VHL protein causes the degradation of hypoxia-induced factors (HIFs), which are transcription factors that contribute to carcinogenesis by stimulating the expression of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) that helps drive tumour cell growth.

Histologically, the tumour cells have a rounded or polygonal shape and abundant clear or granular cytoplasm, which contains glycogen and lipids.

Given below is the histopathological image of clear cell carcinoma.

Cancerous cells produce various abnormal hormones resulting in paraneoplastic syndrome. These include polycythemia, hypercalcemia, cushing syndrome, amyloidosis and hypertension.

The most common site of metastasis is the lungs and bones. Radical nephrectomy is the treatment of choice. But T1a(size less than 4cm) tumours are treated by nephron-sparing surgery or partial nephrectomy to preserve renal function. Drugs that inhibit VEGF and tyrosine kinase inhibitors are used as an adjunct therapy for metastatic disease.

questions.question: The phenomenon of a differential effect of the same gene from different parents is called:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Genomic imprinting

The phenomenon of a differential effect of the same gene from different parents is called genomic imprinting.

Genomic imprinting refers to gene silencing/ inactivation. Here either the maternal or the paternal allele is inactivated resulting in only one functional allele. It occurs by the process of epigenetics, where gene expression is lowered by:

  • DNA methylation
  • Histone deacetylation

Genomic imprinting is best illustrated by two uncommon genetic disorders: Prader-Willi syndrome and Angelman syndrome.

Paternal chromosome 15

(less common)

Clinical features

Elevated ghrelin levels - hyperphagia

Truncal obesity

Severe hypotonia

Small hands and feet with hypotonia

Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism

Cognitive impairment

Severe mental retardation with lack of speech

The image given below is a child with Angelman syndrome:

 

Diagnosis of these syndromes is based on the assessment of the methylation status of marker genes and fluorescence in-situ hybridisation(FISH).

Other options:

Option A: Gonadal mosaicism is a mutation that occurs only in egg or sperm cells and the individual will be phenotypically normal. These individuals with gonadal mosaicism can transmit the disease-causing mutation to the offspring through their mutated
gametes.

Option C: Anticipation refers to earlier onset of disease or increased severity in succeeding generations. This is seen in trinucleotide repeat disorders like Huntington's disease.

Option D: Incomplete penetrance refers to variations in penetrance and expressivity of clinical features. Not all individuals who inherit the mutant gene show a mutant phenotype.

Mnemonic:

Prader–Willi Syndrome: Paternal gene deletion - P for P
Angelman syndrome: Maternal gene deletion (Mothers are Angels, Maternal gene deletion leads to Angelman syndrome)

questions.question: A patient suffering from cholelithiasis underwent cholecystectomy. The image of the specimen is shown below. Which of the following is the correct diagnosis?

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: A 15-year-old boy presents with swelling in the upper diaphyseal part of the tibia. X-ray of the swelling showed a periosteal reaction. A histopathological image of the biopsy is given below. Immunohistochemistry was positive for synaptophysin and mic 2. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ewing sarcoma

The given clinical scenario along with the image showing small round blue cells and immunohistochemistry (IHC) positive for synaptophysin and mic-2 point to a likely diagnosis of Ewing sarcoma. 

Ewing sarcoma is the 2nd most common bone sarcoma in children. The majority of the patients affected are usually <20 years of age. It has a slight male predominance. 

It commonly involves the diaphysis of the long bones like the femur, tibia, fibula, and humerus and flat bones of the pelvis. The majority of Ewing sarcomas have a balanced translocation between the EWSR1 gene on chromosome 22 and the FLI1 gene on chromosome 11. 

Patients present with painful enlarging mass, fever, and anemia. The affected area is usually tender, swollen, and warm. Laboratory findings may show an elevated WBC count and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR). 

A histopathological examination of Ewing sarcoma shows sheets of uniform, round cells arranged in Homer-Wright rosettes. These cells are of neuroectodermal origin and have minimal cytoplasm and abundant glycogen. When they are arranged around a central fibrillary core in the form of clusters, the appearance is termed Homer-Wright rosettes. Immunohistochemistry is usually positive for synaptophysin and mic-2.

Given below is the histopathological appearance of Ewing sarcoma. 

As tumor cells are rich in glycogen, they stain positive for periodic acid Schiff (PAS) stain however, they stain negatively for reticulin.

The image given below shows PAS staining done in Ewing's sarcoma:

Radiological examination of Ewing sarcoma shows a destructive lesion in the diaphysis of long bones. Deposition of periosteal reaction in layers gives an onion-peel appearance (shown below). 

Other options:

Option A: Osteosarcoma is the most common primary malignancy of bone. The histological features of osteosarcoma include pleomorphic cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and abundant mitoses. The diagnosis is definitive with the presence of malignant tumor cells producing unmineralized osteoid or mineralized bone arranged in a typically fine, lacelike pattern.

Given below is the histopathological image of osteosarcoma:

X-ray shows periosteal reaction and it may take the form of a Codman's triangle or it may have a sunray appearance as shown below.

Option C: Neuroblastoma is a tumor of the sympathetic ganglia and adrenal medulla. It is derived from primordial neural crest cells. It is the most common extracranial solid tumor in childhood. On histopathology small round blue cells are seen. These cells are concentrically arranged around a faintly eosinophilic fibrillary material (neuropil). This appearance is called Homer-Wright pseudorosettes (shown below). 

Option D: Osteoclastoma is also known as a giant cell tumour. The tumor cells are primitive osteoblast precursors and express high levels of RANKL. Histologically, the tumors consist of osteoclast-type giant cells with 100 or more nuclei. These cells are usually present against a backdrop of mononuclear stromal cells. 

The image given below shows the histopathological appearance of giant cell tumour/osteoclastoma:

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.question: Which of the following is a marker of natural killer cell?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. CD 94

The marker of the natural killer cells is CD94. It is expressed in natural killer cells and a small subset of T lymphocytes. 

Natural killer cells (NK cells) are essential cells of innate immunity. They act against malignant and virus-infected cells. NK cells are identified by CD16 and CD56 cell surface receptors. 

NK cells' activity is augmented by interferons and upon activation, they bind to glycoprotein receptors on the surface of target cells and release perforins. Perforins create pores in the membrane of the target cells. Through these pores, cytotoxic factors like tumor necrosis factor-beta (TNF-β) enter the cells and destroy them by apoptosis.

NK cells express a phenomenon known as antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC). Here, NK cells have the capability of killing target cells that are coated by IgG antibodies.

The image given below shows the actions of NK cells on cancer cells.

Other options:

Option A: CD68 is expressed on macrophages and monocytes.

Option B: CD 3 is a T-cell receptor marker. They are involved in the transduction of signals to the T cells when an antigen binds to the T cell receptor.

Option C: CD 25 is a component of the IL2 receptor and is important in T cell proliferation and activation.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions is not caused by high-risk strains of human papillomavirus?

Correct answer: D. Laryngeal papillomatosis

Laryngeal papillomatosis is not caused by high-risk strains of human papillomavirus (HPV). It is caused by low-risk HPV strains 6 and 11. 

Laryngeal papillomatosis or juvenile papillomatosis is the most common benign neoplasm of the larynx in children. It is caused by HPV 6 and 11. It involves supraglottic and glottic regions of the larynx. Adult-onset laryngeal papillomatosis involves the anterior part of the vocal cords.

It usually occurs between the ages 3–5 years, but less commonly can also occur in men aged between 30-50 years. Clinical features include hoarseness or aphonia and respiratory difficulty. The recurrence rate is high but they rarely transform to SCC.

Diagnosis is confirmed by direct laryngoscopy and biopsy. Treatment consists of micro laryngoscopy, CO2 laser excision, and topical cidofovir.
