questions.subject: Surgery
questions.question: A 65-year-old man presents with abdominal pain for the past 6 hours, BP- 89/50mmHg, RR- 24/min, saturation 92% with 6 L of oxygen. Radiograph shows extraluminal air in the abdomen. Which of the following must be done before shifting this patient into the OT?
options: Insert central venous cath​eter as initial IV access​ of choice
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1 litre of crystalloid infusion

Volume resuscitation with 1 liter of crystalloid infusion should be done before shifting this patient to the OT for an emergency exploratory laparotomy.

The given clinical scenario in a patient with hypotension and tachypnea with extraluminal gas in the abdomen is suggestive of perforation peritonitis with hemodynamic instability. The immediate step is volume resuscitation to maintain circulating volume and organ perfusion. 

Peritonitis is the inflammation of the peritoneum and can be categorized as local or diffuse and acute or chronic. 

Causes: 

  • Gastrointestinal perforation e.g. perforated ulcer, appendix, diverticulum
  • Transmural translocation (no perforation), e.g. pancreatitis, ischaemic bowel, primary bacterial peritonitis
  • Exogenous contamination, e.g. drains, open surgery, trauma, peritoneal dialysis
  • Female genital tract infection, e.g. pelvic inflammatory disease
  • Haematogenous spread (rare), e.g. septicaemia
  • Miscellaneous- e.g. familial Mediterranean fever

Clinical features: 

  • Abdominal pain, worse on movement, coughing and deep respiration
  • Constitutional symptoms: anorexia, malaise, fever, lassitude
  • nausea +/– vomiting
  • Pyrexia (may be absent)
  • Tachycardia
  • Tenderness +/– guarding/rigidity/rebound of the abdominal wall 
  • Pain/tenderness on rectal/vaginal examination (pelvic peritonitis) 
  • Absent or reduced bowel sounds
  • Septic shock (systemic inflammatory response syndrome [SIRS] and multiorgan dysfunction syndrome [MODS]) in later stages

Management: 

General care of the patient: 

  • Correction of fluid and electrolyte imbalance
  • Insertion of a nasogastric tube and urinary catheter
  • Broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy
  • Aprropriate analgesia

Surgical treatment: Exploratory laparotomy and repair of perforation is the definitive management. Presence of peritoneal signs and hemodynamic instability are indications for urgent surgery.

Other options

Option A: Intubation is not indicated by the patient's current vital signs.

Option B: Initial volume resuscitation can be done with the peripheral large-bore cannula. A central venous catheter may be needed if peripheral access is dificult, vasopressors are administered, patient requires TPN.

Option D: A CT scan, while helpful for locating lesion and confirming the diagnosis, is not indicated for a hemodynamically unstable patient.

Note: 

According to recent ATLS guidelines, crystalloid infusion should be limited to a maximum of 1.5 litres as crystalloid resuscitation beyond 1.5 liters increases the risk of death.

questions.question: A patient with recurrent pain in the right hypochondrium, nausea, and vomiting is diagnosed with biliary dyskinesia. Which of the following is least useful in the diagnosis of this condition?

USG is the least useful investigation in the diagnosis of biliary dyskinesia or sphincter of Oddi dysfunction since the findings can be normal or show non-specific changes such as dilatation of the common bile duct. 

Sphincter of Oddi dysfunction (SOD) is caused due to a structurally or physiologically abnormal sphincter with a higher tone, which fails to relax, causing pain and recurrent episodes of pancreatitis with normal liver function tests. There are two clinical types: biliary SOD and pancreatic SOD. Each type is further classified into types 1,2 and 3.

Option D: Biliary-type SOD should be considered and excluded in post-cholecystectomy syndrome; hence, post-surgery follow-up is essential.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.question: ERCP is least useful in the diagnosis of _____________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Acute pancreatitis without choledocholithiaisis

ERCP is least useful in the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis without choledocholithiasis. 

ERCP stands for Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangio-Pancreatography. It involves the use of a side-viewing endoscope which is passed through the pylorus of the stomach into the second part of the duodenum to visualise the papilla. This is then cannulated, and dye is injected into the pancreatic or bile duct to visualise the pancreatic or biliary tree. It can be therapeutic or diagnostic. It is the best diagnostic modality for viewing the distal biliary tree, but MRCP is preferred as the diagnostic modality unless a therapeutic intervention is also needed. 

Indications of ERCP: 

  • Choledocholithiasis
  • Acute cholangitis 
  • Biliary stricture, biliary leak 
  • Pancreatic duct stricture, pancreatic stones
  • Extrahepatic biliary strictures related to primary sclerosing cholangitis 
  • Endoscopic therapy for some patients with sphincter of Oddi dysfunction 
  • Biliary or pancreatic ductal system tissue sampling 
  • Balloon dilatation of the duodenal papilla or ductal strictures 
  • Sphincterotomy 

The most common therapeutic indication for ERCP is the relief of biliary obstruction due to gallstone disease and benign or malignant biliary strictures. 

Contraindications of ERCP include patients who cannot tolerate anesthesia, patients with type 3 sphincter of Oddi dysfunction, luminal gastrointestinal obstruction (examination limited to an area proximal to the level of obstruction and untreated hemostatic disorder (high risk of bleeding).

Complications of ERCP include duodenal perforation, hemorrhage, pancreatitis and sepsis.

Other options: 

Option A: ERCP can help in ruling out the etiology in cases of recurrent pancreatitis. 

Option B: ERCP can act as both diagnostic and therapeutic in cases of unexplained jaundice. 

Option C: ERCP can be useful in case of a periampullary mass to take a tissue biopsy and cytology.

questions.question: Which of the following nerve is least injured during thyroid surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Marginal mandibular nerve

The marginal mandibular nerve is least likely to be injured during thyroid surgery as it is high up (mandibular margin) than the dissection plane of the approach to thyroid surgery.

Other nerves that might be at risk of injury include:

  • Recurrent laryngeal nerve may be injured if dissection is done below the cricoid cartilage or near the tracheoesophageal groove (option A).
  • Ansa cervicalis may be injured if strap muscles are not cut high enough. (option B)
  • External laryngeal nerve may be injured during ligation of superior thyroid vessels as it lies very close to the superior thyroid artery (option C).

Complications of thyroidectomy:

  • Hemorrhage - most common complication overall; due to slipping of ligature
  • Nerve injury 
    • External laryngeal nerve - hoarseness (more common)

questions.question: eFAST is least helpful in diagnosing which of the following conditions?

Correct answer: C. Retroperitoneal hematoma

Among the given options, eFAST (focussed assessment with sonography in trauma) is the least useful in diagnosing retroperitoneal hematoma as the sensitivity of ultrasound for the detection of retroperitoneal hematomas is extremely poor. 

Computed Tomography (CT Scan) is the investigation of choice for retroperitoneal injury, but it can only be done in a hemodynamically stable patient.

FAST stands for Focussed Assessment with Sonography for Trauma. It is a rapid, non-invasive bedside test for detecting free fluid using sonography used to assess patients for potential thoracoabdominal injuries. 

Technique:

  • The patient is placed in a supine position and the following regions are scanned:
    • Subxiphoid transverse view: assess for pericardial effusion and left lobe liver injuries
    • Longitudinal view of the right upper quadrant: assess for right liver injuries, right kidney injury, and Morison pouch
    • Longitudinal view of the left upper quadrant: assess for splenic injury and left kidney injury
    • Transverse and longitudinal views of the suprapubic region: assess the bladder and pouch of Douglas

eFAST stands for extended FAST and incorporates left and right thoracic views to assess for pneumothorax and haemothorax.

Limitations of eFAST are:

  1. Operator-dependent
  2. Bowel gas and subcutaneous air distort images.
  3. Can miss diaphragm, bowel, and pancreatic injuries
  4. Unreliable for assessment of the retroperitoneum
  5. Cannot reliably exclude injury in penetrating trauma
  6. May need repeating or supplementing with other investigations

questions.question: A patient with unilateral breast cancer is started on tamoxifen. This will increase the risk of?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Endometrial cancer

Tamoxifen increases the risk of endometrial cancer by 1-2%.

The benefit of tamoxifen in breast cancer outweighs the risk of endometrial cancer.

Tamoxifen is a selective estrogen receptor modulator, approved for the treatment of estrogen receptor-positive (ER) breast cancer. It is used only in premenopausal women for 5 years in low-risk patients and for 10 years in patients with a high risk of relapse (node-positive, tumor >5 cm, lymphovascular invasion). It is also known to reduce the incidence of second primary breast cancer in the contralateral breast.

Tamoxifen increases the risk of endometrial cancer in postmenopausal women; hence aromatase inhibitors are used in postmenopausal women. Tamoxifen is also not recommended in patients who have had bilateral mastectomies with ER-positive ductal carcinoma in situ. Other side effects of tamoxifen include bone pain, hot flashes, nausea, vomiting, fluid retention and rarely thrombosis and cataract.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate mesh for use in hernioplasty?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lightweight mesh with large pores

The most appropriate mesh used in hernioplasty is a lightweight mesh with large pores.

Lightweight meshes generally contain less material and induce a less-pronounced foreign body reaction and decreased inflammatory response, which results in better tissue incorporation, increased prosthesis compliance, and decreased patient discomfort and pain.

Meshes with large pores exhibit less inflammatory infiltrate, connective tissue, and scar bridging, which allows increased soft tissue ingrowth. They have greater elasticity and flexibility and also shrink less resulting in lesser adhesions, better tissue incorporation, and decreased patient discomfort and pain. So the best mesh type among the given options is lightweight mesh with large pores.

Meshes used in hernioplasty can be synthetic or biological depending on their composition.

Synthetic meshes are made from polypropylene, polyester, or PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene). 

POLYPROPYLENE POLYESTER PTFE
monofilament multifilament solid
hydrophobic hydrophilic hydrophobic
rigid elastic rigid

PTFE meshes are hydrophobic with a lower risk of adhesion.

Biological meshes are acellular matrix materials derived from humans or animals and have lesser complications. But due to poor collagen deposition and absorption, they rapidly lose mechanical strength and hence their use is restricted to infected environments. 

Note: To promote better tissue integration, a composite mesh was developed which combines the attributes of polypropylene and PTFE by layering the two substances on top of one another.

questions.question: Which of the following gene mutations are involved in carcinoma of the colon?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. APC, k-ras, p53

APC, k-ras, and p53 gene mutations are implicated in carcinoma of the colon.

In the adenoma to carcinoma sequence, the loss of one normal copy of the tumor suppressor gene APC is the first hit, followed by the loss of the intact second copy of the APC gene (second hit). Other changes in the sequence include the mutation of k-ras and the inactivation of the tumor suppressor gene p53, leading to the emergence of carcinoma. The accumulation of these mutations is more important than their occurrence in a specific order. This is known as the Fearon-Vogelstein adenoma-carcinoma multistep model of colorectal neoplasia.

A number of other genes on chromosome 18q are implicated in colorectal cancer, including SMAD2, SMAD4, and DCC.

questions.question: Which of the following are used to stop esophageal variceal bleed?

questions.question: A patient presents with pain in the right upper quadrant on the second postoperative day following a cholecystectomy. Evaluation reveals a collection in the subhepatic space. A bile leak was suspected. Which of the following is the best investigation for this patient?

Correct answer: B. ERCP

Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is the best investigation in a patient suspected of post-cholecystectomy biliary leaks.

Patients with post-cholecystectomy biliary leak usually present with fever, jaundice and abdominal pain.  USG is used for an initial evaluation in such cases and can show a collection in the sub-hepatic space. 

The most common bile leak following cholecystectomy is from the cystic duct. This can be treated by placing a biliary endoprosthesis (stent) in the common bile duct across the origin of the cystic duct.

MRCP shows fluid collections arising from bile leaks but cannot differentiate these from other causes of fluid collections.

ERCP is the best investigation as it has the advantage of being both diagnostic and therapeutic.  ERCP is useful post-cholecystectomy as there is a high likelihood of a retained stone and stone extraction and/or temporary stenting may be required. 

HIDA scan is the most sensitive investigation for biliary leakage.

CT scan can show focal fluid collections, ascites, biliary obstruction, hepatic atrophy, signs of secondary biliary cirrhosis and any vascular injury.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.question: A 35-year-old chronic smoker presents with bluish discoloration of the toe along with intermittent claudication. Which of the following will be the next appropriate investigation in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Duplex scan

Chronic smoker presenting with bluish discoloration of the toe along with intermittent claudication is suggestive of peripheral arterial disease and duplex scanning will be the next appropriate investigation.

Duplex Scanning is a major non-invasive technique that uses B-mode ultrasound to provide an image of the vessel. Most scanners now have color coding, which allows detailed visualization of blood flow in a vessel. Different colors indicate changes in the direction and velocity of flow, with areas of high flow usually indicating stenotic lesions.

Other options: 

Option A: CT Angiography (CTA) is more useful in the evaluation of visceral arterial disease (eg. mesenteric ischemia). It can be beneficial in peripheral artery diseases where a duplex scan shows poor images (aortoiliac segment involvement). CTA is not routinely recommended in peripheral artery disease because of concomitant renal dysfunction in these patients which can lead to contrast-induced nephropathy.

Option B: MR Angiography is time-consuming and expensive, hence not done as the next investigation. It is contraindicated in patients with claustrophobia and metallic implants. 

Option C: Digital subtraction angiography (DSA) is an invasive and expensive procedure compared to other investigations. The benefits of DSA are that it provides dynamic arterial flow information and can be combined with a definitive endovascular intervention when indicated. DSA is indicated only when there is a discrepancy in diagnosis or intervention is planned. Complications associated with DSA include bleeding, hematoma, false aneurysm formation, thrombosis, arterial dissection, distal embolisation, renal dysfunction, and allergic reaction.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.question: A 40-year-old woman presents with complaints of swelling of the right breast over the past 15 days. On examination, there was local rise of temperature, and the swelling was mobile over the chest wall. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Inflammatory carcinoma

In the given scenario, the rapid onset of the disease and the examination findings are suggestive of inflammatory carcinoma of the breast.

Inflammatory breast cancer is the most aggressive subtype of breast cancer. It mimics acute mastitis. The hallmark of inflammatory breast carcinoma is the diffuse tumor involvement of the dermal lymphatics within the breast and the overlying skin, often without a discrete underlying tumor mass (peau d' orange appearance). The patient presents with rapidly progressive swelling of the breast, warmth, erythema and edema. A breast lump may or may not be present. 

A diagnosis of inflammatory breast carcinoma should be suspected when a patient with rapidly progressive swelling with inflammatory skin changes does not respond to antibiotics. The imaging features with ultrasound and a mammograph is non-specific due to the underlying erythema and edema. A biopsy should be done to confirm the diagnosis. 

Treatment includes combined-modality treatment:

  • Neoadjuvant chemo­therapy
  • Mastectomy
  • Radiation therapy
  • Hormonal therapy- for ER-positive tumors
  • Trastuzumab for HER-2-positive tumors

Option B: Giant fibroadenomas occasionally occur during puberty. These are benign solid encapsulated slow-growing tumors over 5 cm in diameter. It presents as a painless lump in the breast. They are managed by excision via a submammary incision.

Option C: Phyllodes tumors usually occur in women over the age of 40 years but can appear in younger women. Phyllodes tumor is mostly benign even though it is also called cystosarcoma phyllodes. It presents as a large tumor with an unevenly bosselated surface. They are usually mobile over the chest wall despite their large size. This tumor does not infiltrate the skin. Nipple retraction is not seen in this condition. Benign lesions can be treated with enucleation or wide local excision. Massive tumours, recurrent tumours and malignant lesions are treated with a mastectomy.

Option D: Galactocele are the most common benign breast lesions in lactating women. It is a cystic enlargement of the mammary gland containing milk. They are mostly detected during lactation or in the third trimester of pregnancy but rarely, may also present after stopping breastfeeding. Clinically, the mass is usually firm and non-tender and presents as a solid tumour-like lesion on physical examination. The patient usually notes the lesion during lactation or some period after lactation. Needle aspiration, followed by excision should it recur, is the standard method of treating galactocele.

Endoscopy is useful for ruling out pseudo-achalasia.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man with IHD presents with sudden, severe, generalized abdominal pain and multiple episodes of vomiting. On examination, the pulse rate is 118bpm, rhythm is irregularly irregular, BP is 90/60 mmHg. The abdomen appears soft, non-distended, and bowel sounds are absent. Which of the following could be a likely diagnosis in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Acute mesenteric ischemia

The given clinical scenario of a patient with sudden onset severe abdominal pain which is out-of-proportion to the physical examination findings along with atrial fibrillation is suggestive of acute mesenteric ischemia. 

Mesenteric ischemia may be acute or chronic. The superior mesenteric artery (SMA) is most likely affected. An embolus is the most common cause of SMA occlusion. Possible sources for SMA emboisation include:

  • Left atrium in atrial fibrillation
  • Previous history of ischemic heart disease/myocardial infarction
  • Vegetations on mitral and aortic valves associated with endocarditis 
  • An atheromatous plaque from an aortic aneurysm.

Other causes of mesenteric ischemia include:

  • Atherosclerosis of mesenteric vessels
  • Vasculitides
  • Venous thrombosis in factor V Leiden mutation
  • Non-occlusive mesenteric ischemia due to alterations in splanchnic blood flow.

The most important clue to an early diagnosis of acute mesenteric ischemia is the sudden onset of severe abdominal pain in a patient with atrial fibrillation or atherosclerosis. The pain is typically in the central abdomen and out of proportion to the physical findings.

Associated clinical features include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal distension, peritonitis, and the passage of bloody stools.

The gold standard for the diagnosis of acute mesenteric ischemia is angiography, and management is laparotomy. The goal of operative exploration is to resect the compromised bowel and restore blood supply via embolectomy.

Other options: 

Option B: A pulsatile abdominal mass is seen in the case of an abdominal aortic aneurysm. Acute pain and hypotension occur with rupture of the aneurysm, which requires an emergency operation. 

Options A and D: Acute severe pancreatitis and peptic ulcer perforation have no association with atrial fibrillation. They usually present with pain over the upper abdomen associated with guarding and rigidity on examination.

questions.question: A 15-year-old girl presented with a slow-growing, rubbery, non-tender swelling on the side of the neck as shown in the image. Examination shows the presence of freckles and skin patches over the face and trunk. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A lateral neck mass in a pediatric patient, which is non-tender and present in association with freckles, and hyperpigmented skin patches (cafe-au-lait spots) is suggestive of neural tumor i.e. neurofibroma. 

Neurofibroma is a benign tumor arising from the connective tissue of the nerve containing ectodermal, neural and mesodermal connective tissue components. It can be single or multiple. It is the most common intradural extramedullary spinal tumor. Neurofibromas can be local, generalized (von Recklinghausen's disease) or plexiform types. Patients present with mild pain or a painless swelling usually in the subcutaneous or cutaneous plane with tingling, numbness and paraesthesia along the distribution of the nerve. Complications of neurofibroma include cystic degeneration, erosion into deeper planes, cord compression and paralysis (spinal neurofibroma) and sarcomatous changes.

Treatment is excision under general or regional anesthesia. Indications for surgery in neurofibroma include symptomatic patients (pain and pressure symptoms), cosmetic problems and malignant transformation (5%).

questions.question: What will be the most likely associated condition with increased TSH and low T4 levels?

questions.question: In e-FAST which of the following body part is included that is not included in FAST?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Thoracic cavity

e-FAST is used to additionally assess the presence of free fluid in the thoracic cavity.

FAST stands for focused assessment with sonography for trauma. It is a rapid diagnostic examination to assess patients with potential thoracoabdominal injuries. It can be performed within 2­-4 minutes.

The sequential order in which FAST is performed: pericardial sac, the right upper quadrant (RUQ), left upper quadrant (LUQ), and pelvis. 4 ‘Ps’ are evaluated in sequence: Pericardial sac → Perihepatic region → Perisplenic region → Pelvis.

Technique:

  • Following regions are scanned:
    • Subxiphoid: assess for pericardial effusion and left lobe liver injuries
    • Right upper quadrant: assess for right liver injuries, right kidney injury, and Morison pouch
    • Left upper quadrant: assess for splenic injury and left kidney injury
    • Suprapubic region: assess the bladder and pouch of Douglas

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.question: Which of the following is the most commonly seen tumor in the retroperitoneal space?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Liposarcoma

Liposarcoma is the most commonly seen tumor in retroperitoneal space.

Retroperitoneal tumors can be benign or malignant. Malignant retroperitoneal tumors may be mesodermal (75%), neuroectodermal (24%), or embryonic remnant (1%) in origin. Rarely it can be urologic or metastatic also. The order of frequency of primary retroperitoneal malignancy is as follows:

  • Liposarcoma
  • Leiomyosarcoma
  • Rhabdomyosarcoma
  • Fibrosarcoma
  • Malignant nerve sheath tumors

Liposarcoma is composed of three histologic varieties (listed in order of decreasing frequency):

  • Well-differentiated and undifferentiated liposarcoma
  • Pleomorphic liposarcoma
  • Myxoid/round cell liposarcoma 

Among the three subtypes, pleomorphic liposarcoma is the most malignant and often metastasizes, while the well-differentiated is the least malignant. Myxoid liposarcoma has intermediate malignant behavior.

Diagnosis is confirmed by contrast-enhanced CT with CT of the chest to look for metastases. 

Surgery is the main modality of treatment. Wide excision with complete en bloc dissection is done. Post-operative radiotherapy and chemotherapy are used as adjuvant methods. Radiotherapy is given at a dose of 5000 cGY, it can be external beam or intra-operative radiotherapy. Chemotherapeutic agents used are mesna, adriamycin, ifosfamide and dacarbazine (MAID regimen).

Correct answer: C. Mass is mobile perpendicular to mesentery attachment line

Tillaux's sign is said to be positive if the mass/swelling is mobile perpendicular to the mesentery attachment line. Tillaux’s sign is seen in a mesenteric cyst.

Mesenteric cysts occur either in the small intestine (60%) or the colon (40%) and can be classified as the following:

  • Chylolymphatic (most common type)
  • Enterogenous
  • Urogenital remnant
  • Dermoid
  • Other causes: traumatic hematoma and cyst formation, tuberculous cold abscess of mesentery and hydatid cyst of the mesentery

They most commonly occur in adults with a mean age of 45 years. It is more common in females than males (2:1). The most common presentation is a painless abdominal swelling near the umbilicus, which is smooth and not moving with respiration with Tillaux's triad: 

  • Soft, smooth swelling in the umbilical region
  • Freely mobile in a direction perpendicular to the mesentery (Tillaux's sign)
  • Zone of resonance around the cyst 

Other presentations include recurrent attacks of abdominal pain due to temporary impaction of a food bolus in a segment of the bowel narrowed by the cyst and vomiting.

Complications of mesenteric cyst include torsion, rupture, infection and hemorrhage into the cyst. 

Ultrasonography and CT are used to demonstrate mesenteric cysts.

Treatment:

  • Chlyolymphatic cyst is managed by enucleation.
  • Enterogenous cyst is managed by removal of the cyst with resection of the adjacent bowel as it arises as a diverticulum or duplication from the adjacent bowel. 

In cases where complete excision is not possible due to the close proximity to vital structures, partial excision or marsupialization should be performed.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.question:
A child is diagnosed with congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, which among the following can be seen in this child?

1. Bilious vomiting
2. Visible peristalsis from right to left
3. Hypochloremia and hypokalemia
4. Metabolic alkalosis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 3 and 4 only

Patients with congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (CHPS) will present with non-bilious projectile vomiting and visible peristalsis observed moving from left to right (not from right to left). Metabolic abnormalities include hypokalemia, hypochloremia and metabolic alkalosis.

CHPS occurs due to hypertrophy of the circular muscle of the pylorus, which results in constriction and obstruction of the gastric outlet. 

  • Patients commonly present between 2 and 8 weeks of age.
  • First-born male infants are at the highest risk.
  • Infants usually present with projectile, non-bilious vomiting.
  • Clinically, an olive-shaped mass is palpable in the right upper quadrant or epigastrium. When the infant is given a test feed, visible peristalsis is usually observed moving from left to right (not from right to left), followed by projectile vomiting.

Metabolic abnormality:

  • Infants with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis develop a characteristic metabolic abnormality i.e. hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria.
  • Persistent vomiting results in loss of hydrochloric acid, leading to metabolic alkalosis (due to loss of H+) and hypochloremia (due to loss of Cl-).
  • Kidneys try to compensate for alkalosis by secreting Na+ and HCO3-. However, sodium loss stimulates aldosterone secretion through the RAAS pathway.
  • Aldosterone causes active reabsorption of sodium in exchange for K+ and H+ ions leading to the development of hypokalemia and paradoxical aciduria, since the body initially loses H+ ions due to the loss of HCl, and instead of compensating for that loss, the body is losing more H+ ions through urine.

Management:

  • The child should be rehydrated and the metabolic abnormality must be corrected before surgery.
  • Ramstedt pyloromyotomy remains the standard surgical procedure for its treatment.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.question:
The components of qSOFA scoring include:

1. Mental status
2. Blood pressure
3. Respiratory rate
4. Heart rate
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2 & 3

The quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (qSOFA) scoring system does not rely on the heart rate.

It is a bedside scoring system that may identify patients with suspected infection, who are at greater risk for sepsis outside the intensive care unit (ICU).

It uses three criteria, assigning one point each:

  • Low blood pressure (SBP≤100 mmHg)
  • High respiratory rate (≥22 breaths per min)
  • Altered mental status

The qSOFA suggests potentially life-threatening sepsis when at least two of the parameters are met.

Note :

The primary method to evaluate the risk of organ dysfunction (sepsis) in patients with suspected infection is by determining the sequential (sepsis-related) organ failure assessment (SOFA) score; which includes an assessment of:

  • Circulation - Systolic BP & need for vasopressors; platelet count
  • Respiration - PaO2/FiO2 & need for mechanical ventilation
  • Mentation - Glasgow Coma Score
  • Hepatic function - Bilirubin
  • Renal function - Creatinine

Organ dysfunction is identified by a SOFA score of ≥ 2

The SOFA score is limited by its requirement of multiple laboratory tests which makes it complex and time-consuming. In order to simplify the scoring process, the "Sepsis -3" task force recommended the quick sepsis-related organ dysfunction assessment "qSOFA" score.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old man presents to the ER with severe abdominal pain. On examination, his HR is 110bpm, BP- 88/60mmHg. On per abdomen examination, guarding is present. The erect abdominal X-ray is shown below. Which of the following would you proceed with, for the management of this case?

1. USG abdomen
2. IV fluids
3. Exploratory laparotomy
4. Elective surgery
5. Conservative management
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 2 & 3

The given clinical scenario and erect X-ray abdomen showing gas under the diaphragm are suggestive of pneumoperitoneum, which is managed by initial resuscitation with IV fluids followed by exploratory laparotomy.

Pneumoperitoneum is the presence of air or gas in the peritoneal cavity. The most common cause of pneumoperitoneum is a perforation of a hollow viscus.  Other causes of pneumoperitoneum in adults include peritoneal dialysis, and mechanical ventilation, after procedures like colonoscopy and endoscopy. In children, it can be caused by necrotizing enterocolitis, hirschsprung's disease, meconium ileus and mechanical ventilation. 

The patient presents with abdominal pain and distension, vomiting, fever, constipation, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, and reduced urine output. Per-abdomen examination can show guarding and rigidity.

An erect X-ray abdomen is highly sensitive for the detection of free intraperitoneal gas. Some of the signs seen in the X-ray include: 

  • Cupola sign is the presence of air underneath the diaphragm, giving a dome-like appearance.
  • Rigler's sign is where both bowel surfaces are seen together as a sharp margin.
  • Falciform ligament sign is the outlining of the falciform ligament with free abdominal gas.
  • Liver/gallbladder edge sign is where the sharp margins of the liver/gallbladder are visible due to the collection of air.

Management includes,

  • Adequate preoperative resuscitation with intravenous fluids followed by correction of electrolyte imbalance, instituting broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics and
  • Early surgical intervention/laparotomy to address the cause of pneumoperitoneum and prevent further contamination of the peritoneal cavity.

questions.question: Which of the following are indications for surgical intervention in abdominal aortic aneurysms?

All the given are indications for surgical intervention in abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA). The indications include:

  • Size >4.5-5 cm in females (option B)
  • Expansion of >0.5 cm within 6 months or >1 cm in one year (option C)
  • Painful, tender aneurysm 
  • Thrombosed aneurysm, aneurysm with distal emboli 

The rupture risk is high for aneurysms >5.5 cm and begins to rise exponentially with an increase in size. Women are at higher risk for rupture than men, with a lower threshold of 4.5 to 5.0 cm (depending on the reference used).

  • Cardiovascular patients in men and women (60-85 years)
  • Men and women >50 years with positive family history 
  • Annual screening in asymptomatic patients with 4-4.5 cm size, size >4.5 cm once in every 6 months.

Management of AAA can be done by open repair or endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR). About 75% of infrarenal aneurysms are suitable for endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR), depending on the morphology of the aneurysm assessed by a CT scan.

Aneurysms that fall below the mentioned indications may safely be followed with CT or ultrasound at 6-month intervals since long-term outcomes to routine follow-up are equivalent to earlier surgical repair of the aneurysm. Smoking cessation is very important and reduces the mortality rate.

  • A well-developed germinal centre may be seen
  • Hurthle (Askanazy) cells that have abundant eosinophilic granular cytoplasm lining the follicles

Hashimoto's thyroiditis is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient areas. It is also known as struma lymphomatosa or lymphocytic thyroiditis. It is an autoimmune disease that results in the destruction of the thyroid gland and gradual & progressive thyroid failure.

  • TSH is raised

    • Thyroid peroxidase (TPO)
    • Thyroglobulin

Option A: Histological features of medullary carcinoma of the thyroid include polygonal to spindle-shaped cells in the form of nests, trabeculae or follicles. questions.subject: Surgery
questions.question: A 45-year-old male patient who presented with a scrotal swelling underwent an orchidectomy. The image below shows the histopathology findings. What is your diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Seminoma

Based on the gross and microscopic appearance of the specimen, the diagnosis is seminoma.

The gross specimen shows a well-circumscribed, pale, gray-white, fleshy, homogenous mass, with a lobulated cut surface, usually devoid of hemorrhage or necrosis. Histopathology shows uniform tumor cells with abundant clear cytoplasm, distinct cell borders, and large central nuclei. There is a sparse lymphocytic infiltrate. Classically, they have a fried egg appearance.

Other options:

Option B: Yolk-sac tumor has a yellowish-white, mucinous appearance. Histologically, they are typically composed of a lace-like (reticular) network of medium-sized cuboidal, flattened, or spindled cells, which generally show less cytologic atypia than embryonal carcinoma. In approximately 50% of tumors, structures resembling endodermal sinuses (Schiller-Duval bodies) may be seen; these consist of a mesodermal core with a central capillary and a visceral and parietal layer of cells resembling primitive glomeruli. 

Option C: Embryonal cell carcinoma appears variegated with foci of hemorrhage or necrosis.  Histologically, the cells grow in alveolar or tubular patterns, sometimes with papillary folds. More undifferentiated lesions may display sheets of cells with cleft-like spaces. The neoplastic cells have an epithelial appearance, are large and anaplastic, and have hyperchromatic nuclei with prominent nucleoli. The cell borders are usually indistinct, and there is considerable variation in cell and nuclear size and shape (pleomorphism). Mitotic figures and tumor giant cells are frequently seen.

Option D: Teratomas also have a variegated appearance but have cysts reflecting the multiplicity of tissue types. Histologically, collections of differentiated cells or organoid structures originating in all 3 germ layers can be seen. Elements may be mature (resembling various adult tissues) or immature (sharing histologic features with fetal or embryonic tissue).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.question: Which is the most common organism causing acute bacterial prostatitis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. E.coli

The most common organism causing acute bacterial prostatitis (ABP) is Escherichia coli.

It is commonly caused by an ascending urethral infection or reflux of infected urine into prostatic ducts. Sexually transmissible infections and other urinary pathogens, such as Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus faecalis may also be responsible.

The patient presents with fever, perineal pain, chills and rigor, and dysuria. Per rectal examination will reveal a tender, boggy prostate. Care should be taken to avoid aggressive palpation or prostatic massage as it can lead to bacterial dissemination and sepsis.

Urine examination and culture should be done. Urine examination reveals threads in urine.

Management:  

Patients with systemic signs of infection should be admitted for IV antibiotics, hydration, and monitoring of laboratory parameters.

Patients who have no signs of systemic infection, who can tolerate oral intake, and who have no urinary retention can be treated with oral antibiotics. Antibiotics are given for 2-6 weeks to ensure the eradication of the infection as antibiotics don't penetrate the prostate capsule easily. 

For outpatient therapy: Ciprofloxacin 500 mg oral every 12 hours or levofloxacin 500 mg OD or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole double-strength tablet oral every 12 hours can be used.

For hospitalized patients: Intravenous ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin with or without an aminoglycoside (gentamicin or tobramycin) or intravenous beta-lactam with or without an aminoglycoside. Gram-positive infections are treated with cephalosporins (cephalexin, cefazolin) or dicloxacillin and vancomycin.

The GSV is the conduit of choice for arterial bypass grafts below the inguinal ligament.

For bypass above the inguinal ligament, while both GSV and PTFE grafts have similar patency rates in the first 2 years, the GSV is superior thereafter and hence preferred over PTFE or any other grafts.

questions.question: Extra mammary Paget's disease is commonly seen in the:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vulva

Extramammary Paget's disease arises most frequently on the vulva. Other sites include the perineum, scrotum, perianal skin, and penis.

Extramammary Paget's disease (EMPD) can be primary or secondary.

  • Primary EMPD is more common and occurs in the absence of an underlying malignancy, thought to arise from intraepidermal parts of apocrine glands or from pluripotent cells from the epidermis.
  • Secondary EMPD arises from an underlying adnexal carcinoma or internal malignancy due to the epidermotropic spread of malignant cells from the underlying tumor.

Visceral malignancies associated with EMPD are carcinomas of the colon, rectum, bladder, urethra, cervix, and prostate. The patient presents with well-defined, moist, erythematous scaly plaques and severe pruritis. Lichenification and excoriations may also be seen.

Diagnosis is confirmed by punch, wedge, or excisional skin biopsy. A systemic workup should also be done to identify any underlying malignancy and they include colonoscopy, cystoscopy, colposcopy, and pelvic examination with pap smear in females. 

Treatment: 

  • Mohs microscopic surgery with 5 cm margin clearance 
  • Radiotherapy 
  • Topical 5-fluorouracil and imiquimod 
  • Chemotherapy 
  • Photodynamic therapy

Endoscopic ultrasonography with a fine needle aspiration (EUS-FNA) is done if CT has failed to demonstrate a tumor. When a tissue diagnosis is required prior to surgery to distinguish between inflammation and neoplasia, EUS-FNA is helpful.

Diagnostic laparoscopy prior to resection can spare an unnecessary laparotomy by identifying small peritoneal and liver metastases.

Percutaneous transperitoneal biopsy of potentially resectable pancreatic tumors is avoided.

Correct answer: A. During feeding

In a child with congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (CHPS), the abdominal mass is best seen during test feed in the right upper quadrant. 

Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis most presents with non-bilious projectile vomiting. It is common between 2 and 8 weeks of age. Hypertrophy of the circular muscle of the pylorus results in constriction and obstruction of the gastric outlet. Male infants are at a higher risk.

Clinically, when the infant is given a test feed, an olive-shaped mass is palpable in the right upper quadrant and visible peristalsis is usually observed moving from left to right across the abdomen.

Infants with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis develop a characteristic metabolic abnormality- hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Persistent vomiting results in loss of hydrochloric acid leading to the development of metabolic alkalosis (due to loss of H+) and hypochloremia (due to loss of Cl-).

All infants with congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis are evaluated with an ultrasound (investigation of choice). It confirms the diagnosis in the majority of cases.

Correct answer: D. Aphthous ulcers

questions.question: The Van Nuys grading system for ductal carcinoma in situ does not include:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hormone receptor staining

Staining for estrogen and progesterone receptors is not part of the Van Nuys system used for grading DCIS. 

The components of the Van Nuys prognostic index (VNPI) are as follows:

  • Size of the tumor
  • Extent of resection margin 
  • Histological variant of DCIS - based on nuclear grade, presence of necrosis, presence of microcalcification
  • Age of the patient

Patients with a high score in this grading system benefit from radiotherapy after excision, whereas those with low-grade and completely excised tumors, need no further treatment.

A score ranging from 1 (lesions with the best prognosis) to 3 (lesions with the worst prognosis) is given for each of the four prognostic predictors. Total scores range from 4 (least likely to recur) to 12 (most likely to recur).

Silverstein Van Nuys prognostic index for DCIS
Parameters Score 1 Score 2 Score 3
Size(mm) ≤15 16-40 ≥41
Margin(mm) ≥10 1-9 <1
Class Grade 1 or 2 without necrosis Grade 1 or 2 with necrosis Grade 3 with or without necrosis
Age(years) >60 40-60 <40
  • Scores 4-7 with >3mm margin: Excision alone 
  • Score 7 with < 3 mm margin, score 8 with > 3mm margin, score 9 with >5mm margin: Excision with RT
  • Score 9 with < 5mm margin & score 10,11,12: Mastectomy

Note: The type of microcalcification seen on imaging, helps in determining the nuclear grade of DCIS. While the linear branching type of microcalcification is associated with high nuclear grade, fine granular type is associated with low nuclear grade.

questions.question: Which of the following statements are true with regards to a keloid scar?
options: The extent does not cross ‌the wound margins
Wide excision of the keloi‌d scar prevents recurrenc​e
Histopathology of a keloid‌ scar shows reduced colla​gen and increased vascula‍rity
A keloid scar forms due to‌ increase in the level of​ growth factors
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. A keloid scar forms due to increase in the level of growth factors

Keloid scars are associated with elevated levels of growth factor leading to increased proliferation of fibrous tissue.

A keloid scar is defined as excessive scar tissue that extends beyond the boundaries of the original incision or wound (option A) and rarely regresses on its own.  It is more common in darker-pigmented ethnicities.

It can arise from surgery, burns, skin inflammation, infections, ear piercing, and even spontaneously. It occurs 3 months to years after the initial insult with even minor injuries causing keloid formation.

It most commonly occurs on the skin of the earlobe, deltoid, presternal, upper back, and rarely extends into the subcutaneous tissue.

The histology of keloid scars shows excess collagen and hypervascularity with collagen fibres arranged haphazardly in loose sheets (option C).

Treatment: Keloid scars do not improve spontaneously with time and excision alone has a high rate of recurrence (option B). The following can be done:

  • Pressure - local moulds or elastic garments.
  • Silicone gel sheeting.
  • Intralesional triamcinolone injection.
  • Excision and steroid injections.
  • Excision and postoperative radiation (external beam or brachytherapy).
  • Intralesional excision.
  • Laser to reduce redness.
  • Vitamin E and palm oil massage.

Barrett's esophagus is a complication of chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), and it is estimated to occur in about 10% of individuals with symptomatic GERD. questions.question: Which of the following drugs causes carcinoma bladder?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cyclophosphamide

Cyclophosphamide (an alkylating agent) causes bladder cancer

The risk of bladder cancer with cyclophosphamide is directly proportional to the duration and intensity of cyclophosphamide treatment. Phosphoramide mustard is the primary mutagenic metabolite that causes bladder cancer in patients exposed to cyclophosphamide.

Painless, gross hematuria is the most common symptom that is indicative of a bladder carcinoma until proven otherwise. 

Depending upon the depth of invasion, bladder carcinoma can be divided into 

  1. Flat, non-invasive carcinoma in situ (CIS)
  2. Non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (70% of cases) - does not invade detrusor muscle but can invade lamina propria. 
  3. Muscle-invasive bladder cancer - invades the detrusor muscle.

Diagnosis is by cystourethroscopy (directly visualizing the growth) and biopsy. Management is as follows: 

  1. Non-muscle invasive bladder cancer:
    1. Transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT) followed by intravesical chemotherapy with mitomycin C or epirubicin
    2. Immunotherapy with regular intravesical instillations of Bacille Calmette Guerin (BCG) in high-risk tumors.
  2. Muscle invasive bladder cancer: Radical cystectomy along with urinary diversion procedure and lymph node dissection +/- neoadjuvant chemotherapy

questions.question: Parathyroid gland post surgery  is commonly transferred to:

Correct answer: D. Brachioradialis

The parathyroid is commonly transferred to the brachioradialis muscle post-surgery. This will facilitate easy removal if there is disease recurrence after surgery.

Parathyroidectomy is indicated in:

  1. Symptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism (HPT):  
  2. Asymptomatic primary HPT with:
    • raise in serum calcium >1mg/dl of the normal range
    • >400 mg urinary calcium in 24-hour urine test
    • < -2.5 Z-score of bone mineral density
    • Age <50yr and failed medical treatment

Parathyroidectomy is performed in neck hyperextension (semi-Fowler position). The thyroid gland is mobilized, and the parathyroid gland with adenoma is identified and resected. The parathyroid tissue is transplanted to the non-dominant forearm.

Pockets are made in the belly of the brachioradialis muscle, and one to two pieces of parathyroid tissue measuring 1 mm each are placed into each pocket. A total of 12 to 14 pieces are transplanted. This is a type of heterotopic transplant.

Miami criteria (confirm the absence of another hyperactive parathyroid): A drop of parathyroid hormone intraoperatively, to more than half the maximum value at 10 minutes postresection is considered an adequate resection in a parathyroid adenoma. However, if there is no drop in PTH level, then a multi-gland disease is suspected and the surgery is converted to a bilateral neck exploration.

Complications of parathyroidectomy include:

  1. Persistent or recurrent hyperparathyroidism
  2. Hypoparathyroidism (presenting as hypocalcemia)
  3. Hungry bone syndrome
  4. Injury to the recurrent laryngeal nerve

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.question: In a blast injury, which of the following organs is least vulnerable to the blast wave?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Liver

In a blast injury, the liver is the least vulnerable to blast wave (primary blast) injury.

Blast injury is a complex type of physical trauma resulting from direct or indirect exposure to an explosion. Primary blast injuries result from the rapid overpressure or shock waves produced by an explosion. These injuries result from the dramatic changes in barometric pressure projecting outwards from the point of detonation. They predominantly cause damage to air-filled hollow organs of the body from rapid pressure change (barotrauma). This includes the middle ear, lungs, and GIT.

The most sensitive and most frequently injured hollow organs are the tympanic membranes > lungs. Blast damage to the lungs is the most common cause of life-threatening injury following an explosion.

Solid organs are the most resistant to blast injuries as the parenchymal disruption requires very high levels of overpressure. 

Classification of blast injuries:

Classification Explanation Injury type Examples
Primary blast Due to air pressure from the blast Shockwave (overpressure) Tympanic membrane injury, blast lung, intestinal blast injury
Secondary blast Fragments from the blast, following a detonation Penetrating/fragmentation All penetrating injuries
Tertiary blast Gross movements of persons, objects, or infrastructure by the blast wind Blunt trauma Blunt and crush injuries. Traumatic amputation.
Quaternary blast Miscellaneous causes Exposure to explosive products or toxic substances Burns, inhalation injury
Quinary blast The intentional addition of biological or radioactive material to the explosive device Environmental contaminants Radiation sickness, infection.

questions.question: A man presents with a slowly progressive swelling over the past 1 and 1/2 years. On examination, it has a variable consistency and appears as shown in the image. What is the probable cause?

Correct answer: C. Pleomorphic adenoma

A slowly progressive swelling, with a variable consistency, lifting the ear lobe, is suggestive of pleomorphic adenoma of the parotid gland.

Pleomorphic adenoma, the most common benign salivary gland tumor, primarily affects the parotid gland, particularly its superficial lobe. It is also referred to as a mixed tumor due to its combination of epithelial and mesenchymal components. This tumor most commonly occurs in females around the age of 40.

Clinical features:

  • Painless, slow-growing swelling
  • Lobulated, firm, variable in consistency
  • Lifts the earlobe
  • No facial nerve involvement
  • Curtain sign positive - cannot be moved above the zygomatic bone.
  • In case of deep lobe involvement, tonsils, and faucial pillars will be pushed medially.
  • Features of malignancy - a sudden increase in size, ulceration of the overlying skin, facial nerve palsy (involvement of facial nerve), painful swelling, and restriction of jaw movements.

Fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) is the investigation of choice in diagnosing pleomorphic adenoma. Open biopsy is contraindicated due to the chances of injury to the facial nerve.

All tumors of the superficial lobe of the parotid gland should be managed by superficial parotidectomy. Radical parotidectomy is performed for malignant pleomorphic adenoma.

Other options:

Option A: Adamantinoma is a low-grade malignant tumor that usually presents with pre-tibial pain and swelling since it most commonly affects the tibial diaphysis.

Option B:  Dermoid cysts present as firm painless subcutaneous nodules and are of 4 types:

  1. Sequestration dermoid - sequestration of epithelium during embryological development.
  2. Tubulodermoid - accumulation of secretions from ectodermal tube/duct
  3. Implantation dermoid - implantation of the epidermis due to trauma
  4. Teratomatous dermoid - having all 3 germ layers (ecto, meso, and endoderm)

Option D: Sebaceous cysts are retention cysts of the sebaceous glands that present as smooth, non-tender, non-transillumination swelling with a punctum (in 70% of the patients).

questions.question: Which nerve is involved in Frey’s syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Auriculotemporal nerve

The auriculotemporal nerve (V3 nerve) is involved in Frey's syndrome (gustatory sweating).

Frey’s syndrome is also known as Dupuy syndrome or auriculotemporal syndrome. It commonly develops after parotid surgery. It is caused by an aberrant regeneration of post-ganglionic parasympathetic nerve fibers crossed along the sympathetic pathways to the sweat glands near the parotid region.

Clinical features are due to the result of salivary stimulation (by the smell or taste of food) leading to the sweating and flushing of the periauricular region on the involved side of the face. A starch iodine test is used for diagnosis.

Treatment ranges from antiperspirants (in mild cases) to tympanic neurectomy or botulinum toxin injection (in severe cases). It can be prevented by incorporating careful extracapsular dissection and closure of the superficial musculoaponeurotic layer during parotidectomy.

Other options:

Option A: Facial nerve is the 7th cranial nerve that supplies the muscles of the face, and results in facial paralysis if injured during parotidectomy

Option B: Oculomotor is the 3rd cranial nerve which supplies the extraocular muscles. If injured during ophthalmic surgeries, it results in ocular paralysis and the eye pointing down and out.

Option D: Glossopharyngeal nerve is the 9th cranial nerve and its injury causes loss of taste sensation from the posterior 1/3rd of the tongue.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding deep vein thrombosis (DVT)?
options: Most common clinical prese‌ntation is pain and tende​rness in calf
Some cases may directly pr‌esent as pulmonary thromb​oembolism
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mostly bilateral

Most cases of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) are unilateral. It is bilateral in only 30% of the individuals.

DVT refers to thrombosis of the deep venous system.

Caused by:

  • Postoperative thrombosis (most common cause)
  • Oral contraceptive pills (OCPs)
  • After childbirth
  • Immobility 

Sites:

  • Pelvic veins—common
  • Leg veins—common in femoral and popliteal veins (common on the left side).

Fever is the earliest symptom, which is also most commonly accompanied by pain and tenderness in the calf and thigh (option C).

The following signs could be elicited:

  • Positive Homan's sign: Resistance of calf muscles on passive foreceful dorsiflexion of the foot.
  • Mose's sign: Gentle squeezing of the lower part of the calf from side to side is painful.
  • Neuhof's sign: Thickening and deep tenderness seen on deep palpation of the calf muscles.

Sometimes, the thrombus may get dislodged and present as pulmonary thromboembolism (option D) with features of dyspnoea, tachypnoea, and chest pain.

Clinical features are unreliable for making a definitive diagnosis (option A), and a venous Doppler is the best modality for confirming DVT. It reveals a non-compressible dilated vein. The likelihood of pulmonary embolism can be predicted using modified Wells criteria.

Patients with DVT should be immediately started with subcutaneous low molecular weight heparin (LMWH). If contraindicated due to renal insufficiency or thrombocytopenia-related conditions, they should be started on fondaparinux (indirect factor Xa inhibitor) or bivalirudin (direct thrombin inhibitor). Anticoagulants should be administered for a minimum period of 3 months. Vena cava filters are used in patients with bleeding risks (like hemophilia).

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding rectal carcinoma?
options: Hartmann’s operation is do‌ne in elderly debilitated​ patients
Adenocarcinoma is a rare v‌ariant of rectal carcinom​a
Early morning spurious dia‌rrhoea and tenesmus can o​ccur

Correct answer: B. Adenocarcinoma is a rare variant of rectal carcinoma

Adenocarcinoma is the most common variant of rectal carcinoma.

Colorectal cancer is:

  1. The second most common malignancy globally
  2. The second most common cancer in women
  3. The third most common cancer in men
  4. The fourth most common cause of death due to cancer. 

Symptoms of rectal carcinoma include:

  1. Painless bleeding - earliest and most common
  2. Alteration of bowel habits - change in frequency and consistency of the stool
  3. Tenesmus - unable to pass a motion even when there is the sensation of needing to evacuate the bowel. It is suggestive of a tumor of the lower half of the rectum 
  4. Early morning bloody diarrhea (option C) - passage of blood and mucus in addition to feces. Pain and weight loss are usually late symptoms

Abdominal examination and digital rectal examination are used for the primary evaluation. Rigid sigmoidoscopy is performed to obtain a biopsy. A synchronous tumor (primary tumor with a different origin than the one currently investigated) is excluded by performing a colonoscopy.

Modified Duke’s classification:

A

Growth limited up to the rectal mucosa (option D)

B

B1: Tumor invading muscularis propria, no lymph node invasion.

B2: Tumors invading into or through serosa, no lymph node invasion.

C

C1: The tumour did not exceed the bowel wall, lymph node metastasis.

C2: Tumour exceeded the intestinal wall and lymph node metastasis.

D

Distant metastasis

Surgery is the mainstay of management for rectal carcinoma. Non-operative management is offered to only those patients who have a complete clinical response to neoadjuvant.

The type of surgery depends on multiple factors (size, location, age of the patient, etc). However, the general consensus is:

  1. Early cancer (T1 and a few T2) is locally excised via the transanal approach.
  2. Most rectal cancer is treated by anterior resection and colorectal/coloanal anastomosis.
  3. Low extensive tumors are treated by laparoscopic abdominoperineal resection(APR) and permanent colostomy.
  4. Hartmann’s operation (option A) is preferred in old and frail patients due to poor anal sphincter and postoperative incontinence.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true about retrosternal goitre?
options: Operated in all patients r‌egardless of symptoms
Sternal incision is always‌ required to operate
It receives blood supply f‌rom the thoracodorsal art​ery
Most of the retrosternal g‌oitres can be removed by ​a neck incision

Correct answer: D. Most of the retrosternal goitres can be removed by a neck incision

Most of the retrosternal goiters can be removed by neck incision (transcervical approach).

Retrosternal goitre is defined as having >50% of the goiter below the suprasternal notch. It can be either primary or secondary.

  • Primary: rare and arises from ectopic thyroid tissue in the mediastinum; receives blood supply from intrathoracic blood vessels. It is not related to thyroid tissue in the neck.
  • Secondary: they are the most common type; an extension of enlarged thyroid from the neck, usually arising from the lower pole of nodular goitre. It receives its blood supply from superior and inferior thyroid vessels.

The majority of patients are asymptomatic or have minimal symptoms. If the gland enlarges within the thoracic inlet, the pressure may lead to dysphagia, tracheal compression, and eventually airway symptoms. Pemberton sign can be positive (facial flushing and dilatation of cervical veins upon raising the arms above the head).

CECT neck and thorax is the investigation of choice.

Over 95% of retrosternal goiters can be removed via a transcervical incision since they are an extension from thyroid tissue in the neck.

Other options:

Option A: Surgical removal of the retrosternal goiter is indicated in patients with significant airway compression, and in young patients who have symptoms such as dyspnoea or dysphagia. 

Option B: Median sternotomy approach is indicated in:

  • Primary mediastinal goiter
  • Malignant retrosternal goitre
  • Very large retrosternal goiter
  • Recurrence in the mediastinum

For a primary mediastinal goiter whose boundaries are completely within the chest, resection is often achieved through median sternotomy or thoracotomy to ensure that the vessels supplying the tumor are properly ligated. Removing the tumor through a cervical approach can result in uncontrolled bleeding and is generally avoided. 

Option C: Blood supply to the retrosternal goiter is from the thyroid vessels (secondary retrosternal goiter).

questions.question: An 80-year-old woman presented with complaints of fatigue. On imaging, she was found to have a scleroatrophic gall bladder with impacted stones in it. A large stone was also present in the common bile duct and the biliary tree is dilated. What is the next step in management?

Correct answer: B. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography

An 80-year-old woman with imaging showing a scleroatrophic gall bladder with impacted stones and a stone in the bile duct is suggestive of chronic cholelithiasis with choledocholithiasis. ERCP is the next line of management for this patient. 

Choledocholithiasis is the presence of stone in the common bile duct (CBD) or biliary tree. It can be primary or secondary:  

  • Primary stones are formed in the CBD or biliary tree itself and are rare.
  • Secondary stones are passed from the gallbladder to the CBD. They are easier to manage than primary stones.

It can be an asymptomatic and incidental finding or present with features such as jaundice (most common), abdominal pain, and fatigue. When there is inflammation of the biliary tree (cholangitis), the patient will have intermittent pain, fever, and jaundice (Charcot's triad). 

Investigations: 

  • Liver function tests will show elevated direct bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase levels. 
  • Abdominal ultrasound is the first imaging modality done and may show gallstones and dilated bile duct (>8 mm). 
  • CT is sensitive for CBD stones. It shows stones, location, ductal stricture or block, ductal dilatation, and intrahepatic biliary changes.
  • MRCP is highly sensitive and specific for CBD stones, but it is only diagnostic and intervention cannot be performed.

Management: 

  • ERCP with sphincterotomy is the procedure of choice, followed by the removal of stones using a dormia basket or placement of a stent.
  • Despite ERCP being an invasive procedure, it has the advantage of being both a diagnostic and therapeutic procedure and is more suited for elderly patients who cannot tolerate anesthesia and surgery.

Other options: 

Option A: Cholecystectomy is not recommended for elderly patients, owing to the risk of old age and associated anesthetic and surgical complications.

Option C: Wait and watch approach can be done for asymptomatic patients, and patients with smaller stones.

Option D: CT is sensitive for CBD stones, but it is only diagnostic and intervention cannot be performed.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.question: A 35-year-old man presented with recurrent episodes of fever with chills. MRCP image is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Primary sclerosing cholangitis

The presence of fever and chills, along with the MRCP showing multiple areas of intrahepatic beading is typical of primary sclerosing cholangitis.

Option B: Caroli's disease is a rare congenital condition characterized by irregular dilatation of the intrahepatic bile ducts with a normal extrahepatic duct system. It is common in both sexes and mostly presents before the age of 30 years with abdominal pain, cholangitis, or end-stage liver disease. MRCP shows irregular, cystic dilation of the large proximal intrahepatic bile ducts with a normal common bile duct. 

Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is an autoimmune condition characterized by inflammatory strictures involving the intra and extra-hepatic biliary tree. It is a progressive condition that leads to secondary biliary cirrhosis. 

MRCP or ERCP will show demonstrate multifocal, diffuse dilatation and strictures of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic biliary trees, this pattern is a beading or chain of lakes appearance. Pseudodiverticula of extrahepatic bile ducts are pathognomic of PSC. MRCP is useful in diagnosis and surveillance, while ERCP is reserved for the treatment of dominant strictures and to exclude malignancy. 

The below image shows a cholangiogram of primary sclerosing cholangitis:

The common age group of primary sclerosing cholangitis is 30-45 years. Men are affected twice as commonly as women. Two-thirds of these cases are associated with ulcerative colitis. It is also associated with Riedel’s thyroiditis and retroperitoneal fibrosis. 10–20% of patients develop cholangiocarcinoma.

Clinical features of a patient with PSC include pruritis, fever, chills, right upper quadrant discomfort, jaundice, and weight loss. 

Liver function tests show a cholestatic pattern with an elevation of ALP and GGT and smaller rises in the aminotransferases. Bilirubin values may be variable.

Liver biopsy excludes other causes of cholestatic liver disease and defines the stage of PSC. It shows onion skin concentric periductal fibrosis. With disease progression, periportal fibrosis occurs, progressing to bridging necrosis, and eventually biliary cirrhosis.

Currently, there is no known effective medical therapy. Surgical management involving resection of extrahepatic biliary tree and hepaticojejunostomy has shown reasonable effects. For patients with advanced liver disease, liver transplantation is the only available option.

Other options: 

Option C: Oriental cholangitis, also known as recurrent pyogenic cholangitis is characterized by recurrent attacks of cholangitis due to bile stasis and stone formation. questions.question: The most common neuroendocrine tumor of the pancreas is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Insulinoma

The most common neuroendocrine tumor of the pancreas is insulinoma (4 per million).

Insulinoma is an insulin-producing tumor of the pancreas, with more than 90% of them being benign. It occurs in >40 years in patients without MEN 1 syndrome and <40 years in patients with MEN 1. It presents with symptoms of hypoglycemia such as weakness, headaches, sweating, faintness, seizures, and altered behavior. These occur after fasting or exertion and improve after glucose intake. 

The investigation of choice for insulinoma is the determination of 72-hour fasting glucose and serum insulin levels. C-peptide and proinsulin levels are also elevated.

Medical management includes:

  • Frequent carbohydrate-rich meals
  • Somatostatin analogs like octreotide are effective in controlling symptoms due to excess insulin secretion. They should be used with caution as they can suppress counterregulatory hormones, such as growth hormone (GH), glucagon, and catecholamines, and precipitously worsen hypoglycemia. 
  • Diazoxide can be used in the initial management of insulinoma as it inhibits insulin release. Its side effects include sodium retention and nausea. 
  • Everolimus has been found to be highly effective in improving glycemic control in patients with insulinoma owing to its antitumor effect and induction of insulin resistance.

Enucleation and pancreatectomy are the definitive surgical management of insulinoma.

Other options:

Option A: Gastrinoma has an incidence of 0.5 to 4 in a million.

Options B & D: Somatostatinoma and VIPoma are much rarer than gastrinoma.

questions.question: A patient comes with long-standing non-pitting edema in the legs. What is the most probable cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lymphedema

Lymphedema is the most probable cause of long-standing non-pitting edema in the limbs.

Lymphedema is the abnormal accumulation of protein-rich fluid in the interstitial spaces of the tissues.

Lymphedema can be primary or secondary.

Primary lymphedema includes: 

  • Lymphedema congenita (0-2 years): more common in males, involves multiple limbs, face, and genitalia. It can be familial or sporadic. The familial type is called Nonne Milroy syndrome.
  • Lymphedema praecox (2-35 years): more common in females, the most common type of primary lymphedema with a peak incidence in puberty. It can be familial or sporadic. The familial type is called Meig's disease.
  • Lymphedema tarda (>35 years): Rare and uncommon.

Secondary lymphedema is more common than primary and is the most common cause of lymphedema overall. Causes include lymph node dissection (axillary or inguinal), post-mastectomy, postoperative radiotherapy, obesity, varicose vein surgery, and trauma.

Complications of lymphedema include infections, skin changes, recurent cellulitis, non-healing ulcers, and lymphangiosarcoma.

Treatment mostly includes patient education and nonsurgical interventions, which include limb elevation, and external compressive garments. When the above methods fail, surgery can be considered.

questions.question: A 41-year-old female patient presented with a tortuous swelling over the left side of the scalp and face as shown in the image given below. On local examination, the swelling was pulsatile. On auscultation, a bruit was heard. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

Correct answer: C. Cirsoid Aneurysm

The presence of a tortuous, pulsatile swelling over the scalp and face is suggestive of a cirsoid aneurysm.

Cirsoid aneurysm is a slow-growing, tortuous swelling that develops due to abnormal arteriovenous connections among the subcutaneous blood vessels. They are usually congenital. However, in some cases, they may be traumatic. The superficial temporal artery is most commonly involved.

Patients present with a tortuous, pulsatile swelling over the scalp or face. They are usually asymptomatic and present to the clinic due to cosmetic deformity. However, some patients may have headache, tinnitus, and/or bleeding. A loud bruit is heard on auscultation.

Angiography is the investigation of choice.

Treatment includes surgical resection, endovascular occlusion or injection of percutaneous sclerosing agents.

options: Most commonly felt in the ‌calf muscles
Day to day distance is var‌iable

Correct answer: B. Most commonly felt in the calf muscles

Intermittent claudication is most commonly felt in the calf muscles because of the involvement of the superficial femoral artery in chronic vascular occlusive disease.

Intermittent claudication:

  • Intermittent claudication is the debilitating cramp-like pain felt in the leg muscles due to reduced blood flow and anaerobic metabolism brought on by peripheral arterial disease.
  • It usually signifies mild to moderate chronic vascular occlusive disease
  • The pain is brought on by walking (option D)

  • Relieved by rest in both the standing and sitting positions, usually within 5 minutes (option A).
  • The distance that a patient is able to walk without stopping is known as claudication distance. It varies only slightly from day to day (option C).
  • The superficial femoral artery (70%) is the most commonly affected artery by claudication and manifests as pain in the calf muscles. 
  • Aorto-iliac occlusion may cause thigh or buttock claudication. Leriche's syndrome occurs due to aortoiliac occlusion and presents with a triad of claudication, impotence, and absent femoral pulses.

Boyd's classification of claudication: 

  • Grade I: Patient complains of pain after walking. If the patient continues to walk, due to increased blood flow in muscle and opening of collaterals metabolites causing pain are washed away and the pain subsides.
  • Grade II: Pain still persists on continuing to walk; but can walk with effort.
  • Grade III: The patient has to take rest to relieve the pain.

Surgery is indicated in an asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) only if its diameter is more than 55 mm in a male patient.

questions.question: Which of the following is the Miami criteria for intraoperative parathyroid hormone (PTH) measurement?

Correct answer: D. Half fall in 10 min

A drop in the level of PTH to less than half the maximum value (corresponding to the preoperative levels)  at 10 min postresection is the Miami criteria.

It is used to determine the extent of resection of the parathyroid gland which is done in a case of primary hyperparathyroidism due to adenoma.

Intraoperative parathyroid hormone monitoring is a commonly used adjunct, which guides the surgeon on when to stop parathyroid exploration and helps in confirming there is no residual hyperfunctioning parathyroid tissue. The PTH levels are expected to drop after the gland is excised due to its short half-life (3-5 minutes). Blood is drawn at various time points and the hormone levels are assessed.

Based on the Miami Criteria, a more than 50% decline in PTH at 10 minutes following parathyroid gland removal compared to the highest baseline level, either the pre-incision or pre-excision, suggests a cure, and the procedure can be terminated.

Indications for parathyroidectomy: 

All symptomatic patients with hyperparathyroidism should be offered surgery. Indications for surgery in asymptomatic patients include: 

Serum calcium levels  0.25 mmol/L (1.0 mg/dL) above the upper limit serum calcium of normal 
Skeletal

  • Vertebral fracture
Renal
  • Creatinine clearance <60 mL/min 
  • 24-hour urinary calcium >10 mmol/dL (>400 mg/day)
  • Increased risk of stone formation by risk analysis 

 
Age  <50 years

questions.question: A 15-year-old boy undergoes bilateral adrenalectomy for phaeochromocytoma. On the third postoperative day, the boy feels lethargic and tired. Blood pressure is 80/60 mm Hg, there is no sign of bleed. What could be the cause of this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Addisonian crisis

The given clinical scenario of hypotension with no presence of bleeding and bilateral adrenalectomy is suggestive of an Addisonian crisis. It is a life-threatening condition caused due to sudden insufficiency of adrenal hormones.

Acute adrenal insufficiency (adrenal or addisonian's crisis) is a medical emergency caused due to a precipitating illness unmasking insufficiency or trauma or severe sepsis causing adrenal hemorrhage (Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome) or surgical removal of the glands. It presents with non-specific symptoms such as shock with fever, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, hypocalcemia and electrolyte imbalances. It may be often misdiagnosed as an acute abdominal emergency.

Adrenal insufficiency can be primary (due to adrenal pathology), secondary (due to pituitary pathology- lack of ACTH) or tertiary (due to hypothalamus pathology- lack of CRH). 

Autoimmune adrenalitis is the most common cause of primary adrenal insufficiency worldwide.

Tuberculosis is the most common cause of primary adrenal insufficiency in India.

Adrenal crisis requires immediate intervention owing to its high mortality rate. Immediate rehydration is initiated with a saline infusion at 1 litre/hr with continuous cardiac monitoring. Glucocorticoid replacement is initiated with an initial bolus injection of hydrocortisone 100 mg followed by 200 mg over 24 hours, preferably by continuous infusion or alternatively by IV or IM injections. Mineralocorticoid replacement is initiated once the daily dose of hydrocortisone has been reduced to <50 mg, since hydrocortisone at higher doses provides sufficient stimulation of mineralocorticoids.

questions.question: A middle-aged man presented to the emergency department with upper abdominal pain after having a heavy meal. On clinical examination, upper abdominal tenderness was noted. On chest radiography widening of the mediastinum with pneumomediastinum was seen. What is the probable diagnosis?
options: Rupture of emphysematous b‌ulla of lung
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Spontaneous perforation of esophagus

The clinical scenario points to a diagnosis of spontaneous perforation of the esophagus.

In a perforated peptic ulcer, patients develop sudden onset severe generalized abdominal pain, tenderness, and board-like rigidity and an erect plain chest X-ray shows gas under the diaphragm (Option B). The foreign body in the esophagus can be asymptomatic or may present with perforation after ingestion. The radiopaque foreign body can be seen with a chest X-ray (Option C).  Rupture of emphysematous bullae of the lung will lead to secondary pneumothorax, which manifests as chest pain and dyspnoea. A plain chest X-ray shows air in the thorax, and the mediastinum is pushed to the opposite side (Option D).

Spontaneous perforation of the esophagus needs immediate diagnosis and intervention due to the higher mortality associated with it. The most common site of perforation is the lower esophagus towards the left esophageal cavity.

Causes: 

  • Iatrogenic perforation (most common)
  • Boerhaave's syndrome (spontaneous emetogenic perforation)
  • Sharp foreign body 
  • Corrosive ingestion 
  • Esophageal carcinoma 

It usually manifests as severe pain in the chest or abdomen after a meal or after a bout of drinking, commonly associated with dyspnoea. On clinical examination, there is rigidity and tenderness in the upper abdomen. The diagnosis is usually confirmed by a chest radiograph which shows pneumomediastinum, pneumoperitoneum, and pneumothorax. Subcutaneous emphysema can be seen in Boerhaave's syndrome. Patients with sepsis will have a fever, tachycardia and tachypnea. 

Treatment includes adequate drainage, antibiotics, closure of the perforation site if possible and supportive measures.
